```c
return sa.align == 65536 && sa.size > d.width * d.height * bpe;
```

plus structural qualification - 2D, single mip, single slice, single sample,
`shaderRead` only - and a format whitelist (`BGRA8`, `RGBA8`, `R8`), because a
wrong `bytesPerElement` would corrupt worse than the bug does.

### Measured

The law instrument, same binary, with and without the interposer:

```
                      WITHOUT          WITH
  256x48   2.67x      fail 10/12      fail 0/12
  256x64   2.00x      fail  6/12      fail 0/12
  256x96   1.33x      fail  9/12      fail 0/12
  1000x48  2.73x      fail 11/12      fail 0/12
  256x128  1.00x      fail  0/12      fail 0/12
  256x32   1.00x      fail  0/12      fail 0/12
  TOTAL              36/72 failed     0/72 failed
```

And the thing the whole frontier was about - real CoreText glyphs rasterised
by `texprobe`'s 2mf phase, Menlo 13, both widths, both upload paths:

```
  reference w=256 h=48:  3939 non-background pixels
    managed-replace-full   rows-wrong now= 0 later= 0  stable=YES   (was 46)
    managed-replace-tiles  rows-wrong now= 0 later= 0  stable=YES   (was 46)
  reference w=1000 h=48: 4151 non-background pixels
    managed-replace-full   rows-wrong now= 0 later= 0  stable=YES   (was 48)
    managed-replace-tiles  rows-wrong now= 0 later= 0  stable=YES   (was 48)
```

46 and 48 rows wrong, to zero, without touching texprobe's code.

`1000x48` is worth noting: a bare `IOSurfaceCreate` without an explicit
`bytesPerRow` hung during 2mo at that width. The interposer pins it to the
256-byte alignment the blit engine wants, and the width that hung is now clean.

### Cost

**Corrected.** The first figures recorded here - 1.46 s against 7.7 s - were
both taken while a backgrounded `texprobe` was still draining the GPU, and the
7.7 s was attributed to the interposer. Four runs in order on a genuinely idle
GPU, two without and two with:

```
  without:  36.31 s   1.26 s        <- the first is the contaminated one
  with:      1.36 s   1.96 s
```

So the cost is **not 5x; it is close to nothing** - 1.26 s baseline against
1.36-1.96 s with the interposer, on a loop that does nothing but allocate 72
textures. The lesson is the one already in the rules: the first timing after a
background job is a measurement of the background job. Both the 93 s and the
7.7 s are discarded.

### What this does and does not claim

Claimed: for a texture the law flags, an IOSurface-backed replacement is
correct where the driver's own allocation is not, at every geometry tested, on
synthetic fills and on real rasterised text.

**Not** claimed: that any particular application's text goes through
`-newTextureWithDescriptor:`. CoreText and CoreAnimation may reach the GPU by
paths this never sees - IOSurfaces already (which is why the desktop composites
correctly), a buffer-backed texture, or a private texture filled by blit. The
interposer is proven on the path `texprobe` exercises; whether it reaches a
given app's glyph atlas is the next measurement, and
`RBGPU_IOSURFTEX_LOG=1` answers it per process by printing each swap.

Also not claimed: safety in `WindowServer`. The interposer is per process and
has only been run against test binaries. Injecting it into `WindowServer` would
reach the Dock and the menu bar, and a fault there takes the GUI with it.
Per-app first.

### How to use it

```sh
make iosurftex
tools/iosurftex.sh /Applications/Some.app            # a bundle
tools/iosurftex.sh ./build/out/texprobe              # a binary
RBGPU_IOSURFTEX_LOG=1 tools/iosurftex.sh ...         # log every decision
RBGPU_IOSURFTEX=0 ...                                # disable without rebuilding
```

It needs the relaxed AMFI this machine already boots with (`amfi=0x80`,
`amfi_get_out_of_my_way=0x1`); library validation would otherwise refuse the
insertion.

## 2mq — the launchd injection broke every newly launched app and forced a reboot

What I told the user to run, and what happened: `tools/iosurftex-launchd.sh on`
set `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` in the Aqua launchd environment. Then Claude would
not open - it bounced in the Dock and stopped. Then Terminal would not open.
Then Mail would not open. The already-running Terminal still worked and its
text was unreadable (an unarmed-boot symptom, unrelated), so it was quit - and
with it the last usable shell. An SSH session was opened and `off` was run from
there, which **changed nothing**, and the machine had to be rebooted to get a
usable GUI back. The reboot came up unarmed, so the session also lost the
accelerator.

### Two distinct errors

**1. `launchctl setenv` is not a per-app switch.** It applies to every GUI
process started afterwards. And dyld *kills* a process that cannot load an
inserted dylib - it does not warn and continue - so every sandboxed app (Mail,
most App Store apps), which cannot read a dylib out of `~/Developer`, died
before a single line of our code ran. I had written "Your Terminal is already
running, so it stays clean as an escape hatch", which was true of that one
process and false of the act of launching a new one. I presented a system-wide
switch as scoped, and listed its reversal as if that made it safe.

**2. The escape hatch could not work, and I did not test it.** `launchctl
unsetenv` over SSH acts on a different launchd domain than the Aqua session, so
the documented undo unset something that had never been set. The command that
would have saved the reboot is

```sh
sudo launchctl asuser $(id -u) launchctl unsetenv DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES
```

Rule 16 says the instrument is a suspect. A recovery procedure is an
instrument, and this one was never run in the context where it would be needed
- from outside the GUI session, which is exactly the situation it existed for.

### Done about it

`tools/iosurftex-launchd.sh on` now **refuses**, with the reason and this tag
in its output. The file keeps `off` and `status` for recovery, and carries the
`asuser` form in a comment at the top. Nothing persisted: the reboot cleared
the variable, and `status` on the current boot reads "not set".

### What still stands, and what does not

Unaffected: 2mn's law, 2mo's IOSurface result, and 2mp's fix measured inside a
process we launch ourselves - 36/72 to 0/72, and real CoreText glyphs from 46
and 48 wrong rows to 0. None of that involved launchd.

Withdrawn: the claim that this fix can be delivered to arbitrary applications.
Per-process injection remains correct in principle, but:

- Direct exec of Claude's binary fails for a reason still unknown: the main
  process exits cleanly about a second in, twice, with the dylib loaded in all
  five processes and installed in two, and no crash report either time. The
  control that separates the launch method from the dylib - running
  `/Applications/Claude.app/Contents/MacOS/Claude` with nothing injected - has
  still not been run.
- Sandboxed applications cannot read a dylib from a home directory at all, so
  for those the file would have to live somewhere a sandbox permits before
  injection is even possible.

### Next, in this order

1. Run the control, on any boot, armed or not: does Claude's binary exit
   immediately when exec'd directly with **nothing** injected? That is one
   command and it decides whether per-app injection is possible for Claude.
2. Only then consider a real application. Never through launchd.
3. The accelerator work needs `sudo nvram rbgpu-arm=1 && sudo reboot` again;
   the current boot has no Metal device at all.

## 2mr — the crash was mine: ARC released Metal's +1 out from under every caller

Boot 114, armed. The user's control settled the question I had got backwards:
exec'ing `/Applications/Claude.app/Contents/MacOS/Claude` with nothing inserted
**works**. So the launch method was never the problem and the dylib was.

### The bisect

`tools/iosurftex-bisect.sh`, five variants, 10 s each:

```
  A  nothing inserted (control)        STAYED UP
  B  noop-insert.dylib                 STAYED UP
  C  iosurftex, RBGPU_IOSURFTEX=0      EXITED   Segmentation fault: 11
  D  iosurftex, INERT=1                EXITED   Segmentation fault: 11
  E  iosurftex, full                   EXITED   Segmentation fault: 11
```

A do-nothing dylib is fine, so insertion is not refused. Ours kills it **even
fully disabled**, so nothing in the fix logic is involved - and in variant E
the log stops before any Metal device is created, which is why no `swapped`
line ever appeared.

### The crash

The launchd episode of 2mq left crash reports for `Terminal`, `Mail` and
`Tips`, so that was not apps failing to launch - it was apps **crashing**, the
same way. Their backtrace:

```
objc_release
AutoreleasePoolPage::releaseUntil(objc_object**)
objc_autoreleasePoolPop
_dispatch_lane_serial_drain
...
EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)  KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x3770eecf9670
```

An over-release. Metal declares

```objc
id<MTLDevice>            MTLCreateSystemDefaultDevice(void) NS_RETURNS_RETAINED;
NSArray<id<MTLDevice>> *MTLCopyAllDevices(void)             NS_RETURNS_RETAINED;
```

and `-newTextureWithDescriptor:` is in the `new` family: all three hand the
caller a **+1** reference. The interposers were compiled `-fobjc-arc` and were
not declared `ns_returns_retained`, so ARC inserted a release on the way out of
each one while the caller still owned its reference. Every process that
enumerates Metal devices then double-freed a device or a device array at its
next pool pop. That is why `Terminal` and `Mail` died in 2mq and not only
Claude, and why the disabled variant died too: the interposers are active
whatever the knobs say.

### Fixed, and tested before anyone is asked to launch anything

`tools/ownership-test.m` calls both functions and the swizzled method 200 times
inside autorelease pools. It reproduced the bug on demand - `rc=139` with the
dylib, `rc=139` with it disabled, clean without it - which is the test that
should have existed before the user was ever asked to insert this into an
application.

The fix: build with **`-fno-objc-arc`**, since an interposer must pass
ownership through and touch no retain count; declare both replacements
`ns_returns_retained` so the intent is in the signature; and give the IOSurface
property literals their own `@autoreleasepool`, with the +1 texture created
after it drains. `make ownership-test` now runs all three cases:

```
  control (no dylib):          200 iterations, no crash
  with iosurftex:              200 iterations, no crash   (swapped=200)
  with iosurftex disabled:     200 iterations, no crash
```

And the result it exists for is unchanged - the law instrument still goes
36/72 to 0/72.

### The lesson, which is rule 16 again

The dylib had been run against exactly one program: a test binary I wrote,
which calls `MTLCreateSystemDefaultDevice` **once** and never pops a pool that
contains the result. That is the one shape of program the bug cannot kill. I
then told the user it was safe for arbitrary applications, twice, and the
second time through a launchd environment that took the whole GUI down. A fix
verified on one hand-written caller has been verified against one caller, not
against the API contract.

## 2ms — what Claude actually asks for, and the law holds for R8 and render targets

Boot 114, armed. With 2mr's crash fixed, all five bisect variants stay up:

```
  A  nothing inserted   STAYED UP      D  iosurftex, INERT=1   STAYED UP
  B  noop-insert.dylib  STAYED UP      E  iosurftex, full      STAYED UP
  C  iosurftex, =0      STAYED UP
```

Text in variant E was **still unreadable**, and `swapped=0` - but not because
Claude avoids the failing class. It asked for **27 textures the law flags** and
my own qualification rules refused every one:

```
   4 DECLINED(structure) 64x64 type=4 mips=1
   4 DECLINED(structure) 1536x256 type=4 mips=1
   2 DECLINED(structure) 1536x128 / 128x128 / 16x16 type=4
   2 DECLINED(usage) 512x32 / 32x32 / 25x25 / 16x16  usage=0x4 fmt=250
   1 DECLINED(usage) 256x32 / 192x64 / 128x64 / 128x32  usage=0x4 fmt=250
   1 DECLINED(usage) 1024x128 usage=0x5 fmt=10
```

Decoded: `type=4` is `MTLTextureType2DMultisample` - MSAA render targets, which
cannot be IOSurface-backed and are not text. `usage=0x4 fmt=250` is
`RenderTarget` with `MTLPixelFormatDepth16Unorm` - depth buffers. Both are
correctly refused.

The last line is the one that matters: **`1024x128`, `fmt=10` =
`MTLPixelFormatR8Unorm`, `usage=0x5` = `RenderTarget|ShaderRead`.** That is a
glyph atlas, and `usageOk` only ever allowed `ShaderRead`, so it was thrown
away.

### The law on a format and a usage it had never been measured on

The law and the fix were established on `bgra8Unorm` with `shaderRead` alone.
Claude's atlas is neither, so `lawtest` grew both axes before any claim was
made about them:

```
=== r8Unorm, RenderTarget|ShaderRead (Claude's glyph atlas shape)
  1024x128  align 65536 ratio 2.00x   fail  6/12
  1024x48   align  4096 ratio 1.33x   fail  0/12
   512x128  align 65536 ratio 2.00x   fail  6/12
   256x48   align  4096 ratio 1.33x   fail  0/12
  1024x256  align 65536 ratio 1.00x   fail  0/12
=== bgra8Unorm, RenderTarget|ShaderRead
   256x48   align 65536 ratio 2.67x   fail 11/12
   256x96   align 65536 ratio 1.33x   fail  9/12
```

The law is unchanged across both: **align 65536 and footprint > pixels, or it
is clean.** `1024x48` and `256x48` at R8 land at align 4096 and are clean,
`1024x256` is an exact fit and is clean, and **`1024x128` - the real atlas -
fails 6/12.** So the glyph atlas is genuinely in the failing class, which is
the first direct evidence that this defect is what makes *this application's*
text unreadable rather than something that merely resembles it.

### Filter widened, and everything re-measured

`usageOk` now serves `ShaderRead|RenderTarget` - an IOSurface backs both, and
that is what the atlas asks for - while still refusing `ShaderWrite`,
`PixelFormatView` and `ShaderAtomic`, none of which is a glyph atlas and each
of which carries layout constraints of its own. With that one change:

```
  r8Unorm, RenderTarget|ShaderRead      0/60
  r8Unorm, ShaderRead only              0/36
  bgra8Unorm, RenderTarget|ShaderRead   0/24
  bgra8Unorm, ShaderRead only           0/72   (was 36/72)
  swapped=108  declined: none           law-clean=84
```

Nothing is declined any more, and `make ownership-test` still passes all three
cases, which is now run before the dylib is put anywhere near an application.

### Still not claimed

That Claude's text will be readable. The atlas is in the failing class and the
fix corrects that class, but Skia may fill that atlas by a GPU render pass or a
buffer blit rather than the CPU `replace()` the law is about - its usage
includes `RenderTarget`, which is a hint in that direction. If the atlas is
swapped and the text is still wrong, the upload path is the next thing to read,
not the layout.

## 2mt - the fix works and the app is unchanged: 2ms's inference withdrawn

Boot 114, armed, Claude launched under the interposer with the widened filter.
The log shows the glyph atlas being served:

```
iosurftex: swapped 1024x128 fmt=10 bpr=1024  (total 1)
iosurftex: swapped  320x832 fmt=80 bpr=1280  (total 3)
iosurftex: swapped 1024x128 fmt=10 bpr=1024  (total 4)
```

and the remaining declines are all correct - `fmt=250` is `Depth16Unorm` and
`type=4` is multisample, neither of which is text. The app is stable. **The
text is unchanged.**

### Withdrawn

2ms said the atlas being in the failing class was "the first direct evidence
that this defect is what makes *this application's* text unreadable". That is
withdrawn. Being in the failing class is necessary, not sufficient, and the
experiment that distinguishes them has now been run: the atlas is served from
an IOSurface, the class is corrected, and nothing on screen moved.

What still stands, because it was measured and not inferred: the law (2mn,
16/16 predicted in advance, extended in 2ms to R8 and to render-target usage),
the IOSurface result (2mo), and the fix inside our own instruments (2mp, 2ms -
36/72 to 0/72, real CoreText glyphs 46 and 48 wrong rows to 0). Those are
facts about this driver. What is *not* established is that this defect is what
the user sees.

The likely reading: Skia fills that atlas with a GPU render pass or a buffer
blit, and GPU writes were correct in **every** test from 2lo onward. A texture
that was never corrupt cannot be fixed.

### The instrument that decides it

The law is about one specific operation - a CPU `replaceRegion` into a
driver-allocated tiled texture. So count them. `iosurftex` now swizzles
`replaceRegion` on `GFXAAMD_MtlTexture` and logs the destination geometry of
every CPU upload.

A trap on the way: the class has **two** separate implementations,
`replaceRegion:mipmapLevel:slice:withBytes:bytesPerRow:bytesPerImage:` and
`replaceRegion:mipmapLevel:withBytes:bytesPerRow:`, and the 4-argument one is
not a forwarder. With only the 6-argument form swizzled, `lawtest`'s 192 known
uploads counted as **zero** - a confident wrong negative that would have been
read as "Claude never uploads by CPU" if it had been pointed at Claude first.
Rule 21 in a new costume: the counter was checked against a case known to be
present before being believed. Both are swizzled now and `lawtest` reports
`cpu-uploads=192`, matching its call count exactly.

### What each outcome will mean

- **No CPU upload into the 1024x128 R8 atlas** - the atlas is GPU-filled, was
  never corrupted, and this entire line of work cannot fix application text.
  The law remains a real driver bug that nothing user-visible depends on, and
  the text cause is somewhere we have not looked.
- **CPU uploads into it** - the atlas *is* filled the broken way, our swap
  should have fixed it and did not, and the swap itself becomes the suspect: an
  IOSurface-backed render-target texture may not behave as the driver expects.

## 2mu — the GPU write path is clean, and a premise of mine was false

Boot 114, armed, `-rbgpulinear` **out** (removed in boot 113 for 2mn's test,
which turned out inert).

### The correction, from the user

I had been reasoning from "Terminal's text is readable, Claude's and Safari's
are not", and built a hypothesis on it: CPU-rasterised text works, GPU-
rasterised text does not. The user states plainly that **Terminal is not
readable on this boot either** - it was readable *only* with `-rbgpulinear`,
which I had them remove two boots ago.

So the split never existed in the form I used it. What exists is: with
`-rbgpulinear` in, Terminal's text is readable and Claude's and Safari's are
not. On this boot nothing is readable, which is a regression I caused.

### 2mn's conclusion needs qualifying

2mn said "there is no kernel-side lever on client texture layout", from
`rbgpu-surf` reading `swz calls=63` before a full `texprobe` run and 63 after.
That is correct **for texprobe's textures** and I generalised it to all
surfaces. It is false for the ~63 surfaces the hook *does* see - the
display/scanout class - and a window's backing store is one of them. Forcing
those linear demonstrably makes Terminal's text readable. The lever exists;
it just does not reach a `newTextureWithDescriptor:` allocation.

Which also means the evidence already in hand had answered this: HANDOFF has
said all along that `-rbgpulinear` buys ~80 % of the widget/Dock/chrome class,
and the user had said Terminal was readable *with it*. The 2kx/2la/2lc variant
of the recurring error - read the evidence in hand before designing the next
experiment - again.

### 2mu, which stands regardless

Does the GPU writing a render target land correctly? A render pass draws a
full-screen quad whose fragment shader writes each pixel's **own coordinates**,
so a displaced row shows up as a wrong value rather than a wrong colour; the
result is read back with the same compute kernel used throughout. A clear would
have been useless here - one value everywhere makes a layout disagreement
invisible.

```
  geometry     align  ratio   driver-private  driver-managed  iosurface
   256x48    65536  2.67x    0/6            0/6            0/6
   256x64    65536  2.00x    0/6            0/6            0/6
   256x96    65536  1.33x    0/6            0/6            0/6
  1024x128   65536  1.00x    0/6            0/6            0/6
   256x128   65536  1.00x    0/6            0/6            0/6
   256x32     4096  1.00x    0/6            0/6            0/6
   512x256   65536  1.00x    0/6            0/6            0/6
```

**Zero failures anywhere**, including the geometries where a CPU `replace()`
fails 11 times in 12. So:

- The GPU write path is correct, for private, managed and IOSurface-backed
  destinations alike.
- The defect the law describes is specific to **CPU uploads**.
- And a render target being in the "failing" class costs nothing when the GPU
  is the one writing it.

### Where that leaves the text

2ms corrected Claude's glyph atlas - the right descriptor, `1024x128` R8Unorm,
confirmed swapped in the log - and the text did not change. 2mu says the GPU
path that fills such an atlas is clean. Together these say the CPU-upload
defect, which is real and now fixable, is **not what scrambles Claude's text**.

What does remains open. The one thing known to move on-screen text is
`-rbgpulinear`, acting on the surfaces that pass through the kernel hook, and
that is where the next look belongs - not in the client-texture path this
session has spent itself on.

### Restored

`-rbgpulinear` goes back in. Removing it was my doing, for 2mn's test, and that
test could not have worked.

## 2mw — the CPU-upload defect CANNOT be Claude's problem, and the proof is mechanical

Boot 115, armed, `-rbgpulinear` in. Claude run under `iosurftex` with
`RBGPU_IOSURFTEX_TRACE=1`, used for a minute, then quit.

```
pid 2137 summary: swapped=0 declined=0/0/0 law-clean=0 fellthrough=0 cpu-uploads=0
101 distinct descriptors across the GPU helper, all of them:
    storage=2 (MTLStorageModePrivate)   x101
    type=2 (2D) x81,  type=4 (2DMultisample) x20
    mips=1 x100,      mips=6 x1
25 textures swapped
CPU UPLOAD lines in the whole log:  0
```

**Claude calls `replaceRegion` zero times.** Every texture it creates is
`MTLStorageModePrivate`, which cannot take a CPU upload at all - the API
forbids it, and `texprobe` learned that the hard way in 2mf when a `.private`
`replace()` segfaulted.

The law of 2mn describes corruption of a CPU `replace()` into a driver-allocated
texture. Claude performs no such operation. So the defect this session found,
characterised, predicted 16/16 and fixed **cannot be what scrambles Claude's
text.** That is not an inference from a failed fix; it is mechanical.

A second screenshot under the interposer, with 25 textures swapped, is
pixel-for-pixel the same kind of scramble as the first. Expected, now.

### What that closes

- The CPU-upload defect is real, obeys a law, and `iosurftex` fixes it. It is
  **not** this machine's presenting symptom. Both halves of that sentence are
  measured.
- Layout is excluded for Claude from the hardware side as well: this boot
  reports `rbgpu-mode seen=5553 m0=5553` - every client resource LINEAR, which
  has no swizzle to get wrong - and the text is scrambled anyway. 2ln said this
  from photographs in boots 103/104; it is now said from the register state.
- Scanout and compositing are excluded: the screenshot carries the corruption,
  so the pixels are already wrong in the surfaces.

### What is left, and it is a short list

Claude's content is produced by the **GPU** into **private** textures. The GPU
paths measured so far are clean: a render pass writing position-derived values
(2mu, 0/6 at every geometry and storage class) and a buffer-to-texture blit
(2lo). Never measured:

1. **MSAA resolve.** 20 of Claude's 101 descriptors are `type=4`, and a
   multisample resolve is a distinct hardware path. Antialiased glyph edges
   come out of exactly this.
2. **Texture-to-texture blit**, which a compositor uses constantly.
3. **Mipmapped sampling** - one descriptor has `mips=6`.
4. **sRGB formats**, which the inventory also shows.

Each is a `texprobe`-shaped userspace measurement needing no boot, and 1 is the
one to do first: it is the largest share of the unexplained population and the
only one with an obvious connection to glyph edges.

### Status correction

`CLAUDE.md`'s three-line status still says the frontier "is NOT a layout
problem", which remains true and is now independently confirmed. It should also
say that the CPU-upload line of work is finished and did not reach the symptom,
so a future session does not re-run it.

## 2mx/2my (2026-10-21) — the first controlled reproduction, and the blind spot every probe shared

### The blind spot, stated plainly

`texprobe`, `lawtest`, `rtprobe`, and today's `blitprobe` and `xprobe` all write
a texture and read **that same texture object** back. A layout that is wrong
*consistently* reads back clean through such a loop. Every "the GPU path is
clean" line in this journal is of that shape, including today's. That is why
measurement after measurement comes back clean while the screen is visibly not.

### What was closed today, by measurement

- **Blit into a 64 KB-tiled PRIVATE texture is correct.** `tools/blitprobe.swift`,
  at Claude's own geometries including the 2048x2048 R8 glyph atlas, with
  glyph-sized sub-rect uploads and texture-to-texture copies. 30 cases, all
  clean. The control - a CPU `replace`, which the 2mn law says must fail -
  failed at all 8 FLAGGED geometries and passed at both untiled ones, 10/10
  with the law, so the detector was known good before its negatives were
  believed (rule 22).
  This kills the hypothesis that motivated it: Skia's atlas is `2048x2048
  fmt=10 usage=0x1`, shader-read-only and private, so a blit is the *only* way
  to fill it - and the blit is right.
- **Cross-consumer reads are correct.** `tools/xprobe.swift`: gpu-write ->
  gpu-read through a FRESH texture over the same IOSurface, gpu-write ->
  cpu-read of the raw surface bytes, and the reverse. 30 cases, all clean.
- **No Metal-to-Metal aliasing.** `tools/vramprobe.swift`: 624 surfaces at
  Claude's own mixed sizes plus 624 multisample textures, each filled with a
  pattern carrying its own id and all kept alive; every one holds its own data.

### The measurement that finally has the right shape

`tools/screenprobe.swift` puts the same self-locating pattern in two real
windows - one drawn by CoreGraphics, one by Metal - and lets the WindowServer
composite them on the same frame. Diffing the two cancels colour management
exactly, so no LUT has to be guessed at.

    direct 512x512      0/262144 differ, max channel difference 0/255
    msaa 512x512        0/262144
    iosurface 512x512   0/262144
    big 900x880         1518/792000, max 5/255, only in the grey calibration
                        ramp - integer-vs-float rounding, not corruption
    bigmsaa 900x880     790054/792000, max 255/255

**In `bigmsaa` the window that was destroyed is the CPU-drawn one.** Blocky,
repeating, and made of the pattern's own colours rearranged. The identical
window at the identical size was clean in `big`, the run immediately before.
The only difference is that the *other* window in the same process had
allocated a 900x880 4x multisample texture.

This is the first time in this investigation that the symptom has been
reproduced in an artifact we control, and it is consistent with two things seen
in the wild: the desktop carries repeated miniature copies of **other windows'**
content, and there are **zero VM faults** - an aliased mapping is a valid
mapping, so nothing faults; the data is just somebody else's.

### Not yet believed, and why

The harness is a suspect before the chip is (rule 16). The script that produced
it killed each probe and immediately started the next at the same screen
coordinates, and a killed process's window surface being recycled while still
displayed would look exactly like this. It was also a single frame, and one
frame is not a result (rule 18).

So `screenprobe.sh` now lets the probe terminate itself and waits for it,
captures twice per run, repeats each mode, and adds a **`bigcpu`** mode that
draws both windows with CoreGraphics and never creates a Metal device. That
mode is the discriminator:

- `bigcpu` corrupts too -> Metal is not involved; a large window backing store
  is enough, and the hunt moves to the WindowServer's surfaces.
- only `bigmsaa` corrupts -> allocating a large multisample texture damages an
  unrelated surface, and the hunt moves to the allocator and to MSAA/FMASK
  sizing for GC 10.3.3 against Navi 21's.
- nothing corrupts -> the one observation was the killed-process artifact, and
  2mx's screen results stand as clean across the board.

**The next action is to run `tools/screenprobe.sh` from the user's Terminal
and read `logs/<stamp>-screenprobe/report.txt`.** It needs no reboot, no kext
load and no sudo; it needs Terminal's Screen Recording permission, which
Claude's own shell does not have.

### Instrument defects found and fixed, four in one session

- The first capture had no windows in it: the Metal shader is compiled at
  runtime and that outlasted a guessed `sleep`. The probe now touches a file
  once the pattern is genuinely on screen and the wrapper waits for it.
- `geometry.txt` came back empty - stdout buffered, process killed before the
  flush. `setvbuf` now.
- The row matcher reported a spurious `shift -256` for half the rows because
  red and green repeat every 256 and it only looked at green. It folds in blue,
  which carries the high bits, and now maps 491/496 rows to identity.
- The CPU control was drawn vertically flipped: CoreGraphics draws images
  bottom-up. Fixed at the source, and the decoder now confirms orientation from
  the calibration strip rather than assuming it.
- `xprobe`'s "meta ~" column is nonsense - `size/px` is already the ratio - and
  its labels truncate at 40 characters. Neither affects its verdicts.

Four instrument defects against one hardware finding is the ratio rule 16 is
about. A negative from an instrument that has not been checked against a case
known to be present is not a negative.

## 2mz (2026-10-21) — the probe's own bug, and what survived killing it

### Half of what 2my measured was this repo's bug

`CPUView` built a `CGImage` over a Swift array's memory inside
`withUnsafeMutableBytes`, so the backing buffer died when the closure exited. A
`CGImage` over caller-supplied bytes may reference rather than copy them, and
CoreGraphics may defer the draw - so it was reading freed memory. It explained
every property of what 2my reported: CPU window only, intermittent, worse on
redraw.

Rebuilt so the pattern is rendered once into a buffer that lives for the life
of the process and is never freed. The effect is unambiguous:

    signature        before the fix              after
    72 row jumps     swap 4/4, refresh 4/4       GONE, 0/16
    84 row jumps     static 2/4, direct 1/4      static 1/4, refresh 3/4, direct 1/4

So the `swap` result that refuted "drawn once" was itself partly an artifact,
and the hypothesis it refuted was never properly on trial. Both are withdrawn.
What remains is the 84/92 signature, in 5 of 16 runs, always on the CPU window.

### What survived, and why it is not memory corruption

The scrambled window holds the probe's own pattern rearranged into blocks, and
the rearrangement is **identical every single time it occurs** - 84 row jumps
and 92 column jumps, run after run, capture after capture. Memory corruption
does not repeat byte for byte. A wrong address mapping does.

`tools/permute.swift` reads the permutation off directly, which the pattern
makes possible because every pixel carries its own coordinates. Colour
management is not guessed at: the CLEAN GPU window in the same capture supplies
the measured intended-to-captured mapping for all 256 levels, and inverting it
makes the scrambled window exactly decodable. On this capture that transform
came out identity, and 251904/251904 pixels decoded.

The displacement is not a constant shift - the histogram is flat at 0.1% per
bucket. It is structured. Reconstructing the source column per 8-pixel block:

    dest x:  0   8  16  24  32  40  48  56  64  72  80  88  96 104 112 120
    src  x: 32  32  48  48  40  40  56  56  48  48  32  32  56  56  40  40

Every displacement is a multiple of 8, bounded inside a tile, repeating on a
64-pixel period. That is a bit permutation of the low address bits: a
**tiled-versus-linear swizzle mismatch** on the window's backing store, one
layout written and another read. The intermittency fits - the backing store
lands tiled on some runs and linear on others.

This is the first reproducible, on-demand, exactly-decodable instance of the
family of defect the user actually sees, and it happens with `-rbgpulinear`
already in boot-args, which is direct evidence that lever does not reach these
surfaces.

### Standing

Five instrument defects were found today against one hardware finding, and two
hypotheses (DCC, "drawn once") were raised and withdrawn. The surviving
measurement is 2mz's permutation. Nothing about a fix is claimed yet.

Next, in order, all userspace and needing no boot:
1. Decode the permutation as a bit map of the linear address - take source and
   destination byte offsets inside one tile and look at the XOR - and compare
   it against the GFX10 64KB_S / 64KB_R_X patterns in `rb_regs.h` and the
   AddrLib notes in `docs/APPLE-STACK.md`. Naming the mode names the fix.
2. Find what decides tiled versus linear for a window backing store, since the
   same window is clean in 11 of 16 runs.

## 2na (2026-10-22) — the corruption is live, and the map is tiling-shaped

### The harness is cleared, at last

Every run stamped the blue channel with a distinct value. Blue was constant
across a window, so it survives any rearrangement of the pixels and names the
run that PRODUCED the surface. In all seven scrambled captures the CPU window
carried the **current** run's stamp:

    static-2 -> 56   swap-1 -> 128   swap-3 -> 176   refresh-2 -> 8
    refresh-3 -> 32  refresh-4 -> 56  direct-1 -> 80

Not a stale surface from an exited process. After five instrument defects in
one session this one is real: a freshly drawn CoreGraphics window backing
store, rearranged, mode-independent, in roughly half of all runs, with a
byte-identical signature (84 row jumps, 92 column jumps) every time.

### What the rearrangement is

`tools/bitfit.swift` extracts the XOR-linear bit matrix of the permutation,
measuring each column by toggling one bit over thousands of reference points
and taking the mode (rule 18, after an earlier one-sample-per-bit attempt
produced a ragged table). Validated against a window known to be clean, where
it returns the identity matrix and predicts 100.00%.

With `p = y*512 + x`, so bits 0-8 are x and 9-17 are y:

    x0 -> x0        y0 -> y0
    x1 -> x1        y1 -> y1
    x2 -> x2        y2 -> y2
    x3 -> y5        y3 -> x5
    x4 -> x4        y4 -> y4
    x5 -> y6, x3    y5 -> y6
    x6 -> y3,y4,x4  y6 -> y6,y4,x6,x4
    x7 -> y5,y6,x6,x7
    x8 -> y4,x8,x4  y7 -> y7,y6,y3,x6,x5
                    y8 -> y8,y4,x4,x3

**x and y bits swap into each other.** That is what a tiled layout does, and it
is why linear, pitch and scale models all fitted at 0.00%, and why nothing
stayed inside its own 128x128 tile under the assumption of an untiled surface.
The named modes still do not fit: 64KB_S, 64KB_S_X and 4KB_D all scored 0.00%
in both directions.

### Why the matrix is believed but the mode is not yet named

The model predicts **94.04%** of decoded pixels, not ~100%. Two things were
done before accepting that as structure rather than noise:

- The high coordinate bits had been encoded in blue as the values 0, 1, 16 and
  17 - a ONE level difference, which no display pipeline preserves. They were
  respaced 15 levels apart (8, 23, 68, 83) and the capture verified to carry
  the new values.
- The matrix was re-extracted from the new capture and came out **identical to
  the same hex digits, with the same agreement percentages**, 94-97% per column.

Two different encodings through two different captures agreeing exactly means
the residual 6% is not decode error. It is either a second term the XOR-linear
form cannot express, or two populations in the same surface. Until that is
resolved the mode is NOT named, and no fix is derived from this matrix.

### Standing

Real, reproducible on demand, deterministic, tiling-shaped, 94% explained by a
bit matrix, mode unnamed. It reproduces with `-rbgpulinear` already in
boot-args, which is direct evidence that lever does not reach this surface
class - and that is the likeliest reason it fixed Terminal and never fixed
Claude.

Next, in order:
1. Find where the residual 6% lives - whether it is concentrated in regions or
   spread - which decides between "a missing term" and "two populations".
2. With a 100% model, match it against the GFX10 equations rather than the
   three hand-coded candidates.
3. Only then: whether the lever that forces LINEAR can be made to reach window
   backing stores.

## 2nf (2026-10-22) — it is the SURFACE, not the drawing path, and not CPU vs GPU

### Two of this session's readings were wrong and are withdrawn

**"The corruption follows a CPU write."** Withdrawn. The probe had the CPU/GPU
difference confounded with which surface was used. An interleaved sweep
separates them:

    right window: my IOSurface, raw CPU stores      0 of 8 scrambled
    right window: my IOSurface, CoreGraphics draw   0 of 4
    right window: my IOSurface, Metal render        0 of 4
    right window: CAMetalLayer                      0 of 8
    left window:  AppKit's own layer backing store  scrambles, ~60% of runs

A CPU write is fine. CoreGraphics drawing is fine. What breaks is **the
surface CoreAnimation allocates for a layer's backing store**, and nothing
else.

**"A CPU-written IOSurface scrambles (2ne)."** Withdrawn, and it was a
misreading of this tool's own output: in the report `cpu` is always the LEFT
window (AppKit's backing store) and `gpu` is the right one, which is what the
mode changes. `cpusurface-1 cpu SCRAMBLED` was the AppKit window, as it is in
every mode. The right window was clean in that run and in every other.

### An instrument bug that scored as a hardware defect

`cgsurface` first reported SCRAMBLED in 4 of 4 runs with a signature of 6 row
jumps and 0 column jumps - nothing like the 84/92 the real defect produces.
Looking at the pixels instead of the metric: the window was simply drawn
**upside down**, and the 6 jumps were the single discontinuity where the grey
calibration strip met the pattern. A `CGBitmapContext` over an IOSurface
already has the surface's first row at its own origin, so the flip the view
context needs is one flip too many there. With it removed, `cgsurface` is
clean 4 of 4.

Had the metric been trusted without looking, this would have been reported as
"CoreGraphics drawing is the trigger" - the exact opposite of the truth.

### What stands

- The defect is in CoreAnimation's own layer backing store. Every surface this
  process allocates itself is correct, however it is written.
- `DetermineSwizzleMode` forced to LINEAR in the app changes nothing: every
  run above carries `patch state: PATCHED` (2nc/2nd).
- The permutation is unchanged and deterministic: 84 row jumps, 92 column
  jumps, the exact map of 2na, with 8x8 micro tiles intact and only their
  placement wrong.

### The caveat that has to stay visible

It is still NOT established that this is the user's symptom. Terminal is drawn
into an AppKit backing store and is **crisp** on this machine, while Claude's
text is GPU-composited through IOSurfaces and is broken - which is the
opposite way round from what this reproducer does. This may be the same
mechanism seen from the other side, or a second defect found on the way. The
honest statement is that a real, reproducible, exactly-characterised bug has
been cornered and its connection to the presenting symptom is unproven.

### Next

The reader of a layer backing store is the WindowServer, not the app, which is
why patching the app's swizzle chooser did nothing. Injecting into the
WindowServer is NOT an option: it is launchd-started, so it would mean exactly
the launchd `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` that rule 21 forbids and that already cost
this project a desktop.

That leaves the kernel side. `-rbgpulinear` hooks
`getPreferredSwizzleMode2` and sees only ~61 calls, all display-class, so
CoreAnimation's backing stores are not going through it. Finding the
allocation path that decides their layout is the next step, and it needs
boots.

## 2ng (2026-10-22) — a per-surface coin flip at allocation, decided once and permanent

### Three candidate explanations killed, cheaply, with no boots

**Window style and level.** A first run of an ordinary titled window at normal
level came back clean 6 of 6 and looked like the reproducer being an artefact
of its own borderless, floating windows. With more samples it is not:

    normalwin   (titled, normal level)    3 of 6 scrambled
    normallevel (borderless, normal)      2 of 6
    direct      (borderless, floating)    4 of 6

6 of 6 clean on a defect that fires near half the time has probability about
1.6% - unlikely, and it happened. Rule 18 earned again.

**Geometry.** Every size tested scrambles, including Terminal's own:

    512x512  3/6     580x380  3/6     256x256  6/6    1024x768 4/6
    900x880  6/6     128x128  6/6     640x480  3/6     800x600  2/6

**Time.** The same window captured at 0.5s and again at 15s:

    run 1  clean / clean          run 4  clean / clean
    run 2  clean / clean          run 5  SCRAMBLED / SCRAMBLED
    run 3  SCRAMBLED / SCRAMBLED  run 6  clean / clean

Identical in all six. Not a transient, and nothing settles.

### What that leaves, and it fits everything

**A surface is either right or wrong from the moment it is created, and stays
that way for its whole life.** Roughly a coin flip, decided at allocation. Not
drawing, not timing, not geometry, not window kind, and not CPU versus GPU -
all measured and excluded.

That resolves every contradiction this investigation has been carrying:

  Terminal crisp              one surface; it won the flip, and a winner stays
  Claude's text broken        Chromium uses MANY surfaces; ~half lose, so
                              something is always visibly wrong
  Safari chrome fine,
  its in-page images broken   chrome is one surface, images are many
  desktop wallpaper broken    its one surface lost
  this probe ~50%             one surface, a fresh flip every run

It also explains why the permutation is byte-identical whenever it occurs: the
loser gets one specific wrong layout, not random damage.

### Where a fix has to go

Not the drawing path and not the app: `DetermineSwizzleMode` forced to LINEAR
in-process changes nothing (2nc/2nd, with every run carrying
`patch state: PATCHED`). The layout of a layer backing store is agreed between
whoever allocates it and the WindowServer that reads it, and the app is not
part of that conversation.

The WindowServer cannot be injected into - it is launchd-started, so that is
exactly the launchd DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES that rule 21 forbids and that
already cost this project a desktop once.

So the kernel side. `-rbgpulinear` hooks `getPreferredSwizzleMode2`, which
sees ~61 calls, all display-class, while these backing stores are allocated in
their thousands. If half of all surfaces draw a wrong layout and forcing
LINEAR removes the disagreement, widening that hook's coverage to every
surface is the fix - and the per-surface coin flip predicts it would fix
Claude, Safari's images, the desktop and the icons all at once.

Next: find which allocation path decides a layer backing store's layout, and
whether the existing hook can be made to cover it. That needs boots.

## 2nh (2026-10-22, boot 118) — it scales with the NUMBER of backing stores

### The boot was checked first, and the baseline re-measured on it

Boot 117 came back up unarmed after the shutdown - `rbgpu-boot` unchanged and
`rbgpu-arm` consumed - and `lawtest` confirmed it at the hardware with no Metal
device at all. Boot 118 is armed (`rbgpu-boot` 118). The two-window probe at
512x512 gives 3 of 6 on this boot, the same as boot 117, so the boot is not a
variable and yesterday's numbers carry over.

### "A per-surface coin flip" was too loose

2ng called it a coin flip at allocation. The rate is not a constant: it depends
strongly on geometry, and far more strongly on **how many CoreAnimation backing
stores the process has**.

Same boot, same 800x600 geometry, same screen position:

    one CPU-drawn window      2 of 6 scrambled
    two CPU-drawn windows    12 of 12 scrambled

And at 512x512, with two windows, the per-window split is the clue:

    window 0 (allocated first)   clean in 4 of 6, then 2 of 6 in a repeat
    window 1 (allocated second)  scrambled in 6 of 6, both times

The first backing store a process allocates is often right. Every one after it
is wrong, and their presence drags the first one wrong too. Grids of four and
six at 512 were scrambled in every window of every round.

Metal is not the variable: creating a device and nothing else (RB_GRIDMETAL=1)
left window 1 at 6 of 6 either way. Position is not the variable: the grid was
moved to the probe's exact coordinates and the split persisted.

### Why this explains the machine

    Terminal                  one window surface, usually right - and crisp
    Claude / Chromium         dozens of layer surfaces, so some are always
                              wrong and the window is never clean
    Safari chrome vs images   chrome is few surfaces, in-page images are many
    this probe                one surface ~33-50%, two surfaces always

It also explains why every single-surface experiment this session looked like a
coin flip: with one allocation there is only one draw.

### Instrument notes

- A grid of N windows at 512 puts anything past the third in a second row that
  falls off a 1080-tall screen, so an N=4 run decoded only two of its windows.
  That row is discarded, not reported.
- With N=1 the decoder is still handed a pair, so its second verdict is empty
  screen and meaningless. Only the first is real.

### Next

The question is now what differs between the first allocation and the later
ones. An address or alignment threshold would fit: the first lands somewhere
acceptable, later ones do not, and adding allocations moves the first as well.

## 2ni (2026-10-22, boot 118) — three more triggers excluded, and where the layout really comes from

### Not an address or pressure threshold

2nh's "later allocations are wrong" suggested the first backing store lands
somewhere acceptable and later ones do not. If that were about addresses or
memory pressure, allocating before the window would poison it. One window at
512x512, 8 rounds each:

    nothing pre-allocated          3 of 8 scrambled
    16 plain IOSurfaces first      2 of 8
    256 MB of ordinary memory      4 of 8

All within noise of each other. **Pre-allocation does not poison the first
window.** The trigger is specific to CoreAnimation's own backing-store
creation, not to where things land in memory.

### Not bytesPerRow

The one property of a surface this probe can vary freely. Surfaces allocated
here are clean at every stride tried - 2048 (natural), 2176, 2304, 3072, 4096 -
0 of 8 captures scrambled in each case.

### CoreAnimation's surfaces cannot be read from outside

`tools/surfdump.c` walks the IOSurface id space and dumps the properties of
anything it can reach, to compare a CoreAnimation backing store against one
allocated by hand. **0 of 20000 ids resolved**: `IOSurfaceLookup` only reaches
surfaces the calling process may use, and CoreAnimation's are not global. The
tool says so rather than printing an empty table (rule 14).

### Where an IOSurface-backed texture's layout actually comes from

This matters because it explains 2nd's negative. The Metal driver has a
separate entry point for them:

    AMD_device_layer::NewTextureWithDescriptor2(objc_object*,
        MTLTextureDescriptor*, __IOSurface*, unsigned long)

A texture made over an existing IOSurface does not get its tiling from
`amdMtl_HWL_DetermineSwizzleMode` - that is the chooser for textures created
from a descriptor alone. So forcing that function to return LINEAR in-process
was never going to touch a layer backing store, and its null result is
explained rather than mysterious.

Two other symbols are worth recording for whoever picks this up:
`amdMtl_HWL_FillInUBMSurfaceInfo`, which carries a static table literally named
`hw2ubmSwizzleMode`, and `amdMtl_HWL_CheckAlignment`.

(The many `...Swizzle...` symbols in this driver are ObjC method-swizzling
machinery - `AMD_InterposedSelector` - and have nothing to do with address
swizzle. Checked rather than assumed; rule 22.)

### Standing

Excluded today, each by measurement: allocation pressure, pre-allocation,
bytesPerRow. Excluded earlier: drawing path, CPU versus GPU, geometry as a
cause rather than a modifier, window style, window level, timing, and the
userspace swizzle chooser.

What remains: the layout of a CoreAnimation layer backing store, decided
somewhere this plugin has not yet reached, and worsening with each additional
backing store a process allocates.

## 2nj (2026-10-22, boot 118) — window backing stores never reach the kernel, and our own lever is a suspect

### Where a layer backing store is NOT

Watched from inside the process with `tools/surfwatch.c`, which interposes
IOSurfaceCreate and IOSurfaceLookupFromMachPort:

    1, 2 and 4 windows   ->  exactly ONE IOSurfaceCreate, always 512x512 id=108
                             ZERO surfaces arriving by mach port

The single create does not scale with the window count, so it is incidental.
Layer backing stores are neither created as IOSurfaces in this process nor
passed into it from the WindowServer by port.

### And not in the kernel either

`rbgpu-si` and `rbgpu-surf` are read straight from NVRAM, which needs no sudo.
Before creating four 512x512 windows and after:

    rbgpu-surf  calls=59      (before)
    rbgpu-surf  calls=59      (after)

Unchanged. **Window backing stores do not pass through the kernel's align
manager.** That closes the last place this plugin can currently see.

### What the kernel DOES see, and why it matters

All 59 calls, with their per-surface rows:

    1920x1080 b32 f26 t1 fl20 s0->1b
    1920x1080 b32 f26 t1 fl20 s0->1b
    8192x4320 b32 f26 t1 fl0  s9->1b
    1920x1080 b32 f26 t1 fl0  s9->1b
    64x64     b32 f26 t1 fl0  s9->16
    forced=59

The 1920x1080 surfaces are screen-sized: the WindowServer's own compositing
buffers. Apple's chooser returns **0x1b = ADDR_SW_64KB_R_X** for them, and
`forced=59` says `-rbgpulinear` rewrites every one of them to LINEAR.

### The suspicion that follows

Every window's pixels reach the screen through those compositing surfaces. We
force them to a layout Apple did not choose, for all 59 of them. If anything
downstream still addresses them as 64KB_R_X, the result is a permutation of
whole micro tiles with their contents intact - which is exactly what 2na
measured.

`CLAUDE.md` already records `-rbgpulinear` as "a SUSPECT in the text defect
(2mm), not neutral", and 2mm's pending test - remove it and see - was never
run. This session has built the instrument that can read the answer precisely
instead of by eye.

**The experiment: remove `-rbgpulinear`, reboot armed, and re-run
`tools/screenprobe.sh`.**

    windows go clean    we have been causing this ourselves, and the lever
                        that fixes widgets and chrome breaks window content.
                        The two classes need separating rather than one global
                        force.
    unchanged           the force is not the cause and the kernel-side
                        compositing surfaces are exonerated, which is worth
                        knowing for the same single boot.

Either way it costs one boot and settles a suspicion that has been carried,
unmeasured, since 2mm.

## 2nk (2026-10-22, boot 119) — `-rbgpulinear` is PROTECTIVE, not the cause

Boot 119, armed (`rbgpu-boot` 118 -> 119, `rbgpu-arm` consumed), with
`-rbgpulinear` removed. The kernel hook confirms the change at the chip rather
than from boot-args alone: `lin=2 forced=0`, so the WindowServer's compositing
surfaces now keep Apple's own choice of `0x1b` (ADDR_SW_64KB_R_X) instead of
being rewritten to LINEAR.

    with    -rbgpulinear   gpu window NEVER scrambled, cpu window ~50%
    without -rbgpulinear   BOTH scrambled, 8 of 8

And the CPU window's signature **changed**: 84 row jumps / 92 column jumps
becomes 77 / 58. It is a different permutation, not the same defect carrying
on unaffected.

So the force is exonerated. Removing it does not reveal a cleaner machine - it
breaks the GPU-rendered window too, which had been clean in every run and every
mode for two days. 2mm's suspicion, carried in `CLAUDE.md` since then as
"`-rbgpulinear` is now a SUSPECT in the text defect, not neutral", is settled
negative.

What it positively establishes: **Apple's chosen 64KB_R_X addressing does not
match what this chip actually does.** Forcing those compositing surfaces LINEAR
removes the disagreement for GPU-rendered content entirely, and for about half
of CPU-drawn window content. The residual - a CoreAnimation layer backing store
that bypasses every allocation path this plugin can see (2nj) - is what LINEAR
does not reach.

### Instrument note

`bitfit` was run on this capture and reported 0.38%. That number is void, not a
finding: it builds its colour LUT from the window it is told is clean, and on
this boot neither window is. It needs a known-good reference in the same frame
and there was none.

### Standing

`-rbgpulinear` belongs IN, now for a measured reason rather than an observed
~80%. Restored at the end of this boot.

## 2nn (2026-10-22, boot 121) — the Lilu user patch CANNOT work: the driver is in the dyld shared cache

Boot 121 carried the WindowServer entry (2nm), `-rbgpumtllinear` and
`-rbgpulinear`, kext UUID `5B28C4CF` matching the build. The user reported
Claude unchanged. Before reading anything into that, `screenprobe` - which is
itself in the proc list and reads its own memory - was asked:

    mtl-patch: original prologue present 1x, LINEAR stub present 0x
    mtl-patch: -> NOT PATCHED

Same as boot 117. So the experiment did not run, again, and "Claude is
unchanged" says nothing about the WindowServer hypothesis.

### Why, and it is structural

    ls /System/Library/Extensions/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver.bundle/Contents/
       MacOS/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver
    -> No such file or directory

**The file does not exist.** A process that has loaded the driver reports that
path through `dladdr`, but the image comes from the **dyld shared cache**.
Lilu's `BinaryModInfo` names a file and patches its pages as they are mapped;
those pages are never mapped from that file because there is no file. So
`onProcLoad` returns `NoError`, the hook logs ARMED, and nothing is patched -
ever.

**2lm, 2nb and 2nm are inert by construction.** The Terminal patch that 2lq
wanted to test, the screenprobe entry of 2nb, and the WindowServer entry of
2nm could none of them ever have applied. This retires the whole line, and it
is rule 20 in its most expensive form: a registration reporting success is not
evidence that a patch applied, and here nothing short of reading the target
process's memory could have revealed it.

The check that would have caught it before a boot was spent costs nothing:
**`ls` the file named in the `BinaryModInfo`.**

### What still works

`tools/mtllinear.c` patches the same bytes successfully, every time, because it
edits the in-memory image with `vm_protect(..., VM_PROT_COPY)` rather than
relying on a file mapping. It is injected per process with
DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES (rule 21), and both it and the probe's independent
self-check confirm PATCHED.

That mechanism cannot reach the WindowServer, which launchd starts - and
putting DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES in a launchd environment is precisely what rule
21 forbids and what already cost this machine a desktop once. So the
WindowServer stays out of reach by any means currently available.

### Where that leaves a fix

The one process whose text the user actually cares about CAN be reached: Claude
itself, and Safari, by per-process injection, which has already been done
safely on this machine (2mv/2mw ran Claude under an injected dylib for a full
trace). Forcing `DetermineSwizzleMode` to LINEAR inside the app is a direct
test of whether the app's own texture layout is part of its symptom, costs no
boot, and has a blast radius of one restartable application.

## 2np (2026-10-22, boot 121) — **CLAUDE'S TEXT IS FIXED**

    tools/mtllinear-app.sh Claude

    mtllinear: PATCHED DetermineSwizzleMode at 0x7ffb21f25a11 (verify ok)  x5
    user: "CLAUDE IS WORKING ... AND IS ACCELERATED"

Five processes - the browser process and its helpers - every one patched and
verified by re-reading the bytes after writing them. Boot 121, armed, with
`-rbgpulinear` and `-rbgpumtllinear` both in boot-args.

**Forcing `amdMtl_HWL_DetermineSwizzleMode` to return ADDR_SW_LINEAR inside the
application makes its text readable.** The defect is the swizzle mode the
userspace Metal driver chooses for client textures, and this chip does not
address surfaces the way that choice assumes.

### Why it took this long, stated plainly

2lg had the answer in 2026-10-20: "client texture layout is computed entirely
in userspace, in `AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver`, and the kernel is never asked",
and it filed that under "out of this plugin's reach". It was right about the
place and wrong that it was out of reach. Three later attempts to reach it
(2lm, 2nb, 2nm) all used Lilu's user patcher, which **cannot** touch this
driver: it lives in the dyld shared cache with no file on disk, so a path-based
`BinaryModInfo` patches pages that are never mapped while `onProcLoad` reports
success (2nn). Every one of them was inert, and the only thing that ever
revealed it was reading the target process's own memory.

`tools/mtllinear.c` works because it edits the in-memory image with
`vm_protect(..., VM_PROT_COPY)` and verifies the bytes afterwards.

### Two defects, not one

This also settles a caveat carried since 2mx and never dropped: the
`screenprobe` reproducer is **not** this symptom. 2nd forced the same function
LINEAR in that probe with every run recording `patch state: PATCHED` and the
scrambling was unchanged - because that probe's defect is an **AppKit layer
backing store**, which bypasses this path entirely (2nj: no IOSurfaceCreate in
process, nothing by mach port, kernel align manager unchanged at calls=59).

    defect A  client texture layout, chosen by DetermineSwizzleMode
              -> FIXED by forcing LINEAR per process (this milestone)
    defect B  CoreAnimation layer backing store, ~50% of allocations wrong,
              permutation measured exactly in 2na -> STILL OPEN

Keeping those apart is why the null result in 2nd did not derail this.

### What is NOT yet done

The fix is per-process and does not survive a relaunch: Claude has to be
started through the launcher. Making it permanent cannot use Lilu for the
reason above. And LINEAR is a correction, not the right answer - the proper
fix is to make the chosen mode match what this chip actually does, which would
also keep tiling's performance.

## 2nr (2026-10-22) — INTELLIJ FIXED TOO, and with tiling kept

2np fixed Claude by forcing the userspace chooser to ADDR_SW_LINEAR. The same
stub applied to IntelliJ IDEA killed it in 3.6 s:

    SIGSEGV (si_addr 0x68) in libawt_lwawt.dylib
    -[EncoderManager getEncoder:renderOptions:]+0x1b2
    <- MTLRenderer_FillSpans <- sun.java2d.metal.MTLRenderQueue.flushBuffer

Relaunching with the dylib injected and `RBGPU_MTLLINEAR=0` came up stable, so
the patch is the cause and not the injection (rule 16).

### Why the same fix broke the second app

The apps differ in what they draw INTO. Electron/Skia renders into
IOSurface-backed textures, which take `NewTextureWithDescriptor2` and never
reach this chooser (2nl), and uses a plain MTLTexture only for its glyph
atlas - so blanket LINEAR fixed the atlas and touched no render target. JBR
renders every Swing surface into a plain MTLTexture. A linear surface is not a
legal render target, `newRenderPipelineState` returned nil, and JBR
dereferenced it at +0x68.

A constant-return stub can never be selective, so `tools/mtlswizzle.c`
replaces it with a detour: 30 bytes of prologue (a whole number of
instructions - the 32-byte uniqueness pattern of 2lm cuts `movq %rdx, %r14` in
half) copied to an RX page with an absolute jump back, and
`movabs %r11, hook; jmp *%r11` over the entry. The hook has the real
signature, so calling the original is an ordinary C call.

### What the hook could measure that the stub could not

The signature, from the mangled name:

    amdMtl_HWL_DetermineSwizzleMode(AMDCommonHwInfoRec*, void* addrLib,
        const MTLTextureDescriptorPrivate*, const AMD_DeviceSettings*,
        uint samples, uint frags, uint& out, bool, bool)

It builds a 0x44-byte ADDR2_GET_PREFERRED_SURF_SETTING_INPUT on the stack
(`movl $0x44, -0x7c(%rbp)`) and asks AddrLib. The flags it fills are
color/depth/stencil/texture/display, derived from format and sample count -
**not** from Metal's usage - so the flags cannot discriminate a render target.

`usage` is at descriptor+0x68, and that was measured, not inferred: the
function tests `0x68(%r14) & 6` = ShaderWrite|RenderTarget, and
`tools/usageprobe.m` then created one texture per usage value and the field
tracked all five. **But +0x68 is the usage as REQUESTED.** IntelliJ exposed
the difference: JBR leaves usage unset, so +0x68 reads 0 while +0xb0 reads
0x17, Metal having expanded an unspecified usage to all of them. Keying on
+0x68 alone called a render target "not a render target" and did not crash
only by luck. The hook ORs the two. usageprobe could never have caught this,
because it always set usage explicitly and the two fields agreed 5/5.

### The finding: every mode the chooser picks is an `_X` mode

Logged from live processes:

    37x48 BGRA8  -> 2  (256B_D)      256x16  -> 22 (4KB_D_X)
    256x48 BGRA8 -> 27 (64KB_R_X)    640x480 -> 27 (64KB_R_X)
    IntelliJ: 512x512 A8 -> 26 (64KB_D_X)   <- the glyph atlas
              1400x941   -> 27 (64KB_R_X)   <- the window surface
              16x16 fmt 253 -> 24 (64KB_Z_X)

`_X` means the swizzle carries a pipe-bank XOR derived from the pipe/bank
configuration. This chip reads GB_ADDR_CONFIG 0x242 (4 pipes, 4 packers, 1 SE)
where Apple's driver is built for Navi 21, and 2na measured the corruption as
**8x8 micro tiles intact with only their placement wrong** - which is what a
pipe-bank XOR computed from the wrong pipe count looks like. A non-X mode
applies no pipe-bank XOR at all, so it is tiled, configuration independent,
and still a legal render target.

Every one of IntelliJ's textures has the render-target bit set in its resolved
usage (0x05, 0x07, 0x17), so usage-gating alone can do nothing for it: its
scrambled text IS the 512x512 A8 atlas at 64KB_D_X. Mode `fix` therefore sends
non-render-targets to LINEAR and maps render targets off the `_X` family:

    22 -> 6   (4KB_D_X  -> 4KB_D)    x8
    26 -> 10  (64KB_D_X -> 64KB_D)   x1
    27 -> 10  (64KB_R_X -> 64KB_D)   x5
    24        (64KB_Z_X) left alone - depth needs _X for HTILE, and is
                                      neither displayed nor CPU-read

**IntelliJ came up completely clean**: menus, project tree, syntax-highlighted
Java, breadcrumbs and status bar all sharp, with no crash. The driver and the
hardware both accepted non-X render targets. This is a better result than
2np's: the surfaces stay TILED and only the pipe-bank XOR is removed, so the
performance tiling buys is kept.

The screenshot also shows the desktop and Finder icons behind the window still
scrambled, which is the control that matters - the chip is in its usual state
and defect B is untouched, exactly as 2nj predicted.

### texprobe is not an oracle for this, and never was

Baseline, unpatched, on this boot: 0/12 failures in every geometry, every
footprint `1.00x (linear)`, "law held in 16/16". Its round trip is
self-consistent because both ends use the driver's own assumption. That is why
it stayed clean for twenty milestones while Claude's text was unreadable. The
only honest oracles for defect A are real applications.

### Made persistent

`tools/rbgpu-app.sh install "IntelliJ IDEA"` builds
`~/Applications/<Name> (GPU).app`, a wrapper bundle whose executable execs the
real binary with the dylib inserted and the policy baked in. Verified through
LaunchServices, which is what the Dock uses: `vmmap` on the resulting process
shows `mtlswizzle.dylib` mapped. It activates an already-running copy instead
of starting a second one, because an app holding a single-instance lock
forwards and exits in a way that looks exactly like a crash (2no).

Rule 21 still forbids the only system-wide form of this. A wrapper per app is
the persistent form that keeps the blast radius at one app.

### What this still cannot reach

Apple platform binaries (Safari, Finder, Mail, WindowServer) strip
DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES whatever amfi is set to, so no injection reaches them.
Defect B is a different path again and is unaffected.

**The lead for a genuinely global fix is now visible and is argument four of
this very function.** `const AMD_DeviceSettings*` comes from the kext, and the
chooser consults it (`testb $0x8, 0x7(%rsi)` with `testb $0x10, 0xcd(%r12)` on
the hw info). If a device-settings field steers the chooser away from the `_X`
family, changing it kernel-side would reach **every process with no injection
at all** - including the platform binaries. That is the next experiment, and
the first one in a while that is worth a boot.

## 2ns (2026-10-22) — can it be global? Three measurements, all negative

2nr ended by naming `const AMD_DeviceSettings*`, argument four of the chooser,
as "the next experiment, and the first one in a while that is worth a boot".
It is not. None of the three routes to a fix that needs no injection survives
contact, and one of them takes a claim from 2nr with it.

### 1. The AddrLib configuration is CORRECT, so the kext cannot fix the math

`amdMtl_HWL_InitAddrLibHwRegFields(_ADDR_CREATE_INPUT*, const AMDCommonHwInfoRec*)`
is four instructions:

    movl $0xd, 0x4(%rdi)        ; ADDR_CREATE_INPUT.chipFamily = 0xd (GFX10)
    movl 0xa4(%rsi), %eax
    movl %eax, 0x30(%rdi)       ; regValue.gbAddrConfig

So AddrLib's **entire** hardware configuration is one field,
`AMDCommonHwInfoRec + 0xa4`, and that record is filled by `gfx10_HwInfoInitData`
from the kernel's `_sAMD_GET_HW_INFO_VALUES`. Read live, from inside a process,
through the 2nq hook which already holds that pointer as argument one:

    swz: AddrLib gbAddrConfig (hwInfo+0xa4) = 0x242
         pipes=4 pkrs=4 se=1 interleave=256
    swz:   hardware GB_ADDR_CONFIG is 0x242 -> AGREES

**It agrees with the chip exactly.**

**This withdraws 2nr's explanation.** "The `_X` pipe-bank XOR is computed from
Navi 21's pipe count against a 4-pipe chip" is false: the userspace AddrLib is
configured from this chip's own GB_ADDR_CONFIG. The `fix` policy still works -
IntelliJ is clean, that was seen - but the reason it works is **not**
established, and the entry that said it was has been corrected. What survives
is 2na's measurement that the permutation is an exact XOR-linear bit matrix,
which still points at the `_X` XOR term; it just no longer points at the pipe
count. Thirty-one instances now of reading a value without establishing what
makes it meaningful - this one caught within the hour, by measuring the field
instead of continuing to reason about it.

It also closes the route: there is nothing in the AddrLib configuration for
the kext to correct, because it is already right.

### 2. AMD_DeviceSettings is built in userspace, not handed over by the kext

    __Z29amdMtl_HWL_InitDeviceSettingsP18AMD_DeviceSettingsP18AMDCommonHwInfoRec
    amdMtl_HWL_InitDeviceSettings(AMD_DeviceSettings*, AMDCommonHwInfoRec*)

Argument four is derived in the process from argument one. It is not an
independent channel from the kernel, so 2nr's lead was a lead to the same
place. The kernel's only channel into any of this is

    AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelDevice::getHardwareInfo(_sAMD_GET_HW_INFO_VALUES*)

and the field of it that configures AddrLib is the one already shown correct.
Whether some *other* hwInfo bit steers the choice (the chooser gates on
`0xcd(%r12) & 0x10` and on settings bits derived from it) is unproven and
would cost boots to explore.

### 3. LSEnvironment in the real app's Info.plist - LaunchServices refuses it

The one route that would have removed the wrapper icon without a launchd
environment: put `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` in the app's own `LSEnvironment`, so
the real app launched normally from the Dock comes up patched. Measured on
IntelliJ, with the original saved to `logs/plist-backups/`:

    _LSOpenURLsWithCompletionHandler() failed for the application
    /Applications/IntelliJ IDEA.app with error -54.

Editing the bundle invalidates its signature and LaunchServices refuses the
app outright - independently of `amfi_get_out_of_my_way`, which only governs
whether dyld will honour the insert once the process exists. Restored, and the
app launches again. It would also have been undone by every app update, where
a wrapper survives one.

### A self-inflicted confound, recorded because it looked like a result

After restoring the plist, IntelliJ still would not start, and left a crash
log identical to 2nr's. The cause was not the restore:

    DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES=.../build/out/mtllinear.dylib

**This Claude process is itself running under 2np's blanket stub**, so every
shell it spawns inherits that variable, and `open -a` propagates it to the app
it launches. The IDE was being started under the one patch known to crash it,
by the act of measuring. `env -u DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` and it came up clean.
Rule 16 in a new costume: the instrument is a suspect, and here the instrument
was the environment the measurement ran in.

### What global actually means now

    third-party apps, signed or ad-hoc or unsigned   wrapper works
    Apple platform binaries (Safari, Finder,
      Terminal, Mail, WindowServer)                  unreachable, full stop
    App Store apps (sandboxed)                       cannot read the dylib
                                                     out of a home directory
    a launchd environment                            forbidden by rule 21,
                                                     and it cost a machine

`tools/rbgpu-app.sh install-all` wraps every injectable app in /Applications
in one pass and names what it skipped and why, so the setup is one command
rather than one per app. The first version of it skipped unsigned and ad-hoc
apps as "unsigned or App Store", which was backwards - those are the easiest
things to inject into - and it also tried to wrap `/Applications/Spotify.app`,
which on this machine has no `Contents` at all.

**The honest answer to "can we fix this globally": not for Apple's own apps,
and not without injecting per process.** The decision is made in the userspace
Metal driver, one copy per process, and the kernel's only input to it is
already correct.

## 2nt (2026-10-22) — the kext route is closed, and 2lo already said why

The question: can the fix be universal, from the kext, with no injection?
Three more measurements, and then the one already in the journal.

### 1. Feeding AddrLib a different gbAddrConfig does NOT help

2ns closed this route for the wrong reason - "gbAddrConfig is already correct,
so there is nothing for the kext to correct". That is the wrong test. The kext
does not need to *correct* it; it needs to make userspace *compute*
differently, and gbAddrConfig is the single value that configures every
swizzle equation AddrLib builds.

`amdMtl_HWL_InitAddrLibHwRegFields` is 22 bytes and self-contained, so
`tools/mtlswizzle.c` gained `RBGPU_GBADDRCONFIG`, which replaces it with
`movl $0xd, 0x4(%rdi); movl $IMM, 0x30(%rdi); ret`. That is a faithful dry run
of changing the value kernel-side: it reaches AddrLib by exactly the path
`AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelDevice::getHardwareInfo` controls, so a value that
works in one process would work in every process.

Identity control first - forcing 0x242, the value the kernel already reports -
reproduced the unpatched modes exactly. Then 0x040: **1 pipe, 1 packer**,
which makes the pipe-bank XOR degenerate, with `RBGPU_SWIZZLE=log` so the
chooser was untouched and still returning `_X` modes.

**IntelliJ came up completely garbled.** Native AppKit chrome ("Welcome to
IntelliJ IDEA", the menu bar) was sharp; every pixel JBR renders was noise.
Zero mode overrides were applied, so `_X` with a degenerate pipe config is
still broken.

A sweep of 0x242/0x040/0x042/0x240 also showed the **chosen mode never
changes** with gbAddrConfig - 22 stays 22, 27 stays 27. The config changes the
math, not the choice, and changing the math this way does not fix it.

So the pipe/packer parameters are not the lever, and the kext has no other
field in that struct.

### 2. The kernel's swizzle translation tables are identity where it matters

`AMDRadeonX6000_AMDHardware::getUbmSwizzleMode` is literally `mov eax, esi;
ret`. `AMDGFX10AlignManager::getAddrSwizzleMode` (table 0xbf4efa0) and
`::getSwizzleMode` (table 0xbf4f120) are identity for every mode the kernel
supports - 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 17, 18, 21, 22, 24, 25, 26, 27 - and map the
rest to invalid (33) or LINEAR. **Every mode actually in play round-trips
unchanged**: the ones userspace picks (2, 22, 24, 26, 27) and the ones `fix`
maps them to (6, 10). There is no kernel/userspace enum mismatch to exploit.

Worth keeping: this also proves the kernel accepts non-X modes, so a
kernel-side non-X choice is legal. It just does not reach the defect.

### 3. pipeBankXor is userspace-only

`amdMtl_ComputePipeBankXor`, `amdMtl_HWL_ValidatePipeBankXor`,
`Addr2ComputePipeBankXor`, `Gfx10Lib::HwlComputePipeBankXor` - all in the MTL
driver. `nm` on AMDRadeonX6000 and AMDRadeonX6800HWLibs finds none. Rule 23
control: the same `nm` returns 6048 symbols and finds 5 swizzle symbols in
that kext, so the empty result is a real absence and not a broken search.

### 4. And 2lo had already settled it on 2026-10-21

> "It is specifically **the CPU-side tiling routine that
> `MTLTexture.replace(region:)` uses for a tiled, multi-byte-per-pixel
> surface.**" - decoded exactly as `y ^ 32` at w=256 and `x ^ 48, y ^ 16` at
> w=1000, BGRA8 failing where R8 is clean, and no other upload path affected.

**That is a memcpy inside the application's own process.** The kernel never
sees those pixels, never computes that XOR, and cannot change the code that
does. 2ln had already measured the other half on hardware: `-rbgpulinear`,
which forces the kernel's own chooser to LINEAR, leaves the text *identically
scrambled in both directions*. The kernel's mode choice does not reach the
userspace CPU tiling path at all.

### The answer

**There is no kext-side universal fix for defect A, and six independent levers
now say so:**

| lever | closed by |
|---|---|
| kernel's own swizzle choice (`-rbgpulinear`) | 2ln, on hardware, both directions |
| AddrLib's hardware config (gbAddrConfig) | 2nt, forced to 1 pipe/1 pkr, still garbled |
| `AMD_DeviceSettings` | 2ns, built in userspace from hwInfo |
| kernel/userspace mode enum translation | 2nt, identity for every mode in play |
| `pipeBankXor` | 2nt, no such code in any kext |
| `LSEnvironment` in the app bundle | 2ns, LaunchServices refuses, error -54 |

The broken code is in the dyld shared cache, runs once per process, and is
reached only from inside that process. Injection is the only lever, which
leaves Apple platform binaries and sandboxed App Store apps permanently out of
reach by this route.

### A boot lost to a charger, and rule 8 earning its place again

The machine restarted mid-session (charger swap). `rbgpu-boot` still read
**121**, unchanged, so the new boot never armed - `rbgpu-arm` is one-shot
(rule 9) and boot 121 had consumed it. `MTLCopyAllDevices` returned **0
devices**: no accelerator at all. The launcher's "the dylib never loaded"
was therefore correct and meant nothing about the dylib - there was no AMD
Metal driver in the process to patch. Caught by an IntelliJ pid of 1236 being
*lower* than the 5856 from ten minutes earlier, which is the only reason the
reboot was noticed before something was read as a result. Boot-args survived
intact (40 of them).

## 2nu (2026-10-22, boot 122) — everything wrapped, and why 2no's first attempt "exited cleanly"

Boot 122 is armed (`rbgpu-boot` 122, one Metal device). Claude relaunched
under `RBGPU_SWIZZLE=fix`, verified from its own memory rather than assumed:
**8 processes HOOKED**, and the overrides are the intended ones -

    override 22 -> 6    (4KB_D_X  -> 4KB_D)              x21
    override 27 -> 10   (64KB_R_X -> 64KB_D)             x7
    override 26 -> 10   (64KB_D_X -> 64KB_D)             x3
    override 27 -> 0    non-render-target -> LINEAR      x3
    override  2 -> 0    non-render-target -> LINEAR      x4

Render targets stayed tiled; only non-render-targets went linear. The user
confirms it reads correctly.

### pgrep cannot see the app a script is running inside

`tools/rbgpu-app.sh verify` reported Claude "not running" while Claude Code
was executing inside it. ps showed pid 1227 as
`/Applications/Claude.app/Contents/MacOS/Claude`; `pgrep -f` with that exact
string, and even `pgrep -x Claude`, returned nothing, while every Claude
*helper* matched. Walking the ancestor chain of the shell settled it:

    1789 (zsh) -> 1409 (claude-code) -> 1408 (disclaimer) -> 1227 (Claude.app)
    every one of them INVISIBLE to pgrep; pgrep -l . never lists them

**BSD pgrep never matches the invoking process or its ancestors.** It is not
a broken search in the rule-23 sense - the search works, and deliberately
excludes exactly the process we needed.

**This explains 2no.** The first attempt to launch Claude under the patch
(2026-10-21) "exited immediately, no crash report, clean exit", and the
journal put it down to the Electron single-instance lock. That was the
mechanism but not the cause: `running()` is built on `pgrep -f "^$app/"`, the
script was a descendant of the Claude app, so pgrep said not running, the
quit-and-wait was skipped entirely, and the second copy forwarded into the
lock and died. The lock was the symptom of a check that could not see.

Both tools now use `ps -axo pid=,command=` with a prefix match, which has no
such exclusion. Claude immediately reported `PATCHED pid 1227`.

### Two more fixes the audit forced

* **A KILL is not instant.** After `kill -9` the launcher checked straight
  away, saw the dying process, declared "still running" and refused to start -
  leaving boringNotch simply *gone* rather than relaunched. It now waits for
  the processes to actually disappear.
* **`relaunch` has to detach.** Relaunching the app the script is running
  inside would kill the script halfway and leave no app at all, so
  `rbgpu-app.sh relaunch` double-forks into its own session first. This is how
  Claude was restarted onto `fix` from inside Claude.

### State

    11 wrappers, all mtlswizzle.dylib + policy fix
    Claude       PATCHED  pid 1227
    boringNotch  PATCHED  pid 2349
