    Happ         UNPATCHED - left alone deliberately: it runs a `happd`
                 daemon and restarting it would drop the user's tunnel
    Safari       no wrapper possible, Apple platform binary
    uBlock Origin Lite   App Store, sandboxed, cannot read the dylib

`tools/rbgpu-app.sh verify` answers "is it really patched" from vmmap on the
live process, which is the only form of that answer worth having (rule 20),
and warns when no IOAccelerator is in the registry, because on an unarmed boot
every reading is void.

## 2nv (2026-10-22) — the seventh lever: the shared cache itself

Six levers were closed in 2ns/2nt, all on the premise that the decision is
made in a per-process copy of a driver that lives in the dyld shared cache.
That premise has one hole: **the cache is a file.**

### The dyld-root route is closed by mechanics, not policy

Metal dlopens
`/System/Library/Extensions/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver.bundle/Contents/MacOS/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver`,
which does not exist on disk (rule 22, confirmed again). Creating a patched
file there would make dyld prefer it - a "root" - and would reach every
process. It needs a loadable standalone copy of the driver, and there is none
to be had:

    dlopen(extracted copy)  ->  exit 139 (SIGSEGV)

    __TEXT        vm 0x7ffb08bf3000   file 0x08bf3000
    __DATA_CONST  vm 0x7ffb412e7b00   file 0x205bfb00   ~870 MB away
    __DATA        vm 0x7ffb434b1ca0   file 0x22789ca0
    __LINKEDIT    vm 0x7ffb80000000   file 0x239d4000   the cache's SHARED linkedit

The image's segments are scattered across the cache and its `__LINKEDIT` is
the cache's global one, shared with every other dylib. A loadable copy means
rebuilding segments contiguously, rewriting every chained fixup, and splitting
one image's symbol, export and binding tables out of a 143 MB shared
linkedit - a full dsc_extractor, whose output is for analysis and generally
does not load either. Closed.

### Patching the cache in place is mechanically open

No extraction needed. `tools/re/dyldcache.py`'s own mapper locates the
function exactly, and the first attempt at the arithmetic was wrong in an
instructive way - the offset was right and the FILE was wrong, because the
cache is split into subcaches and the main file was read instead of `.03`:

    amdMtl_HWL_DetermineSwizzleMode  vm 0x7ffb08d35a11
      subcache  dyld_shared_cache_x86_64h.03
      mapping   vm 0x7ffb00000000+0x1f2d8000 -> file offset 0
      OFFSET    0x8d35a11          30-byte prologue verified byte-for-byte

Conditions, all measured:

    Authenticated Root status      disabled
    /System/Volumes/Preboot        apfs, local, journaled - READ-WRITE
                                   (no remount of / and no new snapshot needed)
    .03                            718.6 MB, root:0755, 36 GB free for a backup
    main cache header              codeSignatureOffset 0, codeSignatureSize 0

### Why it is not done, and what it would take

The blanket LINEAR stub of 2np fits in the 30 bytes but **crashes JetBrains in
3.6 s** and would be applied to every process on the system, WindowServer
included. The policy that actually works, `fix`, needs the usage check at
descriptor +0x68|+0xb0 and the `_X` remap - roughly 60 bytes, so it needs a
code cave in the cache's `__TEXT` plus a redirect.

And the failure mode is not a bad boot, it is **no boot**: if dyld refuses the
modified cache, nothing launches, and the rollback is a Recovery boot to
restore the backup. Rule 21 was learned from a recovery procedure that had
never been tested in the situation it existed for, and this one cannot be
tested from inside a running system. So this is the user's call, not a step
to be taken on judgement.

The patch itself is small and verifiable offline: the find pattern is already
proven unique in this driver's `__text` (2lm counted it), the byte arithmetic
is checked against the live process's own memory, and the whole thing can be
written and validated against a COPY of `.03` before anything on the volume is
touched.

## 2nx (2026-10-22, boot 123) — the cryptex is immutable from a running system

2nw built and verified the shared-cache patch. Installing it does not work
from a booted macOS, and the reason is not any of the things that were
checked first.

### The install failed silently, and the script was at fault

First attempt reported "installed. REBOOT" and the live cache still held the
original prologue afterwards. The script printed that without reading
anything back - **rule 20, broken by the tool whose whole job is to apply a
patch.** What it had actually done was back up the original and write its
checksum, then stop. It could not say which step failed because it checked
none of them. Fixed: every step checked, a failed staging copy prints `df`,
the live file is re-verified after the rename, and a live file that does not
carry the patch is rolled back automatically.

With that in place the real error appeared:

    cp .../dyld_shared_cache_x86_64h.03.new : Read-only file system

### What it is not

Measured, in this order, and all of them exonerated:

    /System/Library/dyld/                    EMPTY - the cryptex copy is the
                                             only one, so not the wrong file
    Cryptexes/OS                             not a mount; same dev as Preboot
    /System/Cryptexes/OS                     a symlink to the Preboot copy
    manifests, .im4m, .dmg near the cryptex  none
    log for cryptex activity this boot       none
    statvfs(.../dyld)                        ST_RDONLY = False
    diskutil info Preboot                    Volume Read-Only: No
    df on the directory                      /dev/disk2s2, 35 GB free
    csrutil status                           Filesystem Protections: DISABLED
    csrutil authenticated-root status        disabled
    csr-active-config                        0xA43, ALLOW_UNRESTRICTED_FS SET

**And CLAUDE.md was wrong about the last one.** It has said `csr-active-config
0xA03` since the file was written; NVRAM reads `43 0a 00 00` = **0xA43**
(UNTRUSTED_KEXTS | UNRESTRICTED_FS | UNRESTRICTED_NVRAM | UNAPPROVED_KEXTS |
UNAUTHENTICATED_ROOT). Corrected.

### What it is

The dyld directory and the subcache carry the `restricted` flag. Clearing it
fails the same way:

    chflags norestricted .../dyld : Read-only file system

An explicit `mount -uw /System/Volumes/Preboot` changes nothing. **`chflags`
failing identically to `cp` is the finding** - it is not the file and not the
disk, it is the subtree, and the policy holding it is governed by none of the
switches above. Apple protects cryptex content by a mechanism that SIP's
filesystem protections, authenticated-root and the CSR bits do not reach.

### The route that remains

Recovery, where that policy is not in force. `tools/cachepatch-recovery.sh`
does it with no python and no perl, because Recovery has shipped neither
since 12.3: it finds the Preboot and Data volumes under `/Volumes` itself,
refuses unless the source matches the target in size, checks the source
carries the right 5-byte signature at block 36149 offset 2577 via `dd | od`,
copies, renames, restores the flags and then **reads the bytes back out of the
installed file** rather than announcing success. `install` and `restore` are
the same code path with different sources and different expected signatures.
Self-tested here against both files: `e9 ea ff 3b 00` for the patched one,
`55 48 89 e5 41` for the original.

Doing the install from Recovery has a property worth naming: it exercises the
exact path the rollback needs. Rule 21 was learned from a recovery procedure
that had never been run in the situation it existed for; this one will have
been run once before it is ever needed.

## 2ny (2026-10-22) — where the shared cache actually lives, and why the route ends

Four Recovery trips, each killed by an assumption of mine, and the last one
returned the answer. The dyld shared cache is **not a file on the Preboot
volume at all**.

### What the Preboot volume really holds

Mounted raw in Recovery (the user's own container, found via the backup
folder - `disk4` there, `disk2` when booted):

    Cryptexes/OS:                               empty
    Cryptexes/OS/System/Library/dyld:           empty
    Cryptexes/Incoming/OS/System/Library/dyld:  empty
    <UUID>/cryptex1/current/os.dmg              2,172,649,472 bytes
    <UUID>/cryptex1/current/os.clone.dmg        identical to it
    <UUID>/cryptex1/current/os.dmg.root_hash    229 bytes
    <UUID>/cryptex1/current/os.dmg.trustcache
    <UUID>/cryptex1/current/apticket.*.im4m     18 of them

The cache lives **inside `os.dmg`**, which macOS **grafts** into
`Cryptexes/OS` at boot. That single fact explains every symptom at once, and
all of them had looked like separate puzzles:

* the grafted tree reports the **same `st_dev` as Preboot**, which is why
  `stat` said it was a plain directory on that volume and why checking for a
  nested mount found nothing;
* it has **no `mount` entry**, so `mount | grep -i cryptex` was empty;
* it is **read-only to root**, which is the EROFS on both `cp` and `chflags`
  that no CSR bit, `Filesystem Protections: disabled` or
  `Authenticated Root: disabled` could lift, because none of them govern a
  graft;
* and it is **absent when the volume is mounted raw**, which is what sent
  three Recovery trips looking for a path that only exists after boot.

It is also, belatedly, why rule 22 is true: `AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver` has no
file on disk because the whole dyld cache is sealed inside a cryptex image.

### Why the patch cannot be delivered

    hdiutil imageinfo os.dmg   Format: UDRW, raw read/write, no checksum,
                               not compressed, not encrypted
    os.dmg.root_hash           IM4P containing `cssy` - the APFS
                               sealed-volume root hash
    apticket.x86legacyap.im4m  IM4M - an Apple-SIGNED IMG4 manifest

The image is raw and editable. The volume inside it is **sealed**, its root
hash is wrapped in an IM4P, and that hash is covered by an Apple-signed
ticket. Editing a byte inside breaks the APFS seal; recomputing the root hash
then requires re-signing the ticket with Apple's private key, which is not
something that can be done.

**This also corrects 2nw.** "The cache's signature is ad-hoc (flags 0x2) with
an empty CMS blob, so nothing is cryptographically pinned" was true of the
cache's *own* embedded signature and is still true - but that signature is
nested inside an outer, Apple-signed cryptex seal that was never looked for.
The conclusion drawn from it, that the edit was verifiable rather than
hopeful, was wrong. The patched file and its 182524 recomputed page hashes
are all perfectly valid; there is simply no way to put them where they would
be read.

### The honest end state

Seven levers were closed in 2ns/2nt because the decision is made in a
per-process copy of a driver. The eighth, the cache as a file, is closed
because the file is inside an Apple-signed sealed image. **Injection per
process is the only delivery mechanism that exists for this fix**, which
leaves Apple's own platform binaries and sandboxed App Store apps permanently
out of reach by any route this project can take.

`tools/cachepatch*.{py,sh}` and `~/rbgpu-cache-backup/` are kept: the
analysis is sound and the tooling verifies correctly, so if a future macOS
ships the cache unsealed, or the graft is ever shown not to verify, it is one
command away. Nothing on this machine was modified at any point - every
attempt failed before writing, which is the one thing that went right.

### What it cost, and the pattern

Four Recovery trips and three reboots, and every one ended on something I
asserted about this machine from general macOS knowledge instead of reading
it: `Cmd-R` on a hackintosh (OpenCore, `PollAppleHotKeys` False), the volume
name (`MACOS - Data`), Recovery's own container, and the booted-system path
on a raw volume. The config that answered the first was in
`logs/efi-backups/` the whole time. Rule 25 states it.

## 2nz (2026-10-22) — rule 22 is WRONG: Lilu is built to patch the shared cache

The user pushed back on 2ny's conclusion - "we own the entire kernel with
OpenCore and kexts and we can't apply a single screen patch?" - and was
right. 2ny closed the *file* route correctly: the cache is inside a grafted,
Apple-signed cryptex image and cannot be edited on disk. But it then treated
that as the end, which was only true because of rule 22, and **rule 22 is
wrong**.

### What Lilu actually has

Read from `third_party/Lilu/Lilu/Headers/kern_user.hpp`, which was in the
tree the whole time:

    codeSignValidatePageWrapper / codeSignValidateRangeWrapper
        -> it hooks cs_validate_page / cs_validate_range
    performPagePatch(const void *data_ptr, size_t data_size)
        "Applies page patches to the memory range - pages in kernel memory"
    patchDyldSharedCache
        "Set on init to decide on whether to use __RESTRICT or patch dyld
         shared cache"
    MapEntry { filename, length, startTEXT, endTEXT, startDATA, endDATA }
    mapAddresses(...)  "Obtains __TEXT addresses from .map files"
    venturaSharedCacheMapHaswell
        "/System/Volumes/Preboot/Cryptexes/OS/System/Library/dyld/dyld_shared_cache_x86_64h.map"

Lilu is **explicitly designed to patch dylibs inside the dyld shared cache**.
It resolves them through the cache's `.map` file and rewrites pages in kernel
memory as they pass code-signing validation. It even hard-codes this
machine's cryptex map path.

### And the map is there, with our driver in it

    $ ls -l .../dyld_shared_cache_x86_64h.map        965305 bytes, 3258 images
    $ grep -A1 AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver .../*.map
    /System/Library/Extensions/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver.bundle/Contents/MacOS/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver
              __TEXT 0x7FFB08BF3000 -> 0x7FFB090F59AE

Byte-identical to what `tools/re/dyldcache.py` derived independently. And the
plugin's existing `kRb2lmMod` already names exactly that path, with
`section = 1` and `SegmentTextText`.

**So 2nn's diagnosis was also wrong.** "A `BinaryModInfo` can only patch a
file that EXISTS" is false for a shared-cache dylib: Lilu does not open that
path, it looks the name up in the map. The *observation* stands - boot 117
really was not patched, measured from the process's own memory - but the
reason is still unknown, and "the file does not exist" was a plausible story
that fitted the evidence and was never tested against Lilu's own source.

That is the recurring error in its purest form yet: a conclusion about a
mechanism, drawn without reading the mechanism, written into the rules, and
then used to close a route for three milestones.

### What remains unknown, and what is now feasible

Unknown: whether Lilu 1.7.3's user patcher functions on macOS 15.8.1. That is
the real question 2lm/2nb/2nm failed to answer.

Feasible: the whole `fix` policy fits inside the range Lilu patches. The
driver's own `__TEXT` contains **28 padding runs of >= 200 bytes**, the
largest 1164 bytes of zeros at `0x7ffb08bf4024`, which is inside
`0x7FFB08BF3000 -> 0x7FFB090F59AE` and within rel32 of the function at
`0x7ffb08d35a11`. So two `BinaryModPatch` entries - the 163-byte cave into
that padding, and the 5-byte detour at the entry - deliver exactly what
`tools/mtlswizzle.c` does per process, but to **every process**, with no
injection, no wrapper, and no write to the cryptex. The seal is irrelevant
because the file is never touched; only the mapped pages are.

### The experiment that costs nothing

Boot A, zero risk: register **only** the cave patch, writing 163 bytes into
padding that nothing calls. Functionally inert by construction. A userspace
prober then reads those bytes out of its own mapped copy. If they are there,
Lilu's user patcher works on this macOS and the universal fix is one boot
away. If they are not, the mechanism is dead and we finally know it, instead
of inferring it a fourth time.

Boot B, only if A succeeds: add the detour.

One variable per boot, and the first one cannot break anything.

## 2ob (boot 124) — Boot A measured: Lilu registered, and nothing was patched

The inert stage ran. Every precondition checked before reading anything
(rule 15), because "not patched" has three boring explanations and only one
interesting one:

    rbgpu-boot            124, up from 123          -> armed boot
    boot-args             -rbgpumtlcave PRESENT
    loaded kext UUID      AC21E22C-EFCC-31BD-BB10-50C8A448EE3C
    built kext UUID       AC21E22C-EFCC-31BD-BB10-50C8A448EE3C  -> not stale
    Metal                 device present

And the registration itself, read out of the IORegistry rather than NVRAM
(the NVRAM diag string is truncated - `d=70` keys, about 40 survive the
write - while `ioreg` carries the whole table):

    mtlcave_section     = 1              not SectionDisabled (rule 20)
    mtlcave_npatches    = 1              cave only, detour withheld
    mtlcave_onprocload  = 0              LiluAPI::Error::NoError
    mtlcave_stage       = "cave only"

**So Lilu accepted the registration and the bytes never arrived.**
`tools/cavecheck` on the live process:

    driver: .../AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver   slide 0xb1d7000
    cave at 0x7ffb1418e5a0    in memory: 00 00 00 00 ...  expected: 55 48 89 e5 ...
    function at 0x7ffb13f0ca11 in memory: 55 48 89 e5 41  (the original prologue)
    VERDICT: NEITHER

That is the same observation 2nn made from inside a process, now with the
registration proven good and the stale-build and unarmed-boot explanations
ruled out. **2lm/2nb/2nm were not inert because of rule 22's story about
files on disk; they were inert for this reason, whatever it is.**

`mtlcave_startTEXT`/`endTEXT` both read 0, but that is **not** evidence: they
are written once, immediately after `onProcLoad`, long before Lilu would
resolve anything from the cache map. Logging a value at a moment when it
cannot yet be meaningful is the recurring error in miniature, and the line is
useless as written.

### Two searches that proved nothing, and were checked

Rule 26, twice, and both times the control saved a wrong conclusion:

* no `2oa` lines in `log show` - but **no `RBGPU` lines at all** appear
  there, and the call site sits in `RGPU::init()` between
  `rbgpu_register_mtllinear_2lm()` and `rbgpu_register_hwblt_2lp()`, which are
  known to run. The absence was the log channel, not the code.
* no Lilu lines either - and the control shows **zero kernel messages of any
  kind** reach `log show` on this machine. Kernel diagnostics here live in
  NVRAM and the IORegistry, nowhere else.

### What is still open

Registration succeeds; the patch does not land. Two candidates remain and
they need different fixes:

1. Lilu 1.7.3's user patcher does not function on macOS 15.8.1 at all - its
   `cs_validate_page` hooks never install.
2. It functions, but cannot reach shared-cache images here - the map is not
   parsed, or `SegmentTextConst` is not resolved for a cached image.

These are separable by a control that does not involve the shared cache: a
patch on an ordinary on-disk binary of our own, with a marker in `__const`
and a function in `__text`. If the marker changes, the patcher is alive and
the cache is the problem; if it does not, the patcher is dead here and no
amount of work on the cache side matters.

Cheaper first, and it needs no boot: Lilu's own SYSLOG lines are in the
kernel buffer, which `sudo dmesg` can read.

## 2oc - why Boot A patched nothing: the byte source is a FILE, and ours has none

`sudo dmesg | grep -i lilu` came back empty, which decides nothing on its own
(rule 26 - and `dmesg` needs a password I do not have, so its own emptiness
was never qualified here). The answer came instead from reading Lilu's
implementation, which settled Boot A with **no boot at all**.

`third_party/Lilu` carries only `Headers/` and `Library/`, so the user
patcher's code was never in the tree. Fetched it: `Lilu/Sources/kern_user.cpp`
(my first three guesses at the path 404'd - `Kernel/`, and tag `1.7.3`, which
**does not exist**: the newest Lilu tag is 1.7.2 while the loaded kext reports
`as.vit9696.Lilu (1.7.3)`, so this machine runs an unreleased master build.
The reading below is master's; it has not been diffed against the loaded
binary).

### The mechanism, from the source

`LiluAPI::onProcLoad` only queues a registration - the header says so
outright ("@return Error::NoError on success", where success means
*registered*). The work happens later in `UserPatcher::registerPatches`,
whose last line is the whole story:

```c
return loadFilesForPatching() && (!patchDyldSharedCache || loadDyldSharedCacheMapping())
       && loadLookups() && hookMemoryAccess();
```

`loadFilesForPatching()` runs **first**, before the cache map is ever parsed,
and it gets the bytes it searches from exactly one place:

```c
auto buf = FileIO::readFileToBuffer(binaryMod[i]->path, fileSize);
if (buf) {
    ...  // findSectionBounds, scan for patch.find, build lookupStorage
}
// no else. no SYSLOG. loadFilesForPatching returns true regardless.
```

Measured here:

```
/System/Library/Extensions/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver.bundle          exists (directory)
.../Contents/MacOS/AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver                         No such file or directory
```

So `buf` is null, the body is skipped in silence, `lookupStorage` stays
empty - and every consumer is guarded on its size: `performPagePatch` needs
`sz > 0`, `patchSharedCache` iterates `0, sz = lookupStorage.size()`. Nothing
to match, nothing patched, no message anywhere. That is `VERDICT: NEITHER`,
exactly.

Of the five `readFileToBuffer` calls in `kern_user.cpp`, four read the `.map`
and the fifth is the one above. `getSharedCachePath` and
`matchSharedCachePath` only ever *match* path strings. **Lilu never reads the
shared cache's bytes.**

### Both earlier readings were wrong, in different directions

* Rule 22 said Lilu's user patcher could never patch our driver. Its
  **conclusion was right as the code stands** - but for a reason it did not
  give, and it generalised that into "a `BinaryModInfo` can only patch a file
  that exists", which overstates it.
* 2nz withdrew rule 22 and declared the route open because Lilu parses the
  cache map. The parsing is real - `loadDyldSharedCacheMapping` reads
  `venturaSharedCacheMapHaswell`, which exists here, lists our driver, and
  gives `__TEXT 0x7FFB08BF3000 -> 0x7FFB090F59AE`, matching `dyldcache.py`.
  But the map supplies **addresses only**. 2nz never asked where the *bytes*
  come from, and concluded the route was open on half the mechanism.

Both preconditions I checked after that were fine and neither was the problem:
`isHaswell` is `cpuHasAvx2` (true on the 7735HS, so the Haswell map is the
right one); Lilu's `KernelVersion` enum knows `Sequoia = 24` and `Tahoe = 25`;
`BinaryModPatch`'s nine fields match our nine positional initialisers in
order; and `RBGPU_MTL_PATH` matches the map's line byte for byte.

### What this says about the patcher - the fork is closed, and neither arm won

2ob's two candidates were both wrong. `loadLookups()` returns `true`
unconditionally (with empty storage its loops simply do nothing), so
`hookMemoryAccess()` **is** reached. **The patcher is alive and its hooks are
installed.** It had zero patterns to look for. The planned on-disk control
binary is unnecessary - it would have measured something already known.

### The route is open after all, and better than the one we were building

For an image in the shared cache, patching does **not** go through
`performPagePatch`'s full-page `memcmp`. It goes through `patchSharedCache`,
which edits live process memory:

```c
auto place = modStart + ref->segOffs[k] + slide;        // modStart = mod->startTEXT, from the .map
orgVmMapReadUser(taskPort, place, tmp, patch.size);
if (!memcmp(tmp, patch.find, patch.size)) {             // patch.size bytes, NOT a page
    vmProtect(taskPort, place & -PAGE_SIZE, PAGE_SIZE, FALSE, RWX);
    orgVmMapWriteUser(taskPort, patch.replace, place, patch.size);
    vmProtect(... RX);
}
```

That is per-process, slide-aware, `vm_map_write_user` into the live image -
which is what 2np's trampoline does from inside the process, only done from
the kernel instead. It would therefore also reach the **Apple platform
binaries** that strip `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` and that `rbgpu-app.sh` can
never wrap.

The only thing `patchSharedCache` needs from the file is `ref->segOffs`, and
that is pure arithmetic on the file's own declared load commands:

```c
off_t segOff = vmsection - vmsegment + sectOff;         // loadFilesForPatching
```

`MachInfo::findSectionBounds` is a plain load-command walk: it takes
`vmsegment = scmd->vmaddr`, `vmsection = sect->addr`,
`sectionptr = ptr + sect->offset`, `sectionSize = sect->size`, and validates
nothing but bounds - no code signature, no LINKEDIT, no dyld info. **Lilu
never checks that the file is the real dylib.** So a small hand-built Mach-O
that merely *declares* the right geometry is a sufficient byte source, and the
addresses close exactly:

```
fn    segOff = 0x7FFB08D35A11 - 0x7FFB08BF3000 = 0x142A11
cave  segOff = 0x7FFB08FB75A0 - 0x7FFB08BF3000 = 0x3C45A0
place = startTEXT + segOff + slide  ->  FN_VM + slide,  CAVE_VM + slide
```

Two hazards found in the same read, before building anything:

* `end = start + size - patch.size` with `start < end`, so a section whose
  size **equals** `patch.size` never scans. The section must be strictly
  larger.
* `pageOff = ((vmsection + sectOff) & -PAGE_SIZE) - vmsection` is computed in
  `vm_address_t`. If `sectOff < vmsection % PAGE_SIZE` it **underflows**, and
  `lilu_os_memcpy(entry->page->p, sectionptr + pageOff, PAGE_SIZE)` then reads
  a wild kernel address. The real dylib is safe by accident (cave sectOff
  0x2F00 against `__const` at ...46A0). A stencil must keep
  `sectOff >= vmsection % PAGE_SIZE` - simplest is a page-aligned `vmsection`
  with `sectOff` shifted up by the same amount, which preserves `segOff`.

### Still unverified

`patchBinary` only reaches `patchSharedCache` when `sharedCacheSlideStored` is
true, set when the `vm_shared_region_slide` hooks fire. Those hooks are
installed by `hookMemoryAccess()`, which does run - but whether they are in
place before the first process maps the cache is not established here, and
there is no log channel on this machine to tell us (2ob). It is the same path
every Lilu shared-cache patch depends on, so it is likely fine; it is an
assumption, not a measurement, and the next boot tests it implicitly.

## 2oe - the precondition probe panicked the boot before the Apple bar

Boot with `-rbgpumtlcave` and build C05C7933/EAC5023E panicked immediately -
"not even the apple bar started to fill in". Qualified before interpreting:

```
loaded kext        EAC5023E  (so the re-install did happen)
rbgpu-boot         124, unchanged from boot A  -> this boot never armed
.panic report      none; newest is 2026-10-20  -> too early for the log
recovery           -rbgpuoff added to boot-args by hand
```

### The suspect is the instrument I added to satisfy rule 14

2od put this in `rbgpu_register_mtlcave_2oa()`, reached from `RGPU::init()`:

```c
auto *stencil = FileIO::readFileToBuffer(RBGPU_MTL_STENCIL, stencilSize);
```

`RGPU::init()` runs at **kext load, during early kernel bootstrap, before the
root filesystem is mounted**. `readFileToBuffer` goes through `vnode_open`,
which needs a root vnode that does not exist yet. The Apple progress bar
appears *after* root mount, so "before the bar" is exactly as far as a boot
gets when it dies there.

The detail that should have stopped this at writing time: **Lilu makes the
identical call, and deliberately not from here.** `loadFilesForPatching` runs
inside `registerPatches`, at user-patcher init, long after BSD is up. 2oc read
that function closely enough to quote it and still copied the call without
copying its timing.

Rule 16 in its purest form - and worse than usual, because the probe existed
only to report a precondition. It reported nothing and cost the boot.

### This boot is NOT a control, and nearly got read as one

`-rbgpuoff` is listed in `PluginConfiguration::bootargOff`, so Lilu disables
the plugin and `pluginStart() -> rgpu.init()` never runs. The machine is
therefore up with EAC5023E loaded and `-rbgpumtlcave` still in boot-args,
which looks exactly like "the suspect code ran and did not panic". It did not
run at all. The theory is untested, not refuted.

Supporting it, short of a boot: the FileIO call is the only new action on the
init path; registration itself is list-appending that 2lm and 2lp already do
safely on every boot today; and the two-mod change adds only a second
`BinaryModInfo` with `count = 0` plus a non-null callback pointer, neither of
which touches a vnode.

### Fix

The probe moves to the binary-loaded callback, which runs at exec time with a
filesystem up, and reports `mtlcave_stencil` once. The init path now has no
FileIO call at all and the "refuse to register" early return is gone with it.
UUID EAC5023E -> 0AE2AA9A.

The next boot tests both things at once: if it boots, the probe was the cause
and the cave measurement comes with it; if it panics again, the remaining new
thing is the two-mod registration and that gets bisected on its own.

## 2of - Lilu disables its own user patcher on Big Sur and newer. Route closed.

Boot 125, fully qualified before interpreting (rule 8, 15):

```
loaded kext   0AE2AA9A == built            not stale
boot-args     -rbgpumtlcave present, -rbgpuoff GONE
rbgpu-boot    125, up from 124             armed
machine       booted normally
```

**2oe is confirmed by that last line.** Removing the `FileIO` call from the
init path fixed the panic; the early-boot vnode read was the cause, as
suspected. Rule 27 stands.

`tools/cavecheck` still reports `VERDICT: NEITHER` (slide 0x14723000, cave
absent, detour absent).

### Qualifying the diag before reading it

`mtlcave_stencil` and `mtlcave_mapsrc` are absent from `RBGPUDiag`. Three
instruments were checked before that absence was allowed to mean anything:

* the log ring is 512 entries and is full of repeating `2en: BOUNDED wait`
  lines, so **no** registration-time line survives - grepping it for `2od`
  returned nothing, and so did a grep for `2lm`/`2lp`, which certainly ran.
  Broken instrument, caught by the control (rule 26).
* the diag table holds 395 of `RBGPU_MAX_DIAGS` 448 keys and the
  "DIAG TABLE FULL" warning never fired, so keys were not being dropped.
* `rbgpu_diag_set_num` calls `scheduleRefreshDiag`, and the 2en traffic keeps
  refreshes flowing, so the published table is current.

So the absence is real: **the binary-loaded callback never ran.** Our
`ProcInfo` is `MatchAny` on `"/"`, which `onPath` matches with `strstr` - it
matches every exec on the system. It fired zero times.

### The one line that explains every inert user patch since 2lm

`Configuration::getBootArguments`:

```c
isUserDisabled = checkKernelArgument(bootargUserOff) ||
    getKernelVersion() <= KernelVersion::SnowLeopard ||
    getKernelVersion() >= KernelVersion::BigSur;
```

`BigSur = 20`; this machine is `Sequoia = 24`. The third term is
unconditionally true, and it is a `||`, so **no boot-arg can switch it off**.

What that does, all of it silent:

```c
bool UserPatcher::init(...) {
    if (ADDPR(config).isUserDisabled) {
        SYSLOG_COND(ADDPR(debugEnabled), ...);   // only with -liludbgall
        return true;                             // NO kauth listener
    }
    ...
}
bool UserPatcher::registerPatches(...) {
    if (ADDPR(config).isUserDisabled) return true;   // silently
    ...
}
```

`init` returns **true**, so `performCommonInit` continues and calls
`activate()`; `registerPatches` returns **true** without reading a file,
parsing the map, or hooking anything. Every layer reports success and the
listener does not exist.

So 2lm, 2lp, 2nb, 2nm, 2oa and 2od were inert for this reason and no other.

### What I got wrong, and how

2oc read `loadFilesForPatching`, `performPagePatch`, `patchSharedCache`,
`mapAddresses`, `findSectionBounds` and `hookMemoryAccess` - six functions
deep - and concluded "the patcher is alive and its hooks are installed,
it simply had nothing to look for". **Every one of those functions is
unreachable on this OS.** The analysis of them was accurate and irrelevant.

This is the recurring error in its canonical form: reading values without
first establishing what makes them meaningful. The specific omission has a
name worth keeping - *check that a subsystem is ENABLED on this OS before
reading how it behaves*. One `grep -n isUserDisabled` would have cost
nothing and saved 2oc, 2od, 2oe, the stencil, and a panicked boot.

Rule 22 is therefore right in its original conclusion for a **third** reason,
simpler than either previous one. The 2oc mechanism (addresses from the map,
bytes from a file) is a true description of code that never executes here.

### Caveat on the source

This is master's `kern_start.cpp`. Tag 1.7.3 does not exist - the newest tag
is 1.7.2 and the loaded kext reports 1.7.3, so it is an unreleased build. The
source has not been diffed against the loaded binary; the EFI was not mounted
and that needs a password. The behavioural evidence is independent of the
source and is what carries the conclusion: a `MatchAny "/"` callback that
fires zero times in hundreds of execs means no listener exists.

### What is still possible

`patchSharedCache`'s *mechanism* is untouched by this - it is just Lilu's
code that cannot run. Every kernel symbol it uses is present in this kernel,
checked directly against `/System/Library/Kernels/kernel`:

```
_cs_validate_range _cs_validate_page _current_map _get_map_min _get_task_map
_vm_map_check_protection _vm_map_read_user _vm_map_write_user
_task_set_main_thread_qos _vm_shared_region_map_file _vm_shared_region_slide
```

and `KernelPatcher` works fine here - it is what routes the AMD functions the
accelerator fix depends on. So the write can be done by this plugin directly:
hook `_vm_shared_region_slide` for the slide, hook `_task_set_main_thread_qos`
for a per-process point with a task, then `_vm_map_read_user` to verify and
`_vm_map_write_user` to place the two patches at
`startTEXT + segOff + slide`. We already know those addresses exactly, so
none of Lilu's file-based pattern discovery is needed and **the stencil
becomes unnecessary**.

That is real kernel code on the exec path of every process, with real panic
risk, and it is a decision rather than a next step.

## 2og - place the shared-cache patch ourselves, from the kernel. Stage A.

2of closed Lilu's user patcher permanently on this OS. The *mechanism* it
would have used is still available to us, so the plugin now does it directly.

### Why this can work where a BinaryModInfo cannot

* Every kernel symbol `patchSharedCache` relies on is present here, checked
  against `/System/Library/Kernels/kernel`: `_get_task_map`,
  `_vm_map_read_user`, `_vm_map_write_user`, `_task_set_main_thread_qos`,
  `_vm_shared_region_slide`, and the rest.
* `KernelPatcher` works - it is what routes the AMD functions the accelerator
  fix depends on.
* A consequence of 2of is in our favour: `isUserDisabled` short-circuits
  **before** `hookMemoryAccess`, so Lilu never routes those functions and
  they are free to take. Rule 3 checked: zero existing routes in this plugin.
* We know the exact unslid addresses, so **none of Lilu's file-based pattern
  discovery is needed and the 2od stencil is unnecessary**.

### Shape

`-rbgpumtlkpatch` installs, from `lilu.onPatcherLoad` (the earliest point
Lilu offers - `processPatcherLoadCallbacks` runs inside `performCommonInit`
before `userPatcher.init()`, and therefore before userspace starts, which
matters because the shared region is created by the first process that needs
it; `processKext` keeps a guarded fallback):

* a hook on `_vm_shared_region_slide` that records arg0 as the slide and
  nothing else - deliberately no `rbgpu_diag_set_num` there, because that
  schedules a thread_call and this fires before the peer exists (2oe's lesson:
  do not put new machinery on a path that has to survive before the machinery
  is up);
* a hook on `_task_set_main_thread_qos` as the per-process point, giving a
  task at exec;
* `vm_protect` + `_vm_map_write_user` to place the bytes.

Stage A is deliberately almost inert: **scoped to processes named
"cavecheck"**, and it writes only the **cave** - 224 bytes into a zero run in
`__const` that nothing branches to. The detour that would make it live is
stage B. `cavecheck` is both the trigger and the verifier, which is the point.

### Checks done before booting it

* **Rule 2**, which cost a boot in 2gb: both prologues disassembled from the
  kernel. `_task_set_main_thread_qos` and `_vm_shared_region_slide` both
  begin `55 / 48 89 e5 / 41 57 / 41 56 / 41 55 / 41 54` - no rel8/rel32
  branch anywhere near the first five bytes. Safe to displace.
* **Imports.** `make plugin` does *not* run `kmutil libraries`, so the new
  undefined symbols were checked by hand: `_vm_protect`, `_proc_selfname`,
  `_memcmp`, all exported by this kernel. A fourth, Lilu's bounded `strstr`,
  was found to be a NEW import - the only other `strstr(` matches in the file
  are comments - and was removed in favour of a six-line local matcher.
  Lilu does `EXPORT` it, but every symbol resolved at load is a way for a
  boot to fail.
* **Header regeneration.** The patch site is ANCHOR bytes before the cave, so
  `gen_cavepatch.py` now emits `RBGPU_MTL_CAVE_ANCHOR` and
  `RBGPU_MTL_CAVE_RESERVED` rather than having the number hand-written
  anywhere. All four byte arrays verified **identical** to the ones already
  being compiled, so the regeneration changed nothing but the defines.
* **Slide trust.** If arg0 of `_vm_shared_region_slide` is not the slide, the
  computed address is wrong, the read-back fails to match `kRbMtlCaveFind`,
  and nothing is written. A wrong slide is therefore reported, not acted on.
  `cavecheck` prints the slide from userspace too, so the two can be compared
  in the same boot.

### What each outcome will mean

```
mtlk_hook_slide / mtlk_hook_qos   0 -> the route failed; nothing else matters
mtlk_slide                        compare against cavecheck's own slide print
mtlk_ready        0 -> a symbol or the slide was missing; nothing was touched
mtlk_match        1 -> THE result: the expected bytes really are at
                       unslid + slide, so the whole address chain is right
                  2 -> already patched;  0 -> wrong address or wrong slide
mtlk_prot_rw      0 (KERN_SUCCESS) -> a cache page can be made writable with
                       plain RW, and Lilu's CS_ENFORCEMENT surgery is not
                       needed. Non-zero -> mtlk_prot_rwx says whether RWX is
                       accepted instead.
mtlk_write        0 -> vm_map_write_user accepted it
mtlk_verify       1 -> read back from the target's own memory and correct.
                       This is the only line that proves anything (rule 20).
```

### Risk, stated plainly

The qos hook runs on **every** exec on the system. The scope check is the
first thing it does and costs a `proc_selfname` plus a substring compare, with
no VM work for any other process - but a fault inside that wrapper would
panic every exec and make the machine unbootable. The rescue is `-rbgpuoff`,
which 2of confirmed disables the plugin outright before `init()` runs.

## 2oi - THE CAVE IS IN. A kernel-placed patch, verified in a live process.

Boot 127, qualified first: built UUID 3424F78C loaded, `-rbgpumtlkpatch`
present, `rbgpu-boot` 127 (up from 126), armed.

```
mtlk_syms        = 15     all four symbols resolved
mtlk_hook_slide  = 1      routed, original non-zero
mtlk_hook_qos    = 1      routed, original non-zero
mtlk_execs       = 2049   the hook fires constantly
mtlk_slide       = 0x8209000
mtlk_map         = 1
mtlk_place       = 0x7FFB111C0570
mtlk_match       = 1
mtlk_prot_rw     = 0      KERN_SUCCESS
mtlk_write       = 0
mtlk_verify      = 1
```

and from the target's own memory, which is the only evidence that counts:

```
tools/cavecheck: slide 0x8209000, cave at 0x7ffb111c05a0
  CAVE (stage A)   PRESENT
    in memory : 55 48 89 e5 53 48 83 ec 18 48 89 d3 48 8b 45 10 ...
    expected  : 55 48 89 e5 53 48 83 ec 18 48 89 d3 48 8b 45 10 ...
```

**A patch placed from the kernel into the dyld shared cache, in a process
that was never given `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`.** Lilu's user patcher took no
part in it and cannot (rule 22).

### Four things measured here, each worth keeping

* **`proc_selfname` is the WRONG name at this hook point.** `mtlk_probe_self`
  = `launchd` while `mtlk_probe_task` = `fsck`, and on the scoped hit
  `mtlk_self` = `zsh` while `mtlk_task` = `cavecheck`. `current_proc()` is
  the *parent*; the exec'ing process is only reachable through the task
  argument, `proc_name(proc_pid(get_bsdtask_info(task)))`. The 2og scope
  matched on `proc_selfname` alone and would never have fired - and would
  have looked exactly like "the address is wrong".
* **The slide is confirmed two independent ways.** `mtlk_slide` = 0x8209000
  from arg0 of `_vm_shared_region_slide`, and `cavecheck` printed the same
  0x8209000 from `_dyld_get_image_vmaddr_slide` in userspace. Arg0 is the
  slide on Sequoia.
* **`mtlk_prot_rw = KERN_SUCCESS`: plain RW is enough.** A shared-cache page
  can be made writable with `VM_PROT_READ|VM_PROT_WRITE`. Lilu only ever
  asks for RWX and pays for it by clearing `CS_KILL|CS_HARD|CS_ENFORCEMENT`
  out of `struct proc` through a hand-rolled field scan. **We never need
  that**, so this does strictly less damage to the process than Lilu would.
* **The write is copy-on-write, per process.** Every process needs its own,
  which is why "verified somewhere" is worth nothing and the cave must be
  confirmed in *this* process before the detour goes in.

### Stage B, and the one ordering rule that makes it safe

`-rbgpumtlkfix` adds the detour. `rbgpu_mtlk_place()` now applies both sites
through one path so they cannot drift apart, and the order is the safety
property: the detour is a `jmp` into the cave, so the cave is written **and
read back** in the same process first, and a failed cave means the detour is
never written. The alternative - a detour jumping into untouched `__const`
padding - is a crash.

`rbgpumtlkscope=<substring>` retargets without a rebuild; default
`cavecheck`. `mtlk_stage` reports 1 or 2.

**Stage B will be the first time this hand-written x86 has ever executed.**
The cave was assembled by `cachepatch.py: build_cave()` and the detour by
`detour()`, and until now both have only ever been compared as bytes. So the
first target is deliberately **TextEdit**: an Apple platform binary, which
strips `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` and therefore *cannot* be fixed any other way,
has visible text to judge, and can be killed without ending the session.
A bug in the cave crashes TextEdit, not the machine.

### Also fixed here

`tools/cavecheck.m` was printing "CAVE PRESENT - Lilu's user patcher WORKS on
this macOS", which is now exactly wrong and would mislead a future session.
Both verdict strings now name the kernel-side patcher and point at `mtlk_*`.

A stale-build near miss, caught by the UUID rule: a `git stash` round-trip
used to check whether `___strlcpy_chk` was a pre-existing import left the
object files newer than the sources, so `make plugin` reported success and
produced the *previous* UUID. `efi.sh install` deletes those two objects for
exactly this reason; a bare `make plugin` does not.

## 2oj - TextEdit is not an oracle, and the cave verified before executing it

The user asked, before arming stage B, whether TextEdit rendering text
correctly *right now* was expected. It is, and it kills TextEdit as the
target.

This defect is the swizzle mode the userspace driver picks for **client
MTLTextures**. Electron and JBR hit it because they render text into plain
textures themselves. Native AppKit apps draw text through CoreGraphics into
CALayer backing stores, and 2nj measured that those surfaces reach **neither**
this chooser nor the kernel's align manager - that is Defect B. TextEdit was
never affected by this one.

The sharper point: if TextEdit never calls `DetermineSwizzleMode`, stage B
there executes the cave **zero times** and tests neither correctness nor
crash-safety. It would have been a wasted boot, and the "it still renders
fine" result would have looked like success. 2og's choice of TextEdit was
made on "Apple platform binary, cannot be reached any other way" without
asking whether it is affected at all - the recurring error again, one step
removed.

### An honest correction to the value of this work

"Reaches the Apple platform binaries that strip `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`" has
been repeated since 2oc as the prize. It is not established that **any**
platform binary is broken by *this* defect rather than by Defect B, and the
first data point - TextEdit - says it is not. What the kernel patcher
definitely buys: no per-app wrappers, no `~/Applications/<App> (GPU).app`, it
survives app updates, it needs no user action, and it reaches sandboxed App
Store apps, which cannot load an inserted dylib from a home directory at all
(rule 21). That is what the user asked for originally - "a fix for everything,
out of the box from the kext" - so the goal stands. The platform-binary claim
should stop being stated as a benefit until one is shown affected.

### The cave verified statically, before its first execution

Disassembled `kRbMtlCaveRepl[ANCHOR..ANCHOR+163]` by assembling the bytes
into an object file (no raw-binary disassembler is available here - no
capstone, no llvm-mc, and `objdump -b binary` produces nothing):

```
push rbp; mov rsp,rbp; push rbx; sub 0x18,rsp
mov  rdx,rbx                  ; rbx = the descriptor
copy 0x10/0x18/0x20(rbp) to the new stack   ; out*, bool, bool
call <trampoline>             ; the relocated original
mov  0x68(rbx),rcx ; or 0xb0(rbx),rcx       ; usage, BOTH offsets
test 0x4,cl ; jne                           ; render-target bit
xor  eax,eax                                ; non-RT -> LINEAR
cmp  0x1b,eax ; ja                          ; in-range guard
lea  0xe(rip),rcx ; movzbl (rcx,rax),eax    ; table lookup
pop rbx; pop rbp; ret
```

and the 28-byte table is exactly `nox()`: `21->5 22->6 23->6 25->9 26->10
27->10`, identity elsewhere, **Z modes 20 and 24 untouched**. No mismatches.

One thing that needed checking rather than assuming: the cave modifies
**`%eax`** and never dereferences the `out` pointer after the call, which
looks wrong against a signature whose 7th parameter is `uint &out`. It is
right: `tools/mtlswizzle.c`, the hook that demonstrably works, also ignores
`out` and ends in `return want`. The function returns the mode; `out` is
something the caller may or may not consume. The cave matches the proven
contract.

### The target that does answer something

**IntelliJ IDEA**, process name `idea`: broken unwrapped, fixed by this exact
policy through the DYLD trampoline, so it is a true oracle - and it answers
the question that actually matters, which is whether the wrappers can be
retired. Explicitly **not** Claude, which is this session's host.

## 2ok - stage B lands: cave AND detour live in a real app, nothing crashed

Boot 128. Qualified first, and the qualification is the whole story:

```
built/loaded   EE7D0B93 (stage B code ran, so not stale)
boot-args      -rbgpumtlkfix  rbgpumtlkscope=TextEdit
rbgpu-boot     128, up from 127   armed
mtlk_stage     2
mtlk_scope     "TextEdit"
```

The scope was still `TextEdit` from the 2og plan - the switch to `idea` was
never applied - so **IntelliJ was never targeted** and its text being broken
is the correct result, not a failure. Rule 15 again: read which boot-args are
actually there before interpreting anything.

What did happen, in TextEdit:

```
mtlk_self   "xpcproxy"      mtlk_task  "TextEdit"
mtlk_match     1   mtlk_prot_rw  0   mtlk_write  0   mtlk_verify   1
mtlkd_match    1   mtlkd_prot    0   mtlkd_write 0   mtlkd_verify  1
```

**Both sites placed and read back correct in a live application.** And
TextEdit is pid 441, launched this boot, still running, with no crash report
of any kind. So the detour is live in a real process and the machine and the
app are both fine.

A third confirmation of the naming finding, from a different angle:
`mtlk_self` is `xpcproxy` this time, not `zsh` or `launchd` - whatever
`current_proc()` is at that hook point, it is never the process being
exec'd. Only `proc_name(proc_pid(get_bsdtask_info(task)))` is.

### What this does and does not prove

Proved: the kernel-side patcher can place a 224-byte cave and a 5-byte detour
into the dyld shared cache of an arbitrary process, per-process and
copy-on-write, with plain RW protection, and the process keeps running.

**Not** proved: that the cave's machine code ever executed. 2oj established
that TextEdit draws text through CoreGraphics into CALayer backing stores and
so may never call `DetermineSwizzleMode` at all. "TextEdit did not crash" is
therefore consistent with both "the cave is correct" and "the cave was never
called". That distinction is exactly what the next boot settles, because
IntelliJ definitely calls it.

### Also corrected

CLAUDE.md's status paragraph still read "first target TextEdit, an Apple
platform binary that no other route can reach", which 2oj already withdrew.
Fixed there too, not just in the journal.

## 2ol - THE UNIVERSAL FIX WORKS. Unwrapped IntelliJ, text correct, from the kext.

Boot 129, `rbgpumtlkscope=idea`, `-rbgpumtlkfix`. The user launched
IntelliJ IDEA normally - no `env -u`, no `(GPU)` wrapper - and **the text is
correct**.

Qualified before being believed, because this is the claim the whole project
has been reaching for:

```
pid 413    /Applications/IntelliJ IDEA.app/Contents/MacOS/idea   the plain bundle
ps eww     no DYLD_* in its environment AT ALL                   no injection
wrapper    no ~/Applications/IntelliJ IDEA (GPU).app instance running
scope      "idea"     mtlk_cavehits 4     mtlkd_verify 1
boot       129, up from 128, armed
```

and the obvious confounds ruled out: `-rbgpulinear` and `-rbgpumtllinear` were
both set in boots 124-128, during which unwrapped IntelliJ was broken every
time, so neither explains the change. The only new variable is
`-rbgpumtlkfix`.

**This is the first time the hand-written cave has executed**, and it produced
the right answer. 2oj's static verification of it - usage OR'd from +0x68 and
+0xb0, render-target bit test, non-RT to LINEAR, 28-byte `nox()` table with Z
modes untouched - is now confirmed dynamically.

### An instrument mistake worth recording, caught in the same breath

My own verification printed "wrapper matches: 3", which looked like three
wrapped IntelliJ processes running and would have invalidated the result.
They were **my own `grep` command lines**, visible in `ps` output because the
pattern `(GPU)` appears in the shell command that searches for it. Rule 23's
cousin: `ps` shows the searcher alongside the searched. Also in the same
check, `awk '$2=="idea"'` against `ps -axo comm=` silently matched nothing,
because `comm=` prints the **full path**, not the basename - so the
DYLD-environment test did not run at all and reported nothing, which looked
like a pass. Both were caught only by printing the raw rows instead of a
count.

### What is now true

The fix is delivered **by the kext**, into any process named by
`rbgpumtlkscope`, with no wrapper, no injected dylib, no user action, and no
change to the app bundle. It survives app updates, because nothing about the
app is touched. The route 2ns declared closed - "there is NO global fix, the
decision is made in the userspace driver, one copy per process" - was right
about the *place* and wrong about the reach, in exactly the way 2lg was.

### What is next, and the risk in it

The scope is still a single substring. Widening it is the remaining work, and
it is not free: blanket LINEAR **crashes** JBR (2np), and while the `fix`
policy is strictly gentler, it has now been proven on exactly one application.
Widening should go app by app, or by a list, and the mechanism should keep a
way to exclude a process that misbehaves. The per-app wrappers in
`tools/rbgpu-app.sh` can start being retired, but not before the apps they
cover are each confirmed under the kernel path.

Defect B - the CoreAnimation backing store - is untouched by any of this and
remains open.

## 2om - the universal fix: every process, with an escape hatch

2ol proved one app. This makes it general.

### What changed

* `rbgpumtlkscope` is now a **comma-separated list**, and `*` matches every
  process. The default stays `cavecheck`: going universal has to be an
  explicit act, never something a stale boot-arg does by accident.
* `rbgpumtlkexclude=a,b` is checked **first**, so it always wins. That is the
  escape hatch for an app that misbehaves under the `fix` policy - settable
  over SSH with `efi.sh bootarg` and a reboot, no rebuild.
* **Reporting is throttled.** The detailed per-site keys are written for the
  first 8 patches only. `rbgpu_diag_set_num` takes a lock and scans ~400 keys,
  and in universal mode this runs on every exec on the system - about 2000 per
  boot (`mtlk_execs` = 2049, 2081 in previous boots). Unthrottled it would
  have been the slowest thing in the plugin, which is how 2fa/2ez turned a
  publisher into something indistinguishable from a wedge. Two counters are
  always maintained: `mtlk_patched` and `mtlk_failed`.
* **Scope now prefers the task name.** 2oi/2ok measured `proc_selfname` as
  `launchd`, `zsh` and `xpcproxy` in three different boots, so matching on it
  drags in children of a matched process - boot 129 patched `jspawnhelper`
  for exactly that reason. `selfname` is now only a fallback for when
  `get_bsdtask_info` yields nothing.
* Removed `rbgpu_mtlk_name_matches`, now dead, in the same change (rule 6).

### Leftover (GPU) wrappers are safe, and the reason is worth keeping

A wrapper and the kernel patch in the same process looked dangerous: our
detour is placed at exec, *before* dyld runs, so `mtlswizzle` would copy an
already-patched prologue into its trampoline, and the `jmp rel32` inside it
would be relocated and point somewhere wrong - rule 2's hazard exactly.

It cannot happen. `mtlswizzle` searches for a **32-byte** pattern and refuses
unless it finds exactly one match (2lm needed 32 bytes for uniqueness: 14
bytes gave 2099 hits). After our patch:

```
occurrences of the 32-byte kFind in kRbMtlCaveRepl : 0
detour changes the first 5 bytes: 55 48 89 e5 41 -> e9 8a 1b 28 00
```

The function site no longer matches because the first five bytes changed, and
the cave's trampoline holds only **30** original bytes - two short of the
pattern. So `hits == 0`, `mtlswizzle` prints REFUSING and does nothing. The
kernel patch stands and the wrapper is inert. This is luck rather than design,
and it only holds while the pattern is longer than the trampoline's copy - so
do not shorten `kFind` below 31 bytes.

A first check of this was wrong and caught itself: a hand-typed 16-byte
prefix of `kFind` reported 1 occurrence inside the cave, which would have
meant the wrapper patches our trampoline. Parsing the real 32-byte array out
of `mtlswizzle.c` instead of retyping it gave 0. Rule 26 again - the
instrument was a hand-typed constant.

### Recommended first universal boot

`rbgpumtlkscope=*` with `rbgpumtlkexclude=WindowServer,loginwindow`.
WindowServer is the one process whose failure costs the GUI, and 2nj already
measured that its CoreAnimation surfaces reach neither this chooser nor the
kernel align manager - so excluding it gives up almost nothing and removes
the worst outcome. Drop the exclusion in a later boot if it is worth testing.

### Cost, stated honestly

Patching every process writes two copy-on-write pages per process (one for
`__text`, one for `__const`), so a universal boot costs roughly 8 KB of
private memory per process that execs. Across ~2000 execs that is a few tens
of MB transiently, most of it freed as short-lived processes exit. The
per-exec work is two reads, two protects, two writes and two read-backs.

## 2on - UNIVERSAL. Every app, Safari included, no wrappers, from the kext.

Boot 130, `-rbgpumtlkfix`, `rbgpumtlkscope=*`,
`rbgpumtlkexclude=WindowServer,loginwindow`.

```
mtlk_execs    2049
mtlk_patched  2045
mtlk_failed      8
mtlk_cavehits 2050
mtlk_stage       2
Safari        pid 457, no DYLD_* in its environment
```

The user reports **every single app correct, Safari included, and all images
loading**. Nothing is wrapped, nothing is injected, no app bundle is
modified.

### This settles the question 2oj withdrew

2oj struck out "reaches the Apple platform binaries that strip
`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`" because TextEdit was evidence *against* it and
nothing was evidence *for* it. **Safari answers it:** it is a platform
binary, it was affected by this defect, and the kernel path fixes it.
The withdrawal was right at the time - there was no evidence - and the claim
is now re-established on a measurement instead of an assumption. TextEdit
remains correctly explained: it was never affected, because AppKit text does
not reach this chooser (2oj).

### The defect was never only about text

"All pictures load" is new. Images were affected too, which means the mis-set
swizzle mode damaged ordinary sampled textures and not just the surfaces
applications render glyphs into. Every milestone from 2lg to 2ol called this
"the text defect" because text is where it was first *noticed*; the name was
always narrower than the fault.

### Two honest caveats on the numbers

* **The counters are racy by construction.** `g_mtlkPatched` and
  `g_mtlkFailed` are plain `uint64_t` increments on a path that runs
  concurrently on every exec, with no atomics, so `2045 + 8 = 2053` against
  `cavehits = 2050` does not balance and is not meant to. They are
  magnitude indicators, not an audit. Making them atomic would be easy and
  is not worth putting more work on that path.
* `mtlk_exclude` printed as `"WindowServer` with the rest missing. That is my
  own reader - `tr ',' '\n'` splits the IORegistry dump on commas, and the
  value legitimately contains one. The stored value is correct. Rule 26: the
  instrument again, this time only cosmetically.

The 8 failures are almost certainly execs that happened before
`_vm_shared_region_slide` fired, which take the `mtlk_ready = 0` path and
touch nothing. That is a guess, not a measurement, and it is cheap to confirm
later by reporting the reason per failure.

### What this retires

`tools/rbgpu-app.sh` and the whole `~/Applications/<App> (GPU).app` scheme are
now obsolete: the kext covers every process, survives app updates, needs no
user action, and reaches sandboxed App Store apps and platform binaries that
the wrapper scheme could never touch (rule 21, 2ns). Leftover wrappers are
harmless (2om), so they can be removed at leisure rather than urgently.

Also worth re-testing now, separately and one at a time: `-rbgpulinear` and
`-rbgpumtllinear` are both still in boot-args. The first predates all of this
and was credited with ~80 % of the widget/Dock artifacts (boot 104); the
second is provably inert (rule 22). Neither has been evaluated against a
working universal fix, and `-rbgpulinear` in particular is a *kernel* forcing
of the same decision this patch now makes correctly in userspace, so it may
now be redundant or actively harmful.

### Still open

Defect B - the CoreAnimation layer backing store, rearranged in about half of
allocations (2na, `tools/screenprobe.sh`) - is a different path (2nj) and
nothing here should be assumed to have touched it. It needs its own run of
`screenprobe.sh` to say anything.

## 2oo - both halves on by default. The desktop needs the kernel force too.

Boot 131: `-rbgpulinear` and `-rbgpumtllinear` both removed,
`rbgpumtlkexclude` empty - so **WindowServer and loginwindow were patched for
the first time**. `mtlk_patched = 2195`, `mtlk_failed = 10`, capture in
`logs/20261022-222826-plugin`.

Two results, one good and one a regression.

**WindowServer is safe to patch.** The machine booted, the GUI came up, and
the exclusion I had recommended turns out not to be needed. That removes the
last special case from universal mode.

**The userspace fix alone is NOT a stable desktop.** With `-rbgpulinear` gone,
apps came up correct and then went wrong again after idle or a tab switch, and
Terminal and other native apps were broken regardless. That is consistent with
everything measured before: the kernel-side force and the userspace chooser
are two **different** paths, and surfaces reallocated later - or belonging to
native AppKit apps, which never reach the chooser at all (2oj) - are only
covered by the kernel one.

### So both are now ON BY DEFAULT, no boot-arg, no setup

* The linear force: on unless `-rbgpunolinear`. `-rbgpulinear` is no longer
  read anywhere in the plugin - it is the default behaviour now, and the arg
  is simply ignored if left in boot-args.
* The kernel-side patcher: on unless `-rbgpumtlkoff`, stage B, scope `*`.
  `-rbgpumtlkpatch` still selects the inert cave-only stage, and
  `rbgpumtlkscope` / `rbgpumtlkexclude` still override.

This is safe to default because the patcher **fails safe by construction**:
every site is read back and compared against the expected bytes before
anything is written, so if an OS update moves the driver the comparison fails
and nothing is patched at all. `-rbgpuoff` remains the blunt rescue (rule 27).

### 2mm's suspicion of -rbgpulinear is retired, and explained

2mm filed `-rbgpulinear` as a *suspect* in the defect, reasoning that it makes
the kernel compute a linear layout while the userspace driver still lays the
surface out in 64 KB tiles - so the two disagree and every geometry whose
tiled footprint exceeds its pixel bytes renders wrong. That was right, and the
universal fix removes the disagreement: userspace now returns LINEAR for
non-render-targets too, so both sides agree.

Stated as a hypothesis, not a result: the render targets userspace deliberately
keeps **tiled** (mapped off the `_X` family) are still computed linear by this
force, and nothing yet explains why *that* pair does not also disagree. It
works; why it works is not established, which is the same honest gap 2nr/2ns
left around the `_X` family itself.

### A latent bug found while making the change

`g_rb_2ld_on` was initialised lazily inside `hooked_swizmode_2la` but **read**
by `hooked_surfinfo_2lf`. If the latter ran first, it saw 0 - neither 1 nor 2 -
and the force silently did not apply. It is now resolved once through
`rbgpu_2ld_state()`, callable from either hook, and reported as
`linear_force`. Whether this ever actually happened is unknown; the ordering
was never guaranteed.

### Still not measured

`tools/screenprobe.sh` has not been run since the universal fix - the newest
screenprobe logs are from 10:05 this morning, long before 2on. **Defect B's
status is unknown**, and the "goes wrong after idle" symptom above is
suspiciously close to a backing-store reallocation, so it may well be Defect B
rather than a third thing. That is the next measurement, and it should be run
on a boot with this build, where the config is stable.

## 2op - BOOT 132: flawless desktop from the defaults, and DEFECT B IS GONE

Boot 132, build `A0DD3CA4-4ECD-3EAA-8C1E-1DF8F7BEB768`, the 2oo default-on
build. The user's words: *"everything is flawless... not a single artifact or
even an off pixel... it's perfect"*, and `tools/screenprobe.sh` came back
**CLEAN on every test**.

### What this boot actually tested - the defaults, not the args

Boot-args at install (`logs/efi-backups/20261023-000431-install/config.plist`)
still carry `-rbgpumtlcave -rbgpumtlkfix rbgpumtlkscope=*`, so the honest
question is whether anything ran from a boot-arg rather than from 2oo's new
default. Checked against the built binary rather than assumed:

```
$ grep -n 'checkKernelArgument("-rbgpumtlkfix")' src/plugin/kern_start.cpp
  none - the arg is not read
$ strings build/out/.../RembrandtGPU | grep -E 'rbgpumtlk|rbgpu.*linear'
  -rbgpumtlkoff  -rbgpumtlkpatch  -rbgpunolinear  rbgpumtlkexclude  rbgpumtlkscope
```

`-rbgpumtlkfix` and `-rbgpulinear` survive **only inside log-message text**;
neither is read anywhere. So:

* **The linear force ran from its default.** `-rbgpulinear` was already out of
  boot-args at boot 131 and is now unread; `-rbgpunolinear` is absent. PROVEN.
* **The patcher ran from its default enable and its default stage.** The arg
  that used to enable it is dead text, and `-rbgpumtlkpatch` is absent, so
  stage B came from the default. PROVEN.
* **The scope string came from `rbgpumtlkscope=*`**, not from the default. The
  default is also `*`, so the resulting state is identical, but the default
  scope string itself is still untested on hardware. A boot with that arg
  removed would close it; nothing depends on it.

### Defect B no longer reproduces - with the control this time

`screenprobe.sh` ran `refresh` x4, repeats 4: **32 of 32 captures CLEAN**, row
jumps 0 and column jumps 0 in every one, CPU window and GPU window alike
(`logs/20261023-000923-screenprobe/report.txt`).

Rule 26 says a clean instrument is not evidence of absence until it has been
checked against a case known to be present, and texprobe has already burned
us by being clean at baseline (0/12). So the same four `refresh` blocks were
pulled out of the two earlier runs that used them, broken down per block:

| run | instrument | scrambled captures |
|---|---|---|
| `20261022-013727` | refresh x4 | **20 / 32** |
| `20261022-015825` | refresh x4 | **18 / 32** |
| `20261023-000923` | refresh x4 | **0 / 32** |

And across all 28 earlier screenprobe runs, every single one that produced a
report had `cpu SCRAMBLED` captures - the three immediately before the fix
(`direct`, 10:01-10:05 on 10-22) were **100 % scrambled, GPU window included**.
The probe was never clean here before tonight. The negative result is real.

### An independent, in-process proof the detour is live

screenprobe's own `reportMetalDriverPatch` walks its `_dyld_image` list and
searches the **loaded** `AMDRadeonX6000MTLDriver` `__TEXT` for the 32-byte
original prologue of `amdMtl_HWL_DetermineSwizzleMode`:

```
10-22 10:01 / 10:05  (14 launches)  original prologue present 1x  -> NOT PATCHED
10-23 00:09          ( 4 launches)  original prologue present 0x  -> patched
```

The prologue is **gone from screenprobe's own address space**. screenprobe is
a plain Swift binary launched from a shell script that nothing special-cased,
so this is the universal fix verified a third independent way - from inside an
ordinary process, by code that predates the kext patcher and knows nothing
about it.

It also confirms 2om's "a leftover `(GPU)` wrapper is a safe no-op" from the
other direction: the same 32-byte search that `mtlswizzle` uses to decide
whether to patch now finds **0** matches, which is exactly why it refuses.

**One instrument bug fixed, not reasoned around.** That reading printed
`INCONCLUSIVE`, because the verdict was written when there were only two
possible readings - prologue intact, or mtllinear's 14-byte constant stub in
its place. The kext's 5-byte detour leaves *neither* pattern findable (the
cave's trampoline holds only the 30 displaced bytes, two short of 32), so the
success case fell into the "don't know" branch and read like a failure.
`tools/screenprobe.swift` now distinguishes all three and names the kext
detour explicitly.

### What this closes

* **Defect B** - the CoreAnimation layer backing store that came out
  rearranged in about half of allocations, open since 2nj/2na and the last
  named rendering defect. It does not reproduce. 2on's warning not to assume
  the universal fix touched it was the right caution and the measurement has
  now answered it the other way.
* **The "wrong after idle or a tab switch" symptom** of boot 131 was Defect B,
  or at least shares its cause: it is gone on the same boot that cleans up
  screenprobe, and the kernel linear force is what covers it. No third defect
  needs to be hypothesised.

### What is still open, and must not be quietly dropped

* **WHY the `_X` swizzle family is wrong on this chip.** Unchanged since 2ns.
  gbAddrConfig reads 0x242 and agrees with the hardware; 2na's XOR-linear bit
  matrix still points at the `_X` XOR term and nothing has explained it. The
  fix is a policy that works, not an understanding.
* **Why the render targets the policy keeps TILED do not disagree** with the
  kernel's linear computation, when that disagreement is precisely 2oo's
  explanation for why the force is needed at all. Both halves being on cannot
  be the whole story, and this is the loose thread.
* **The display half has never started** (§4) - still the boot framebuffer.

### The cleanup, same milestone

Rule 6 - when a fix moves upstream, remove the downstream patch it replaces -
applied to everything the universal fix made dead.

**Deleted from `src/plugin/kern_start.cpp` (~590 lines):** the 2lm userspace
force (`-rbgpumtllinear`), the 2lp hardware-blit force (`-rbgpuhwblt`), and
the whole 2oa/2oc/2od shared-cache attempt (`-rbgpumtlcave`, `-rbgpumtlfix`),
including `kRb2lmMod`, `kRb2lpMod`, the contiguous `kRbMods[2]` array, the
stencil probe `rbgpu_mtlcave_binary_loaded`, `rbgpu_mtlcave_mapped_mod` and
the three registrars called from `RGPU::init()`. Every one of them was a Lilu
`BinaryModInfo`, and Lilu's user patcher cannot run on this OS (rule 22), so
all of it reported success and did nothing.

**Kept, deliberately:** `#include "rbgpu_mtlcave.h"` and all four byte arrays
- `kRbMtlCaveFind/Repl` and `kRbMtlFnFind/Repl` are what the kernel-side
patcher compares and writes. Only the Lilu `BinaryModPatch` wrappers around
them went.

**Deleted tools:** `tools/gen_stencil.py` (2og: the kext knows the unslid
addresses, so no byte source on disk is needed), `tools/rbgpu-app.sh` and
`tools/mtllinear-app.sh` (the `(GPU)` wrapper machinery; all 11 wrappers were
removed in 2on). The `stencil` Makefile target went with them.

**Kept, with the reason, so this is not re-litigated:**

| kept | why |
|---|---|
| `tools/cachepatch.py` | a live dependency - `gen_cavepatch.py` imports it |
| `cachepatch.sh`, `cachepatch-recovery.sh`, `docs/CACHE-RECOVERY.md` | the *undo* for a cache install. An undo is worth keeping even for something rule 24 says cannot succeed |
| `tools/iosurftex-launchd.sh` | already neutered to recovery-only; it is the undo for the 2mq disaster that needed a reboot |
| `tools/mtllinear.c` | still a live option of `screenprobe.sh` (`MTLLINEAR=1`) |

**Verified, not assumed:**

* `make plugin` from a clean object dir: **0 errors, 41 warnings** - the same
  count as before the deletion, so no new diagnostic and nothing left unused.
* UUID moved `A0DD3CA4` -> `29E0049F`.
* The four dead arg strings are **absent** from the binary; the live ones
  (`-rbgpumtlkoff`, `-rbgpumtlkpatch`, `-rbgpunolinear`, `rbgpumtlkscope`,
  `rbgpumtlkexclude`) are all present.
* `gen_cavepatch.py` re-run after losing its `gen_stencil.py` pointer
  reproduces `src/plugin/rbgpu_mtlcave.h` **byte-identical**.
* `make kext`: `hosttest: all passed`. `make tools`: every target still builds,
  no dangling rule.

A side effect worth having: the removed `rbgpu_diag_set_num` keys
(`mtllinear_section`, `mtllinear_procs`, `hwblt_section`, `hwblt_scope`,
`hwblt_onprocload`, `mtlcave_section`, `mtlcave_startTEXT`, `mtlcave_endTEXT`)
free slots in the diag table, which §6 records as full at `d=73`.

**This is behaviour-neutral by construction and unverified on hardware.** The
installed build is still `A0DD3CA4`, which is the one that produced the
flawless boot 132. `29E0049F` should behave identically - the deleted code
could not execute - but "could not execute" is a reading of Lilu's source, not
a measurement of this build, so it owes one boot before that is stated as
fact.

## 2oq - the display half, surveyed statically: macOS HAS NO DCN 3.1.2, and it does not matter

All of this is read-only - no boot, no load, no write. Four findings, in the
order they change the plan.

### 1. There is no DCN 3.1.2 code anywhere in macOS

Apple's DAL is real AMD display-core source compiled into
`AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer`, from `ampc/SunburstE/dal/...`. Its compiled
directories top out at **DCN 3.0 / 3.0.2**:

```
dal/dc/dcn10  dcn20  dcn21  dcn30  dcn302
dal/dc/dml/dcn20  dcn21  dcn30
dal/dc/clk_mgr/dce100  dce110  dcn10(rv1)  dcn21(rn)
```

Rule 26 - a search is an instrument - so the pattern was checked against a
case known to be present before the absence was believed:

| pattern | hits |
|---|---|
| `dcn30` (control) | **58** |
| `dcn31`, `dcn312`, `dcn_3_1`, `vba_31` | 0 |
| `yellow_carp`, `yellowcarp`, `rembrandt`, `3_1_2` | 0 |

Zero in `AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer`, and zero in `AMDSupport`,
`AMDRadeonX6000`, `AMDFramebuffer` and `AMDRadeonX6800HWLibs` too - none of
which carries a DAL at all. **This chip is DCN 3.1.2 (DMU 3.1.3). Apple's
newest is 3.0.2.** There is no code here to coax, which is the opposite of the
accelerator half, where GC 10.3.0 paths drove GC 10.3.3 once `vram_base_offset`
was right.

Note `clk_mgr/dcn21/rn_clk_mgr` - Renoir, an APU. Apple does have one APU
display path, two DCN generations too old.

### 2. §4's blocking prerequisite is dead - the linkability worry was unfounded

`AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer.kext`'s `OSBundleLibraries` are **all public KPIs**:
AppleGraphicsDeviceControl, IOACPIFamily, IOGraphicsFamily, IOPCIFamily and
the `kpi.*` set. Nothing private, nothing unlinkable. `OSBundleRequired` is
`Safe Boot`. And Apple's own kext *imports* `IOFramebuffer` symbols from
IOGraphicsFamily - `getVBLTime`, `moveCursor`, `showCursor`, 66 in all - so
`IOFramebuffer` is an exported class we can subclass from our own kext.

The exact personality that would have to accept `0x16811002`:

```
AMDRadeonNavi21Controller  IOClass AMDRadeonX6000_AmdRadeonControllerNavi21
                           IOProviderClass IOPCIDevice   (not AtiFbStub)
                           IOMatchCategory ATIFramebuffer  IOProbeScore 1000
AMDGPUWrangler             IOClass AMDRadeonX6000_AmdGpuWrangler
                           IOProviderClass IOPCIDevice
                           IOMatchCategory IOFramebuffer   IOProbeScore 60000
```

Both match `IOPCIDevice` directly, in **different** match categories, and
neither lists `0x1681`. **But finding 1 makes this route pointless**: even a
matching personality would instantiate a Navi 21 controller whose DAL has no
DCN 3.1.2 resource pool, hwseq, DML or clk_mgr. It would match and then fail,
or worse, program a 3.0 register layout into a 3.1.2 chip.

Also measured: `AMDRadeonX6000Framebuffer` is **not loaded** (`kextstat` lists
AMDSupport, X6000HWServices, X6000 and X6800HWLibs; not it), so its
OSMetaClasses are not registered and a personality naming that IOClass would
have nothing to instantiate until the kext itself is loaded.

### 3. What the desktop is actually running on, and why animations are poor

```
.Display_boot  <class IONDRVFramebuffer>
  IOFBConfig = { "IOFB0Hz" = Yes, "IOFBModes" = ( ONE mode: 0x780 x 0x438 ) }
  IOFBMemorySize = 8294400          (1920*1080*4)
  no vblank, flip, or refresh property of any kind
```

`system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType` prints a resolution and **no refresh
rate**. `IOFB0Hz = Yes` is IOKit's marker for a framebuffer with no refresh
clock, and there is exactly one mode, taken from firmware.

So the two things the user asked for have **one** cause: there is no display
driver at all, only the generic NDRV boot framebuffer. No vblank means
WindowServer cannot pace to the panel and animates off a timer; one fixed mode
means no resolution or refresh change; every present is a copy into the
firmware's buffer rather than a flip. The 7 MB in About This Mac is the same
fact (2lj recorded it as cosmetic, and it is, but it is cosmetic *because* this
is the boot framebuffer).

### 4. The hardware is ALREADY programmed and scanning out

From `logs/20261020-175624-plugin/pci.txt`, a level-2 probe this project
already took:

```
OTG0_CONTROL    0x00011201     bit0 OTG_MASTER_EN = 1   -> LIVE
OTG1..3_CONTROL 0x00000300     bit0 = 0                 -> off
OTG4/5_CONTROL  0x00000000                              -> absent (4 pipes)
DCHUBP_CNTL0    0x300f1002     distinct from 1/2/3      -> HUBP0 is the feeder
DCHUBP_CNTL1..3 0x000f101b/2b/3b
DMCUB firmware  4.0.15.47 running (4.0.21.71 on ROM)    -> DMUB is UP
```

The firmware brought DCN 3.1.2 up, OTG0 is running, HUBP0 is feeding it, the
DMCUB is loaded, and 1920x1080 is on the panel right now. **Nothing needs to
bring DCN up.** `src/common/rb_regs.h` already carries OTG0-3
CONTROL/H_TOTAL/V_TOTAL and HUBP0-3 SURFACE_CONFIG/PRIMARY_ADDR - precisely
the registers this needs.

### The plan this produces

Not "implement DCN 3.1.2" (tens of thousands of lines, and Linux's dcn31 is
the only reference), and not "make Apple's DCN 3.0 DAL drive a 3.1.2 chip"
(finding 1: the offsets, DML, clk_mgr and DMUB ABI all differ). Instead,
**adopt the pipe the firmware is already running**:

| step | what | writes DCN? |
|---|---|---|
| a | read `OTG0_H_TOTAL`/`V_TOTAL` + pixel clock -> the real timing | no |
| b | our own `IOFramebuffer` subclass reporting that timing and the firmware buffer, so macOS stops saying 0 Hz | no |
| c | enable and handle OTG0's vertical interrupt -> a real vsync for WindowServer | **yes** |
| d | write `HUBP0_PRIMARY_SURFACE_ADDRESS` at vblank -> tear-free page flip | **yes** |

Steps (a) and (b) are inside the probe's existing hardware rules. **Steps (c)
and (d) are not**: `rb_probe.c` permits no writes except `MM_INDEX`/
`MM_INDEX_HI`, and these are writes to a live display pipe. That is the user's
decision, like an SMU message group, and it carries a specific hazard worth
saying out loud - a wrong OTG or HUBP write **blanks the panel**, and rule 12
records that a user rebooting a black screen is indistinguishable from a hang.
Steps (a)/(b) also will **not** fix animations on their own; only (c) will.

Honest scope: the rendering half is finished, and the accelerator was the hard
part. The display half is a new subsystem rather than a remaining 10 %, but
finding 4 makes its first useful milestone - a real framebuffer with a real
vblank - much smaller than finding 1 alone would suggest. Mode setting,
external displays, brightness, DSC and PSR are all beyond it and all need the
DCN 3.1.2 code that does not exist here.

### Step (a)'s instrument, built the same day

The display plan's step (a) - get the real timing - needed registers the probe
did not have. Fetched `dcn_3_1_2_offset.h` and `_sh_mask.h` from
torvalds/linux master (`734bef54`), and the first thing they did was **confirm
the three DCN offsets already in `rb_regs.h`**: `regOTG0_OTG_H_TOTAL` 0x1b2a,
`regOTG0_OTG_V_TOTAL` 0x1b2f, `regOTG0_OTG_CONTROL` 0x1b41, all `BASE_IDX 2`,
exact matches. The headers are not copied into the tree (1.5 MB and 6.5 MB,
per UPSTREAM.md's existing policy); all eleven new offsets are tabulated there
with their Linux names.

**The refresh rate needed a different measurement than I first reached for.**
H_TOTAL and V_TOTAL cannot give it - that needs the pixel clock, which sits
behind the DCCG dividers and DISPCLK. `OTG0_OTG_STATUS_FRAME_COUNT` can, and
is read-only.

My first design was to count frames in a fixed window inside `rb_probe.c`.
Two things were wrong with it, and both are worth recording because the fix
was a better design rather than a patch:
