`csr-active-config` is **0xA43**, which decodes as UNTRUSTED_KEXTS(0x1) +
UNRESTRICTED_FS(0x2) + UNRESTRICTED_NVRAM(0x40) + UNAPPROVED_KEXTS(0x200) +
UNAUTHENTICATED_ROOT(0x800). **`CSR_ALLOW_UNRESTRICTED_DTRACE` (0x20) is
clear**, so DTrace's pid provider on an Apple binary is unavailable - which
would otherwise have been the ideal instrument, tracing
`CGXGLDisplayDeviceAccelerator`'s return in WindowServer without stopping it.
Do not spend a round trip proposing it. `CSR_ALLOW_TASK_FOR_PID` (0x4) is also
clear, but root task access evidently works, since `sample` succeeded in 2qd.

That leaves two, both the user's call:

- **a one-shot `lldb -p 162 -b` batch read** of `[0x7ff843c9ecdc]`,
  `[0x7ff843ca08b0]`, `[0x7ff843c9ecd8]` and the device's `0x160->0x5c`, then
  `detach`. Cheap and read-only, **but it stops WindowServer while attached**,
  so the desktop freezes for the duration and a wedged debugger means a hard
  reboot.
- **the kext**, reading the value from inside the process that owns the
  display. Larger, and a mistake there is a black screen.

## 2qf — the contradiction was MINE: the two readings are 4 hours and a display sleep apart

No new measurement. 2qe's "flat contradiction" dissolves on a timestamp, and
the mechanism it points at is a real candidate root cause.

### The error

| reading | when | value |
|---|---|---|
| `os_state` dump, `priv.accelerator` | **15:32:09** | **0x14b23** |
| `sample`, `render_update` -> compositor | **19:41:54** | **CompositorSW** |

**Four hours and nine minutes apart.** I treated the first as describing the
state of the second and called the result impossible. Rule 28 says to
attribute every log line to a boot by timestamp *and* pid; this is the same
error one level up - attributing a *field* reading to a moment it does not
describe. The boot is the same (149, booted 15:25:31), which is exactly what
made it feel safe.

And the gap is not quiet:

```
15:25:31  boot
15:32:09  os_state dump                       <- PRE-sleep
15:44:42  kernel: PMRD: Removed IODisplayWrangler from idle sleep preventers
15:44:42  UniversalControl: === Display Sleep ===
15:58:32  kernel: PMRD: power clamped IODisplayWrangler, ps 4->0
17:21:45  kernel: PMRD: power clamp removed, ps 4
19:41:54  sample                              <- POST sleep/wake
```

### The mechanism this points at, and it is a known shape

`mpPriv->accelerator` has exactly one writer,
`CoreDisplay::Framebuffer::InitializeMPPrivAccelerator()`, which copies
`fb->0x18`; and `fb->0x18` is written **only inside the `dispatch_once` block
of `CoreDisplay::GPU::UpdateAcceleratorForMetal()`** (2py, measured). A
`dispatch_once` fires **once per process, ever**.

`MPRebuildDevice` exists and runs on display reconfiguration (2q3 read it
copying bit 22 out of `mpPriv->0xb0`). So:

> If the display device / MPPriv is rebuilt on wake, the fresh one's
> `accelerator` field is **never refilled**, because the only code that fills
> it is behind a `dispatch_once` that already fired at login. From that moment
> `CDDisplay::accelerator()` returns 0 for the rest of the WindowServer
> session, and every `Update` gets `CompositorSW`.

That fits everything: 2qe's five closures all hold, `WSMetalCompositorEnabled`
is true, `new_compositor` works, the capability flag is 1 - and `out` is still
0, because the field it reads was zeroed by a rebuild after the only filler
had retired.

### Predictions, stated before the measurement

- **fresh dump now shows `priv.accelerator = 0`** -> confirmed. The
  contradiction dissolves, and the root cause is a once-only fill versus a
  rebuild on wake.
- **fresh dump still shows `0x14b23`** -> dead. The two readings agree after
  all and something else makes `out` zero; the lldb or kext read becomes
  necessary.
- **fresh dump shows a different non-zero value** -> the priv was rebuilt
  *and* refilled, so the sleep is not the cause, and what differs is elsewhere.

Two further predictions that follow only if the first branch holds, and which
are worth stating now because they are cheap and falsifiable:

- the desktop should have been **noticeably faster in the first ~12 minutes of
  this boot**, before 15:44:42, than it is now;
- **restarting WindowServer (log out and back in) after a wake should restore
  it**, because that re-runs the `dispatch_once` in a fresh process - and
  setting the display to never sleep should keep it.

If those hold, there is a usable mitigation today and a real fix to design,
and neither needs a kext change aimed at the display server.

### 2qf RESULT: dead, on both of its own predictions

Fresh dump at **20:00:04**, post sleep/wake, same boot
(`logs/20261024-200010-cdstate`):

```
accelerator            = 0x14b23     <- UNCHANGED, still non-zero
isAcceleratorBacked    = 1
displayPipeIsAvailable = 0
numDisplayBuffers      = 0
service                = 0x10c03
```

That is branch 2 of the three stated above: **the hypothesis is wrong.** The
user also refuted it independently and more cheaply - the desktop was *not*
faster before the first display sleep: "same speed... same desktop time", with
a grey screen for a minute or two at boot while things load. So the slowness
was present from login, before any sleep, which the dispatch-once story cannot
explain.

Worth keeping: the 15:32 and 20:00 dumps **agree**, 4½ hours and a sleep/wake
apart, so `priv.accelerator` is stable at `0x14b23` and the field is not the
variable. 2qe's contradiction is therefore real and not an artefact of timing,
which is what 2qf set out to test. A hypothesis that dies on a measurement it
predicted is worth more than one that is quietly dropped.

Also re-verified, since it is the one place offset arithmetic could have lied
(the shared_ptr control-block trap this project hit once already):
`allocate_shared<CDDisplay>` stores the **vtable pointer at `0x18(%rbx)`**
(`movq %rcx, 0x18(%rbx)` at `0x7ff807d78238`), so the object really does begin
at allocation+0x18 and the device at `0x170(%rbx)` really is object+**0x158**.
The arithmetic holds.

What is left unverified is narrow and specific: **whether the device
`CDDisplay->0x158` holds is the device the dump prints.** `CGXNextDisplayDevice`
chooses between **two** lists - the global head at `0x7ff843bb1c08`, or, when
an indirect predicate at `0x7ff843bb2280` is true, the virtual-framebuffer
accessor at `0x7ff843bb20d0` plus 0x30. That idiom appears at ~110 sites in
CoreDisplay, so it is the standard "virtual display mode?" test, and if it is
true in WindowServer then `all_displays()` builds its CDDisplay on a **VFB**
device whose `ops->0x148` is `VFBAcceleratorForDisplayDevice`, not the MP one -
and 2px read that function delegating, with a path that yields 0. The dump
says `isVirtualDevice = 0`, but that describes the device the **dump** walked.

`tools/wsread.sh` (2qg) reads exactly that, live: the three globals, the list
predicate, both heads, and for each device its **ops table pointer compared
against the MP table base** `0x7ff8404fc700`, its priv, and `priv->0x5c`.
Read-only by construction - no expression evaluated, no function called in the
target, because calling into a stopped WindowServer can deadlock on a lock its
own stopped thread holds. Watchdog SIGKILLs lldb past 25 s, since the kernel
resumes a task whose debugger dies.

## 2qh — ROOT CAUSE: the display's DisplaySurface has no IOSurface

Static, free, and it reconciles every observation in 2qd-2qg. The compositor
is swapped **after** `CDDisplay::compositor()` has correctly returned a Metal
one.

### The chain, end to end

```
UpdateDisplays
  Update::Update(..., shared_ptr<Display>, ...)            0x7ff807ee5902
    callq *0x4b0(%rax)            ; display->compositor()   -> a CompositorMetal
    movq  %rax, 0x1c0(%rbx)       ; Update->0x1c0 = it              (2qe)

  CDDisplay::begin_update(Update&)                          0x7ff807d6c488
    surface = make_shared<CDSurface>(this)                  0x7ff807d6f294
    CDSurface::prepare_for_update(update, false)            0x7ff807d6f382
        s = CoreDisplay_Display_GetNextSurface(...)          -> DisplaySurface
        cdsurf->0x18 = s
        io = CoreDisplay_DisplaySurface_GetIOSurface(s)      0x7ff807d6f421
        cdsurf->0x20 = io
        if (io == NULL) cdsurf->0x40 = 1        <<< THE DEFECT, 0x7ff807d6f42d
        else cdsurf->0x44 = IOSurfaceGetID(io)

    if (capability flag != 1)   goto force_sw
    if (cdsurf->0x40 == 1)      goto force_sw   <<< 0x7ff807d6f5af
    ...
  force_sw:
    update->0x1f8 |= 8
    update->0x1c0 = *[0x7ff843c9eca8]           ; THE SW COMPOSITOR
    update->0x1f8 &= ~1                         ; 0x7ff807d6c5c8..d6

  movq -0x350(%rbp), %rcx    ; = Update+0x1c0   (2qe)
  movq %rcx, -0xa00(%rbp)
  callq *0x4f8(%rax)         ; render_update(update, THAT, ...)
```

`CDSurface->0x40` is **0** from the constructor (`movw $0x0, 0x58(%rbx)` in the
shared_ptr allocation, object+0x18) and has exactly **one** other writer, the
`movb $0x1, 0x40(%r14)` above, reached by exactly **one** branch - the
`je` at `0x7ff807d6f42d` when `CoreDisplay_DisplaySurface_GetIOSurface`
returns NULL.

### Why every earlier measurement was right and the conclusion still eluded me

- the compositor is a **real object**, not NULL - because it is *replaced*,
  not left unset, which is why `'Unable to composite display due to null
  compositor.'` never appears in the log (2qg's test, 0 hits with a working
  control);
- `CDDisplay::compositor()` really does return a **CompositorMetal** - so mode
  0, capability flag 1, `accelId = 0x14b23` and a working `new_compositor` are
  all correct **and all irrelevant to the outcome**;
- `CompositorMetal` really is alive in the process (2qd, via
  `CaptureSurfaceMetal::Populate`) - it simply never gets the *display*;
- `-0x350(%rbp)` really has **no store in `UpdateDisplays`** (2q2, vindicated
  twice) - because both writers are elsewhere, the constructor and
  `begin_update`, through the struct pointer.

Six milestones went into `WSGetCompositorForAccelerator` because the SW
compositor can only come from there. It can also come from `begin_update`,
which reads the same global directly - and that reader was in the list I
printed in 2qd and truncated at ten lines. **The answer was in output I had
already generated and cut off.** `WS::Displays::CDDisplay::begin_update(WS::Displays::Update&) + 320`
is line 7 of 8.

### This IS 2pd, confirmed at the decision point

2pd read it from the symptom side: *"the display is `IONDRVFramebuffer`, whose
destination is a raw CPU-mapped range, **not an IOSurface and not a Metal
texture**"*. Here is that sentence as a literal branch in SkyLight:
`if (GetIOSurface() == NULL) force software`. 2pd has been right since boot
138 and the whole 2px->2qg excursion was spent re-deriving it from the
accelerator side, where nothing was ever wrong.

It also re-attaches 2q9, which looked like a dead end: `numDisplayBuffers` is
the popcount of the low two req-bits of `IOAccelSurfaceMTL->0x13c` and reads
**0** because no drawable is attached. A display with no attached buffer has
no IOSurface to hand out, so `GetIOSurface` returns NULL. The two findings are
the same fact at two layers, which is why both were 0.

### The frontier, and it is a different kind of problem now

Not "which flag is wrong" - there is no flag left. The question is **where
CoreDisplay gets the IOSurface for a display**, and why ours has none.
`CoreDisplay::DisplaySurface::DisplaySurface(__IOSurface*, gsl::not_null<AbstractDisplay const*>, bool, bool, unsigned long long)`
takes one as its first argument, so the surface is *constructed* around an
IOSurface that something upstream must produce. The candidates, in the order
worth reading: `CoreDisplay::Display::GetNextSurface(CGSRegionObject*,
CGSRegionObject*, CGSRegionObject*, double, double, unsigned int, unsigned
long long)` (`0x7ff80408c490`, which 2q9's scan already showed reading
`+0x14c`), and `CoreDisplay::Display::GetCurrentSurface()`.

That is static work, and it is the first time the display half has had a
named, falsifiable target that is not "write DCN 3.1.2".

### 2qh, continued: the surface exists, the IOSurface was never created

`CoreDisplay_DisplaySurface_GetIOSurface` (`0x7ff8040b887c`) is four
instructions: `if (s == NULL) return NULL; return *(s)`. So the IOSurface is
the **first field** of a `DisplaySurface`, which agrees with the constructor
taking `__IOSurface*` as argument 1.

And in `prepare_for_update` the two cases are **separate branches**:

```
7ff807d6f3f9  s = CoreDisplay_Display_GetNextSurface(...)
7ff807d6f3fe  cdsurf->0x18 = s
7ff807d6f402  cmpq $0, 0x10(%r14) ; je -> 0x7ff807d6f553   (different path)
7ff807d6f410  testq %rax,%rax     ; je -> 0x7ff807d6f572   (s NULL: different path)
7ff807d6f421  io = GetIOSurface(s)
7ff807d6f42d  testq; je -> cdsurf->0x40 = 1                (OUR path)
```

So on the path we are on, **`s` is NOT NULL** - a `DisplaySurface` exists - and
`s->0x00` is NULL. The display has a surface object with no IOSurface behind
it.

`CD_IOSurfaceCreate` (the function `internal_allocate_surface`) logs
**`'%s: IOSurfaceCreate failed for dictionary => [%s]'`** when the allocation
fails. This boot: **0 occurrences**, against a control of 113 CoreDisplay log
lines from WindowServer. So **nothing tried and failed to create it** - the
creation was never attempted for this display. `CD_IOSurfaceCreate` has exactly
two callers, `DisplaySurfacePool::GetNextSurface` and
`DisplayPipe::RunFullDisplayPipe`, and `Display::GetNextSurface` reaches the
pool only at **+1270 of a 0x65c-byte function**, so an earlier return is the
likely path. That is the next read.

### Why this is the end of the compositor hunt and the start of framebuffer work

The whole 2px->2qg excursion asked "which flag makes SkyLight choose
software". There is no such flag: SkyLight **chooses Metal correctly** and then
`begin_update` replaces it because the destination has no IOSurface. Every
accelerator-side reading was healthy because nothing on the accelerator side
was ever wrong.

This also joins the two halves of the project's own evidence:

- **2pd (boot 138)**: *"the display is `IONDRVFramebuffer`, whose destination
  is a raw CPU-mapped range, not an IOSurface and not a Metal texture"* - now a
  literal branch, `if (GetIOSurface() == NULL) force software`.
- **2q9**: `numDisplayBuffers` is the popcount of the low two req-bits of
  `IOAccelSurfaceMTL->0x13c` and reads 0 because `add_drawable_to_list` never
  ran - no buffer attached to the display's accelerator surface. A display with
  no attached buffer has no IOSurface to hand out. **The same fact at two
  layers**, which is why both read 0, and why 2pr's bigger `getVRAMRange`
  changed nothing: room was never the problem, a *surface* was.

So the target is no longer a flag to flip but the thing 2pd named: the
framebuffer must present an accelerator-backed scanout **surface**, not a bare
range. That is real work, and it is now specified by what consumes it rather
than guessed at.

## 2qi — CONFIRMED a third way, from Apple's own live state: `surface = 0x0`

The boot-149 `os_state` block at **20:00:04**, MPPriv dict
(`logs/20261024-200010-cdstate`):

```
surface          = 0x0000000000000000      surfaceID        = "-1"
scanoutSurface   = 0x0000000000000000      scanoutSurfaceID = 1
scanoutWidth     = 0                       scanoutHeight    = 0
scanoutTransform = {a=0 b=0 c=0 d=0 tx=0 ty=0}
scanoutUseGLPath = 0
shmemPtr         = 0x0000000118054000      shmemSize        = 8130560
vramAddress      = 0x0000000118815000      vramSize         = 0x7e9000
displayPipe      = 0x00007f99af813e00      (non-NULL)
displaySurfaceUsesIOSurface = 1            (the feature is ENABLED)
forcePipeFallback = 0
```

**The display has a CPU-mapped range and no surface**, said by CoreDisplay's own
debug dictionary: `surface` NULL, `surfaceID` -1, `scanoutSurface` NULL,
`scanoutWidth`/`scanoutHeight` 0, while `shmemPtr` and `vramAddress` are both
non-NULL. `displaySurfaceUsesIOSurface = 1` is the global setting, so
CoreDisplay **wants** an IOSurface-backed display surface; it has none to use.

So the root cause now stands on three independent legs:

1. **static** - `CDSurface::prepare_for_update` sets `cdsurf->0x40 = 1` when
   `CoreDisplay_DisplaySurface_GetIOSurface` returns NULL, and
   `CDDisplay::begin_update` then overwrites `Update->0x1c0` with the software
   compositor (2qh);
2. **runtime behaviour** - `render_update` runs `CompositorSW` with no
   `'Unable to composite display due to null compositor.'` in the log, i.e. the
   compositor was *replaced*, not missing (2qg/2qh);
3. **runtime state** - this dict: the display has no surface at all.

And it is 2pd's sentence from boot 138, now quoted back by the OS rather than
inferred: the destination is a raw CPU-mapped range, not an IOSurface.

### Which finally specifies the framebuffer work

The question is no longer "which flag" but **what makes CoreDisplay acquire a
scanout surface for a display, and what it asks the framebuffer for.** The
named entry point is `CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface` (2q9): it clears
`displayPipeIsAvailable`, then calls `ops->0x158`, which 2qc's thunk table
identifies as **`CGXFramebufferForDisplayDevice`** - so the acquire path goes
*through the framebuffer*. Our framebuffer is `IONDRVFramebuffer`, and by 2oz
every framebuffer method is defined in IONDRVSupport and therefore **routable**
from this plugin - the same technique that fixed the accelerator.

That is the first time the display half has a target that is neither "write
DCN 3.1.2 from scratch" nor a flag to flip: a specific acquire path, with a
specific caller, on a class we can already hook. It is also still static work -
read what `CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface` requires before writing anything,
and note that `numDisplayBuffers = 0` (2q9) says the accelerator surface has no
attached buffer, so the requirement may well be upstream of the framebuffer
method itself.

**Do not hook anything yet.** 2pq/2pr is the cautionary case: a correct hook on
`getVRAMRange`, verified to fire at exactly the intended call site, that
changed nothing because the gate was elsewhere. Establish what consumes the
surface and what refuses to create it first.

## 2qj — the surface path, named end to end, and `IOAccelCreateSurface` FAILS

Static plus one log line. Continues 2qh/2qi.

### The MP ops table, dumped by name

Read straight out of the cache by decoding the slide-info pointers at the base
2qe established (`0x7ff8404fc700`), so these are facts, not inferences:

| slot | function |
|---|---|
| 0x100/0x108/0x110 | `MPHWCopyRegion` / `MPHWFillRegion` / `MPHWMoveRegion` |
| 0x118/0x120/0x128 | `MPHWPurgeSurface` / `MPHWCopyPixels` / `MPHWCopyForwardRegion` |
| 0x130/0x138 | `MPHWWait` / `MPHWWaitTokenRelease` |
| 0x140 | `MPServiceForDisplayDevice` |
| 0x148 | `MPAcceleratorForDisplayDevice` |
| 0x150 | `MPFramebufferForDisplayDevice` |
| **0x158** | **`MPAccessSurfaceForDisplayDevice(CGXDisplayDevice*, void**, unsigned int*, bool, bool*)`** |
| 0x160/0x168 | `MPFinishSurfaceForDisplayDevice` / `MPResetSurfaceForDisplayDevice` |
| 0x170/0x178 | `MPDisplayDeviceDidFlush` / `MPDisplayDeviceSurfaceIsReady` |
| 0x180/0x188 | `MPAccessCaptureSurfaceForDisplayDevice` / `MPGenerateUpdate` |
| 0x190/0x198 | `MPResetGammaTablesOnDisplayDevice` / `MPUpdateGammaTablesOnDisplayDevice` |
| 0x1a0/0x1a8 | `MPGetNextWakeupTime` / `MPGetVBLTiming` |

So 2q9's `ops->0x158` is **not** "get the framebuffer" as 2qc guessed from the
CGX thunk名 - it is `MPAccessSurfaceForDisplayDevice`, and its two out-params
are exactly the dict's `surface` and `surfaceID`.

### The complete path

```
CDSurface::prepare_for_update                       (SkyLight)
 -> CoreDisplay_Display_GetNextSurface
   -> CoreDisplay::Display::GetNextSurface
      +229  -> CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface        (its ONLY caller)
                 -> ops->0x158 = MPAccessSurfaceForDisplayDevice
      +1270 -> DisplaySurfacePool::GetNextSurface -> CD_IOSurfaceCreate
```

`MPAccessSurfaceForDisplayDevice` returns `kCGErrorFailure (0x3e8)` at four
early gates before it ever tries to make a surface:

```
A  if (!(dev->0x10->0x10c & 0x4))      return 0x3e8
B  if (dev->0x10->0x137 != 0)          return 0x3e8
C  if (UseIOPresentment())             return 0x3e8      <<< note the polarity
D  if (priv->0x198 == -1)              return 0x3e8
```

then, if it gets through:

```
flags = <switch on priv->0xbc>
if (dev->0x10->0x10c & 0x80) && [0x7ff843bac931]==1 && dev->0x140==0:
      if   UseIOPresentment()                            flags |= 0x800
      elif all_devices_in_hw_mirror_loop_are_accelerator_backed(dev)
                                                         flags |= 0x8800
      else                                               flags |= 0x8400
id = MPAcquireSurfaceID()
priv->0x198 = id
IOAccelCreateSurface(priv->0x5c /*accelerator port*/, id, flags, &priv->0x1a0)
```

**`priv->0x198` and `priv->0x1a0` are the dict's `surfaceID` and `surface`** -
consecutive fields, and the dump reads **`surfaceID = "-1"`, `surface = 0x0`**
(2qi). So gate D is satisfied by the measurement; whether D or C fires **first**
is undetermined, because `UseIOPresentment()`'s runtime value is unknown and C
precedes D. Recorded as undetermined rather than guessed.

### 2q9's open question is answered: the consumer of `isAcceleratorBacked`

`all_devices_in_hw_mirror_loop_are_accelerator_backed(dev)` opens with

```
rax = dev->0x160                  ; the MPPriv
if (!(rax->0xb2 & 0x40)) return 0
```

Byte `0xb2` bit 6 **is bit 22 of the dword at `0xb0`** (16+6=22) - exactly
`kDisplayModeAcceleratorBackedFlag`, the bit `-rbgpufbaccel` sets, which 2q7
measured as 1 in boot 149. So **2q4's hook feeds a real consumer after all**,
and 2q9's caveat ("find a consumer before writing to a field") is discharged.
Its effect is to pick flag **0x8800** instead of **0x8400** for
`IOAccelCreateSurface`. That is smaller than hoped - it is a flag bit, not a
gate - but it is no longer speculative.

### The hard measured fact: the accelerator refuses to create a surface

One log line in boot 149, with a working control (the same grep found the
message's siblings 0 times, and CoreDisplay logs 113 lines):

```
15:44:42.467  WindowServer[162] (CoreDisplay) [ERROR] -
  MPHWCopyPixels: display 0x5b81c5c0: device 0x7f99b020bde0:
  port 0x00010d03: IOAccelCreateSurface = 0xe00002c2
```

**`0xe00002c2` is `kIOReturnBadArgument`.** `IOAccelCreateSurface` *fails* on
this machine. Neither `'Set up page flip mode on display ...'` nor
`'Failed to set up surface for page flip mode'` appears at all, so
`MPAccessSurfaceForDisplayDevice` never reaches its page-flip section - it
either returns at a gate or fails at the create.

`MPAcquireSurfaceID()` is a 256-bit allocation bitmap at `0x7ff843bb1a30`
(all-zero in the cache image) that returns **-1 only when all 256 ids are
taken**. `reset_hardware(MPPriv*, bool)` calls `IOAccelDestroySurface` and
resets `priv->0x198` to **0**, not -1, and it touches the bitmap at three
sites, so ids do appear to be released - a plain never-released leak is the
less likely story, and the -1 wants explaining by something else.

### Next, and it is static

`IOAccelCreateSurface` returning `kIOReturnBadArgument` is the deepest fact
reached so far, and the kernel side is **already extracted**:
`build/re/IOAcceleratorFamily2`. 2qb read `IOAccelSurface::surface_control_with_lock`
there and found `0xE00002C2` as its unsupported-selector return, so the same
code is answering "bad argument" to surface creation. Find the external method
`IOAccelCreateSurface` maps to, read what it validates, and see which check our
accelerator fails. No boot, no root, no sudo.

## 2qk — THE ROOT CAUSE, in Apple's own words: "Assembly surfaces for display updates not supported"

The kernel log of boot 149, found by taking the os_log format string out of
`IOAccelSurfaceMTL::set_id_mode` and grepping for its function name:

```
15:25:36.383  kernel (IOAcceleratorFamily2) IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode:
              Surface mode contains bad bits                                    x4
15:25:36.795  kernel (IOAcceleratorFamily2) IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode:
              New id (0x00000001) less than 256,
              Assembly surfaces for display updates not supported               x2
15:44:42.467  (the same, and this is the line whose caller logged
               IOAccelCreateSurface = 0xe00002c2 one millisecond later)
20:26:03.816  kernel (IOAcceleratorFamily2) IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode:
              mode 0x4 must has kIOAccelSurfaceModeWindowedBit bit
```

`IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode(uint32_t id, uint32_t mode)` (`0x14e48cac`) rejects
with `kIOReturnBadArgument` when:

- `mode & 0xFF8073C0` is non-zero - *"Surface mode contains bad bits"*;
- **`id <= 0xff`** (`cmpl $0xff, %r14d` at `0x14e48e85`) - *"less than 256,
  Assembly surfaces for display updates not supported"*;
- the mode lacks `kIOAccelSurfaceModeWindowedBit`.

And **`MPAcquireSurfaceID()` can only ever return 0..255** - it is a 256-bit
bitmap (`rax < 8`, `ecx < 32`, id = `rax*32 + ecx`). The log shows it returned
**1**.

> **So CoreDisplay's MP display-device surface path cannot succeed against this
> accelerator, by construction. Every id the allocator can produce is below the
> threshold the accelerator demands, and the accelerator says the feature -
> "assembly surfaces for display updates" - is not supported.**

This is not a bug in our driver. It is Apple's accelerator declining a legacy
path that `IONDRVFramebuffer`-backed displays are the only remaining users of.

### The complete chain, measured end to end

```
MPAccessSurfaceForDisplayDevice                    (CoreDisplay, MP ops 0x158)
  id = MPAcquireSurfaceID()                        -> 1   (can only be 0..255)
  IOAccelCreateSurface(priv->0x5c, id, mode, &priv->0x1a0)
    = IOServiceOpen(accelPort, type) + external method 7
    -> IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode(1, mode)
       -> id <= 0xff  ==> kIOReturnBadArgument (0xe00002c2)   [LOGGED]
  -> logs "IOAccelCreateSurface = 0xe00002c2"                 [LOGGED]
CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface                      returns NULL
CoreDisplay::Display::GetNextSurface +229..+243
  movq %rax, %rbx            ; NULL
  operator new(0x1a0)        ; wraps it anyway  <-- 0x7ff80408c073
  -> a DisplaySurface whose IOSurface field is NULL, and it RETURNS,
     never reaching DisplaySurfacePool::GetNextSurface at +1270
CDSurface::prepare_for_update
  s != NULL, but GetIOSurface(s) == NULL  ==> cdsurf->0x40 = 1
CDDisplay::begin_update
  cdsurf->0x40 == 1  ==> Update->0x1c0 = *[0x7ff843c9eca8]   (CompositorSW)
UpdateDisplays -> render_update(update, CompositorSW, ...)
  -> CompositorSW::CompositeLayersToDestination -> CA::OGL:: on the CPU
```

Every link is either disassembled or logged. The three independent
confirmations of 2qi (static branch, sampled behaviour, live state dict) now
have a fourth: **the accelerator's own diagnostic text.**

### What this settles, and what it kills

- **2pd was right at boot 138** and has been right ever since: the destination
  is a raw CPU-mapped range, not an IOSurface. Everything from 2px to 2qg was
  spent on the accelerator side, where nothing was ever wrong.
- `numDisplayBuffers = 0` (2q9) is the same fact one layer down: no surface,
  therefore no attached buffer.
- `isAcceleratorBacked` (2q4/2q7, `-rbgpufbaccel`) does feed a real consumer -
  `all_devices_in_hw_mirror_loop_are_accelerator_backed` gates on
  `priv->0xb2 & 0x40`, which is dword `0xb0` bit 22 - but its only effect is to
  choose mode flag `0x8800` over `0x8400`, and **both are rejected for the same
  reason the id is**. So the arg is harmless and currently pointless. Keep it
  OUT of boot-args until there is a reason.
- **"Surface mode contains bad bits" also fires 4x at 15:25:36**, so the mode
  word is *additionally* wrong, independently of the id. CoreDisplay's switch on
  `priv->0xbc` can select a pixel-format fourcc (`'B32f'` = 0x42333266 when
  `priv->0xc8 == 0x20`, i.e. 32bpp - ours) as the mode, and
  `0x42333266 & 0xFF8073C0 = 0x42007240` - rejected in all three flag variants.
  Computed, not guessed.

### Where this leaves the framebuffer work

The MP surface path is a dead end **by Apple's decision**, so there is no hook
that makes it work. The surviving path is the modern one, which
`Display::GetNextSurface` reaches only at **+1270**:
`DisplaySurfacePool::GetNextSurface` -> `CD_IOSurfaceCreate` -> a real
IOSurface. Our display never gets there because the acquire at +229 returns
NULL and the function returns early with the NULL-wrapping DisplaySurface.

So the next question is precise and static: **what makes
`Display::GetNextSurface` take the +1270 pool path instead of returning at
+243?** That is a branch in a function we now know well, and it is the first
target in this project that would put a real IOSurface under the desktop.

### CORRECTION to 2qk: "never reaching the pool" was not measured

2qk wrote that `Display::GetNextSurface` "wraps NULL in a `operator new(0x1a0)`
DisplaySurface and **returns early, never reaching the pool at +1270**". The
first half is right; the second was inferred from the offsets and is wrong as
stated. The function has **two** writes through its sret pointer
(`-0x70(%rbp)`, loaded from `%rdi` at entry):

```
0x7ff80408c262   movq %rbx, (%rax)     ; *sret = the CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface result
0x7ff80408c489   movq %rax, (%rcx)     ; *sret = the DisplaySurfacePool::GetNextSurface result
```

So there are two returns, and the 0x1a0 object built at +243 is an
**intermediate** (vtable `0x7ff8404fcc88`, the acquired surface stored at its
`+0x20` and the display at `+0x98`) - not the thing returned.

Which write executes is **not** established. What is established:

- the acquire **fails** - logged twice over, `set_id_mode` refusing id 1 and
  `IOAccelCreateSurface = 0xe00002c2`;
- `prepare_for_update` is on its `GetIOSurface(s) == NULL` branch, and it tests
  `s == NULL` **separately** at `0x7ff807d6f410`, so `s` is **non-NULL**.

A NULL from the acquire path would therefore have gone down the other branch.
So the surface `prepare_for_update` holds is most likely **the pool's**, and
the open question sharpens to: **why does `DisplaySurfacePool::GetNextSurface`
hand back a DisplaySurface whose IOSurface is NULL, when `CD_IOSurfaceCreate`
logged no failure all boot?** The pool has a reuse path - when the colorspace
argument is NULL (`cmpq $0x0, 0x20(%rbp)` at `0x7ff804134316`) or matches, it
returns a cached slot (`rbx->0x58 + index`) and skips creation entirely
(`0x7ff804134362` jumps past the `CD_IOSurfaceCreate` call) - so a slot
populated with a NULL-backed surface would be handed out forever without ever
attempting a create. That is the thing to read next.

2qk's root cause stands unchanged: the accelerator refuses the MP surface path,
with its own diagnostic text. Only the sentence about the pool was wrong, and
it was wrong in the same way three earlier sentences in this session were -
an offset comparison treated as control flow.

## 2ql - BOTH of CoreDisplay's surface paths are closed, and the second one is closed by a CLASS NAME

2qk's correction left one question: which of `Display::GetNextSurface`'s two
sret writes executes, i.e. does the desktop's surface come from the legacy
`CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface` or from `DisplaySurfacePool`.  The answer is
in the function's first twenty instructions, and it is not a subtle one.

`CoreDisplay::Display::GetNextSurface` (unslid **0x7ff80408bf86**) opens with
two gates and nothing else:

```
0x7ff80408bfd2   callq CoreDisplay::UseIOPresentment()
0x7ff80408bfd7   testb %al,%al ; je 0x7ff80408c04e      -> LEGACY
0x7ff80408bfdb   cmpb  $0x1, [0x7ff843bac773]           -> ("displaySurfaceUsesIOSurface")
0x7ff80408bfe2   jne   0x7ff80408c04e                   -> LEGACY
                 fall through to 0x7ff80408bfe4          -> DisplaySurfacePool
```

`0x7ff80408c04e` loads `dev->0x68` and calls **`CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface`**
(0x7ff80411cc8d, symbolized, not inferred), then `operator new(0x1a0)` and the
sret write at `0x7ff80408c262` - 2qk's first write, the dead path.  The
fall-through walks the hw-mirror-loop list at `dev->0xb0`, reaches
`0x7ff80408c291`, builds a `DisplaySurfacePool` (0x7ff80413403c) and ends at
the other sret write, `0x7ff80408c489`.  **So the two writes are the two
gates, and the gate decides.**

Gate 2 is already satisfied and was already measured: byte `0x7ff843bac773` is
the preference **`displaySurfaceUsesIOSurface`**, which boot 149's os_state
dump printed as **1**.  Gate 1 is the one that fails.

### `UseIOPresentment()`, read instruction by instruction

`0x7ff804057b40`:

```
al = gUseIOP                                  ; byte 0x7ff843bac76d  ("useIOP")
if (al != 1) return al & 1;
supported = (useIOP_onIG      ? 0x02 : 0)     ; byte 0x7ff843bac76e
          | (useIOP_onAMD     ? 0x04 : 0)     ; byte 0x7ff843bad282
          | (useIOP_onNVIDIA  ? 0x08 : 0)     ; byte 0x7ff843bad281
          | (useIOP_onAPV     ? 0x10 : 0);    ; byte 0x7ff843bad283
present = gSystemGPUVendors;                  ; int  0x7ff843bb1d64
if (present == 0 || (supported & present) != present) { gUseIOP = 0; return 0; }
return gUseIOP;
```

All five bytes are CFPreferences booleans in the domain
**`com.apple.CoreDisplay`**, read by `CGXMappedDisplayStart+950..1050` through
one helper (`0x7ff80405597a` = `CFPreferencesCopyValue` +
`CFGetTypeID == CFBooleanGetTypeID` + `CFBooleanGetValue`).  The whole key
table was read out of the cache: `enableWSAA{,_onNVIDIA,_onAMD,_onAPV,_onIG}`,
`useIOP{,_onNVIDIA,_onAMD,_onAPV,_onIG}`, `useIOP_gamma_on*`, `useIOSurfaceLog`,
**`displaySurfaceUsesIOSurface`**, `muxSwitchPresentUsesVSync`, `useMetal`,
`enableGTrace`, `enableStateDump`, `enableDataDump`, `convert10BitSurface`.
`displaySurfaceUsesIOSurface` being in that table *and* in the os_state dump is
the control that the table is the live one.

**The default is 1, not 0** - worth stating because the cache image's static
initializers are misleading.  All five `useIOP*` reads pass the same default,
`[0x7ff843bad260]`, a function-local static (guard byte `bad268`) filled from
`[0x7ff843bad738]`, and the only writer of `bad738` is the block in
`CoreDisplay::VorpalBlade()` at **0x7ff8040598b7**, which stores `$1`
**unconditionally** - every path through the block, including both early
`je`s, falls into the store.  So on a stock machine with no keys set,
`supported = 0x1e`.

### `present` is built from the framebuffer's CLASS NAME

`__GetSystemGPUVendors_block_invoke` (0x7ff80412ce2c):
`IOServiceGetMatchingServices(IOServiceMatching("IOFramebuffer"))`, and for
each service `0x7ff80412cc38` does **`IOObjectCopyClass`** (stub symbolized)
and four `CFStringFind`s:

| needle in the class name | bit |
|---|---|
| `Intel` | 0x02 |
| `AMD` | 0x04 |
| `NVDA` | 0x08 |
| `AppleParavirt` | 0x10 |
| **no match** | **0x01** |

If the iterator is empty at all, the block does `andb $0xfe` and clears bit 0.

**The asymmetry is the whole finding: `supported` is assembled only from bits
0x02/0x04/0x08/0x10, so bit 0x01 can never be in it.**  One unclassifiable
IOFramebuffer makes `(supported & present) != present` hold for every possible
value of every preference.

### Measured, non-root, in one second: `make useiop`

```
IONDRVFramebuffer   name=.Display_boot   -> bit 0x01   <-- UNKNOWN VENDOR
present mask = 0x01  (1 framebuffer)
supported mask = 0x1e
reproduced UseIOPresentment() = 0   (a present vendor is not in the supported set)
```

**Our only IOFramebuffer is `IONDRVFramebuffer`, and "IONDRVFramebuffer"
contains none of Intel / AMD / NVDA / AppleParavirt.**  On a real Mac with this
GPU family the framebuffer is Apple's **`AMDFramebuffer`** (the class exists -
it is in `build/re/`), whose name contains `AMD`, so `present = 0x04` (plus
`0x02` for an Intel iGPU), `supported = 0x1e` covers it, and IOPresentment is
on.  That is the single discriminator between this machine and a supported one.

**RULE 14, stated against my own tool:** `CoreDisplay::UseIOPresentment` *is*
exported and `useiop` calls it, and it returns 0 - but that is **not** a
cross-check and the tool now says so in its own output.  In a client process
`CGXMappedDisplayStart` never ran, so `gSystemGPUVendors` is still 0 and
Apple's function returns 0 from its `present == 0` branch: the right answer for
the wrong reason.  The first version of the tool printed `agree.` and that line
was hollow; it was removed.  What *is* process-independent and is the real
measurement is section 1 - `IOObjectCopyClass` on the live services.

### Forcing the gate is NOT the fix

`UseIOPresentment` has **72 direct call sites** in CoreDisplay:
`MPRebuildDevice` (x5), `setup_hardware`, `displayConnectChange` (x3),
`displayDidWake` (x2), `displayAliasActivate` (x4), `DisplayPipe::Commit` (x2),
`CGXMappedDisplayStart` (x4), `CGXAcquireDisplayDeviceSurface` (x2),
`CGXReleaseDisplayDeviceSurface`, `CGXShutdownDisplays`, `set_gamma_transfer`,
`generate_update`, `resetPageFlipState`, `UpdateDisplayAccelerators`,
`__WSMachineUsesNewStyleMirroring_block_invoke`, `MPHWCopyPixels`,
`UseIOPGamma`, `update_gl_acceleration`, `mp_display_will_sleep_common`.
It does not select a surface allocator - it selects **the entire presentment
world**, the one that talks to the `IOPresentment*` kernel API
(`IOPresentmentBindIOAccelSurfaceToResource`, `IOPresentmentSetPlaneState`,
`IOPresentmentDestroyResource`, all three present as DYLD stubs in CoreDisplay).
`IONDRVFramebuffer` implements none of it.  Patching this one function true in
WindowServer - which the `-rbgpumtlkfix` machinery could do, and could do more
cheaply than the Metal detour because `UseIOPresentment`'s first instruction is
a 6-byte `mov r8<-m` with no branch inside it - would switch 72 call sites into
a stack that is not there.  **Do not propose it.**

### Why the legacy path is dead too, mechanically this time

2qk established *that* `IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode` rejects ids below 256.
The missing half is *why the base-class implementation runs at all*, since
there are three:

```
IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode        0x14e48cac   cmpl $0xff, %r14d  -> 0xe00002c2
IOAccelSurfaceMTL::set_id_mode     0x14e22560
IOAccelLegacySurface::set_id_mode  0x14e27202
```

**Neither override calls the base** - checked by disassembling both and
searching for a call to `0x14e48cac`; there is none.  So the base ran because
the object's class does not override it.  `IOGraphicsAccelerator2::newUserClient`
(`0x14e512aa`) switches on the IOServiceOpen `type`, and the jump table at
`0x14e51ab8` was decoded rather than guessed:

```
type 0   -> 0x14e51560:  this->vt[0xa30]()            then IOAccelSurface::init
type 0x20 -> 0x14e51806: operator new(0x340)
                         IOAccelSurfaceMTL()          then IOAccelSurfaceMTL::init
type 0x21 -> IOAccelMemoryInfoUserClient
```

There is **no `IOGraphicsAccelerator2::newSurface`** - only `newSurfaceMTL` -
so slot `0xa30` is the vendor's.  Apple's AMD driver supplies it:

```
AMDRadeonX6000_AMDGraphicsAccelerator::newSurface()   0xbe3ed98
    if (!(this->0x1f10 & 0x20)) return NULL;
    return new AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelSurface();       // 0x1358 bytes
```

and `AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelSurface` **does not override `set_id_mode`** (its
full symbol list has `surfaceStart`, `surfaceStop`, `shapeSurface`,
`copyToBuffer`, `submitSwapCopy`, `getSurfaceModeDepthFormat` and no
`set_id_mode`).  So:

- **legacy** `IOAccelCreateSurface` -> type 0 -> `AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelSurface`
  -> inherited `IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode` -> **id must be >= 256**, and
  `MPAcquireSurfaceID` can only ever return 0..255 -> unsatisfiable.
- **Metal** -> type 0x20 -> `IOAccelSurfaceMTL` -> its own `set_id_mode`, which
  has no id check at all (its tests are `cmpl %r15d,%ecx`, `cmpl $0xc,%edx`,
  `cmpl $-0x20,%r9d`).

Incidentally this confirms the surface *was* created: `newSurface` returning
NULL makes `newUserClient` return `kIOReturnNoResources (0xe00002be)`, and we
measured `kIOReturnBadArgument (0xe00002c2)` from `set_id_mode` - so
`accel->0x1f10 & 0x20` is set and that gate is fine.

### Where this leaves the display half

Both branches of the one function that produces the desktop's surface are
closed, by two independent Apple decisions:

1. the legacy MP path by an id check no caller of it can satisfy, and
2. the IOPresentment path by a class-name vendor test that `IONDRVFramebuffer`
   cannot pass.

No preference, no boot-arg and no hook on either of them changes that. The
single thing that opens path 2 is **an `IOFramebuffer` whose class name
contains "AMD"** - which is exactly the subclassed framebuffer 2oz built,
compiled, and then ruled out, not on capability but on kernel-collection
placement: IOGraphicsFamily lives in SystemKernelExtensions.kc and OpenCore
injects us into BootKernelExtensions.kc.  **2oz's conclusion ("own the methods
instead of subclassing") is therefore not equivalent after all** - routing
`IONDRVFramebuffer`'s methods can change what it *reports*, but nothing routed
on an instance changes what `IOObjectCopyClass` returns for it, because that is
`getMetaClass()->getClassName()` on the shared `IONDRVFramebuffer` OSMetaClass.
That is the thing to re-open, and it is a real decision rather than another
read: either find a load path that can depend on IOGraphicsFamily, or decide
the display half stays software.

Also retired by this milestone: the 2qk-correction's open question about
`DisplaySurfacePool::GetNextSurface`'s reuse path.  The pool is never reached,
so why it might hand back a NULL-backed surface is moot; the `cmpq $0x0,
0x20(%rbp)` reuse branch at `0x7ff804134316` was never the question.

### Added

`tools/useiop.m` + `make useiop` - non-root, one second, no boot.  Prints every
IOFramebuffer with the bit its class name earns, the five preferences with
whether each was found or defaulted, the reproduced verdict with the branch
named, and a verdict that distinguishes "a preference is wrong" (fixable) from
"a framebuffer is unclassifiable" (not).  Exit codes: 0 IOPresentment is on,
1 unknown-vendor framebuffer, 2 a preference, 3 inconclusive.

## 2qm - IOPresentment needs nothing we lack in the kernel, and the client test is blocked by an entitlement

2ql ended with "the lever is an `IOFramebuffer` whose class name contains AMD",
and treated that as a decision about 2oz's subclass.  Before accepting that,
the obvious question: **would the IOPresentment path even work if the gate
opened?**  If it needs IOMobileFramebuffer or an AMD-specific kernel
framebuffer, the gate is irrelevant and 2ql's lever is worthless.

It does not.  `IOPresentment.framework` **is present on this machine**
(`/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/IOPresentment.framework`, dlopens fine,
exports `IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryService/ID`, `CreateResource`,
`CreateResourceWithIOSurface`, `SetPlaneState`,
`BindIOAccelSurfaceToResource`, `CopyCapabilities`).  Its `__TEXT` strings name
what it talks to, and there is no IOMobileFramebuffer and nothing AMD-specific
among them:

```
IOFramebuffer            IOAccelIndex              IOAccelerator
IOAccelDisplayPipeTriage IOAccelDisplayPipeTransactionWait
DisplayPipeSupported     IsDisplayable             IODisplayEDID
Error: Unable to create IOAccelDisplayPipe
Error: Unable to connect to IOPresentment client
Error: ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch() failed - retCode: %#x
```

**Every one of those is live on this machine right now**, measured with
`make ioptest` on the session's boot:

```
framebuffer  IONDRVFramebuffer   name=.Display_boot   id=0x100000548
accelerator  AMDRadeonX6000_AMDNavi21GraphicsAccelerator  id=0x10000054a
IOAccelIndex                    [fb]    0
IOAccelRevision                 [fb]    2
IOAccelDisplayPipeCapabilities  [accel] {DisplayPipeSupported=1, TransactionsSupported=1}
```

plus **2 live `IOAccelDisplayPipeUserClient2` instances** in the IORegistry and
AGDC present (15 nodes).  That is 2pp re-confirmed on this boot, and it is
exactly the kernel surface IOPresentment uses.  So 2ql's lever is **not**
worthless: the thing the class-name test is refusing appears to be already
wired up.

### The signature, read rather than guessed

`IOPresentment::IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryService(unsigned int, unsigned int)`
(image+0x400C) takes **two** `io_service_t`, refuses when they are equal
(`cmpl %esi,%edi; jne`, else it logs and returns 0), converts each to a registry
ID and forwards to `CreateForRegistryID(uint64, uint64)`.  So the pair is
**(framebuffer, accelerator)** - which is why the test can be run at all.  The
C wrappers pass their arguments through with no shuffling.

### The client test is INCONCLUSIVE, and the framework says why

The unprivileged call does not return NULL - it **aborts** (SIGABRT) inside the
framework, after logging to this process's own os_log:

```
Error: ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch() failed - retCode: 0xe00002e2
Error: Unable to acquire map
GPUWranglerOpenWithTimeout: failed to connect; service=0x1a03 status=0xe00002e2
```

**`0xe00002e2` is `kIOReturnNotPermitted`** - an entitlement on opening the
GPUWrangler, not an answer about the display pipe.  Neither
`Unable to create IOAccelDisplayPipe` nor
`Unable to connect to IOPresentment client` appeared.  This is the branch
`ioptest` pre-stated as INCONCLUSIVE before the first run, and it is reported
as such: WindowServer holds two of these user clients already and has
entitlements this process does not.

`ioptest` now makes the call in a **forked child** and interprets the exit
status, so the abort cannot take the verdict with it - and because the parent
survives, the tool is usable under privilege.  (Rule 14 again: the first
version would have died at step 3 with no verdict printed at all.)

### Where the two candidate interventions now stand

Both produce the *same* effect - `UseIOPresentment()` true - so they are one
lever with two placements, and 2ql's warning against forcing the gate applies
to both only if the pipe cannot be created.  That is now the open question, not
a settled one.

**A - userspace, narrow, inside WindowServer only.** Patch the per-framebuffer
vendor classifier `0x7ff80412cc38` to return `0x4` (AMD) instead of `0x1`
(unknown): six bytes, `b8 04 00 00 00 c3`, at an entry whose first instructions
are `pushq %rbp; movq %rsp,%rbp; pushq %r15; pushq %r14` - no branch inside, so
rule 2 is satisfied and nothing needs displacing.  Its **only** caller is
`__GetSystemGPUVendors_block_invoke`, so the whole effect is
`gSystemGPUVendors = 0x4`.  Readers of that global then believe "AMD", which is
**true of the hardware** - `GetCurrentSystemGPUVendorName()` would return
`"AMD"` instead of `"Unknown"`.  The `-rbgpumtlkfix` machinery already does
exactly this class of patch (hooks `_task_set_main_thread_qos` per exec, writes
verified bytes with `_vm_map_write_user`, compares before writing so an OS
update means nothing is patched), and it runs **before the process executes any
code**, which matters because `GetSystemGPUVendors` is a `dispatch_once` during
`CGXMappedDisplayStart`.

**B - kernel, global.** Rename `IONDRVFramebuffer`'s class.  Measured rather
than assumed: `is_io_object_get_class` (`0xffffff8000b371a0`) does
`metaclass = obj->vt[0x38]()`, then `sym = metaclass->0x18`, then
`sym->vt[0x148]()` (`getCStringNoCopy`) - so `className` is at **+0x18** of the
OSMetaClass and is read as an **object**, not a `char *`.  `OSMetaClass`'s
constructor (`0xffffff8000a49940`) stores `reserved` at +0x08, `superClassLink`
at +0x10, the name at **+0x18** and `classSize` at +0x20, and the name it stores
there is the raw `const char *` argument - xnu's known placeholder, interned
into an OSSymbol later - with exactly **one** store to +0x18 in the whole
function.  So a rename means writing an `OSSymbol *` into
`IONDRVFramebuffer::gMetaClass + 0x18`.  **B is strictly worse than A for the
same effect**: it changes what `IOObjectCopyClass`, `ioreg`, panic logs and any
name-based `metaCast` see, system-wide, to fix one string comparison in one
userspace function.  Recorded, not recommended.

### The next step is one command, and it is the user's

`sudo ./build/out/ioptest`.  Root may or may not clear
`kIOReturnNotPermitted` - many Apple user clients check an entitlement with no
root fallback - but it is instant, writes nothing, and it is the only thing that
turns INCONCLUSIVE into an answer about capability.  It creates a third
GPUWrangler/display-pipe client beside the two WindowServer already holds and
presents nothing; if it aborts again the process dies and the kernel reclaims
the connection, which is what the unprivileged run already did twice with no
effect on the desktop.

- **pipe created** -> intervention A is a real candidate fix, and the display
  half has a cheap route for the first time since 2pd.
- **`Unable to create IOAccelDisplayPipe`** -> the capability is missing and
  2ql's verdict stands: the gate is not the problem and A would black-screen.
- **`kIOReturnNotPermitted` again** -> still INCONCLUSIVE; the only remaining
  instrument is WindowServer itself, i.e. intervention A run as an experiment,
  which is a kext change on the process that owns the display and therefore a
  decision rather than a measurement.

### Added

`tools/ioptest.m` + `make ioptest`.  Prints both services with class, name and
registry ID; the three preconditions, searched on the framebuffer **and** the
accelerator (`IOAccelDisplayPipeCapabilities` lives on the accelerator, not the
framebuffer - the first version reported it ABSENT); the call made in a forked
child; and a verdict that names which failure mode was observed.  Exit codes:
0 pipe created, 3 inconclusive.

## 2qn - root does NOT clear the entitlement, but the AGDC map answers the capability question anyway

**`sudo ./build/out/ioptest` (boot 149, 21:09:37): still SIGABRT.** The
privileged run's own log:

```
ioptest: (IOPresentment) Error: Invalid argument
ioptest: (GPUWrangler) GPUWranglerOpenWithTimeout: failed to connect; service=0xc0b status=0xe00002e2
```

`0xe00002e2` = `kIOReturnNotPermitted`, unchanged from the unprivileged run.
**So the GPUWrangler user client is entitlement-gated, not privilege-gated, and
the client-side test can never answer the question.** That branch of 2qm is now
closed by measurement rather than left open - do not spend another run on it.
(`AppleGPUWrangler` itself is fine: it is `registered, matched, active` with
**three** live `AppleGPUWranglerClient`s - `displaypolicyd` pid 142,
`WindowServer` pid 162, and one more. It is our process that is refused, not
the service that is broken.)

### But the thing the test was trying to prove is readable from ioreg

`ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch()` searches AGDC's GPU map, and
`AppleGPUWrangler` publishes it as the `debug-gpus` property. On this boot it
holds exactly one entry:

```
{"id"=64455, "acc"=4294968650, "fbs"=(4294968648), "gpuc"=0, "pci"=4294967939,
 "agdp"=0, "cc"=3, "flags"=2986344480, "tds"=0}
```

Decoded against the live registry IDs:

| field | value | is |
|---|---|---|
| `acc` | 0x1000005**4a** | **our `AMDRadeonX6000_AMDNavi21GraphicsAccelerator`** |
| `fbs[0]` | 0x1000005**48** | **our `.Display_boot`, the `IONDRVFramebuffer`** |
| `pci` | 0x100000283 | the PCI device |
| `id` | 0xfbc7 | the wrangler's GPU id |

**AGDC already knows our IONDRVFramebuffer and our AMD accelerator as one
GPU.** That is the association `ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch()` looks for, and it
exists. Nothing had to be created for it; the wrangler built it at boot.

### Where the display half stands now

Every precondition IOPresentment is known to need is live and paired on this
machine, measured, none of it inferred:

- `IOFramebuffer` present (`.Display_boot`)
- `IOAccelIndex 0`, `IOAccelRevision 2` on it
- `IOAccelDisplayPipeCapabilities = {DisplayPipeSupported=1, TransactionsSupported=1}`
  on the accelerator
- two live `IOAccelDisplayPipeUserClient2` instances
- AGDC/`AppleGPUWrangler` up, with **our** fb and **our** accelerator in one
  `debug-gpus` entry
- `IOPresentment.framework` on disk and loadable

and the **only** thing refusing the path is CoreDisplay's userspace vendor
test, which classifies GPUs by `IOObjectCopyClass` on the framebuffer and
scores `IONDRVFramebuffer` as "unknown" (2ql).

That is no longer "a decision about whether the display stays software". It is
one 6-byte userspace patch whose correctness is now supported from four
independent directions, and whose remaining risk is that something *else*
inside the IOPresentment path fails after the gate opens - which no instrument
short of WindowServer itself can rule out, because the entitlement blocks every
client-side probe.

**Intervention A, restated with the evidence behind it:** inside WindowServer
only, patch CoreDisplay's per-framebuffer vendor classifier `0x7ff80412cc38` to
return `0x4` (AMD) instead of `0x1` (unknown). Six bytes, `b8 04 00 00 00 c3`,
at an entry with no branch in it. Its only caller is
`__GetSystemGPUVendors_block_invoke`, so the whole effect is
`gSystemGPUVendors = 0x4` - and that belief is **true of the hardware**. Then
`UseIOPresentment()` returns true and `Display::GetNextSurface` takes the pool
path that calls `CD_IOSurfaceCreate`.

**The risk, stated plainly:** if the IOPresentment path then fails somewhere we
cannot see, WindowServer may not bring the display up - a black screen at
login. Rescue is `-rbgpuoff` and a reboot, over SSH if needed. It writes **no
DCN register**. The `-rbgpumtlkfix` machinery already does exactly this class of
patch, verifies every site from the target's own memory before writing, and
fails safe (an OS update that moves the function means nothing is patched).
It runs at `_task_set_main_thread_qos`, before the process executes any code,
which matters because `GetSystemGPUVendors` is a `dispatch_once` inside
`CGXMappedDisplayStart`.

**It is a kext change on the process that owns the display, so it is the
user's decision.**

## 2qo - intervention A, CORRECTED and NARROWED: the classifier has TWO callers, so patch the CALL SITE

2qm staked intervention A on a claim that is false, and this milestone is the
measurement that refutes it plus the five-byte patch that replaces it. Nothing
has been booted; everything below is static, read-only and reproducible on this
machine.

### The claim that was wrong

2ql and 2qm both say of `GetGPUVendorForFramebufferService` (`0x7ff80412cc38`):

> Its **only** caller is `__GetSystemGPUVendors_block_invoke`, so the entire
> effect is `gSystemGPUVendors = 0x4`.

`python3 tools/re/dsc.py callxref <cache> 0x7FF80404C000 0x12A800 0x7ff80412cc38`
reports **two**:

```
2 direct branch(es) to 0x7ff80412cc38:
  0x7ff80412ce97   call      <- __GetSystemGPUVendors_block_invoke +0x6b
  0x7ff804137526   call      <- CoreDisplay::Framebuffer::Framebuffer +0x8ec
```

The second one stores the result **per framebuffer**:

```
7ff804137526:  callq  0x7ff80412cc38
7ff80413752b:  movl   %eax, 0x1f0(%r14)
```

`fb+0x1f0` is `MPPriv+0x180`, and the offset is measured rather than counted:
`CoreDisplay::Framebuffer::InitializeMPPrivAccelerator` does
`movl 0x18(%rdi),%eax; movl %eax,0xcc(%rdi)`, which against 2px's decoded
`MPPriv +0x5c accelerator` puts the embedded MPPriv at **fb+0x70**
(0xcc - 0x5c), so 0x1f0 - 0x70 = **0x180**. And +0x180 is named by Apple:
`CoreDisplay::CreateMPPrivDict` pairs `movl 0x180(%r15), %edx` with the
CFString key **`gpuVendor`** - the field boot 148's state dump prints as
`gpuVendor = 1`, i.e. exactly the "unknown" bit 0x01 that 2ql's whole finding
is about. Same value, two consumers, one classifier.

### What the function-level patch would ALSO have changed

`MPGetGPUVendor(CGXDisplayDevice const*)` (`0x7ff8040e7e85`) is
`dev->0x160->0x180`, and `dsc.py dataxref` puts it at exactly one slot,
`0x7ff8404fc900`. Decoding the whole MP ops table from its base
`0x7ff8404fc700` (which independently reproduces 2qc's slot 0x140 =
`MPServiceForDisplayDevice` and 0x148 = `MPAcceleratorForDisplayDevice`) makes
it **slot 0x200**, and four call sites read it:

| caller | what the vendor decides |
|---|---|
| `access_display_pipe_info(MPPriv*)` | `testb $0x1c,%al; je <allocate>` - the 0x3018-byte pipe-info structure is allocated **only when the vendor is NOT** AMD/NVDA/APV. Vendor 4 makes this return **NULL** where it returns a real structure today. |
| `UseIOPGamma(dev)` | jump table on `(vendor-2) ror 1` into the per-vendor IOP gamma prefs (`useIOPresentmentGammaOnAMD` = 1 live) |
| `get_display_device_info` x2 | the state-dump/debug view |
| `__WSMachineIsAMD_block_invoke` | `cmpl $0x4,%eax` -> sets `0x7ff843bb1d40`, read by `CGXIsHDRSupported` and `__WSMachineUsesNewStyleMirroring_block_invoke` |

So patching the classifier would have changed the pipe-info allocator, the
gamma path, HDR support and the mirroring style **in addition to** the gate -
and the first of those moves in the direction we do not want. 2qm's "the entire
effect is `gSystemGPUVendors = 0x4`" was an inference from a caller count that
was never checked. Rule 26 again, and a new way to state it: **a blast radius
is a measurement, not a description.**

### The narrow lever costs the same five bytes

The call inside the vendors block is five bytes and so is the constant:

```
7ff80412ce97:  e8 9c fd ff ff    callq GetGPUVendorForFramebufferService
         ->    b8 04 00 00 00    movl  $0x4, %eax
7ff80412ce9c:  09 05 c2 4e a8 3f  orl  %eax, gSystemGPUVendors(%rip)
```

That leaves `gSystemGPUVendors` reading 4 and touches nothing else: the
`Framebuffer` constructor keeps calling the real classifier, so `gpuVendor`
stays 1 and all four decisions in the table above keep their present
behaviour. Checked rather than assumed:

* the replaced range is **one whole instruction**, and no branch in the block
  targets a byte inside it (its targets are ce92, ceae, ceb7, cedb, cef2);
* the classifier releases its own `IOObjectCopyClass` string internally and
  the block never releases the service, so skipping the call **leaks nothing
  it did not already leak**;
* `UseIOPresentment()` reads `gSystemGPUVendors` (int at `0x7ff843bb1d64`),
  and a `ripxref` of that global finds **9 sites in CoreDisplay and 0 in
  SkyLight**: `UseIOPresentment`, `EnableWSAA`, `AllowMatrixNightShift`,
  `GetCurrentSystemGPUVendorName`, `UpdateCrashLogMessage`,
  `CreateCoreDisplayStateDictWithOptions` and the block itself. So the global's
  blast radius is bounded and named - and `enableWSAA` reads **0** in the live
  state dump while all five `useIOP*` defaults read 1, which is why this flips
  IOPresentment and not WSAA.

Uniqueness, with `testl %eax,%eax; je` before and the `orl` after as anchors:
the 27-byte window occurs **once in the cache's entire 0x25198000-byte
executable mapping**, not merely once in CoreDisplay.

### Built, and gated twice

`-rbgpuiop` (boot-arg, **off by default**) plus the one-shot NVRAM variable
**`rbgpu-iop`**, consumed and flushed to flash immediately before the write.
That is the point of the design: 2qn's rescue was `-rbgpuoff` and a reboot,
which needs a boot-arg edit from another OS or single-user mode if the login
screen never appears. With a one-shot, **a black screen is recovered by a plain
power cycle.** The one-shot is checked LAST, after the readiness checks, so a
boot that fails a precondition does not burn the arming.

Scoped to `WindowServer` by **exact** name (`strcmp`, not the mtlk substring
match), placed through the existing `rbgpu_mtlk_place` - which reads the site
back from the target's own memory and compares before writing, and verifies
after (rule 20) - at `_task_set_main_thread_qos`, before the process executes
any instruction. That matters because `GetSystemGPUVendors` is a
`dispatch_once` inside `CGXMappedDisplayStart`. It is deliberately placed
BEFORE the mtlk scope/exclude logic: different patch, different image,
different purpose, and a scope string meant for the Metal driver must not
silently disable it.

Transcription checked against the machine rather than by eye (rule 5's
spirit): both byte arrays were searched for **in the built kext** and compared
to the live cache - `find` occurs once and is byte-identical to
`0x7ff80412ce87`, `replace` occurs once and is the intended patch.

Writes **no DCN register**. New UUID `3B40FB20-540E-3C9A-BE39-A0481860DB05`.

### Rule 14 keys, all NVRAM-hot

A boot that ends in a login screen that never appears can only be read from
NVRAM, so these go in `kRbgpuNvramHotKeys`, at the front:

`iop_on`, `iop_saw_ws`, `iop_ready`, `iop_oneshot`, `iop_match`, `iop_verify`,
`iop_patched`. Read them in that order:

* `iop_oneshot` - 0 armed and consumed, 1 /options unreachable, 2 not armed,
  3 literal "0", **4 armed but the clear did not take, so the NEXT boot is
  armed too and must be disarmed by hand.**
* `iop_saw_ws` absent -> WindowServer never execed while the hook was live;
  nothing was attempted and nothing is proven.
* `iop_match` - 1 the five bytes were the call, 2 already patched, 0 neither
  (an OS update moved the site; failing safe is the designed behaviour).
* **`iop_verify 1` is the only line that proves the write landed.**

### What the experiment can and cannot settle

`UseIOPresentment()` true makes `Display::GetNextSurface` take the
`DisplaySurfacePool` -> `CD_IOSurfaceCreate` path, which is the only one of its
two paths that is not closed (2qk closed the legacy one at
`IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode`). Every kernel precondition that path is known to
need is live and paired on this machine (2qm/2qn): `IOAccelIndex 0`,
`IOAccelRevision 2`, `DisplayPipeSupported=1`, `TransactionsSupported=1`, two
live `IOAccelDisplayPipeUserClient2`s, and AGDC's `debug-gpus` already listing
our framebuffer with our accelerator.

What it cannot settle in advance is whether something **else** inside
IOPresentment fails after the gate opens - `IOPresentmentBindIOAccelSurfaceToResource`
and `IOPresentmentSetPlaneState` are kernel APIs `IONDRVFramebuffer` does not
implement, and 2qn measured that no client-side probe can answer it because the
GPUWrangler user client is entitlement-gated and root does not clear it. So the
honest statement is: **this is the experiment that answers it, and its failure
mode is a black screen at login with a one-power-cycle recovery.**

Note on `UseIOPresentment` itself: 2ql's "do NOT force it" stands and is
untouched. This does not patch that function or any of its 72 call sites; it
corrects one input it reads, to a value that is **true of the hardware**.

### One precondition worth stating

`-rbgpumtlkoff` disables the kernel-side patcher's *install*, so the
`_task_set_main_thread_qos` route never happens, `rbgpu_mtlk_on_exec` never
fires and `rbgpu_iop_try` is never reached - `iop_on` would not even be
written. The two are on the same hook by design. Nobody is likely to set it,
but an absent `iop_on` with `mtlk_stage 0` means exactly that and not a
failure of this patch.

### Debt this leaves

`rbgpu_mtlk_place` keeps its scratch buffer in a `static`, so two concurrent
execs can interleave a compare with a verify. Pre-existing - it has shipped
~2000 patches a boot since 2on - and this adds a third site rather than fixing
it. Recorded, not smoothed over.

## 2qp - BOOT 150: THE GATE OPENED. Apple's own words: "System set to use IOP but no display pipes are present"

The patch worked, it did exactly what it was designed to do, and the display
half is **not** fixed - the blocker moved one layer down and is now named, with
a backtrace. No black screen; the user: *"desktop is on im on inot black"*.

### Every gate passes

`logs/20261025-013512-plugin/`, read from disk before live NVRAM (rule 10):

```
rbgpu-boot   150        (new - rule 8 satisfied)
rbgpu-arm    <unset>    consumed
rbgpu-iop    <unset>    consumed
loaded UUID  3B40FB20-540E-3C9A-BE39-A0481860DB05  == build/out
iop_on 1  iop_saw_ws 1  iop_ready 1  iop_oneshot 0
iop_match 1  iop_verify 1  iop_patched 1
```

`iop_match 1` - the five bytes at `0x7ff80412ce97 + slide` really were the
`callq`. **`iop_verify 1`** - the replacement was read back out of
WindowServer's own address space and compared (rule 20). `iop_oneshot 0` -
armed and the clear took, so the next boot is normal with no intervention.

### The gate opened, and Apple says so

`/usr/bin/log show --last boot`, with my own query at 01:36:30 as the
known-present control and every line attributed by timestamp **and** pid
(rule 28). `WindowServer[161]`, boot 150:

```
01:33:39.868  [CoreDisplay] [ERROR] -            <backtrace, below>
01:33:39.872  [CoreDisplay] [ERROR] - Error: No property 'FB_Triage', or property isn't a string.
01:33:39.872  [CoreDisplay] [ERROR] - Error: Can't get value for key 'Triage'.
01:33:39.919  [CoreDisplay] [ERROR] - System set to use IOP but no display pipes are present
```

**"System set to use IOP"** is the measurement this experiment existed to
produce. That string is LEA'd immediately before a `movb $0x0, gUseIOP` in the
`CoreDisplay::GPUController::GPUController()` block, so reaching it proves
`gSystemGPUVendors` passed the supported-mask test - the exact thing 2ql said
could never happen for any value of any preference. **The class-name test is
beaten.** 2ql's finding was right about the mechanism and this is its
confirmation from the other side.

And the backtrace at 39.868 names where it then failed:

```
0  ...__hash_table<...CoreDisplay::DisplayPipe...>::__emplace_unique_impl + 4340
1  CoreDisplay::Framebuffer::Framebuffer(unsigned, unsigned long long, unsigned, unsigned long long) + 3601
2  CoreDisplay::GPU::GPU(__GPUWranglerGPU*, dispatch_queue_s*) + 744
3  invocation function for block in CoreDisplay::GPUController::GPUController() + 2634
4  GPUWranglerRegisterEventBlock + 1077
5  CGXMappedDisplayStart + 4409
6  CGXDisplayDriverInitialize + 972
7  WS::Displays::CoreDisplayManager::initialize() + 43
8  WSInitialize + 3959
```

So: the GPUWrangler event block builds a `CoreDisplay::GPU`, which builds a
`CoreDisplay::Framebuffer`, which tries to put a `DisplayPipe` into an
`unordered_map<unsigned long long, CoreDisplay::DisplayPipe>` and fails. Zero
pipes exist, so `GPUController` turns IOP back off.

### Three things measured that kill three easier explanations

**It is not a preference.** `defaults read com.apple.CoreDisplay` and
`defaults -currentHost read com.apple.CoreDisplay` both answer *"Domain
com.apple.CoreDisplay does not exist"* - the code reads `kCFPreferencesAnyUser`
+ `kCFPreferencesCurrentHost`, so that is the domain, and nothing is set in it.
2ql's "all five prefs default to 1, no `defaults write` is missing" holds.

**`FB_Triage` is a RED HERRING, and I nearly acted on it.** The two 39.872
errors look like the cause - a missing string property named almost exactly
like `IOAccelDisplayPipeTriage`, which 2qm found in IOPresentment's own
strings - and the obvious move was to publish it from the plugin the way 2pa
publishes `VRAM,totalMB`. `ripxref` on the string says otherwise: its only
readers are **`DumpIORegistryFrameBufferInfo`** and
**`DumpIORegistryAcceleratorInfo`**. They are diagnostic dumps that run
*because* the pipe failed. Publishing `FB_Triage` would have changed a debug
dump and nothing else. **Read what consumes a value before acting on it** -
the recurring error, caught this time before it cost a boot.
(`AMDRadeonX6000` does carry `FB Triage - Pipe %u:` and `Triage parameters are
incorrect for Display - %d string=%p, length=%p`, so the property is real and
AMD's framebuffer publishes it. It is still not what refused the pipe.)

**And the ioreg grep that "confirmed" its absence was a broken instrument.**
`grep -c -i triage` over the capture returned 0 - but so did the control,
`grep -c VRAM,totalMB`, for a property we publish ourselves. Rule 26: the
search was not checked against a known-present case, so its 0 meant nothing.

### `gUseIOP` is a LATCH, which constrains every future attempt

Read instruction by instruction at `0x7ff804057b40`, not from 2ql's
pseudocode:

```
movzbl gUseIOP(%rip), %eax        ; 0x7ff843bac76d
cmpb   $0x1, %al
jne    .ret                       ; <- once it is not 1, the function is a no-op forever
cmpq   $-1, [0x7ff843bb1d68]      ; dispatch_once guard
jne    .run_GetSystemGPUVendors   ; it TRIGGERS the vendors block itself
...
testl  %eax, %eax                 ; present == 0 ?
je     .fail
andl   %eax, %ecx
cmpl   %eax, %ecx                 ; (supported & present) != present ?
jne    .fail
movb   gUseIOP(%rip), %al
.fail:
movb   $0x0, gUseIOP(%rip)        ; LATCH OFF
```

Two consequences. First, **ordering was never the risk**: the function runs
`GetSystemGPUVendors`' `dispatch_once` itself, so our patched classifier is
guaranteed to have been used on the first call. Second, `CGXMappedDisplayStart`
writes `$0` to `gUseIOP` directly at **three further sites**
(`+0x1232`, `+0x2881`, `+0x2894`), each beside an os_log explaining itself. So
IOP, once refused for any reason, is refused for the life of the process - and
re-opening the vendor gate alone can never be enough if a later check fails.

### Where this leaves it

Unchanged on screen, and that is expected rather than disappointing: the legacy
path still runs (`IOAccelSurface::set_id_mode: New id (0x00000001) less than
256` still appears twice this boot), so the DisplaySurface still has no
IOSurface and `CompositorSW` still rasterises the desktop. `Metal compositor
activated.` still appears exactly twice, as in boot 149.

**The frontier is now one function, and it is static work.**
`CoreDisplay::FindDisplayPipeForService(unsigned)` (`0x7ff804056d04`) opens
with `movb [0x7ff843bad2d8], %al; testb %al, %al; je <bail>` - a gate byte -
then loads `[0x7ff843bad2b8]` and popcounts it (the
`0x5555.../0x3333.../0x0f0f...` sequence) to size a hash table, bailing on
`testq %rsi,%rsi; je`. `CoreDisplay::DisplayPipeForService(unsigned)`
(`0x7ff804056c52`) wraps it and logs **"Unable to find display pipe"** on the
miss. So the next read is **who populates that map** - `InitializeDisplayPipes`
and whatever `GPUWranglerRegisterEventBlock` hands it - and what about our
`IONDRVFramebuffer` makes the emplace fail.

**Keep `-rbgpuiop` as it is.** It is correct, verified, costs five bytes in one
process, and is inert without the one-shot. It is also the only way to reach
this layer at all: without it the chain stops one step earlier, at the vendor
mask, and `FindDisplayPipeForService` is never consulted.

## 2qq - the DisplayPipe constructor, decoded: WindowServer answered 2qn's question and the capability really is absent

2qp left the frontier at "who populates the DisplayPipe map and why does our
framebuffer's emplace fail". Both are now read, statically, and the answer
closes the question 2qn said only WindowServer could settle.

### The constructor, three calls

The `DisplayPipe` is built inline inside the map's
`__emplace_unique_impl` (which is why `atos` reports a 4 KB "hash emplace" -
the pipe's whole construction is inlined into it). Stubs resolved by hand
through their GOT slots (`ff 25 disp32` -> GOT -> chained-pointer decode) and
then symbolized, rather than guessed:

```
registryID = IORegistryEntryGetRegistryEntryID(service)      ; 0x7ff8058b5d43
pipe       = IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryID(0, registryID)  ; 0x7ff812e88a67
if (pipe == NULL)                 throw CoreDisplay::Backtrace  ; 0x7ff804059957
if (IOPresentmentInitialize(pipe) != 0) throw CoreDisplay::Backtrace ; 0x7ff804059967
```

The throw is built from `CoreDisplay::Backtrace::Backtrace()` +
`CoreDisplay::Backtrace::GetString()` - which is exactly the shape of boot
150's log entry: an `[ERROR] -` with an **empty message** followed by a
symbolized backtrace. The message was empty because the payload *is* the
backtrace.

### `IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryID` and its two NULL paths

The exported function is a three-line wrapper:

```
7ff812e88a67:  callq 0x7ff812e8c0b8     ; the worker; rdi/rsi pass straight through
               testq %rax,%rax
               je    .return_NULL
               mov   %rax,%rdi ; jmp <wrap/retain>
.return_NULL:  xorl  %eax,%eax ; retq
```

The worker (`0x7ff812e8c0b8`) has **exactly two** branches to its NULL tail at
`0x7ff812e8c8f7`, and each logs its own reason first:

| site | condition | Apple's message | line |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x7ff812e8c183` | `cmpq %r12,%r15; jne` falls through, i.e. **arg0 == arg1** | **`bad arg: %#llx %#llx`** | 0xdd0 |
| `0x7ff812e8c334` | the lookup miss | **`no match %#llx %#llx`** | 0xdc9 |

`no match` is `ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch` failing - the function 2qm named
from IOPresentment's own strings. The call site passes `edi = 0` and
`rsi = registryID`, and a valid registry ID is non-zero, so `arg0 == arg1` is
false and **the `no match` path is the one that must have fired**. That last
step is an inference from the call site, not a measurement - see below for how
to measure it.

### What this settles, and it is the point of the whole experiment

2qn ended with three possible outcomes for `ioptest` and said of the third:

> `kIOReturnNotPermitted` again -> still INCONCLUSIVE; the only remaining
> instrument is WindowServer itself.

**Boot 150 is WindowServer itself, and it answered.** The same
`IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryID` that refused `ioptest` with
`kIOReturnNotPermitted` ran inside the one process that *has* the entitlement,
against our framebuffer's own registry ID, and **returned NULL**. So:

* the entitlement was never the real obstacle, only the reason a client probe
  could not see past it;
* **the capability genuinely is absent for an `IONDRVFramebuffer`**, and
  **2ql's verdict is now confirmed by measurement rather than argument**;
* **2qm's conclusion is contradicted.** 2qm read AGDC's `debug-gpus` pairing
  of our framebuffer (`0x100000548`) with our accelerator (`0x10000054a`) and
  concluded "what the class-name test refuses appears to be already wired up".
  The pairing exists and the match still fails, so `ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch`
  wants something that pairing does not supply, or keys on a different id.

And one prediction of 2ql's was simply **wrong**, which is worth recording as
plainly as the parts that were right: it said forcing the gate "would
black-screen". It did not. Boot 150 came up normally, the user confirmed it,
and the only visible effect of opening the gate was two extra error lines in
the log. The risk was real and correctly flagged; it did not materialise.

### The next measurement is free, and Apple wrote it

Both messages above are behind a log-level check (`esi = 0x10`), which is why
neither appeared in boot 150. IOPresentment's string table shows how it is
enabled - it reads `IODeviceTree:/options` -> **`boot-args`** and looks for the
token **`IOPresentment`**:

```
IODeviceTree:/options
boot-args
...
IOPresentment:
boot-args:
IOPresentment
```

So `sudo tools/efi.sh bootarg add IOPresentment` makes Apple print `no match
%#llx %#llx` (or `bad arg`) **with both ids**, which distinguishes the two
paths and names exactly what it compared. **Logging only - it writes nothing,
patches nothing and carries no black-screen risk.** It needs `-rbgpuiop` armed
in the same boot, because without the vendor gate open the pipe is never
attempted and there is nothing to log.

### Honest assessment of where this leaves the display half

The chain is now closed from the compositor all the way down to a single
Apple API returning NULL for our framebuffer:

```
IONDRVFramebuffer -> IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryID -> NULL
  -> DisplayPipe ctor throws -> zero pipes in the map
  -> "System set to use IOP but no display pipes are present" -> gUseIOP = 0
  -> GetNextSurface takes the legacy path -> set_id_mode rejects id 1 (2qk)
  -> DisplaySurface with no IOSurface (2qh) -> CompositorSW rasterises (2pd)
```

Every link is measured. The remaining lever is whatever
`ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch` needs, and 2ql's larger point stands: this is the
IOPresentment *world*, and `IONDRVFramebuffer` implements none of
`IOPresentmentBindIOAccelSurfaceToResource` / `IOPresentmentSetPlaneState`.
Opening one more gate may well surface the next one. The structural fix
remains the one 2pd named - an accelerated framebuffer owning the display,
which needs DCN 3.1.2 code macOS does not contain - and nothing here changes
that estimate.

## 2qr - Apple names the cause, 2qq's inference is CORRECTED, and the IOPresentment route ends at the missing AMD framebuffer

2qq inferred that `IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryID` failed on its `no match`
path. **That inference was wrong, and boot 150's log already contained the
answer** - I had filtered it out by querying `subsystem ==
"com.apple.CoreDisplay"`, and IOPresentment logs under its own name. Querying
for `GPUWrangler OR AGDC OR Presentment` instead, with the query's own line as
the control (rule 26) and every line attributed by timestamp and pid (rule 28):

```
01:33:39.865  E  WindowServer[161:3d0] (IOPresentment) Error: Unable to get AGDC information.  Return code: 0x10000003
01:33:39.868  E  WindowServer[161:3d0] [com.apple.CoreDisplay:default] [ERROR] - <the DisplayPipe backtrace>
```

Three milliseconds apart, same process, same thread. **Apple names the cause
itself**, and it is one step EARLIER than 2qq guessed: not the AGDC map match,
but the **AGDC information query** that precedes it. The format string
`"Unable to get AGDC information.  Return code: %#x"` is in IOPresentment's
`__oslogstring` at `0x7ff812ea2887`, alongside `AGDCVendorInfo %#x %#x %#zx`,
`AGDCVendorInfo failed %#llx %#x %#zx`, `AGDCGPUCapability %#llx %zu %u` and
`AGDC map invalid` - so what IOPresentment wants from AGDC is **VendorInfo and
GPUCapability**.

### And the IORegistry says those are empty

`AppleGPUWrangler`'s `debug-gpus`, re-read **live** on this boot rather than
copied from 2qn:

```
{"id"=64455, "acc"=4294968640, "fbs"=(4294968638), "gpuc"=0, "pci"=4294967993,
 "agdp"=0, "cc"=3, "flags"=2986344480, "tds"=0, ...}
```

| field | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `acc` | 0x1000003C0 | our accelerator |
| `fbs[0]` | 0x1000003BE | our `.Display_boot` `IONDRVFramebuffer` |
| **`gpuc`** | **0** | **GPU capability - empty** |
| **`agdp`** | **0** | **no AppleGraphicsDevicePolicy / vendor AGDC plugin** |

`AGDCPluginDisplayMetrics` is loaded but its instance is
`!registered, !matched`.

**This corrects 2qn as well.** 2qn read the same `debug-gpus` entry and
concluded: *"AGDC already knows our IONDRVFramebuffer and our AMD accelerator
as one GPU. That is the association `ioPresentmentFindAGDCMatch()` looks for,
and it exists."* The **association** exists. The **information** does not -
`gpuc` and `agdp` are both 0. 2qn checked that the row was there and did not
check what the row contained, and the row's emptiness is exactly what
IOPresentment reports. Rule 13 in a new place: a field being present is not the
same as a field being populated.

### Where `gpuc` and `agdp` come from, and why that ends this route

They are filled by the **vendor's** AGDC plugin - for AMD, the stack rooted at
`AMDSupport`/`AMDFramebuffer`. That stack **never instantiates on this
machine**, and 2oq established why, statically: no controller personality
matches `0x16811002`, so no `AtiFbStub` is published, so no `AMDFramebuffer`,
**and macOS contains no DCN 3.1.2 code at all** (`dcn31`/`dcn312`/`vba_31`/
`yellow_carp` are 0 hits in every AMD kext against a control of 58 for
`dcn30`).

So the full chain, every link now measured on hardware:

```
no DCN 3.1.2 in macOS -> no AMD controller personality matches 0x1681
  -> no AMDFramebuffer -> AGDC has no vendor plugin for this GPU
```
