no corresponding type and is fed by something else.

**That reconciles 2sd.** Answering all five types filled the five groups that
do not gate anything, and left untouched the one group that does. It is no
longer surprising that boot 170's log was byte-identical: the thing being
refused was never one of the five.

### The candidate, named but NOT established

IOPresentment's string table carries two IORegistry property names, both
referenced from `ioPresentmentPopulateIOFramebufferEntries`:
**`kAGDCGPUCapability`** and **`kAGDCVendorInfo`**. Our AGDC service publishes
**neither** — `rbgpu_agdc.cpp` sets only `NeedsPolicyDriver`,
`IOUserClientClass` and `RBGPUAGDCBridge`.

That is a co-location of key names, **not** a read of where `PlaneArray` is
filled, and it is recorded as a hypothesis only. The project's own rule is to
find the consumer before writing a field (2q9/2qa), and that read has not been
done. Do not publish `kAGDCGPUCapability` on the strength of this paragraph.

### Next

Read `__GatherAGDCDisplayPipelineCapabilities` (`0x7ff812e979dc`) itself and
find where the plane group is filled and from what. It is the one function
that sits between the AGDC replies and every capability CoreDisplay later
reads, and both remaining unknowns — the plane count and why
`System Gamma - Unknown` survived a successful type 2 reply — are inside it.
Static, no boot.

## 2sg — the plane count cannot come from AGDC at all, and 2rg had already read the function I went to read

No boot. Two results, one of them about method.

### The method failure first

I read `__GatherAGDCDisplayPipelineCapabilities` and `__GatherAGDCLogicalDeviceCapabilities`
from scratch and reported the bit-0 gate at `0x7ff812e979b7` as a finding.
**2rg had already read all of it**, by address, and `rb_agdc.h`'s own comment
on `+0xa4` cites that function by name. Worse, 2rg had already settled the
question I was about to pursue. One `grep GatherAGDCLinkCapabilities
docs/JOURNAL.md` at the start would have cost nothing and saved the whole
detour. That is the project's own recurring error — **read the evidence
already in hand before designing the next experiment** — and it is now
recorded for the third time (2kx/2la/2lc, 2s5, here).

### What is actually established, combining old and new

`__GatherAGDCDisplayPipelineCapabilities` (`0x7ff812e979dc`, 0x111a bytes)
issues **attribute 0x711 exactly sixteen times and nothing else**. Its
immediates are the sixteen qwords `0x800000001 … 0x800008000` — stored at
struct+0x04, so type at +0x04 and **count 8 pre-loaded at +0x08**, which is
`rb_agdc.h:178`'s claim confirmed from the caller's side — plus `0x196c`, the
struct size, and `0x2006`, its failure code. Four distinct callees, 16/16/32/32
calls. Sixteen queries is exactly what boots 169 and 170 measured
(`agdc_extcap_calls = 16`).

`__GatherAGDCLogicalDeviceCapabilities` (`0x7ff812e9781a`) issues **0x921
once** and copies the whole 0xb0 reply into the capability block — `reply+0x2c`
lands at `0x19b28`, the field its caller divides by hTotal × vTotal, which
independently re-confirms 2rd/2rg's `IODetailedTimingInformationV2`-at-+0x04
embedding from a third direction. It returns 0x808 with no device, 0x80E on a
failed or empty 0x921.

`__GatherAGDCLinkCapabilities` (`0x7ff812e98af6`) is reached only when
link-config `+0x08` bit 0 is set, which we deliberately clear. **2rg already
measured that this is a dead end**: it issues 0x925 and 0x988 and all it
ultimately writes is `this->0x19c78`, which has *four writers and ZERO readers
in the entire image*. Setting bit 0 "would cost two answerable queries and
change nothing".

### The deduction

Those three functions are the **entire** AGDC input to
`IOPresentmentCreateCapabilities`. The plane count is in none of them:

- not the sixteen 0x711 queries — boot 170 answered all five answerable types
  and the plane group and the pipe state did not move (2sd);
- not the 0x921 logical-device reply — we answer it correctly as of boot 169
  (`agdc_link_result 0`) and the copy is wholesale, so there is no field of it
  we are withholding;
- not the link gather — unreachable by our own choice, and measured inert.

So **the plane count does not come from AGDC**, and `PlaneArray` having no
corresponding capability type (2sf) is not an accident of naming — there is no
AGDC query that carries it. `_IOPresentmentSetPlaneCount` has no caller inside
IOPresentment, so CoreDisplay sets it, and CoreDisplay's
`IOPCapabilities::PlaneCount` must be fed from something that is not the AGDC
gather.

### Where that points

IOPresentment links against `IOAccelDisplayPipe*` symbols — a DYLD stub for
`IOAccelDisplayPipeTransactionSetPlaneEmpty` sits in its stub table. That is
the IOAccelerator user library over `IOAccelDisplayPipe` in
IOAcceleratorFamily2, the same class whose `signalVBLInterrupt` we have been
feeding since 2s5, and whose vendor half `AMDRadeonX6000` already implements
in full (2s4, `AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelDisplayPipe`). A plane count sourced
there rather than from AGDC is consistent with every measurement in this
sequence, and it would explain why four milestones of AGDC work moved nothing.

It is a direction, not a result. The next read is the `IOAccelDisplayPipe`
plane interface — kernel side, `IOAcceleratorFamily2`, where `nm` works and
`dumptable.py` decodes the vtables — **not** more of the dyld cache. And 2rg's
closing line in its own entry already said where this was going: "Still
absent: the bind/transaction/scanout backend, **all plane state**".

Nothing was built. No boot was spent.

## 2sh — NullMoth's two personalities are a blueprint, and they reframe why the AGDC work could not have worked

No boot, no code. The user asked whether the other third-party drivers help.
`/Library/Extensions` still holds `NVAccel`, `NVRM`, `NVRMAGDC` and `NVRMFB`,
so the architecture is on this disk and its Info.plists are readable without
touching anyone's source. 2rv already noted the `NVRMFBClaim` line; the full
personality set is new here and it says more than the one line did.

```
NVRMFB.kext
  NVRMFBClaim   IOProviderClass=IOPCIDevice  IONameMatch=display
                IOMatchCategory=IOFramebuffer   IOProbeScore=30000
  NVRMFB        IOClass=NVRMNVDAFramebuffer  IOProviderClass=NVRMDisplay
                IOProbeScore=1000
NVRMAGDC.kext
  NVDAGDCLoader IOClass=NVDAGDCLoader  IOProviderClass=IOResources
                IOResourceMatch=IOKit  IOMatchCategory=NVDAGDCLoader
```

### Three things that transfer

**1. How to displace `.Display_boot`.** `IOMatchCategory = IOFramebuffer` +
`IONameMatch = display` on `IOPCIDevice` at **`IOProbeScore` 30000**. 2oz
established the provider and category; the probe score is the part that
outbids `IONDRVFramebuffer`, and here it is as a worked example rather than a
guess.

**2. The framebuffer attaches to the driver's OWN service, not to PCI.**
`NVRMFB`'s real class takes `IOProviderClass = NVRMDisplay` — a service the
claim stage publishes. So the shape is two-stage: a cheap high-score claim
wins the display category, then the real framebuffer matches on the driver's
own node. Nothing about that requires Apple's framebuffer kext.

**3. `IOResources` matching sidesteps the wrangler race entirely.**
`NVDAGDCLoader` matches `IOProviderClass = IOResources`,
`IOResourceMatch = IOKit` — it loads as soon as IOKit is up, with no race to
win. Our bridge publishes on the PCI device and races `AppleGPUWrangler`,
which is the whole of 2rx/2rz/2r0 and the reason `-rbgpuagdcearly` exists and
wedges. This is a different mechanism for being early. It would **not** fix
the wedge — boots 164/169/170 won the race and wedged anyway — but it is a
cleaner way to be early than the notification race, and worth holding.

### What this reframes

Every AGDC milestone from 2s9 to 2sd fed capabilities to a framebuffer that
**structurally cannot participate**. `IONDRVFramebuffer` is the generic NDRV
driver; it implements none of the IOFramebuffer hooks IOPresentment needs, and
2s3's pre-statement said as much before any of those boots. So the capability
work was answering questions on behalf of a driver that was never going to be
asked the next one. That is a better explanation of 2sd's null result than
anything in 2sd or 2se.

And it suggests the path that does not dead-end on missing DCN code: **our own
`IOFramebuffer` subclass**, winning the category the way `NVRMFBClaim` does,
implementing the plane/transaction hooks — while leaving scanout exactly where
it already is. We do not need DCN 3.1.2 to scan out: OTG0 is already running
(`OTG0_CONTROL 0x00011201`, DMCUB 4.0.15.47, 143.898 Hz measured) and the GOP
framebuffer is BAR0 offset 0 (2pr). Firmware did the mode-set permanently at
boot. What `IONDRVFramebuffer` withholds is not pixels, it is the hooks.

**This is a design hypothesis, not a measurement.** It is also a large build
and its failure mode is a black screen, rescuable with `-rbgpuoff`. Nothing
should be written until the plane-count read in `IOAcceleratorFamily2` says
whether the transaction path can be satisfied at all.

### What does NOT transfer, and the licence line

NVIDIA display hardware shares nothing with DCN 3.1.2, so no register, timing
or sequence knowledge crosses over — only the IOKit-side shape above, which is
match-dictionary configuration read from this machine's own
`/Library/Extensions`. Measured and still true (2rv): `NVRMFBClaim`,
`NVRMNVDAFramebuffer`, `NVDAGDCLoader` and `NVRMDisplay` instantiate **zero**
instances here, and boot 170 loaded only Lilu and our plugin. It is a
blueprint, not a working example on this machine.

**An RDNA 3 iGPU driver is the one that could carry display code**, because
Phoenix is DCN **3.1.4** and this chip is DCN **3.1.2** — the same
`DCN_VERSION_3_1` grouping this project's own register rule keys off. Which
project that is, and its licence, is **not** known here and must come from the
user. **NootedRed and NootRX remain hard-blocked** by the ChefKiss Open
Knowledge License v1 §2/§3: if the RDNA 3/4 iGPU drivers are ChefKiss work,
Claude cannot read or analyse them and findings must come from the user in
their own words. "WhateverXe" is unknown here and nothing is assumed about it.

## 2si — the wedge is NOT `wait_for_queue_slot_gated`, and eight instructions prove it

No boot. Kernel side, `build/re/IOAcceleratorFamily2`, where `nm` and
`objdump` work properly.

### The queue, in full

```
IOAccelDisplayPipe::wait_for_queue_slot_gated()           0x14e60526
    eax = this->0x23c - this->0x238
    if (eax != 4) return;                  // <- a free slot: returns at once
    do { commandSleep(gate, this, 0); }     // gate = this->0xb0, vt[0x1e0]
    while (this->0x23c - this->0x238 == 4);
```

```
IOAccelDisplayPipe::transaction_queue_gated(txn)          0x14e60466
    if (this->0x2a4 == 0) { this->0x2a4 = 1; vt[0x888](this); }   // enable vbl
    txn->0x58 = vt[0x8b8](this, txn);                             // stamp
    slot = this->0x23c % 4;                 // signed mod: lea/cmovns/and -4/sub
    *(this + 0x118 + slot*0x48 + 0x40) = txn;
    vt[0x1b0](this->0x88->0x380, txn+0x60);
    sfence;
    this->0x23c++;                          // write index
```

So the ring is **four entries**, base `0x118`, stride `0x48`; `0x23c` is the
write index, `0x238` the read index, and **the depth is the compiled constant
4**. There is no queue-depth field, no plane count and no capability anywhere
in it. Both functions agree, read independently.

### What that forces

`wait_for_queue_slot_gated` sleeps **if and only if exactly four transactions
are outstanding**. On a pipe that has never queued one, `0x23c - 0x238` is 0,
`0 != 4`, and the function **returns on its second instruction**. It is
structurally incapable of blocking an idle pipe.

And boot 168 measured that nothing was ever queued: `fb_vbl_ot_armed` absent
with `diag_used` 571 of 768, so `0x2a4` was never set, so
`transaction_queue_gated` never ran.

**Therefore WindowServer was not blocked in `wait_for_queue_slot_gated`.**

### The claim this withdraws

CLAUDE.md has carried, since 2s2, that *"past the gate WindowServer submits a
display-pipe transaction and blocks in Apple's own
`IOAccelDisplayPipe::wait_for_queue_slot_gated` — `commandSleep` with no
deadline, THREAD_UNINT, zero os_log refs"*. The description of the sleep is
accurate; **the location is wrong**, and it has been wrong since 2s2. 2s2 read
what the function does when it sleeps and never read the condition under which
it is reached. That is rule 13 — a return code, or here a sleep, is not a
result until the code that reaches it has been read — applied to this
project's own conclusion.

Boot 168 and 2s2 were in direct conflict for four milestones and nobody put
them side by side. Boot 168 wins.

Also corrected: the transaction-interrupt flag is `this->0x2a4`, not `0x281` as
earlier notes had it. The vtable call is dump offset `0x888`
(`enable_vbl_interrupt`), used as a direct jump through the vtable symbol, so
rule 7's dump-offset form applies and 2s5's table agrees.

### Where it actually blocks — inferred, not measured

Positive evidence, from boot 169 and 170's own logs: **56 byte-identical
`DisplayPipeState` dumps and `Clean` appearing zero times in 156 KB.** A
kernel `commandSleep` produces one dump and then silence. Fifty-six identical
dumps is a **retry loop in userspace**, and the only function that both calls
`AreOperationsSupportedInHW` and enters `RunGPUDisplayPipe` is
`CoreDisplay::DisplayPipe::Commit` (`0x7ff80411633c`, 2sb).

So the wedge is most likely a **livelock in CoreDisplay's Commit**, not a
kernel sleep at all. That fits every measurement in this sequence: no
transaction ever queued, no AGDC error in the log, no kernel wait reachable,
nothing ever Clean, and a machine that stops responding without panicking.

**This is an inference from the dump count, not a measurement.** What `Commit`
retries on is unread, and that is the next thing to read — in the dyld cache,
`0x7ff80411633c`, chunked (2sb's `dscdis.sh` truncation applies).

Nothing was built. No boot was spent.

## 2sj — nullarc's framebuffer uses NONE of the path 2s2–2si chased, and that is the redirection

No boot. The user supplied `luuumi-dev/nullarc` and `Almosst-DEV/Cobalt64`.
2mk already cleared nullarc's licence (MIT or GPL-2.0-only own code,
PolyForm-NC for `src/phxaccel`/`src/nmplugin`/`tools/nvmtl-patches`, **no AI
restriction**) and surveyed its four echelons — but 2mk was about the glyph
defect, and never asked the question that is now the whole frontier.

`Cobalt64` is MIT, RDNA 4 / Navi 48, a preview tested on one PC, not yet
installable. Architecturally the furthest of the three from gfx1033 and the
least mature; nothing to take now.

### `PhxAMDFB` (src/phxaccel/accel/phxfb.cpp), read for the display path

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| superclass | **`IOFramebuffer`** — not `IONDRVFramebuffer`. Takes over the mode the firmware GOP already lit, replacing the firmware framebuffer at boot |
| IOPresentment | named in **one comment**; the code never uses it |
| `IOAccelDisplayPipe` | comments only |
| display-pipe transactions | comments only; no transaction code |
| `SetPlaneState`, `BindIOAccelSurfaceToResource`, plane state | **absent entirely**, code and comments |
| DCN register writes | **none** — "writes nothing to the display engine". `measureRefresh` maps BAR5 and only **reads** OTG0 timing and frame counter |
| mode | one mode, measured refresh, 32-bit direct, built-in |
| scanout | `getApertureRange` returns the **boot console's physical surface** |
| vblank | `registerForInterruptType` accepts up to **four** VBL handlers, driven by a `thread_call` at panel refresh |
| accelerator hooks | `callPlatformFunction` for VRAM alloc/free and GPU-VA, emulating an NVIDIA RM interface so the accelerator can allocate surfaces |
| who composites | **not this class.** `PhxAccel` / `NMXAccel` composites for WindowServer; this supplies the framebuffer side |

### The redirection

**A working RDNA 3 driver, on DCN 3.1.4 — the same `DCN_VERSION_3_1` grouping
as our 3.1.2 — gets WindowServer compositing at 120 Hz while using none of
IOPresentment, AGDC transactions, plane state or display-pipe queues.**

So the path 2s2 through 2si chased is **optional**. 2s3's "there is no
transactions-off mode" was true of `IOPresentmentCreateForRegistryID`
specifically, and the correct inference was not "we must satisfy
IOPresentment" but "we need not go through IOPresentment at all".

Everything that path cost — the AGDC bridge's capability work (2s9–2sd), the
plane-count hunt (2se–2sg), the queue read (2si) — was elimination inside a
subsystem a working driver skips. The eliminations stand as facts; their
relevance does not.

And note how closely their framebuffer matches instruments we **already have
measured and working**: OTG0 read-only sampling (`otg_err 0`, 143.898 Hz,
2rn/2s9), the GOP surface at BAR0 offset 0 (2pr), a timer-driven vblank to
multiple registrants (`-rbgpuvbl`/`-rbgpuvblpump`/`-rbgpufbvbl`, de-aliased
for multiple handlers in 2s5), and the single firmware mode the NDRV already
reports. We have been building the parts of their framebuffer for weeks
without the framebuffer.

### Why this project is better placed than nullarc was

nullarc had to write **all four** echelons because Apple's driver stops at
RDNA 2 (Navi 21/23) and gfx1103 has nothing to reuse. **Our chip is gfx1033 —
inside the generation Apple still supports**, and our accelerator already
works: `AMDRadeonX6000_AMDNavi21GraphicsAccelerator` is attached and Metal
compute is bit-exact. We would need only the framebuffer half.

**The open question that decides it, and it is NOT established:** will Apple's
`AMDRadeonX6000` composite for a framebuffer that is not Apple's? nullarc's
compositor is their own `NMXAccel`, so their result does not answer it.

### A claim I went to verify and could NOT

`phxfb.cpp` carries a comment that **CoreDisplay disables IOPresentment for
framebuffers whose class name lacks "AMD"**. If true it would explain this
entire sequence at a stroke, since ours is `IONDRVFramebuffer`. So it was
checked rather than believed.

**It is unverified, and the obvious evidence for it is something else.** The
only bare `"AMD"` string in that region of the cache (`0x415ad4a`) sits in a
watchdog message table beside `"Intel"`, `"Transaction hang (IG IOFB)"`,
`"IOAF waiting for GPU work completion stamp (IG 3D Driver)"`, `"AMD
transaction hang or work overload (AMD IOFB)"` and `"CD surface count issue
(CoreDisplay)"` — **vendor tags for hang diagnosis, not a class-name gate**.
Both `IONDRVFramebuffer` hits in the cache are the property name
`IONDRVFramebufferGeneration`, not a comparison. The claim may still be true
elsewhere in CoreDisplay; it is **not** to be acted on as fact.

### One real measurement that fell out of looking

Those watchdog strings are exactly the diagnoses CoreDisplay emits for a hung
transaction, so the wedged boots were checked for them. **Zero hits** for
transaction hang, work overload, surface-count issue or IOAF waiting, in
**both** boot 169 and boot 170 — against a control of 112 hits for a
known-present pattern and **757** CoreDisplay/WindowServer lines in the same
file.

So CoreDisplay's own watchdog never fired. There was no transaction to hang,
which is independent support for 2si: the loop never reaches submission, and
the wedge is not a wait on submitted work.

### Licence note for whatever gets built

Reading `src/phxaccel` is permitted and 2mk established that. **Copying from
it carries PolyForm-NC** (noncommercial only) and would attach that to the
derived files here. Learning the architecture — that an `IOFramebuffer`
subclass over the firmware-lit mode is sufficient — is not copying. Which
side of that line any future framebuffer kext sits on is the user's decision,
not Claude's, and should be made before code is written rather than after.

Nothing was built. No boot was spent.

## 2sk — the accelerator id's producer, and the lookup is NOT what fails

No boot. 2sj redirected away from IOPresentment; nullarc's compositing runs
through **Metal**, and 2pu had already named the Metal-vs-software decision end
to end. This picks up 2pu's one open question.

### 2pu's decision, restated

```
WSGetCompositorForAccelerator(accelId)          0x7ff807c9b78c
    mode = *0x7ff843c9ecdc                      ; 0 Metal, 1 SW, 2 debug
    if (mode == 2)                  return debug;
    if (mode != 0)                  return SW;
    if (accelId == 0)               return SW;          ; (a)
    if ((*0x7ff843ca08b0 & 1) == 0) return SW;          ; (b)
    return getMetalCompositorFor(accelId);
```

Mode is 0 — `Metal compositor activated.` is logged every boot — so the
software path is taken by **(a)** or **(b)** and nothing else. 2pu could not
say which, because the id arrives through `CDDisplay`'s vtable slot +0x60 and
that slot is chained-fixup encoded.

### The producer, read without needing that vtable

`CGXAcceleratorForDisplayDevice` is a stub in SkyLight, imported from
CoreDisplay, where the implementation is **`MPAcceleratorForDisplayDevice`**
(`0x7ff8040e6825`). Its own log string gives the real signature:

```
CGError MPAcceleratorForDisplayDevice(const CGXDisplayDevice *const, int32_t,
                                      CGXDisplayAccelerator *,
                                      CGXDisplayAcceleratorID *)
```

```
    if (outID) *outID = 0;
    *outAccel = 0;                                  ; BOTH pre-zeroed
    rec = lookup(dev->0x160, idx);                  ; 0x7ff8040ebef2
    if (!rec) { log("%s: Invalid device alias (%d)"); return 0x3e9; }
    *outAccel = rec->0x5c;
    if (outID) *outID = rec->0x98;
    return 0;
```

The lookup walks a linked list off `dev->0x160`, matching a record on its
`+0x60` and `+0x64` fields (bounds-checked `<= 0x20`, rejecting negative
indices).

**So `accelId == 0` — test (a), the one that routes to the software compositor
— is exactly what a failed lookup leaves behind**, because both out-params are
zeroed before it and the failure path returns without writing them. It is also
what a found record holding zero in that field produces. Two routes to the
same zero.

### And the measurement: the lookup is not failing

The failure path logs `MPAcceleratorForDisplayDevice: Invalid device alias
(%d)`. **That string appears in ZERO captures in `logs/`**, against a control
of **704** CoreDisplay lines in the same file.

So CoreDisplay **finds** the record. The accelerator id is whatever
`rec->0x5c` / `rec->0x98` holds, and 2pu's open question narrows: it is not a
failed lookup. Either the record carries zero in that field, or test (b) — bit
0 of `*0x7ff843ca08b0` — is the one failing.

**Caveat on that negative**: the failure logs through `0x7ff80405f052`, and
whether that is an always-on error channel or a gated category has **not**
been checked. 704 CoreDisplay lines show the subsystem is logging, which is
why the negative is worth recording, but it is not the same control as
catching this specific logger with a known-present line.

### What is now worth doing, in order

1. Find what writes the record's `+0x5c` / `+0x98`. That names the condition
   under which a display gets a non-zero accelerator id, and it is the whole
   display half if the answer is a property or an IOKit association we can
   publish.
2. Find the writers of the flag at `0x7ff843ca08b0`, to settle test (b). A
   `ripall` for that address is the instrument, and it must be chunked.
3. Only then consider nullarc's route (our own `IOFramebuffer`), which is a
   much larger build. 2sj's reading stands — their framebuffer needs none of
   IOPresentment — but if a non-zero accelerator id is all that stands between
   `CompositorSW` and `CompositorMetal` on the framebuffer we already have,
   that is a far smaller change for the same result.

The user has cleared PolyForm-NC for this project, so copying from
`src/phxaccel` is permitted if it comes to that.

Nothing was built. No boot was spent.

## 2sl — ROUTE A IS OPEN: the KC split blocks EFI injection, NOT a runtime-loaded kext. 2oz/2qs/2ql corrected.

Static, no boot, one minute of measurement. This reverses the conclusion that
has closed the display half since 2oz, and it is the first time the load path
itself was tested rather than inherited.

### The measurement

A throwaway kext bundle whose only content is four undefined references to
`IOFramebuffer` — its vtable, its metaclass, its `start` and its
`OSMetaClass` constructor, i.e. exactly what a *linked subclass* needs:

```c
extern char _ZTV13IOFramebuffer[];
extern char _ZN13IOFramebuffer10gMetaClassE[];
extern char _ZN13IOFramebuffer5startEP9IOService[];
extern char _ZN13IOFramebufferC2EPK11OSMetaClass[];
void *rb_linktest_refs[4] = { ... };
```

`OSBundleLibraries` extended with `com.apple.iokit.IOGraphicsFamily`,
`IONDRVSupport` and `IOAcceleratorFamily2`, then:

```
$ kmutil libraries -p .../LinkTest.kext
For extension com.rembrandtgpu.probe:
  __ZN13IOFramebuffer10gMetaClassE   in SystemKernelExtensions.kc: com.apple.iokit.IOGraphicsFamily (599)
  __ZTV13IOFramebuffer               in SystemKernelExtensions.kc: com.apple.iokit.IOGraphicsFamily (599)
  __ZN13IOFramebuffer5startEP9IOService      in SystemKernelExtensions.kc: com.apple.iokit.IOGraphicsFamily (599)
  __ZN13IOFramebufferC2EPK11OSMetaClass      in SystemKernelExtensions.kc: com.apple.iokit.IOGraphicsFamily (599)
```

**All four resolve, out of `SystemKernelExtensions.kc`.** `kmutil libraries` is
the same instrument the `make kext` step has used since the beginning to prove
every import resolves; here it is pointed at the one dependency the project
decided was impossible.

### The error, and it is a specific one

The "2oz trap" is real and the CLAUDE.md check that guards it is correct — but
it guards **the Lilu plugin**, which OpenCore injects into
`BootKernelExtensions.kc`, where a system-KC dependency genuinely cannot bind.
That constraint was then carried over to *any* kext of ours:

- **2oz** built the `IOFramebuffer` subclass and ruled it out "on
  kernel-collection placement".
- **2qs** measured the split live and correctly — IOGraphicsFamily at
  `0xffffff7f95c94000`, our plugin at `0xffffff8004043000` — then wrote
  "Route A (our own linked `IOFramebuffer`) is closed by the KC split" and
  recorded the display half as closable.
- **2ql** ended "either find a load path that can depend on IOGraphicsFamily,
  or decide the display half stays software."

The load path was in the repository the whole time. `tools/load.sh` loads
`RembrandtProbe` with `kmutil`, at runtime, after the desktop is up; a kext
loaded that way links against **every** loaded collection, system KC included.
`src/kext/Info.plist` simply never declared a system-KC library, so the
capability was never exercised. Nobody tested it; three milestones reasoned
about it.

### Independent confirmation, from a driver that works

`luuumi-dev/nullarc`'s own install description splits its kexts exactly along
this line (fetched from its README):

- **`PhxBringup.kext` → `EFI/OC/Kexts`** — the OpenCore-injected half, which
  brings the GPU up before WindowServer and needs no system-KC dependency;
- **`PhxAccel.kext` → installed as an auxiliary kernel collection** — and
  `PhxAccel` is the kext that contains `PhxAMDFB`, their `IOFramebuffer`
  subclass.

So the one working RDNA 3 driver on a Hackintosh uses the EFI slot for the
Lilu-like half and the **AuxKC** for the framebuffer half. That is the same
split this project already has, with the second half unused.

### Correction to 2sj, on nullarc's class-name claim

2sj recorded their comment that CoreDisplay gates IOPresentment on "AMD" in
the framebuffer's class name as **"unverified, do not act on it"**, because the
bare `"AMD"` string found near that region of the cache is a hang-watchdog
vendor tag. That caveat was about the wrong string. **2ql had already measured
the gate itself**, instruction by instruction:
`__GetSystemGPUVendors_block_invoke` runs `IOObjectCopyClass` over every
`IOFramebuffer` service and `CFStringFind`s `Intel`/`AMD`/`NVDA`/
`AppleParavirt`, a no-match earning bit `0x01` which `supported` can never
contain — and `make useiop` prints it live: `IONDRVFramebuffer name=.Display_boot
-> bit 0x01`, `present 0x01`, `supported 0x1e`, verdict 0. nullarc's comment is
**confirmed, by our own prior measurement**, and `PhxAMDFB` contains `AMD` for
precisely this reason. The 2sj caveat is withdrawn.

### The personality numbers, read rather than guessed

| kext | IOClass | IOProviderClass | IONameMatch | IOMatchCategory | IOProbeScore |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IONDRVSupport | `IONDRVFramebuffer` | `IOPCIDevice` | `display` | **`IOFramebuffer`** | **20000** |
| AMDFramebuffer | `AMDFramebuffer` | `AtiFbStub` | `display` | **`IOFramebuffer`** | 65050 |

One driver wins per (provider, `IOMatchCategory`), so a personality with
`IOProviderClass = IOPCIDevice`, `IONameMatch = display`,
`IOMatchCategory = IOFramebuffer` and a score above 20000 **displaces
`IONDRVFramebuffer`** rather than joining it. That matters beyond winning the
match: `present` is the OR over *all* `IOFramebuffer` services, so an
AMD-named framebuffer **added beside** `.Display_boot` would give
`present = 0x05`, and `(0x1e & 0x05) != 0x05` keeps the gate shut. Displacing
is not an optimisation here, it is the requirement.

### A staging lever found in the same read

`kmutil load --load-style start-only|match-only|start-and-match`. **`start-only`
loads the kext without sending its personalities to the catalog** — the class
registers, nothing matches, nothing touches the display. So the first hardware
test of a framebuffer kext can be "does it load and register without a panic",
with the match a separate, later step (`kmutil load -P <personality>`). That is
the kind of two-stage experiment rule 16 asks for, and it is free.

### What is NOT established

- **That the load is accepted**, as opposed to resolvable. `kmutil libraries`
  checks symbols; `kmutil load` additionally wants authorization. SIP is 0xA43
  (UNTRUSTED_KEXTS + UNAPPROVED_KEXTS set) and `RembrandtProbe` loads ad-hoc
  signed today, so the precedent is good — but the precedent is for a kext
  with no system-KC dependency, and AuxKC rebuilds are a separate mechanism.
  Measure it with `start-only` before anything else.
- **Whether `Apple`'s `AMDRadeonX6000` will composite for a non-Apple
  `IOFramebuffer`.** Unchanged from 2sj; nullarc's compositor is their own.
- **Where in `/Library/Extensions` vs AuxKC this lands.** CLAUDE.md forbids
  Claude installing there; it is the user's action, like the EFI.

### What this does to the frontier

The display half is **not closed**. The thing 2ql named as the single lever —
"an `IOFramebuffer` whose class name contains AMD" — is buildable, by the
load path the repo already uses, and a working driver on comparable silicon
ships exactly that shape. 2s2–2sk's eliminations keep their value as
eliminations; the route around them is now open rather than hypothetical.

## 2sm — THE FRAMEBUFFER KEXT IS BUILT, AND ITS VTABLE IS VERIFIED SLOT BY SLOT AGAINST APPLE'S

Static, no boot. `src/fbkext/` + `make fbkext` + `tools/fbload.sh`.

### The vtable risk, retired before a line was written

2qs's objection to building our own framebuffer was "a hand-built vtable one
slot wrong is a panic on the path that owns the display, vtable layout is not
stable across OS updates". That objection is about *synthesising* a vtable
(route C). A **compiled subclass** does not synthesise one — the compiler emits
it from the header — so the risk reduces to a single checkable question: does
`third_party/MacKernelSDK/Headers/IOKit/graphics/IOFramebuffer.h` describe the
same layout as the IOGraphicsFamily this machine runs?

Measured both ways, with the project's own instrument.

**Apple's table**, `dumptable.py build/re/IOGraphicsFamily __ZTV13IOFramebuffer`
— 2824 bytes, and the declared order in the header matches the named entries
exactly, from `open` at dump +0x988 through:

```
+0x988 open          +0x990 close          +0x998 isConsoleDevice
+0x9a0 setupForCurrentConfig  +0x9a8 serializeInfo  +0x9b0 setNumber
+0x9b8 getApertureRange (pure)  +0x9c0 getVRAMRange  +0x9c8 enableController
... +0xa08 setDisplayMode ... +0xa60 getConnectionCount ...
+0xae0 registerForInterruptType  +0xae8 unregisterInterrupt
+0xaf0 setInterruptState  +0xaf8 getNotificationSemaphore   <- last slot
```

The header's last virtual is `getNotificationSemaphore`, and the table ends
there. Also a free confirmation of rule 7 and of CLAUDE.md's recorded call
offsets: `getVRAMRange` dumps at 0x9c0 and is documented as call offset 0x9b0;
`registerForInterruptType` dumps at 0xae0, documented 0xad0. Both hold.

**Our table**, dumped out of the built kext: `__ZTV16RBAMDFramebuffer` is
**2824 bytes — byte-for-byte the same size**. No slot added, none removed, so
every override replaced an existing entry rather than extending the class. Then
each override checked individually against `nm`:

```
+0x998 isConsoleDevice   +0x9b8 getApertureRange   +0x9c0 getVRAMRange
+0x9c8 enableController  +0x9d0 getPixelFormats    +0x9d8 getDisplayModeCount
+0x9e0 getDisplayModes   +0x9e8 getInformationForDisplayMode
+0x9f0 getPixelFormatsForDisplayMode  +0x9f8 getPixelInformation
+0xa00 getCurrentDisplayMode  +0xa08 setDisplayMode
+0xa18 setStartupDisplayMode  +0xa20 getStartupDisplayMode
+0xa38 setAttribute      +0xa40 getAttribute      +0xa60 getConnectionCount
+0xa68 setAttributeForConnection  +0xa70 getAttributeForConnection
+0xae0 registerForInterruptType   +0xae8 unregisterInterrupt
+0xaf0 setInterruptState

22 of 22 slots carry the expected override
```

With controls: the three slots we deliberately did **not** override —
`setApertureEnable` (0xa10), `setCLUTWithEntries` (0xa28),
`getTimingInfoForDisplayMode` (0xa48) — read 0 in the unlinked image and appear
in `nm -u` as undefined `__ZN13IOFramebuffer…` imports, which is what an
inherited slot looks like before the kext is linked into a collection. A pass
with no control would have been the same hollow result the first `useiop`
printed (rule 14 against our own tool).

### The build

`make fbkext` → `build/out/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext`, `-Wall -Werror`, clean, and
the target **fails the build** unless `kmutil libraries` both accepts the bundle
and shows an `IOFramebuffer` symbol resolving out of `SystemKernelExtensions.kc`
— so a broken dependency can never be discovered on hardware. It reports:

```
LINK 83 symbols from the system collection, 283 from boot
```

`make plugin` re-checked afterwards: still **0** from the system collection and
**0** `IOGraphicsFamily` in its Info.plist, so the 2oz trap guard is intact.
The two kexts have **opposite** requirements and the Makefile now enforces each
one separately, which is the thing that was conflated for five milestones.

### What it does, and what it deliberately does not

Every number is read off this machine, not chosen. `.Display_boot`'s live
`IOFBConfig` carries one mode, ID 100, `DM = 80070000 38040000 3fd58f00
00000000`: width 0x780 = 1920, height 0x438 = 1080, refresh `0x008fd53f` in
16.16 = **143.83 Hz**, maxDepthIndex 0. `IOFBMemorySize` reads **8294400** =
1920·1080·4 exactly, so rows are unpadded and `bytesPerRow` is **7680**. The
aperture is a sub-range of BAR0 at offset 0 (2pr), BAR0 read from
`assigned-addresses` as `0x8_8000_0000`, 256 MB. The 16.16 refresh has an
independent control: the BAR5 OTG sampler measured 143.908 Hz by latching both
endpoints on an `OTG0_FRAME_COUNT` edge (2rm/2rn).

It **writes nothing to the display engine** — `enableController` returns success
because OTG0 is already running (`OTG0_CONTROL 0x00011201`, DMCUB 4.0.15.47),
and `setDisplayMode` *refuses* anything but the firmware's mode rather than
silently accepting it. That is 2sj's shape, and it is also the only honest one:
we have no modeset.

The `'vbl '` interrupt is delivered from a `thread_call` at the measured period,
because 2s4 measured that the pipe needs a `'vbl '` callback at the panel's
rate, not a particular source for it, and the comparable driver does the same
(2sj). Phase is not locked to scanout; the rate is right. Stated, not hidden.

`registerForInterruptType` **declines every type except `'vbl '`** instead of
returning success, because a registration that reports success without
installing anything is exactly what rule 20 forbids.

### The class name is the point

`RBAMDFramebuffer`. It contains `AMD` and none of `Intel` / `NVDA` /
`AppleParavirt`, so `__GetSystemGPUVendors_block_invoke` scores it **0x04**
instead of the 0x01 that `.Display_boot` earns and that no `supported` mask can
contain (2ql).

The personality therefore **displaces** `IONDRVFramebuffer` rather than joining
it — same `IOProviderClass` (`IOPCIDevice`), same `IONameMatch` (`display`),
same `IOMatchCategory` (`IOFramebuffer`), `IOProbeScore` 30000 against its
20000, plus `IOPCIMatch 0x16811002` so it can never claim a display on another
machine. Displacing is **required, not tidier**: `present` is the OR over all
`IOFramebuffer` services, so an AMD-named framebuffer added *beside*
`.Display_boot` gives `present = 0x05` and `(0x1e & 0x05) != 0x05` keeps the
gate shut.

### Arming, and why a bad boot costs one power cycle

`probe()` refuses unless NVRAM `rbgpu-fb` is set, and consumes it with
`IONVRAM-FORCESYNCNOW-PROPERTY` **before** returning — the same two details the
accelerator arm paid for: the bounded retry for the `/options` race (2in) and
the durable flush, because a removal that never reached flash cost the boot loop
of 2026-10-12 (2dg). Unarmed, the kext is inert and `IONDRVFramebuffer` matches
as usual. This matters more here than for the accelerator, because this one owns
the panel: a failure has no SSH window if it also takes the console.

### `tools/fbload.sh`, staged by risk

- **stage 1, `sudo tools/fbload.sh`** — `kmutil load --load-style start-only`.
  No personality reaches the catalog, so the class registers and nothing
  matches; the display is untouched. It answers the one thing 2sl left open:
  the symbols **resolve**, but is the **load accepted**? `kmutil libraries`
  does not check authorization, so that is a separate claim and gets its own
  measurement.
- **stage 2, `sudo tools/fbload.sh beside`** — stages the `IOMatchCategory` to a
  private one so the service attaches *alongside* the boot framebuffer. Three
  readings available nowhere else: does `IOFramebuffer::start()` complete on a
  non-Apple subclass here, does the service appear in the registry, and does
  `make useiop` report **0x04** for our class name. **The verdict staying 0 in
  stage 2 is expected and is not a failure** — that is the 0x05 arithmetic
  above. Stage 2 proves the bit, not the gate. Writing that down before the run
  is the point; it is the prediction, and a stage-2 "failure" that was predicted
  cannot later be read as one.
- **stage 3** — the auxiliary collection at boot, with the displacing
  personality. That is an install, so it is the user's step, and it is the only
  stage that can actually open the gate.

The script refuses to load at all when `rbgpu-fb` is unset, so a forgotten
`nvram` cannot be mistaken for a broken kext.

### Still not established, and it is the honest list

- **That the load is accepted** — stage 1 exists to measure exactly this.
- **Whether `IOFramebuffer::start()` completes** on our subclass on this
  machine. Stage 2.
- **Whether Apple's `AMDRadeonX6000` will composite for a non-Apple
  `IOFramebuffer`.** Unchanged since 2sj; nullarc's compositor is their own, and
  this is the one question no static read here can settle.
- **What happens past the gate.** 2qp already opened `UseIOPresentment` by
  patching the classifier's call site and met *"System set to use IOP but no
  display pipes are present"*, and the display-pipe arc from there (2qq→2sk)
  ends in the wedge. Opening the gate with a real framebuffer is a different
  input to the same machinery, not a different machinery. Nothing measured so
  far says the wedge will not come back, and nothing says it will.

### 2sm addendum — the loadability question, taken as far as static analysis goes

`kmutil print-diagnostics` is "perform all possible tests on a specified kext,
and indicate whether the kext is loadable" — the dry run 2sl asked for. On the
framebuffer kext:

```
Diagnosing build/out/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext...
Error:
	Filesystem error: Invalid ownership (501:20) should be (0:0) ...   [x7]
	Authenticating extension failed: Bad code signature
Resolving dependencies for build/out/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext...
Dependencies: OK
```

**With the control that makes it mean something** — `RembrandtProbe`, which
loads on this machine every time `tools/load.sh` is run:

```
Diagnosing build/out/RembrandtProbe.kext...
Error:
	Authenticating extension failed: Bad code signature
Resolving dependencies for build/out/RembrandtProbe.kext...
Dependencies: OK
```

**The same two errors and the same `Dependencies: OK`.** So the ownership and
signature complaints are artifacts of reading the bundle out of `build/out`
(user-owned, ad-hoc signed) rather than the root:wheel staged copy `fbload.sh`
makes, and they are not a property of the framebuffer kext. The one
substantive line — full dependency resolution, which is exactly the system-KC
link in question — **passes**. A negative here would have been worth a lot;
this is the positive, and it is as far as static work reaches. Whether
`kmutil load` *authorizes* it still needs stage 1.

### The stage-3 rescue, named before stage 3 is proposed

A framebuffer kext in the auxiliary collection that fails at boot can take the
console with it, which is worse than the AGDC wedge because it leaves no SSH
window. Two layers:

1. **The one-shot.** `probe()` consumes `rbgpu-fb` durably before touching
   anything, so the *next* boot is unarmed. A plain power cycle is the first
   and usually only move. This is the same guarantee 2s8 measured for the
   accelerator arm, where the wedge still wrote its NVRAM note and still
   consumed its one-shots.
2. **`kmutil trigger-panic-medic`** — "delete and disable loading of third
   party kexts in order to safely boot into a target volume", Recovery only.
   The command for this machine, with both facts rule 25 was written for:
   Recovery is reached with **SPACE at the OpenCore picker** (not Cmd-R), and
   the system volume is **`MACOS`** (`diskutil info /` → Volume Name MACOS;
   the Data volume is `MACOS - Data`):

   ```
   kmutil trigger-panic-medic --volume-root /Volumes/MACOS
   ```

   Recorded now, while the machine is up and the names can be read off it,
   rather than looked up from a black screen. Four Recovery trips were each
   ended by a detail asserted instead of measured (2ny).

## 2sn — STAGE 1 PASSED ON HARDWARE: the kernel bound IOGraphicsFamily to our kext, and the vendor arithmetic is clear

The user ran `sudo tools/fbload.sh`. No reboot, no display disturbance, nothing
matched. Two results, one of them stronger than the measurement it confirms.

### 1. The load was accepted, and the kernel itself names the dependency

```
201    0 0xffffff7f98089000 0x1ff9  0x1ff9  com.rembrandtgpu.fb (0.1.0)
                                    97E170CD-72E5-3858-B32D-F85F4D6CBB39 <139 18 7 6 3>
```

and, from `kextstat` in the same boot:

```
139   18 0xffffff7f95c94000 0x2efea  com.apple.iokit.IOGraphicsFamily (599)
 18   37 0xffffff8002886000 0x35000  com.apple.iokit.IOPCIFamily (2.9)
141    4 0xffffff7f95ce8000 0x8ffc   com.apple.iokit.IONDRVSupport (599)
```

**Index 139 in our dependency list IS `IOGraphicsFamily`.** The link is not a
static claim from `kmutil libraries` any more — the running kernel resolved it
and recorded it.

And the load address settles it from the other side. 2qs measured the split
with these exact numbers: *"IOGraphicsFamily `0xffffff7f95c94000`, our plugin
`0xffffff8004043000` — all `0xffffff80…`, the boot KC. 2oz's blocker
confirmed."* Our framebuffer kext loaded at **`0xffffff7f98089000`** — the
`0xffffff7f9…` range, beside IOGraphicsFamily and IONDRVSupport, **not** the
boot-KC range the plugin lives in. The same instrument that was read as proof
the route was closed now shows us inside the region it was measuring. The
measurement was always right; only the conclusion drawn from it was wrong.

`kernelmanagerd`'s own account of the decision, which is the part
`kmutil libraries` could not speak to:

```
directLoadAuxiliaryExtensions: [com.rembrandtgpu.fb v0.1.0 ... signed @none ...]
extensionsNeedingApproval:     []
approvalsRequiredFromSyspolicyd: false
unsupportedExtensions:         []
safebootBlockedExtensions:     []
```

So: an **auxiliary** load, ad-hoc signed (`signed @none`), **no** syspolicyd
approval required, not unsupported, and not safeboot-blocked. The UUID matched
`build/out` (97E170CD…), per the standing rule.

No `RBAMDFramebuffer:` log lines appeared, which is **correct and was predicted**:
`--load-style start-only` sends no personality, so `probe()` never runs and the
one-shot was neither read nor consumed. An absence that was stated in advance is
a result; this one is.

### 2. The vendor arithmetic for stage 3, measured rather than assumed

`make useiop`, live, and `ioreg -rl -c IOFramebuffer`:

```
IONDRVFramebuffer   name=.Display_boot   -> bit 0x01   <-- UNKNOWN VENDOR
present mask = 0x01  (1 framebuffer)
supported mask = 0x1e
reproduced UseIOPresentment() = 0
```

**Exactly one IOFramebuffer service exists on this machine.** That had to be
checked rather than assumed, because this machine also carries
`/Library/Extensions/NVRMFB.kext` (`com.nullmoth.NVRMFB`, alongside `NVAccel`,
`NVRM` and `NVRMAGDC`) — an NVIDIA framebuffer kext from the nullmoth driver,
which the stage-1 output listed in the auxiliary contents. **It publishes no
`IOFramebuffer` service**, so it contributes no vendor bit.

That matters concretely. `present` is the OR over all framebuffers, so a second
unclassifiable one would have kept the gate shut no matter what we did, and
stage 3 would have failed for a reason nothing in the kext could fix. With
`.Display_boot` displaced and ours in its place the mask becomes `present =
0x04`, `supported = 0x1e`, and `(0x1e & 0x04) == 0x04` — the gate opens. Free
to measure now, expensive to discover from a black screen.

Also noted without being chased: `.Display_boot`'s registry id read
`0x1000004c9` earlier this session and `0x1000004c3` now. The node has been
recreated in between. Not pursued, and not used for anything.

### An instrument defect, found by its own output

`fbload.sh`'s registry line was `ioreg -c IOFramebuffer -k IOClass | grep '^+-o'`,
and it printed **`+-o Root`** — saying nothing at all about framebuffers, while
looking like an answer. That flag pair does not filter the way it reads. Fixed
to `ioreg -rl -c IOFramebuffer | grep -E '^\+-o|"IOClass"'`, which is what
produced the one-framebuffer result above, and the failure case now prints
"no IOFramebuffer service found" rather than a bare `Root`. Rule 26 again, on
our own script, caught only because a control existed elsewhere in the same run.

### What stage 1 did NOT establish

That `IOFramebuffer::start()` completes on this subclass. Nothing constructed an
instance — that is exactly what stage 1 avoids, and exactly what stage 2 is for.

### 2sn addendum — two claims in the kext were false in the beside configuration, fixed before stage 2 was offered

Reviewing stage 2 before proposing it found that `isConsoleDevice()` returned
**true unconditionally** and `getConnectionCount()` returned **1
unconditionally**. Both are correct for the instance that displaced
`IONDRVFramebuffer`. Beside it, both are **false statements about hardware we
are not driving**:

- a second framebuffer claiming the console invites `IOFramebuffer` to hand the
  kernel console to an instance that is not driving the panel — on the driver
  that *is* the screen, that is a black screen with no SSH window;
- claiming a live connection beside the real framebuffer conjures a second
  1920x1080 display for WindowServer.

Neither is a configuration flag, and neither needed one. Which configuration an
instance is in **is readable from the instance**: only one driver wins a given
(provider, `IOMatchCategory`) pair, so an instance whose own `IOMatchCategory`
is `IOFramebuffer` took that category from IONDRVSupport's personality and
therefore owns the panel and the console. `ownsPanel()` reads exactly that, and
both answers now follow from it; an instance with no category property at all
answers "no", because the safe direction for an unknown is the one that touches
nothing. `start()` logs which configuration it came up in, so a capture says so
rather than leaving it to be inferred.

This is rule 17's shape — do not state something about the hardware that is not
so — caught by asking what stage 2 would actually assert rather than by running
it. Re-verified after the change: the vtable is still **2824 bytes**,
`ownsPanel` is **not** in it (0 hits, it is non-virtual), and the UUID moved
97E170CD → A62398A7.

## 2so — STAGE 2 PASSED: `IOFramebuffer::start()` completes on a non-Apple subclass, and Apple's display stack attaches to it

The user ran `sudo tools/fbload.sh beside`. Every prediction 2sn stated in
advance held, and the one thing static analysis could not reach is now measured.

### 1. The service exists, started, and Apple's own drivers joined it

```
+-o RBAMDFramebuffer  <class RBAMDFramebuffer, id 0x100000700,
                       registered, matched, active, busy 0 (1 ms), retain 10>
  |   "IOClass"         = "RBAMDFramebuffer"
  |   "IOMatchCategory" = "RBAMDFramebufferBeside"
  |   "IOProbeScore"    = 30000
  |   "IONameMatched"   = "display"
  |   "VRAM,totalMB"    = 4096
  |   "model"           = "AMD Radeon 680M"
  +-o AppleMCCSControlModule       ("IOProviderClass" = "IOFramebuffer")
  |   +-o AppleMCCSParameterHandler
  +-o AppleUpstreamUserClientDriver
```

`registered, matched, active` requires `start()` to have returned true, so
**`IOFramebuffer::start()` completes on our subclass on this machine.** And the
stronger result is the children: `AppleMCCSControlModule` matches on
`IOProviderClass = IOFramebuffer`, so **Apple's own display stack metacast our
class to `IOFramebuffer` and attached to it.** The vtable verification of 2sm
predicted that; this is it happening on hardware.

`<140 18 7 6 3>` — and index **140** is `IOGraphicsFamily (599)` in this boot.
Note it was **139** last boot: `kextstat` indices are not stable across boots,
so the dependency must be confirmed by resolving the index in the same boot,
never by the number. Recorded because the number was nearly treated as the fact.

### 2. The class name earns the AMD vendor bit, measured in the classifier

```
IONDRVFramebuffer   name=.Display_boot      -> bit 0x01   <-- UNKNOWN VENDOR
RBAMDFramebuffer    name=RBAMDFramebuffer   -> bit 0x04
present mask = 0x05  (2 framebuffers)
supported mask = 0x1e
reproduced UseIOPresentment() = 0
```

**`-> bit 0x04`.** That is the whole thesis of 2ql/2sl confirmed against a real
service: our class name scores as AMD in `IOObjectCopyClass` + `CFStringFind`.
The verdict staying **0** is the result 2sn predicted in writing — `0x1e & 0x05
!= 0x05` while `.Display_boot` is still present — so it is not a failure, and
because it was predicted it cannot be read as one later. Stage 3's arithmetic
follows directly: displace `.Display_boot`, the `0x01` goes away, `present`
becomes `0x04`, and the gate opens.

### 3. The hardening of 2sn's addendum worked, and the registry proves it

The beside configuration was supposed to claim no console and no connection.
Measured by comparison, which is the only way this means anything:

| | `.Display_boot` | `RBAMDFramebuffer` |
|---|---|---|
| `AppleDisplay` child | **yes** | **no** |
| `IOFBConfig` | 1 | **0** |
| `IOFBMemorySize` | 1 | **0** |

`getConnectionCount()` returning 0 from `ownsPanel()` means **no display was
created for a panel we are not driving** — no phantom second display, exactly
as designed, and confirmed from the registry rather than from the absence of a
complaint. The one-shot `rbgpu-fb` is **absent** afterwards, so `probe()` ran
its armed path and consumed it durably.

### The error in this milestone, which was mine and nearly went into the journal

The kext's own `IOLog` lines did not appear in the capture. I went looking for
why, found `RembrandtProbe` with **106 lines** in `log show --last boot`, and
was about to record "a sibling kext's IOLog reaches the unified log and ours
does not" as a finding about our kext.

It was the same boot error rule 28 was written for, one level up. `uptime` reads
**up 4 minutes**; `log show --last boot` returned **two** `Darwin Kernel
Version` banners; `--start/--end` printed *"Wall Clock adjustment detected -
results might be strange"*. The machine had rebooted at ~23:04, those 106 lines
were from a **previous** boot, and `RembrandtProbe` is **not loaded at all**
now — its control count in this boot is **0**, identically to ours. So the
control did not discriminate anything, and **the absence of our log lines
carries no information whatsoever.**

What makes the conclusion safe without it: the registry dump, the consumed
one-shot and `kextstat` were all read live, in the current boot, and each one
independently requires `probe()` and `start()` to have run and succeeded. The
log was never the evidence; it only looked like the evidence because it was
missing.

### Two instrument defects, both found by their own output

- `CONTAINS "RBAMDFramebuffer"` matched every `kernelmanagerd` line carrying
  the bundle **path**, so the capture filled with noise shaped like output.
  Now `BEGINSWITH "RBAMDFramebuffer:"`, over a 15-minute window rather than
  `--last boot`, and the empty case prints that absence here is **not** a
  result and points at the registry instead.
- `make useiop && ./build/out/useiop` printed the whole correct report and then
  **"make useiop failed; run it by hand"** — because `useiop` exits **1** when
  an unknown-vendor framebuffer is present, which is its *verdict*. Build and
  run are separate steps now, and the exit code is printed with what it means.

Rule 26, twice, on our own script, in one run.

### Where this leaves stage 3

Both of the things stage 1 and 2 existed to measure are answered: the load is
accepted and binds `IOGraphicsFamily` in-kernel (2sn), and the subclass starts
and is accepted as an `IOFramebuffer` by Apple's drivers (2so). Nothing about
the framebuffer itself is unmeasured now.

What remains is entirely about the configuration change: displacing
`IONDRVFramebuffer` makes us the console and the only framebuffer, which is the
first time our code owns the screen, and it needs the auxiliary collection at
boot. The known wall behind it is unchanged — 2qp opened this gate by patching
the classifier and met *"System set to use IOP but no display pipes are
present"* — and the open question is whether that is fatal to the **surface**
path or merely noisy beside it. The reason it may come apart:
`Display::GetNextSurface` calls `UseIOPresentment()` only as a branch
predicate, and the pool path it then takes reaches `CD_IOSurfaceCreate`, which
touches no `IOPresentment*` API; the `DisplayPipe` is a separate object with a
separate constructor. 2qh's chain says a non-NULL IOSurface alone is what keeps
`CompositorMetal`. Not established, and stated as the hypothesis stage 3 tests.

### 2so addendum — stage 3 splits in two, and the reason is rule 21

Stage 3 was going to be one step: install to `/Library/Extensions`, arm, reboot.
That bundles two different risks into one boot, and one of them has never been
tested.

**The untested one is the fallback.** Unarmed, `probe()` returns `nullptr`, and
IOKit is then supposed to match `IONDRVFramebuffer` instead — same provider,
same `IOMatchCategory`, lower score. That is standard IOKit behaviour and it is
what makes a permanent install safe by design, because every future boot
attempts the match. But it has **not** been exercised: in stage 2 our `probe()`
returned `this`, and the category was private, so nothing ever competed. Rule 21
is exactly this lesson — *test a recovery procedure in the situation it exists
for* — and the recovery procedure here is "the installed kext declines and the
boot framebuffer takes over".

So:

- **stage 3a — install and reboot UNARMED.** The kext is in
  `/Library/Extensions`, the AuxKC carries it, the displacing personality is
  live, and `rbgpu-fb` is **not** set. Expected: `probe()` declines,
  `IONDRVFramebuffer` matches, the desktop is exactly as it is today, and
  `ioreg` shows our kext loaded with **no** `RBAMDFramebuffer` service. That
  proves the install is inert by default and that the fallback works — which is
  the property every later boot depends on.
- **stage 3b — `sudo nvram rbgpu-fb=1` and reboot.** The real test, and the
  first time our code owns the screen.

If 3a does **not** come up normally, stage 3b is off the table until it does,
and the install comes straight back out. Splitting costs one extra boot and buys
the only safety property that matters for a permanent install.

**The failure modes of 3b, ranked, with what covers each:**

1. *Black screen, kernel alive.* The most likely bad outcome, and the mildest:
   **SSH still works**, so the capture and the uninstall are both available.
   This is strictly better than the AGDC wedge, which takes WindowServer with
   it.
2. *Panic during our `start()`.* The one-shot is consumed and flushed with
   `IONVRAM-FORCESYNCNOW-PROPERTY` **before** anything touches hardware — now
   not just implemented but *demonstrated*, since stage 2 consumed it — so the
   next boot is unarmed and 3a's behaviour is what comes up. One power cycle.
3. *Panic so early the flush does not land.* `armedOnce()` returns before any
   mapping, any PCI access and any `IOFramebuffer::start()`, so there is no
   code path between the flush and the risk. Not impossible, covered by 4.
4. *Unbootable.* `kmutil trigger-panic-medic --volume-root /Volumes/MACOS`
   from Recovery — SPACE at the OpenCore picker, system volume `MACOS`, both
   read off the live machine in 2sm rather than recalled.

**A known gap in the kext, stated before the boot rather than after it:** we
publish no gamma. `.Display_boot` carries `IOFBGammaCount 256`,
`IOFBGammaWidth 8`, `IOFBGammaHeaderSize 12`; we inherit
`IOFramebuffer::setGammaTable` and publish none of those keys. CoreDisplay's
wedge logs showed `System Gamma - Unknown` as the one operation that never
resolved (2sa), so gamma is plausibly load-bearing somewhere downstream.
Deliberately **not** implemented yet: adding unmeasured machinery before the
first owning boot is how 2cy happened. If 3b comes up with wrong colours or a
gamma complaint, that is the first thing to add, and it will then be a response
to a measurement.

## 2sp — the AuxKC rebuild is blocked by a broken password prompt, not by consent; and a staged kext is inert after a reboot but not absent

The user ran the 3a install. `cp`, `chown` and `chmod` succeeded —
`/Library/Extensions/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext` is there, `root:wheel` — and
`kmutil rebuild` got as far as accepting the kext and then failed:

```
Attempting to add the following extensions (1):
[+] com.rembrandtgpu.fb  0.1.0  /Library/Extensions/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext
Attempting to remove the following extensions (1):
[-] com.rembrandtgpu.fb  0.1.0  /private/var/tmp/RBAMDFramebuffer.stage/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext
Requesting user approval (times out in 60 seconds)...
Error Domain=com.apple.LocalAuthentication Code=-6
  "Biometry is not available on this device."
```

So the collection builder **accepts** the kext; the step that fails is the
interactive approval, and `kmutil rebuild` takes no flags at all (`--help`
lists only `-h`).

### What the blocker is NOT

`spctl kext-consent status` reads **`Kernel Extension User Consent: DISABLED`**.
That is SIP's `CSR_ALLOW_UNAPPROVED_KEXTS` (0x200, set in this machine's 0xA43)
doing its job, so there is **nothing to approve in System Settings** and no
syspolicyd gate in the way. Worth stating because "kext blocked" normally means
exactly that, and chasing the Privacy & Security pane here would have been a
dead end.

What fails is `kmutil rebuild`'s own `LocalAuthentication` call — an
admin-password prompt — and it asked for **biometry** on a machine that has
none, erroring instead of falling back to a password.

### The second finding, which changes the procedure

`tools/load.sh` has said since it was written that a staged kext "is gone after
a reboot". Measured now:

```
/private/var/tmp/RBAMDFramebuffer.stage          PRESENT
/private/var/tmp/RembrandtProbe.stage            PRESENT
/private/var/tmp/MHelper.stage                   PRESENT
```

and the AuxKC's own contents list **both** of our kexts at their staged paths:

```
com.rembrandtgpu.fb     0.1.0  /private/var/tmp/RBAMDFramebuffer.stage/...
com.rembrandtgpu.probe  0.1.0  /private/var/tmp/RembrandtProbe.stage/...
```

So the **load** does not survive a reboot — `kextstat` after the 23:04 reboot
showed the probe absent, with its file present and its AuxKC entry intact — but
the **file** and the **collection entry** both do. `/private/var/tmp` is not
cleared at boot.

The distinction is not pedantry. The staged copy of the framebuffer carries the
**beside** personality (`IOMatchCategory = RBAMDFramebufferBeside`), and it is
sitting in the AuxKC next to the `/Library/Extensions` copy that carries the
**displacing** one. Nothing observed suggests it would auto-load — the probe is
the control, and it did not — but entering a boot where the installed copy is
meant to win the `IOFramebuffer` category with a second copy of the same bundle
id present in the collection is exactly the kind of thing that produces a
result nobody can attribute. It gets removed first.

`load.sh`'s comment is corrected rather than deleted, with what was measured.

Also noted: the mechanism by which `/Library/Extensions` kexts reach the AuxKC
clearly works on this machine — `NVAccel`, `NVRM`, `NVRMAGDC`, `NVRMFB`,
`HighPointRR` and `HighPointIOP` are all in it at their `/Library/Extensions`
paths. So this is a question of which command does it, not whether it can be
done.

### The three ways forward, in risk order

1. **Let the boot-time rebuild do it.** `kernelmanagerd` rebuilds a stale AuxKC
   during boot, and with consent DISABLED there is nothing interactive to
   satisfy there. The collection is stale right now (our installed copy is not
   in it), the kext is correctly owned, and **stage 3a is a reboot anyway** — so
   this costs nothing extra and is tried first. Either the next boot lists the
   `/Library/Extensions` path in the AuxKC or it does not, and that is a clean
   fact either way.
2. **`sudo kmutil create -z -n aux …`** — `create` *does* carry
   `-z/--no-authorization`, unlike `rebuild`. This is the documented bypass, and
   it is the fallback rather than the first move for one reason: it rewrites the
   collection that the user's **working** nullmoth RTX driver depends on. That
   risk is fully covered by copying the single 18.6 MB
   `/Library/KernelCollections/AuxiliaryKernelExtensions.kc` aside first, which
   makes it reversible, but it is still a bigger step than a reboot.
3. Re-running `kmutil rebuild` and hoping for a password dialog. Recorded as an
   option and ranked last: the error names the biometric policy specifically, so
   there is no reason to expect a different answer on a second run. Do not spend
   a round trip on it before 1.

## 2sq — PANIC: `kmutil unload` of a live framebuffer. My command caused it, and my one-shot guarantee did not hold.

The user ran the 3a cleanup line and the machine panicked. Both faults are mine
and neither is in stage 3 — **the `/Library/Extensions` copy never loaded and
stage 3a never ran.**

### The panic, named to the byte

`logs/Kernel-2026-10-26-231753.panic`, kept in the repo:

```
panic(cpu 2 ...): Kernel trap at 0xffffff7fab2a56aa, type = 14=page fault
CR2: 0x0000000000000120
R12: 0x0000000100000700          <- the registry id of our stage-2 instance
Panicked task ... pid 122: kernelmanagerd

kext_request -> OSKext::handleRequest -> OSKext::removeKext
  -> IOCatalogue::terminateDriversForModule
  -> IOGraphicsFamily: IOFramebuffer::terminate(uint)
  -> IOService::terminatePhase1 -> scheduleTerminatePhase2 -> terminateWorker
  -> IOWorkLoop::runAction -> IOService::actionStop
  -> IOGraphicsFamily: IOFramebuffer::stop(IOService*) + 0x48    <-- PANIC
```

`R12 = 0x100000700` is **exactly** the `id` of the `RBAMDFramebuffer` service
2so recorded, so there is no ambiguity about which object was being torn down.

Disassembling `IOFramebuffer::stop` (`0x14fbc662`) gives the fault instruction
at `+0x48` to the byte — `0x14fbc6aa - 0x14fbc662 = 0x48`:

```
0x14fbc699   movq 0x118(%r15), %rsi      ; this->0x118
0x14fbc6a0   movq 0x1c8(%r15), %rax      ; this->0x1c8  - valid, did not fault
0x14fbc6a7   movq (%rax), %rax           ; *(this->0x1c8) == NULL
0x14fbc6aa   movq 0x120(%rax), %r12      ; <-- CR2 = 0x120
0x14fbc6b1   movq %r12, %rdi
0x14fbc6b4   movq %r13, %rdx             ; r13 = "stop"
```

`r12` becomes the first argument of a call whose third argument is the literal
`"stop"`, i.e. another `IOGraphicsWorkLoop::timedCloseGate`. So `this->0x1c8`
points at a framebuffer-group table and `[0]` is the group's first framebuffer,
whose `+0x120` is its workloop. **Our instance never joined a group**, so `[0]`
is NULL.

That is consistent with everything 2so measured about the beside instance:
`getConnectionCount()` 0, no `AppleDisplay` child, no `IOFBConfig`, no
`IOFBMemorySize` — it never completed configuration. **`IOFramebuffer::stop()`
assumes a configuration that a never-configured framebuffer does not have.**
It is Apple's code, reached through a lifecycle Apple's own framebuffers never
enter.

Ruled out by the disassembly rather than by argument: my `stop()` releases the
aperture before calling super, which was the obvious suspect. The fault is on
`*(this->0x1c8)`, a field we never touch, so the release ordering is not the
cause. Noted because it would have been the natural thing to "fix".

**The fix is in the instructions, not the code.** `fbload.sh` ended every run
with `To unload: sudo kmutil unload -b com.rembrandtgpu.fb`, and I put that same
command at the head of the 3a cleanup line. It now says, with the reason and the
disassembly: **to remove this kext, REBOOT; do not run `kmutil unload`.** A
reboot tears the instance down without running that path.

A code-level guard — refusing termination so an unload is declined instead of
fatal — is **not** written yet, deliberately. `terminateDriversForModule` calls
`terminate()` directly, so whether `requestTerminate` is even consulted on this
path is unread, and adding a guard whose mechanism has not been verified is
rule 20's error. It needs a read first.

### The worse defect: the one-shot was STILL SET after a reboot

```
nvram rbgpu-fb   ->   rbgpu-fb    1
```

2so recorded the one-shot as consumed, on the strength of `nvram rbgpu-fb`
returning "not found" **in the same boot**. That reads IODTNVRAM's *in-memory*
copy. It does not establish that the removal reached flash, and the value came
back after the reboot.

So the claim I have repeated at every stage — *"a bad boot costs exactly one
power cycle, because `probe()` consumes the key durably before touching
anything"* — **is not established, and the evidence now points the other way.**
2qy already recorded that a one-shot can fail to clear (`mcr_oneshot 4`); this
is that failure mode again, in the one place where the consequence is the
framebuffer arming on a boot nobody armed.

An alternative explanation exists and has not been excluded: the user may have
set the key again. That is why this is written as "not established" rather than
"the clear failed" — but the safe reading is the dangerous one, and everything
downstream now assumes the one-shot is **not** a reliable disarm.

What that means concretely, and it is the whole safety story of this work:

- `/Library/Extensions/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext` + `rbgpu-fb=1` in flash = the
  framebuffer arms on the next boot where the AuxKC carries it. **That
  combination must not be left on the machine**, so the kext comes out and the
  key is deleted explicitly with `nvram -d`.
- The durability has to be **measured across a reboot** before stage 3b is
  proposed again: set it, consume it, reboot, read it. Until that measurement
  exists, there is no one-power-cycle guarantee and 3b has no safety net
  except `trigger-panic-medic`.
- Rule 9's existing wording ("the one-shots are one-shot") is too confident for
  this case and should be read with 2qy's caveat in front of it.

### State of the machine as of this entry

Measured, not assumed: `kextstat` lists only `com.rembrandtgpu.plugin`; the
AuxKC carries `com.rembrandtgpu.fb` **only** at its stale
`/private/var/tmp/RBAMDFramebuffer.stage` path, not the
`/Library/Extensions` one; and the sole `IOFramebuffer` is `.Display_boot` with
its `AppleDisplay` child. So the desktop is back to its normal configuration and
the installed copy has never loaded. The boot-time AuxKC rebuild did **not**
pick it up, which also leaves 2sp's option 1 answered: **no**.

## 2sr — the one-shot clear is NOT durable, the kernel says why, and rule 9 already had the answer

The user confirms they did not re-set `rbgpu-fb`. So 2sq's alternative is
excluded: **the clear genuinely failed**, and the key survived a reboot after
`removeProperty` + the FORCESYNCNOW write + a read-back that returned absent.

### What the kernel does, read rather than assumed

`/options` is an **`IODTNVRAMVariables`** on macOS 15, not `IODTNVRAM`, and:

```
IODTNVRAMVariables::removeProperty(const OSSymbol*)      0xffffff8000b219e0
    ... jmp IODTNVRAM::removePropertyWithGUIDAndName     0xffffff8000b228f0

IODTNVRAMVariables::setProperty(const OSSymbol*, OSObject*)
    ... callq IODTNVRAM::setPropertyWithGUIDAndName
```

and the two destinations differ in exactly the way that matters:

| | calls `IODTNVRAM::syncInternal` |
|---|---|
| `setPropertyWithGUIDAndName` | **yes** |
| `removePropertyWithGUIDAndName` | **no** |

`removePropertyWithGUIDAndName`'s entire call/jump set is
`clientHasPrivilege`, `handleSpecialVariables`, `memcmp`, `strcmp`, `strncmp`,
`record_system_event`, `__stack_chk_fail` and internal branches. **There is no
commit in it.** A removal is in memory until something else flushes.

And `IONVRAM-FORCESYNCNOW-PROPERTY` is referenced by **exactly one function in
the whole kernel** — `IODTNVRAM::setPropertyWithGUIDAndName` — found by mapping
the string's file offset `0x9c31d1` through `__cstring`
(vmaddr `0xffffff8000c1f080`, offset `0x937080`) to **`0xffffff8000cab1d1`** and
xrefing that address across the image.

So the pieces exist and are wired, which is why this is recorded as "the
read-back proves nothing" rather than "the sync is a no-op": our FORCESYNCNOW
write does reach the only function that honours it. What is **not** read is
`handleSpecialVariables`' return path — whether it can make
`setPropertyWithGUIDAndName` return before `syncInternal`, and whether the GUID
`IODTNVRAMVariables::setProperty` passes is the one the special-variable check
wants. That is the remaining unknown, and it is deliberately left unread,
because the fix below does not depend on the answer.

**An instrument note, and it is rule 26 almost verbatim:** my first pass
grepped each function for `callq` and reported that
`IODTNVRAMVariables::removeProperty` makes **no calls at all** — because it
ends in a `jmp`, a tail call. Rule 26 already records "a `callq *0xNNN(` grep
cannot see a tail jump through a loaded register"; this is the same trap with a
direct target. The grep now matches `(callq|jmp)`.

### The fix, which rule 9 had already written down

CLAUDE.md rule 9, as it has stood for many milestones:

> And a one-shot can fail to clear (2qy, `mcr_oneshot 4`), so between
> experiments take the *boot-arg* out: the feature needs the arg *and* the key,
> so without the arg a stuck key is inert.

Every other gated feature in this project follows that. **The framebuffer kext
did not** — I gave it an NVRAM key alone and then built a safety argument on
top of the key's durability, which rule 9 explicitly says not to trust. The
guarantee I repeated at every stage ("a bad boot costs one power cycle") rested
on the one mechanism the project had already measured to be unreliable.

`probe()` now requires **both**:

```c
char flag[16];
if (!PE_parse_boot_argn("-rbgpufb", flag, sizeof(flag))) {
    LOG("-rbgpufb is not in boot-args; NOT arming whatever NVRAM says ...");
    return false;
}
```

so the durable disarm is `sudo tools/efi.sh bootarg remove -rbgpufb` — an edit
to a file, with a backup, which is durable in a way the NVRAM one-shot
demonstrably is not. The one-shot stays for what it is actually good at: making
a single armed boot single, so a repeat takes a deliberate `nvram` command. It
is no longer load bearing.

The in-memory read-back is kept but now logs what it is: *"one-shot removal
accepted IN MEMORY - this does NOT prove it reached flash (2sq); the durable
disarm is `efi.sh bootarg remove -rbgpufb`"*. A refusal path that publishes the
value it refused, and a success path that publishes the limit of what it
proved.

`fbload.sh` refuses the beside stage without the boot-arg, so a missing arg
cannot read as a broken kext. CLAUDE.md records both this and the
`kmutil unload` panic in the hard rules.

### What this costs and what it buys

Stage 3b now needs an EFI edit as well as an `nvram` command, which is a bigger
setup — and that is the correct price. The thing it buys is that the dangerous
combination 2sq left on the machine (**an installed kext plus a key that would
not clear**) can no longer exist: without `-rbgpufb` in `config.plist` the kext
cannot arm, whatever NVRAM holds.

Built, `-Wall -Werror` clean, UUID moved to AE8133E2. Not loaded anywhere; the
kext is out of `/Library/Extensions` and the key deleted.

## 2ss — the boot-arg check was a substring grep, and the kernel is stricter than our tooling

Immediately after 2sr added the boot-arg requirement, a state check printed:

```
rbgpu-fb in NVRAM : not found          (good - the user disarmed it)
kext in /L/E      : absent             (good)
-rbgpuownfb arg   : PRESENT            (<-- WRONG. Nobody added it.)
fb kext loaded    : 0
```

The check was `nvram boot-args | grep -q -- '-rbgpufb'`, and this machine's
boot-args contain **`-rbgpufbvbl`, `-rbgpufbvram` and `-rbgpufbaccel`**, each of
which contains `-rbgpufb` as a substring. `-rbgpufb` is in fact a prefix of six
names in this project: `-rbgpufbaccel`, `-rbgpufbmatch`, `-rbgpufbvbl`,
`-rbgpufbvram`, `-rbgpufbvramrange`, `-rbgpufbvramrangeall`.

A false positive in a **safety** check, reading as armed. That is the worst
place for one, and it was mine, written in the same milestone that moved the
safety story onto that very check.

### The kernel, read rather than feared

`PE_parse_boot_argn` (`0xffffff8000b92970`) scans a token up to a separator and
then:

```
0xb92a38   rbx = r8 - r13          ; rbx = LENGTH of the token in boot-args
0xb92a4b   strncmp(token, name, rbx)
0xb92a52   je   -> +0x100          ; first rbx bytes equal
0xb92a77   strlen(name)
0xb92a7c   cmpq %rax, %rbx         ; token length == strlen(name)?
0xb92a7f   jne  -> reject          ; <-- EXACT LENGTH REQUIRED
```

**So `PE_parse_boot_argn` never prefix-matches.** A token `-rbgpufbvram` has
length 12 against `strlen("-rbgpufb") == 8`, so it is rejected. Consequences,
and the second is worth more than the first:

1. The kext was **never** actually at risk of arming off `-rbgpufbvram`. The
   hazard existed only in our shell tooling.
2. **The project's existing prefix pairs are safe too** — `-rbgpufbvram`
   against `-rbgpufbvramrange`, and the `-rbgpumtlk*` family. That was an open
   worry the moment the collision was noticed, and it is now closed by
   measurement rather than left as an assumption. Lilu's
   `checkKernelArgument` wraps `lilu_get_boot_args` → `PE_parse_boot_argn`, so
   the plugin inherits the same exact semantics.

### Fixed two ways, because one was not enough

- **The check is now whole-token**:
  `nvram boot-args | tr ' \t' '\n\n' | grep -qx -- '-rbgpuownfb'`. Verified on
  the live machine **with a control in the same run**, which is the only form
  of this that means anything:

  ```
  new form: absent (correct)
  old form: PRESENT   <- the false positive, reproduced
  ```

- **The arg is renamed `-rbgpufb` → `-rbgpuownfb`.** The kernel did not need
  this; humans and greps do. A name that is a prefix of six others in the same
  family is a trap for every future `grep` anyone writes, including the user's.
  `-rbgpuownfb` shares no prefix relationship with any existing arg (`-rbgpuoff`
  is the nearest, and neither is a prefix of the other), and it says what it
  does: this is the arg that lets our framebuffer **own** the panel.

Rebuilt clean. CLAUDE.md gains rule 30 for the boot-arg semantics and three
more entries in rule 26's list of instruments that lied: `ioreg -c X -k Y` not
filtering (2sn), a tool's exit code being its verdict (2so), and a direct tail
`jmp` hiding a call (2sr).

### 2ss addendum — the accelerator arm has the same exposure, and the code already suspected it

`rbgpuConsumeArming()` in `RembrandtGPUPeer.cpp` opens with a comment written
long before tonight:

> Caveat: if this setup uses OpenCore's emulated NVRAM, a variable cleared here
> may not survive a forced restart, in which case the next boot is armed again.
> Recover from single-user mode (Cmd+S) with `nvram -d rbgpu-arm`.

**That caveat was speculation when it was written. 2sq/2sr measured it true**,
and 2sr found the kernel-side reason
(`removePropertyWithGUIDAndName` calls no sync at all). So the comment should
now be read as a fact, and the recovery it names is the right one.

But the accelerator's arming is an **OR**, not an AND:

```c
if (checkKernelArgument("-rbgpuarm")) {
    rbgpu_log("Peer: -rbgpuarm set; accelerator ARMED by boot-arg (NVRAM untouched)");
    return true;
}
... else fall through to the rbgpu-arm NVRAM one-shot ...
```

so the NVRAM key alone still arms it, and a key that fails to clear arms the
next boot too. **2s8's claim — "the wedge still consumes its one-shots, so it
does not re-arm itself and a plain power cycle comes up clean" — rests on the
same mechanism now measured unreliable.** Boots 165–167 did come up clean, so
it evidently works often; it is not a guarantee.

Deliberately **not** changed here. Making the accelerator require both would
alter a workflow the user has relied on for many milestones, and `-rbgpuarm`
arming on its own looks like a deliberate convenience rather than an oversight.
It is the user's call, and the honest statement meanwhile is: **an armed
accelerator boot may repeat, and the disarm that always works is removing the
boot-arg or `nvram -d rbgpu-arm` from single-user mode.**

What the framebuffer kext does differently, and why: it requires **both**,
because it is the one component that can take the console and leave no SSH
window. The cost of a repeat there is categorically worse than for the
accelerator, where a wedge still leaves NVRAM and a power cycle.

## 2st — the wrangler pairs Apple's accelerator to our framebuffer, and the Metal compositor activates

Boot of 2026-10-26 23:42, `uptime` 3 mins at capture, both one-shots set
