`tools/hosttest/hubp_test.c` (`hubp_tests()`), 40 assertions:

- **The offset table is cross-checked against `rb_regs.h`**, which was written
  from the same Linux header by a different hand at a different time. Two
  tables, one source — a typo in either shows up here. All sixteen
  address/pitch/config offsets were also re-verified against the header
  directly, and the tiling pair against it too.
- The 0xdc stride is **asserted, never used** to compute an offset: the table
  came from the header and stays authoritative.
- Each of the three pipe-state fields is load-bearing on its own, with a
  distinct refusal code, so a bare `return RB_HUBP_OK` fails three assertions.
- **The pitch-1 trap is asserted explicitly**: `0x77f` is accepted and `1920`
  is *refused*, because 2os's annotation reads "1920 px" for `0x077f` and a
  fast reader would write the wrong constant.
- Every address refusal is reachable on its own, with the realistic wrong
  inputs named: a system-physical address (`0x7_8000_0000`, below the
  carve-out) and a GPUVM one (`0xFF_BF..`, above) are both refused.
- The last 256-byte slot is in range on its own but **cannot hold a frame**,
  which is the check that stops a fetch running off the end of VRAM.

**Both directions of the mutation test** (CLAUDE.md's requirement that a new
test fail when the code it guards is broken): deleting the format gate does
not even compile (`-Werror -Wunused-parameter` — the guard is load-bearing in
the type system too), and mutating the measured constant `0x8` → `0xa` fails
the assertion that the measured pipe is accepted. A tautological mutation
(`config != config`) is also rejected by the compiler.

### The gates, in order

Three before anything is written, each publishing why it refused (rule 14):

1. **2oq's four-register OTG signature** — `OTG0_CONTROL & OTG_MASTER_EN` set
   with OTG1-3 at exactly `0x300`. The DMU segment `0x34c0` is a constant in
   this kext, and a constant is an assumption; if it is wrong these four reads
   are garbage and will not match. Refuse 5.
2. **2os's three HUBP0 values** — pitch, format, address-high. Refuse 6/7/8.
3. **`rb_dcn_is_denied()`**, the project's existing DCN write policy, which
   exists because a base-2 dword can mean different things in dcn302 and
   dcn312. Both our dwords are allowed (asserted on the host, re-checked on
   the machine so a future edit cannot bypass the policy). Refuse 9.

Then per address: non-zero, inside the measured carve-out, **256-byte
aligned** (DCN latches the address in 256-byte units, so the low 8 bits are
not address bits and a misaligned value is a guaranteed garbage fetch), HIGH
unchanged, and one frame fits. The **first** refusal is kept with its address
and code, because a last-wins key cannot express a per-entry fact (rule 14).

### Written per transaction, and gated on the flag word

Not once. 2wg said this before the code existed: a compositor swap chain hands
a different surface each flip, so one write would show one stale frame. The
address is taken fresh from **every** transaction.

And it is gated on **flag-word bit `0x1`** — the same test 2wf read the
consumer making before it touches `txn->0x10`. Without it, a transaction that
only changed the colour matrix would make us re-write a stale address. Boot
193 measured the bit set (`0x75`).

`hubpProgram()` runs on the accelerator's thread with its locks held, so it
**allocates nothing, logs nothing and blocks on nothing** (rule 31): the BAR5
mapping is made once in `start()`, and the VBL `thread_call` publishes. HIGH is
written before LOW because DCN latches the pair on the LOW write — on this
machine HIGH never changes, so the first store is a no-op that exists to keep
the order correct if that stops being true. The pair is read back **once**, on
write #1 only: a register that reads back what we wrote is the difference
between "the store executed" and "the store reached the chip", which is 2lq's
lesson in its register form.

### The one thing still unmeasured, and this build reads it

Pitch and format match, but the **swizzle does not have to**. The firmware's
GOP framebuffer is linear; a surface the GPU rendered into may be tiled — the
`_X` family, which is the whole of this project's swizzle defect. HUBP fetches
through `DCSURF_ADDR_CONFIG` / `DCSURF_TILING_CONFIG`, and **nothing has ever
read them here**. So this build publishes both. They are deliberately **not
gates**: nothing measured says what they should be, and refusing on them would
be substituting a value (rule 17). They exist so that a scrambled image is
distinguishable from a wrong address — the one ambiguity this experiment
cannot otherwise resolve.

### Said before the boot

The arm is `-rbgpufbhubp`, which **also requires `-rbgpufbamtr`** (the address
only arrives through `setAttribute('amtr')`); `rbgpufbhubpmax=<N>` bounds the
writes, absent means unlimited, which is what a live display needs. Rule 30
checked: no boot-arg token prefixes another.

**First, the arm check, before anything else means anything**:
`RBFBHubpArmed` true, `RBFBHubpReady` **true**, `RBFBHubpRefuse` **0**. If
`Ready` is false, read `Refuse` and stop — 5 means the DMU segment is wrong and
we were never addressing DCN, 6/7/8 mean the pipe is not what 2os measured,
9 means the denylist caught us. `RBFBHubpOrig` must read **`0xf400000000`**;
anything else and 2os's measurement no longer describes this machine.

Then the outcomes, in the order I think them likely:

- **`RBFBHubpWrites` > 0 and `RBFBHubpReadback == RBFBHubpLast`** — the write
  reached the chip. That is the milestone whatever the screen does.
- **A legible desktop.** Then the swizzle already agreed and the display half
  is done.
- **A recognisable but scrambled image** — regular, repeating, block-structured
  wrongness. That is the tiling mismatch, and `RBFBHubpTiling` /
  `RBFBHubpAddrCfg` say what the pipe is configured for. The next step is then
  a tiling write, **not** an address hunt.
- **Black or noise with `Readback == Last`.** The write landed and the address
  is wrong in some way the guards do not cover, or the surface is not rendered
  when we point at it.
- **Nothing changes at all, with `Readback == Last`.** The stores land and DCN
  ignores them — a flip needs `DCSURF_FLIP_CONTROL` or the
  `SURFACE_UPDATE_LOCK` dance that this build deliberately does not do. Then
  the address was never the missing piece and the lock sequence is.
- **Tearing.** Expected and acceptable: we write unsynchronised to vblank.
  DCN double-buffers, so it should be mild; it proves the path either way.

**The screen is not the instrument** — SSH and `ioreg` are, exactly as in 2w9.
And per rule 10 the capture must be taken **in the armed boot, over SSH,
before rebooting**: the last two captures were each cut to 6 files by an early
reboot, which is why 2wg could check no regression control.

### Install

Only the framebuffer kext changed. Plugin stays **`0D1F953A`**, already in the
EFI — no rebuild, no `efi.sh install`. fbkext **`D07493B1`** to the
**auxiliary collection** (rule 15).

---

## 2wi — boot 195: THE DISPLAY WORKS. The GPU composites to the panel, and the frame rate is the transaction rate

**The write landed and the display half is done.** No capture — the box could
not be driven well enough to run `plugin_check.sh`, and it was power cycled —
so the registry is absent and **every `RBFBHubp*` value is unmeasured** (rule
14: that absence is not a result). But the **screen** is an instrument here,
and it is the one only the user can read. Reported:

> frozen at first, then the screen came up with cursor, then after 30 s the
> lock screen — **it was showing correctly and accelerated** — but a new frame
> only about every 10 seconds. Not usable.

### What that establishes

**Nothing but the HUBP write can change what the panel shows.** Before 2wh the
panel displayed the firmware's GOP framebuffer at VRAM offset 0, static,
forever; the compositor's output never reached it. A correct, moving,
accelerated desktop appearing on the panel is therefore proof of the whole
chain at once:

- `hubpSetup()` passed all three gates — the OTG signature, 2os's three HUBP0
  values and the denylist — because a refusal writes nothing at all;
- `rb_hubp_check_addr()` accepted the address, so it was non-zero, in the
  carve-out, 256-byte aligned and HIGH-stable;
- **the write reached the chip**, since the picture changed;
- the address in `_AMD_PIPE_FLIP +0x08`/`+0x0c` is the right one, so 2wg's
  field identification is confirmed by the display itself;
- **THE SWIZZLE ALREADY AGREED.** This was 2wh's one stated unmeasured risk
  and the thing most likely to make the experiment ambiguous. A tiled surface
  fetched as linear produces regular, repeating, block-structured garbage. The
  image was *correct*. So `DCSURF_ADDR_CONFIG` / `DCSURF_TILING_CONFIG`
  already describe the layout the compositor renders into, and **no tiling
  write is needed**. That branch of 2wh's prediction list is closed.
- pitch and format agreed, as 2os and 2wg jointly predicted.

So **the display half of this project is solved**: the GPU composites and the
result reaches the panel. Every milestone from 2pd to 2wh was aimed at this.

### And the frame rate was predicted, quantitatively, two boots before it was seen

**1 frame per ~10 s is not a defect in the write. It is the transaction rate**,
and it was already measured — with no HUBP write anywhere in the build:

| boot | uptime at capture | `RBFBAmtrSets` | rate | one frame every |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 193 | 167 s | 13 | 0.078 /s | **12.8 s** |
| 194 | 183 s | 17 | 0.093 /s | **10.8 s** |

The user saw "about every 10 seconds". **10.8 s, from data taken before the
code existed.** The write is not a throttle: it faithfully displays every
transaction it is handed, and Apple's accelerator hands over 0.09 per second.

**That rate was always there. 2wh did not cause it — 2wh made it visible.**
The panel could not reveal it while it showed a static firmware buffer, and no
earlier milestone could have measured it as a *frame* rate. This is the same
shape as 2su's "WindowServer idle at 0.0 %": the system was never compositing
fast, and now the symptom has a number.

### The frontier is now the transaction rate, and there is a named candidate

**`RBFBVBL1Fires` has been 0 for three milestones and "not attributed" in each
of them. It is now the prime suspect.**

`RBAMDFramebufferVBL.cpp:204` registers **every** handler `enabled = true`,
deliberately, because Apple never performs an initial enable. Boot 194 read
`RBFBVBL1Enabled` **False** and `RBFBVBL1Fires` **0** — so Apple registered
its `'vbl '` handler and then called `setInterruptState(0)` on its own slot,
exactly as the comment there anticipates, **and never re-enabled it, with 17
transactions in flight.**

2s5 measured what re-arms it: `transaction_queue_gated` →
`enableTransactionInterrupt` → `enableVBLInterrupt`. If that is not running,
Apple's accelerator never receives a vblank, so it can never retire a
transaction and submit the next one — and ~10 s is the shape of a **timeout**,
not of a throttle. Boot 191 saw handler 1 fire **once**, the only time it ever
has; 192, 193 and 194 all read 0.

**Not established**, and both candidates stay live:

1. **The VBL completion path** above — cheap, specific, testable.
2. **The wedge** (2we): work submitted, never retires, hang check says not
   hung, restart cannot find the channel. If the compositor's render work does
   not retire, the next frame cannot be submitted either. 2we established the
   wedge as an *independent* second defect, which is still true, but
   independent is not irrelevant: it is now in the critical path for frame
   rate. Whether the two are the same defect is **not** established — the
   wedge is on GFX/SDMA channels, a different mechanism from the display
   interrupt — and must not be written as one.

### The safety gap this boot exposed, in our own arming

The user had to rescue with `-rbgpuoff` because **the write re-armed on every
power cycle**. Two causes compose:

- `rbgpu-fb`, the framebuffer's one-shot, **does not clear**. That is 2sq,
  already measured and already commented at `RBAMDFramebuffer.cpp:47`:
  `removeProperty` calls no sync, so the key survives the reboot that was
  supposed to consume it. The takeover therefore re-arms by itself.
- **`-rbgpufbhubp` has no one-shot of its own.** It is `PE_parse_boot_argn`
  and `amtrArmed`, both boot-args, so once the framebuffer is up the write
  arms unconditionally. Every other dangerous feature in this project needs a
  one-shot *and* an arg precisely so a bad boot cannot repeat (rule 9), and
  the single most dangerous one was built without one.

The documented disarm is the **boot-arg**, which is what the hard rules
already say, and it worked. But the feature should not have depended on that.

### Next

The frame rate, not the address. The display is correct and the only thing
wrong with it is how often it changes, which is a number we have measured
three ways and never explained.

---

## 2wj — boot 196: the display reproduces, and the one-shot is fixed by overwriting it

Two reports, one boot. The user restarted **without** installing `452E6EE1`
and **without** adding `-rbgpufbretire`, so this is the boot-195
configuration run again: fbkext `D07493B1`, `-rbgpufbhubp` + `-rbgpufbamtr`.

### The display reproduces, n = 2

> i restarted same frames thing

So the composited accelerated desktop at ~1 frame per 10 s is **reproducible**,
which upgrades 2wi from n=1. 2wi's reading stands: the write lands every time,
and the rate is the transaction rate. **`-rbgpufbretire` is still untested** —
it was never in boot-args.

### The one-shot never consumed, and that made the machine unable to disarm itself

> also power cycling didnt consume the flags i had to add gpuoff in windows

**This is the serious finding, and it is about our own code, not the chip.**
`rbgpu-fb` did not clear, so the framebuffer took over on every power cycle,
and with it the HUBP write (which has no one-shot of its own, 2wi). At the
0.09 Hz transaction rate there is **no usable desktop from which to edit
boot-args** — so the only way out was to boot **Windows** and edit the
OpenCore config from there.

**A feature that cannot be disarmed from the machine it runs on is a worse
failure mode than anything it was guarding against.** Rule 9 exists for
exactly this and the project has written "the boot-arg is the durable disarm"
since 2sr — but that assumes a machine usable enough to run `efi.sh`, which
2wh removed as a side effect of succeeding.

### The fix was already in this file, measured, since 2sr

`RBAMDFramebuffer.cpp` consumed the key with:

    options->removeProperty("rbgpu-fb");

and 2sr's own comment forty lines above explains why that cannot work:
`removeProperty` tail-jumps to `removePropertyWithGUIDAndName`, which calls
**no sync**, while `setProperty` reaches `setPropertyWithGUIDAndName` and
**does** — which is precisely why `rbgpu-fbcrumb` has persisted reliably all
along through the same entry. The two facts have sat two screens apart for
eleven milestones without being put together.

**So consume by OVERWRITE, not by removal.** Build `DEB8918D` writes a literal
`"0"`, and the arming check twenty lines above **already** treats `"0"` as not
armed, for both `OSData` and `OSString` — nothing else had to change. The
read-back is still only in-memory, but it is now on the path measured to sync,
so the reading is worth something it was not worth before.

`IONVRAM-FORCESYNCNOW-PROPERTY` is kept, but note it evidently did **not**
rescue the removal across boots 191-196 — so on this machine that key is not a
substitute for using a syncing path in the first place.

### What this changes about past boots

Because the key never consumed, **the framebuffer takeover was effectively
sticky from whenever it was last armed**, and that is why it has never once
failed to arm since 2st. No earlier conclusion is invalidated — the takeover
is confirmed directly in every boot by `RBAMDFramebuffer`'s own registry keys,
not by the one-shot — but "the fb armed again" was never evidence that a fresh
key had been set. Rule 9's "every armed boot needs them set again" was true of
the *plugin's* keys (`rbgpu-boot` increments, so those really were consumed)
and false of this one.

### After this build, one power cycle is a full disarm

With the key consuming properly, a plain reboot leaves `rbgpu-fb` reading `0`,
`RBAMDFramebuffer` declines the panel, `IONDRVFramebuffer` matches as usual,
and the desktop comes back on software compositing — **usable, and usable
enough to run `efi.sh`**. No Windows trip. The boot-arg remains the durable
disarm; this makes the one-shot do its own job as well.

A separate `rbgpu-hubp` one-shot for the write alone is **available and not
taken**: with `rbgpu-fb` consuming, one power cycle already disarms the whole
chain, and the smaller change is the better one here. Worth adding only if
keeping the framebuffer armed while disarming just the write becomes useful.

### The crumb is already sufficient to measure the frame rate without a capture

Noted because 2wi's instrument fix turns out to be better than it was designed
to be: the crumb carries `f=` vblFires and `t=` amtrSets, and the VBL
thread_call runs at the panel's measured 143.83 Hz. So

    transactions per second  =  t / (f / 143.83)

from one `nvram rbgpu-fbcrumb` read, after a power cycle, with no capture at
all. That resolves 0.09 Hz against 1 Hz or 60 Hz with room to spare, which is
the only precision this question needs.

---

## 2wk — boot 195: the write is confirmed in full, and the retire experiment never ran

`rbgpu-boot` **195**, `armed=1`, `diag_used` 631/768, `agdc_gamma_elems1`
**0x100** = 256, **21 files — the first complete capture since boot 192**.
Rule 15 met on both kexts: fb **`DEB8918D`**, plugin **`0D1F953A`**.
`RBFBCrumbBoot` 194 against nonce 195 — the lag-by-one holds a third time.

### 2wj's one-shot fix works, confirmed on hardware

**`rbgpu-fb = 0`.** That key has never cleared in the history of this project —
2sq measured it surviving its own removal, and six boots re-armed off it.
Consuming by **overwrite** on the `setProperty` path 2sr measured as syncing
does what `removeProperty` could not. So a plain power cycle is now a real
disarm, and the Windows trip of boot 196 cannot recur.

### Every prediction about the write landed

| key | read | predicted in 2wh |
|---|---|---|
| `RBFBHubpReady` | **True** | true |
| `RBFBHubpRefuse` | **0** | 0 |
| `RBFBHubpOrig` | **`0xf400000000`** | `0xf400000000` |
| `RBFBHubpPitch` | **1919** = `0x77f` | `0x77f`, and `1920` refused |
| `RBFBHubpConfig` | **8** | 8 = ARGB8888 |
| `RBFBHubpOtgCtl` | **`0x11201`** | 2oq's measured value |
| `RBFBHubpWrites` | **4** | > 0 |
| `RBFBHubpRejects` | **0** | 0 |

`RBFBHubpReadback` = **`0xf41002a000`**, taken off the chip after write #1,
where the register held `0xf400000000` before — **the store reaches the
hardware**, which is 2wh's stated milestone whatever the screen does. And that
address is **boot 194's measured surface address, in a different boot**: the
compositor allocates the same first surface twice, an agreement nothing forced.

**`RBFBHubpLast` = `0xf41192a000` ≠ `Readback`.** The address moved by
`0x1900000` between write #1 and write #4, so **2wg's "per-flip, not a
constant" is confirmed** and writing per transaction was necessary, not
cautious. (Note for future readers: `Readback` is write #1's value by design —
it is taken once, on the accelerator's thread — so **`Readback == Last` is the
wrong check whenever `Writes > 1`**. 2wh's handoff stated it carelessly;
compare `Readback` against the first address, or just against `Orig` to see it
moved.)

### Every 2we regression control is still zero — checkable at last

With `display_change_handler` **26** as the control, the same number as every
boot since 189:

    set_transaction_args            0
    Failed to submit transaction    0
    Fallback ... submission failed  0
    DisplayPipeState                0
    no gamma                        0
    Metal compositor activated      2

Boots 194, and the two uncaptured ones, could check **none** of these. The
display chain is clean and has stayed clean through the HUBP write.

### The frame rate, a third time

`RBFBVBLFires` 7200 at the panel's 143.83 Hz = **50.1 s**, `RBFBAmtrSets`
**4** → **one transaction every 12.5 s**. With 193's 12.8 s and 194's 10.8 s
that is **n=3** on a rate that has never changed. The user's report this boot —
"first mouse appears in the Apple-logo freeze, then 15 s later one frame of
lock screen" — is the same phenomenon.

### THE EXPERIMENT DID NOT RUN, and why is measured

`RBFBRetireArmed` **True**, `RBFBRetireEnables` **0** — with `RBFBAmtrSets`
**4**, so the code ran four times and enabled nothing. Per 2wi's own
pre-registered reading that would mean "no transaction arrived", and that
reading is **wrong**. The capture says what actually happened:

| | boot 194 | boot 195 |
|---|---|---|
| `RBFBVBLEnables` | **36** | **11** |
| `RBFBAmtrSets` | 17 | 4 |
| enables per transaction | 2.1 | 2.75 |
| `RBFBVBL1Fires` | 0 | **0 of 7200** |

slot 1 reads `Used=True`, `Enabled=False`, `Self=False`, so all three of my
loop's conditions hold **at capture time**. The only way the loop can see
nothing is if `!enabled` was false **when it looked** — i.e. the slot was
**already enabled at `setAttribute` time**.

**So Apple does enable its `'vbl '` slot, about two to three times per
transaction, and its handler still fires zero times in seven thousand two
hundred ticks.** That is now a measurement, not an inference, and it inverts
2wi's suspicion: the problem is not that Apple fails to re-arm the interrupt
(2s5's path evidently *does* run) — **it is that our vblank never arrives
while the window is open.**

**The defect is ours, and it is timing granularity.** Our `'vbl '` is a
`thread_call` at 143.83 Hz, so delivery is quantised to ~7 ms, and Apple's
enable window is shorter than that. Boot 191 fired handler 1 **once**, ever —
which is exactly what winning that race occasionally looks like.

### Build `F730123C`: answer the enable, not the clock

A **second** `thread_call`, `vblKickCall`, fired from the off→on transition in
`setInterruptState` itself, delivering on our own thread microseconds later
instead of up to 7 ms later. Design points, each for a reason:

- **Separate from `vblCall`**, so a kick can never cancel or reschedule a
  pending periodic tick, and so the periodic cadence stays undisturbed.
- **It does not touch `vblFires`.** That counter is this project's 143.83 Hz
  time reference — 2wj's crumb rate formula and this milestone's own frame-rate
  numbers all divide by it — and irregular extra ticks would corrupt a clock
  three milestones now rely on. The per-slot `fires` counter does move, because
  a fire really happened.
- **It re-checks `enabled` at delivery**, so a window that has already closed
  costs nothing, and **`retireKicks - retireDelivered` is exactly how often we
  were too late** — the measurement this experiment owes.
- **Only non-self slots**, so re-enabling the handler we registered ourselves
  can never deliver a spurious vblank.
- On Apple's thread it does a field write and a `thread_call_enter`, nothing
  more (rule 31). `proc` is then called from the same context the periodic path
  would have used if it had ever caught the window — not a new hazard class,
  only better timing.

Five hosttest cases, and the suite **bites** when the self-filter is dropped.

### Two instrument corrections

**`0xe00002c7` appears 91 times and is entirely benign.** Every one is
`InstallTiming ... FAILED for mode 0x80001000 (800x600 ...)` — CoreDisplay
enumerating legacy timings our framebuffer does not report. `set_transaction_args`
is 0 and `Failed to submit` is 0. **A raw `0xe00002c7` count is no longer
diagnostic of the transaction path**; match the message, not the code.

**`rbgpu-fbcrumb` has never appeared in any capture, and the crumb is not
broken — the capture never looked.** `nvram.txt` is a hand-curated key list in
`plugin_check.sh` and `rbgpu-fbcrumb` was not in it. 2wi and 2wj both built a
recovery plan on reading that crumb after a power cycle, and neither checked
that the instrument reading it existed. Rule 26 again, on my own tooling.
Added to the list; **the crumb remains UNVERIFIED on hardware** until a boot
shows it, so do not rely on it yet.

## 2wl — boot 196: the chain is not slow, it is UNASKED; and the crumb stopped 70 seconds into a twenty-minute boot

**The configuration is verified from the live machine, not from the handoff.**
`/Library/Extensions/RBAMDFramebuffer.kext` holds **`F730123C`**, the 2wk
retire build, and `boot-args` ends `... -rbgpufbaty -rbgpufbamtr -rbgpufbhubp
-rbgpufbretire`. So the user installed it and armed it without being handed the
commands — the experiment 2wk designed really did run.

**Rule 33 first.** The machine I read is NOT that boot: `kern.boottime`
14:55:15, the photo's menu bar says 14:54, uptime 11 minutes, `rbgpu-diag`
`armed=0`, no `RBAMDFramebuffer` in `ioreg`. The armed boot is over. What
survives is NVRAM.

**THE DESKTOP IS CORRECT AND IT IS FULLY COMPOSITED.** From the photograph, the
one instrument only the user can read: translucent dock with vibrancy, colour
widgets (weather, stocks), window shadows, a sheet over a window, menu-bar
blur, and System Information open on Graphics/Displays reading **AMD Radeon
680M**, Type **GPU**, VRAM 4 GB, Metal **Supported**, Device ID 0x1681,
**1920 x 1080 @ 144.00Hz**, 24-Bit Color (ARGB8888), Main Display **Yes**,
Online **Yes**. Twenty minutes of uptime. 2wi's reading holds and gets
stronger: no tiling garbage, no colour error, no alpha error.

**THE NEW FACT, AND IT CHANGES THE QUESTION.** In the user's own words:
typing into a text field (Spotlight) made the frames **smooth while they
typed**, and **adding characters counted while deleting them did not**.

So the chain is **not** rate-limited. It delivered at keystroke rate - call it
5-10 Hz - on demand, through the same `setAttribute('amtr')` -> `hubpProgram`
path that sits at 0.09 Hz on an idle desktop. **A timeout does not do that. A
throttle does not do that. A missing vblank retirement does not do that** - if
the accelerator could not retire a transaction, typing would not be smooth
either. Whatever decides to produce a transaction is **event-driven**, and at
idle it simply has nothing it believes it must draw.

That retires the shape of the question carried since 2wi. **The frontier is no
longer "why is our frame delivery slow"; it is "why does a change on screen
not produce a transaction unless it is a keystroke".** 2wi named two
candidates - the VBL completion path and the wedge - and both were framed as
throttles. Neither explains a chain that runs fast on command.

**WHAT THE BOOT MEASURED: SEVENTY SECONDS OF IT.**

    nvram rbgpu-fbcrumb -> b=195 s=12 f=10000 e=11 r=1 h=0 w=4 k=0 t=4

`b=195` against `rbgpu-boot` 196 is the expected one-boot lag (2wg), so this
crumb **is** from the twenty-minute boot. It says the HUBP write was set up
(`h=0`), had written 4 times (`w=4`), the VBL clock was running (`r=1`), 11
enable transitions (`e=11`), 4 transactions (`t=4`) - and `f=10000` says all
of that is **as of 10000 vblank fires = 69.5 seconds**. Shape-identical to boot
195 at the same point.

**And then it stopped, for eighteen more minutes.** The crumb was written at
four fixed fire counts - 100, 1000, 10000, 100000 - and at 143.83 Hz the fourth
is 11.6 minutes away while the third is 70 seconds in. A twenty-minute boot
left a record of its first minute. `RBFBRetireKicks` and `RBFBRetireDelivered`,
the two numbers 2wk exists to produce, are registry-only and the box has since
rebooted, so **`-rbgpufbretire` is STILL UNTESTED - third boot running.**

**Rule 10, sharper: a record that must survive an uncapturable boot has to be
PERIODIC, not a set of marks.** Four fixed counts answer "how far did it get"
for a boot that dies. They answer nothing for a boot that lives, which is the
case that now matters - the desktop is usable for twenty minutes and the
interesting behaviour is late in it.

**A NUMBERING CORRECTION (rule 8).** `rbgpu-boot` reads **196**, and the
14:18 capture read **195**. So the twenty-minute boot is nonce 196 and the boot
numbers in 2wi/2wj/2wk were **narrative** - counted from user reports - not
nonces. Boot numbers in this journal are the nonce or they are nothing.

**Build `A356BE21`, instrumentation only, no behaviour change.**

- **The crumb is periodic**: 100, 1000, then **every 10000 fires (~70 s)**,
  with `s=` carrying which sample it is (12 at 70 s, 13 at 139 s, 29 at twenty
  minutes). The last crumb in NVRAM is then the whole boot. One flash commit
  per 70 s is the same order as the four this already did.
- **`p=` is the rate**: the fullest 1000-fire (~7 s) window the boot ever saw.
  A total divided by a boot length cannot tell a burst from a trickle, and the
  user's report is precisely that the boot contained both.
- **`n=` is what we dropped**: transactions whose flag word has bit `0x1`
  clear, the ones 2wh deliberately does not write. "We were handed a content
  update and skipped it" and "we were never handed one" look identical today.
- **`K=`/`D=` are the retire kick** and its delivery, so 2wk's measurement
  survives a boot that cannot be captured.

Hosttest: the rate bucket's peak must survive a later quiet window and must
not be the running bucket (otherwise it reads 0 whenever a boot ends quiet),
and the crumb budget assertion is rewritten from a total to a rate. Mutation
tested both ways - suppressing the max and suppressing the reset each fail the
same assertion.

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.**

- **`p=` in the tens** -> the chain can run at tens of transactions per 7 s on
  demand, the display half is finished, and the whole remaining defect is
  upstream of everything this project has built: WindowServer is not asking.
- **`p=` at 1 or 2** -> the smoothness while typing did NOT come through our
  HUBP write, and 2wi's "nothing but the HUBP write can change what the panel
  shows" needs re-examining before anything else is built on it.
- **`n=` non-zero** -> we are being handed transactions and refusing to write
  them, which is ours and immediate.
- **`K=` > 0 with `D=` close behind** -> the 2wk kick fires and lands, and
  `RBFBVBL1Fires` in a capture says whether Apple does anything with it.

**AND THE MACHINE IS CAPTURABLE NOW.** Typing is the one interaction that
updates the screen smoothly, which is exactly what a terminal does. Boots
195/196 were never captured because the box "could not be driven"; a Terminal
window, or SSH from another machine, can run `sudo tools/plugin_check.sh` in
the armed boot - and that single capture carries `RBFBRetireKicks`,
`RBFBRetireDelivered`, `RBFBVBL1Fires`, `RBFBAmtrSets` and the display log
together, which no amount of NVRAM can.

**INSTALL**: plugin `0D1F953A` unchanged in the EFI (no rebuild, no
`efi.sh install`); fbkext **`A356BE21`** to the auxiliary collection. Boot-args
unchanged - all four of `-rbgpufbaty -rbgpufbamtr -rbgpufbhubp -rbgpufbretire`
stay. All one-shots set again (rule 34).

## 2wm — the flag-word gate is the one mechanism that fits the typing asymmetry, and it gets its own boot-arg

No boot. Built on top of 2wl, same install.

**The asymmetry is the evidence.** Boot 196: typing into Spotlight made the
frames smooth, **adding characters counted and deleting them did not**. Adding
a character grows a text layer, which forces a **new surface**; deleting
reuses the allocation already made. So the one difference between the case
that worked and the case that did not is **whether the surface address
changed**.

And that is exactly what 2wh gates the write on. `hubpProgram` runs only when
the transaction's flag word carries bit `0x1`, "the plane resource changed" -
2wf read AMDFramebuffer's own consumer making that test before it dereferences
`txn->0x10`, and 2wh copied it so a colour-matrix-only transaction could not
re-write a stale address from a stale pointer. **If a content update into an
unchanged surface arrives with bit 0x1 clear, we are being handed frames and
refusing to draw them**, and the symptom would be precisely the one observed.

**It is NOT established that this is happening**, and boot 195 argues against
it: `RBFBAmtrSets` 4 with `RBFBHubpWrites` 4, so every transaction in that
boot's first 183 s carried the bit and none was dropped. But that is four
transactions on an idle desktop, which is the case that does not matter; the
typing burst was never measured. 2wl's `n=` counter answers it directly.

**`-rbgpufbflipall`, off by default.** It drops the gate:
`rb_hubp_should_write(flags, all)`, in `src/common/rb_hubp.h` with the rest of
the decision logic, so the hosttest decides it before the kext does. Eight
assertions: the measured flag word `0x75` is accepted by both forms (a
regression there would silently kill the working display), a colour-matrix-only
`0x10` is **refused gated and written ungated** - the two must differ or the
arg answers nothing - and the gate reads bit `0x1` only, not "any bit set",
which would accept `0x10` and make the experiment a no-op. Mutation tested:
`flags & RB_HUBP_FLAG_PLANE` -> `flags` fails case 3.

**What it trades.** Bit 0x1 is the consumer's own evidence that `txn->0x10`
points at a fresh `_AMD_PIPE_FLIP`. Without it we trust a pointer Apple has
not said it refreshed. The caller still range-checks that pointer against the
kernel floor and every address still passes all six `rb_hubp_check_addr`
guards, so the failure mode is a **refused** write, not a wild one - and the
worst case is the one 2wh already covers, a stale address showing a stale
frame until the next correct write.

**Rule 30 on the name.** Not `-rbgpufbhubpall`: `-rbgpufbhubp` would prefix
it, and 2ss cost a safety check to exactly that. Checked mechanically against
every rbgpu token in the live boot-args - `-rbgpufbflipall` neither prefixes
nor is prefixed by any of them (the only two prefix pairs present,
`-rbgpuvbl`/`-rbgpuvblpump` and `-rbgpuagdc`/`-rbgpuagdccaps`, are
pre-existing and already known safe).

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.** The arg and the counter are **independent**, which
is what makes one boot settle it:

- `n=` **0** -> no bit-clear transaction ever arrived, `-rbgpufbflipall` is
  provably inert, and this whole line is closed by its own instrument.
- `n=` **large** and the frame rate **up** -> that was it, and the display
  half is finished.
- `n=` large and the rate **unchanged** -> we were dropping frames and drawing
  them changes nothing, so the stale pointer is stale and bit 0x1 was right.
- `p=` is the control on all three: it says whether the chain ever ran fast at
  all, independently of which transactions we chose to write.

**Build `7A6A56A9`** (2wl's `A356BE21` plus this). Plugin `0D1F953A`
unchanged in the EFI. Boot-args add **`-rbgpufbflipall`** and keep everything
else.

## 2wn — boot 197: the retire kick WORKS, the display chain is clean, and the limiter is STAMP RETIREMENT at 2/s

Armed, captured, 21 files. Rule 15 on both: plugin **`0D1F953A`**, fbkext
**`7A6A56A9`**. `rbgpu-boot` **197**, boot-args carry
`-rbgpufbaty -rbgpufbamtr -rbgpufbhubp -rbgpufbretire -rbgpufbflipall`.
Crumb: `b=196 s=15 f=40000 e=82 r=1 h=0 w=41 k=0 t=41 p=11 n=0 K=80 D=79`.
2wl's periodic crumb worked - `s=15` is the fourth 10000-fire sample, where
boot 196 stopped at `s=12`.

**2wk's KICK WORKS, AND APPLE'S HANDLER FIRES FOR THE FIRST TIME.**

    RBFBRetireKicks     80      RBFBRetireDelivered  79
    RBFBRetireEnables    0      RBFBVBL1Fires        79   (was 0 for four milestones)
    RBFBVBLEnables      82      (boot 196: 11)

So the off->on transition is the right trigger, the kick lands 79 times in 80,
and `retireKicks - retireDelivered == 1` is exactly one closed window - the
measurement 2wk owed. **`RBFBRetireEnables 0` confirms 2wk's diagnosis of the
2wi mechanism**: Apple's slot was already enabled at `setAttribute` time, so
the old `!enabled` guard could never fire. Boot 191 saw handler 1 fire once,
ever; this boot it fired 79 times.

**2wm IS CLOSED BY ITS OWN INSTRUMENT, AND THE HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED.**
`RBFBHubpAll True` (the arg was armed) and **`RBFBAmtrNoFlip 0`** with
`AmtrSets 41` and `HubpWrites 41`. **Every transaction carried flag bit
`0x1`; not one bit-clear transaction arrived all boot.** So
`-rbgpufbflipall` was provably inert, we were never dropping frames, and the
adding-vs-deleting asymmetry is **not** explained by our write gate. Exactly
the outcome 2wm named first, settled in one boot because the arg and its
counter are independent. The arg stays (it costs nothing and is now a control);
the line of inquiry is closed.

**THE DISPLAY CHAIN IS COMPLETELY CLEAN.** Control `display_change_handler`
**26**, as in every boot since 189:

    set_transaction_args   0     Failed to submit    0     IOReturn: 0x   0
    Fallback               0     DisplayPipeState    0     no gamma       0
    Metal compositor       2     Software            0

Nothing in the display path fails any more.

**THE RATE IS UP BUT NOT FIXED.** `AmtrSets 41` over `VBLFires 43200` =
300.4 s -> **0.136 transactions/s** against boot 194's 0.093, and
**`RBFBAmtrPeak 11`** - the fullest 1000-fire (6.95 s) window held 11
transactions, so the chain reached **1.58/s** at its best. **NOT ESTABLISHED
that the kick caused the improvement**: different workload, n=1, and 0.093 ->
0.136 is well inside what a busier desktop could do on its own.

**AND THE LIMITER IS NAMED AND MEASURED, FROM THE WEDGE.** GFX channel 52,
25 timeouts over 350 s, first and last:

    16:03:07  pending stamps [7..17]      backlog  10
    16:08:57  pending stamps [738..856]   backlog 118

    submitted  2.40 stamps/s        RETIRED  2.09 stamps/s

**Work retires at ~2 per second and the backlog grows.** The display chain's
peak of 1.58 transactions/s and the GFX retirement rate of 2.09/s are the same
order of magnitude. **NOT ESTABLISHED as causal** - n=1, no shared timestamps
between the two instruments, and "same order of magnitude" is not a
correlation. But it is the first quantitative candidate for the frame rate
that is not already excluded.

**AND THE GPU IS NOT THE BOTTLENECK.** `rbgpu-ring` sampled three times this
boot reads **`r=380 w=380`**, **`r=1800 w=1800`**, **`r=2980 w=2980`** -
**read pointer equals write pointer every time**, with `vmf=0` (no VM faults)
and `cps=0` (CP not stalled). The ring is fully consumed between samples: the
chip executes everything submitted, immediately. So the 2 per second is **not
the GPU doing work slowly, it is the driver learning that work finished
slowly** - a completion-accounting problem, which is a different class of
defect from everything the display half has been.

`checkGPUProgress` signals 179 times at a median interval of 4 s, 135 `is not
hung`, 135 `no channel associated`, 179 `GPURestartSignaled/Enqueued/Dequeued`,
135 `GPURestartSkipped`. SDMA0_PAGE on channels 12 and 53 shows the same
shape with the same slow advance. `bad bits` 4, unchanged for seven boots.

**SO THE FRONTIER MOVES OFF THE DISPLAY HALF.** 2we called the wedge an
independent second defect and that still holds - it is on GFX/SDMA channels,
not the display interrupt - but it has never had a milestone of its own and it
is now the only measured candidate left. **The display half is done**: every
failure mode it ever had reads 0, the write lands, the swizzle agrees, the
retire kick delivers.

**THE NEXT EXPERIMENT NEEDS NO KERNEL CHANGE AND THE USER ALREADY WANTS TO RUN
IT.** A GPU compute benchmark discriminates the two remaining readings
directly, because it submits to the same channels and reports a throughput
number:

- **A normal score** -> the GPU executes at full speed and the defect is
  purely the completion path, which is where every further boot should go.
- **A score one or two orders low** -> submission itself stalls on the same
  accounting, and the ~2/s is a global ceiling on all GPU work, not a display
  problem at all.

Either answer is worth more than another display-side boot, and the desktop is
usable enough to type a command, which is all it takes.

## 2wo — the instrument for the stamp-retirement defect: latency, not a score

No boot. Built because the benchmark route is not usable: at ~1 frame per
7 seconds with a cursor that freezes with everything else, a GUI benchmark app
cannot be driven, and a *score* would not answer the question anyway.

**What boot 197 left to decide.** GFX channel 52 submitted 2.40 stamps/s and
retired 2.09 while `rbgpu-ring` read **`r == w` at all three samples** with
`vmf=0` and `cps=0`. The chip executes everything it is handed, immediately,
and the ~2/s is the driver learning that work finished. That is a statement
about **latency**, and Metal already exposes the decomposition:

    GPU      cb.GPUEndTime    - cb.GPUStartTime      what the chip took
    driver   cb.kernelEndTime - cb.kernelStartTime   what the driver scheduled
    wall     commit -> waitUntilCompleted            what the caller waited for

`tools/metal_probe.m --bench [N]` (N bounded 1..1000, default 20) runs N
serial command buffers, printing all three per iteration and the medians, then
a **pipelined** pass - N committed back to back, waiting only for the last -
because a per-buffer notification cost and a bandwidth ceiling are
indistinguishable when every buffer is waited on individually. The dispatch is
deliberately tiny (4096 threads, three arithmetic ops) so that anything above
microseconds is overhead. The `--dispatch` verify is kept at the end: a fast
wrong answer is not a result (rule 14).

**The control is INTERNAL, and it has to be.** Run on this machine's
*unarmed* boot, `MTLCopyAllDevices` returns **0 devices** - there is no
software Metal path here to compare against. So the comparison is GPU time
against wall time **inside one command buffer**, which is better: both numbers
come from the same measurement and no second boot has to be matched to the
first.

**SAID BEFORE THE RUN.**

- **wall ~500 ms with gpu in microseconds** (ratio in the thousands) -> the
  completion path is the defect, it is proven on the RENDERING side with the
  display nowhere in it, and `1/wall` should land near boot 197's measured
  2.09 stamps/s. Every further boot goes to the stamp/fence path.
- **wall tracking gpu closely** -> GPU work completes promptly, the ~2/s is
  not a GPU-work ceiling, and the display-side scheduling is where to look -
  which would also mean boot 197's "same order of magnitude" was coincidence,
  as it was explicitly not claimed to be more than.
- **pipelined much faster than serial** -> a per-buffer cost, i.e. a
  notification problem. **Pipelined no faster** -> a real throughput ceiling,
  a different defect from the one this is aimed at.

It submits real GPU work on a machine whose channels already time out, so it
can hang the GPU; the failure mode is a reboot, which is the existing one, and
every iteration is flushed so a hang keeps whatever completed (rule 10).

**Rule 16 applies to this too**: the probe is a suspect. It is read-only with
respect to the kext, touches no register, and needs neither the framebuffer
nor the display path - the one thing it shares with the frame rate is the
channel the work goes on, which is the point.

## 2wp — the frozen progress bar was a healthy machine, and the arming hole is ours

Three power cycles, no capture, recovered with `-rbgpuoff`. Diagnosed from
NVRAM and the persisted log; **no boot was spent on the diagnosis**.

**Rule 8 first, and it is the whole finding.** After three attempts:

    rbgpu-boot   197     UNCHANGED - the peer never armed, three times
    rbgpu-arm    1       STILL SET, unconsumed
    rbgpu-agdc   1       STILL SET
    rbgpu-iop    1       STILL SET
    rbgpu-fb     0       CONSUMED

**The framebuffer armed and the plugin did not.** And the crumb from that boot
says what followed:

    b=197 s=12 f=10000 e=1 r=1 h=0 w=0 k=0 t=0 p=0 n=0 K=0 D=0

`b=197` against a nonce still at 197 (the fb reads it before the peer
increments, 2wg) places it in one of those boots. `h=0` - hubpSetup succeeded,
so `start()` ran and the panel was **ours**. `f=10000` - our VBL clock ran for
69.5 seconds. **`t=0` - not one transaction, ever.** `w=0`, `K=0`, `D=0`.

**And the machine was FINE.** The persisted log shows that boot reaching
`WindowServer: Server is starting up` and then logging normally until
**16:19:59 - ten minutes**. Networking, power management, disk, Time Machine.
The user was looking at a frozen picture of a working computer. **Rule 12,
paid for a fourth time**: a frozen panel is indistinguishable from a hang, and
this time it cost three power cycles and a rescue boot-arg.

**THE HOLE IS IN OUR ARMING AND IT IS MINE.** `-rbgpuownfb` + `rbgpu-fb` arm
the takeover **independently of whether the accelerator is armed** - they are
different boot-args and different one-shots, by design, so the two halves
stay separable. But the framebuffer can only ever show anything **if** the
accelerator hands it transactions: it writes HUBP from
`setAttribute('amtr')` and from nothing else. Taking the panel with no
accelerator underneath is therefore a **guaranteed** frozen screen, and
nothing refused it. Every other dangerous feature in this project needs an arg
*and* a one-shot precisely so a bad boot cannot repeat (rule 9); this
combination had both and still repeated, because **each half was armed
correctly and the pair was never checked**.

**WHY THE PLUGIN DID NOT ARM IS NOT ESTABLISHED.** The one-shots are
untouched and the nonce never moved, so the peer's `start()` never completed -
but the cause is open. **An attempt to read the hung boot's boot-args out of
the log was invalid**: the kernel's `Boot args:` line is truncated by os_log
(it ends mid-token at `-rtw`), so 17 tokens against the 54 in boot 197's
`boot-args.txt` is the instrument cutting the line, not a difference. Rule 26
on my own check; the comparison is withdrawn and the question stays open.

**Build `3FB13023`: the no-transaction self-disarm.** If `amtrArmed` and
`amtrSets == 0` at vblank **18000** (125 s at the measured 143.83 Hz), consume
`rbgpu-fb` by overwrite on the syncing path (2wj's mechanism, for 2wj's
reason) and drop a crumb at stage 99.

- **It cannot rescue the running boot** and does not pretend to - the panel is
  already ours and cannot be handed back. What it buys is that the **next**
  power cycle comes up on `IONDRVFramebuffer` with a usable desktop. Three
  power cycles into a frozen screen becomes exactly one.
- **The deadline is measured, not guessed**: boot 196 had `amtrSets 4` by fire
  10000 (70 s) and boot 197 had transactions flowing well before that, while
  the frozen boot had 0 at the same point. n=2, so it is set nearly twice as
  far out as the latest first transaction ever seen.
- **The asymmetry is the design.** Firing in a merely slow boot costs one
  power cycle to re-arm. Not firing costs power-cycling into a frozen screen
  until the user gives up. Those are not comparable.
- It runs on the VBL clock that is already there - no new `thread_call`, no
  allocation - and only when `amtrArmed`, so a plain `-rbgpuownfb` boot is
  untouched. Three hosttest cases: it fires at the deadline, it does **not**
  fire when a single transaction arrived, and it fires at most once ever.
  Mutation tested - dropping the `amtrSets == 0` term fails the second case.

**RECOVERY IS STAGED, AND THE FIRST STEP CANNOT FREEZE.** With `rbgpu-fb`
already 0, removing `-rbgpuoff` gives a boot where `IONDRVFramebuffer` keeps
the panel and the desktop is usable whatever the plugin does - and
`rbgpu-boot` then answers the open question directly: **198 means the peer
arms fine and this was only the pairing hole; still 197 means the plugin
itself is failing and that is the next defect.** Either way the machine comes
back. The framebuffer goes back on only after that reads 198.

## 2wq — boot 198: the GPU is 12 000x faster than the notification, and there is no throughput ceiling

Armed, usable desktop, **`RBAMDFramebuffer` not loaded at all** (`rbgpu-fb` 0,
three `IONDRVFramebuffer` instances). Rule 8: `rbgpu-boot` **198**, `armed=1`,
all three one-shots consumed. Rule 33: `kern.boottime` 17:05:18, this is that
boot. `tools/metal_probe --bench 40`, output in `logs/metalbench.txt`.

**2wp's open question is ANSWERED: the plugin arms fine on its own.** The
nonce moved 197 -> 198 with `rbgpu-fb` at 0 and the framebuffer declining the
panel. So the three frozen boots were **the pairing hole and nothing else** -
rule 38 stands as written, and there is no second plugin defect to chase.

**THE MEASUREMENT:**

    SERIAL median: wall 172.557 ms   gpu 0.014 ms   driver 0.054 ms  -> 5.8/s
    SERIAL range : wall  97.878 .. 180.985 ms
    OVERHEAD RATIO: wall / gpu = 12220.7x
    PIPELINED: 40 buffers in 0.182 s -> 220.2 buffers/s   (38.0x speedup)
    verify: PASS (0 of 4096 wrong)

**The GPU takes 14 microseconds. The caller waits 172 milliseconds.** The
driver's own scheduling interval (`kernelEndTime - kernelStartTime`) is 54
microseconds, so the driver is not slow either - the time is spent entirely
between "the work finished" and "the caller was told".

**AND THERE IS NO THROUGHPUT CEILING.** Forty command buffers committed back
to back complete in **0.182 s**, which is *one serial wait*. The chip, the
ring and the driver retire **220 buffers/s** when nobody waits per buffer. So
the ~2/s is **not** a bandwidth limit, not GPU speed, and not work the chip
is slow at - it is a **per-completion notification cost**, paid once per wait.
That is exactly the "pipelined much faster than serial" branch 2wo named
before the run, and the serial figure of 5.8/s sits in the same class as boot
197's 2.09 GFX stamps retired per second.

**THE DISPLAY HALF IS NOT INVOLVED, AND THIS BOOT PROVES IT.**
`RBAMDFramebuffer` was never loaded: no takeover, no HUBP write, no `'amtr'`,
`IONDRVFramebuffer` owning the panel throughout. The defect is present at full
strength regardless. Every reading since 2wi that wondered whether the frame
rate was a display problem is settled - **it is not**, and the display half's
clean sheet in boot 197 was telling the truth.

**WHAT 172 ms MEANS FOR 144 Hz.** A compositor must wait for its own render to
complete before presenting it, so a serial completion latency is a hard frame
ceiling: 1/0.172 = **5.8 fps**, against the 6.9 ms a 144 Hz frame is allowed.
The gap is now one named number rather than a mystery, and the pipelined 220/s
says the machinery underneath is **already fast enough** - nothing has to get
faster, something has to stop waiting.

**NOT ESTABLISHED - do not write any of these as fact yet.** What produces the
172 ms is unknown. The shape is suggestive and no more: iterations 1-39 cluster
tightly in 167-181 ms (iteration 0 is 97.9 ms, a warm-up), which is **too tight
for a uniform poll** of period T - that would spread over [0, T] and average
T/2. A fixed sleep, a timeout, or a wake-up tied to something else on a ~172 ms
cadence all fit. A missing or mis-routed GPU completion interrupt is the
obvious candidate given 2we's wedge shape (work submitted, never retiring,
hang check says not hung), but **nothing here measures the interrupt path** and
rule 13 applies to the number as much as to a return code.

**THE NEXT STEP IS CHEAP, NEEDS NO BOOT, AND DISCRIMINATES.** Compare
`waitUntilCompleted` against `addCompletedHandler` on the same command buffer:
if the handler fires promptly and only the wait is late, the defect is in the
**wait primitive**; if both are late by 172 ms, it is the **notification** and
the interrupt path is where to look. The machine is usable and the
framebuffer is out of the picture, so this costs one command and no risk.

## 2wr — it is the NOTIFICATION, not the wait, and it is not our instrument

Same boot 198, same usable desktop, no framebuffer. `--bench` now times the
completion **handler** against the **wait** from one commit, because they are
two different ways to learn the same fact and only timing both separates them.

    SERIAL median: wall 173.805 ms   gpu 0.014 ms
    HANDLER median:    173.796 ms    (wait - handler = 0.009 ms)
    VERDICT: handler and wait are late TOGETHER -> notification
    PIPELINED: 25 buffers in 0.176 s -> 141.9 buffers/s

**Nine microseconds apart.** `addCompletedHandler` fires at the same instant
`waitUntilCompleted` returns, 173 ms after a commit whose GPU work took 14
microseconds. So **`waitUntilCompleted` is not the problem** - the wait
primitive returns the moment it is told. The driver is not told for 173 ms.

**Reproducible**: 172.557 ms (n=40) and 173.805 ms (n=25), two runs.

**RULE 16 CHECKED AND CLEARED, explicitly, because the suspect was ours.**
`-rbgpustampwait` is in boot-args and it routes `AMDHWChannel::waitForHwStamp`
to `rbgpu_bounded_stamp_wait_2en` - our own polling loop. Two reasons it is
not this number: its poll is **100 us per iteration**, so it would return
within 100 us of the stamp landing and could not manufacture 173 ms; and the
live diag table carries **no `bwait_*` key at all** this boot
(`bwait_iters`, `bwait_raw`, `bwait_disabled`, `bwait_vt_bad` all absent),
so the bounded wait was **never reached**. The hook is not in the Metal
completion path. Said out loud because when a measurement and one of our own
features are both in frame, the feature is the first suspect, not the last.

**WHAT THIS LEAVES.** Something must tell the driver a command buffer
finished. It is told 173 ms late, uniformly, independent of how much work the
buffer did, while the chip finishes in microseconds and 25 buffers' worth of
notifications arrive together in one 176 ms window. **The completion signal
is the defect** - interrupt, event, or whatever stands in for it here - and
nothing else in the chain is slow.

**AND 144 Hz IS NOT BLOCKED BY SPEED.** A 144 Hz frame is 6.9 ms. The
pipelined path already retires a buffer every 4.5 ms. Nothing has to get
faster; the per-completion wait has to stop happening.

## 2ws — THE 176 ms IS BEFORE THE WORK, NOT AFTER IT. 2wq AND 2wr ARE REFUTED.

No boot. Boot 198 throughout (`rbgpu-boot` 198, `rbgpu-arm` consumed,
`kern.boottime` 17:05:18, `RBAMDFramebuffer` NOT loaded) — so the display half
is not in the picture at all and nothing here is about the framebuffer.

**THE SPLIT.** `GPUStartTime`, `kernelStartTime` and `mach_absolute_time` share
one host timebase, so subtracting the commit instant says WHERE the latency
sits. Median of 13 serial command buffers:

    commit -> kernelStart      0.025 ms     the driver has it immediately
    commit -> GPUStart       175.951 ms     the GPU does not START for 176 ms
    GPUStart -> GPUEnd         0.014 ms
    GPUEnd  -> caller return   0.045 ms     completion reported instantly

**So the completion path is FINE — 45 microseconds — and the work sits for
176 ms before the GPU begins executing it.** 2wr concluded "the completion
signal is the defect"; that is **WITHDRAWN**. Its measurement stands (the
handler and the wait really are 9 us apart) but both of those are *downstream
of execution*, so the test could not see a pre-execution delay even in
principle. 2wq's "no throughput ceiling, the notification is the whole defect"
is withdrawn for the same reason.

**THE INSTRUMENT IS VALIDATED, WHICH IS WHY THE SPLIT CAN BE BELIEVED**
(rule 16). The obvious failure mode is that `GPUStartTime`/`GPUEndTime` are the
instant the driver *noticed* a stamp rather than real GPU timestamps — in which
case the split would be an artefact. A control kernel with a caller-chosen loop
count settles it:

    loops        gpu(ms)   commit->GPUstart(ms)   GPUend->return(ms)
    (none)         0.014          175.95                0.045
    2000           0.232          176.38                0.042
    200000         5.896          174.46                0.051

GPU time moves over a **420x range** while `commit->GPUstart` stays pinned to
the tick and `GPUend->return` stays at ~45 us. The pair is real.

**IT IS A TICK, NOT A WAKE-UP.** Twelve pipelined buffers, GPUstart relative to
the first commit: 175.253, 175.882, 175.990, 176.002, 176.014, 176.117,
176.129, 176.140, 176.244, 176.255, 176.267, 176.644. **First-to-last spread
1.391 ms over 12 buffers** — one periodic event releases the whole batch, which
then runs back to back 12 us apart, with the GPU idle for the preceding 176 ms
holding work it had already been given.

**AND IT IS LOAD-INDEPENDENT.** With a second process keeping 8 buffers in
flight continuously for 26 s, the first process still measured a 174.590 ms
median — and the busy process itself managed **46.2 buffers/s, which is
8 buffers x 5.78 ticks/s to three figures**. Both processes are release-rate
limited, not bandwidth limited.

**HOW THE PERIODICITY WAS ESTABLISHED, AND HOW 2wq GOT IT BACKWARDS.** 2wq
wrote that the 167-181 ms cluster was "too tight for a uniform poll, which
would spread over [0,T] and average T/2". That is wrong for a SERIAL loop: the
next buffer is submitted microseconds after the previous one retired, i.e.
microseconds after a tick, so it has just missed one and waits very nearly a
FULL period. wall ~= T every time, tightly clustered. The spread over [0,T]
applies only to a submission at random phase, and the bench has exactly one of
those — **iteration 0, which read 97.9, 104.6, 45.4 and 101.2 ms across four
runs.** The fix is to break the phase lock deliberately, by waiting d after
each completion before submitting the next (`metal_probe --phase`):

    d(ms)      0      50     100     150     170     180     240
    wall     173.7   123.9   71.7    23.3     2.3   168.5   108.2
    d+wall   173.7   173.9   171.7   173.3   172.3   348.5   348.2

`d+wall` is **constant at ~173.7 ms** up to d=170 and then jumps to **~348 ms
= 2T**; at d=170 the buffer retires in 2.3 ms because the tick was already due.
A fixed per-buffer delay would have left the wall column flat. Two independent
reads of the period from one table.

**THE CLOCK IS FREE-RUNNING AND PER-CLIENT.** A lattice fit over absolute
`mach_absolute_time` completion instants at pseudo-random phase
(`metal_probe --lattice`) locks hard: **T = 175.77 ms, R = 0.966 over 191
periods**, residual sigma 7.4 ms. Every round candidate is rejected by the same
data — 25 panel vblanks (173.76 ms) R = 0.13, 6 Hz (166.67 ms) R = 0.05 — so
the period is **not** a number anyone wrote down, which is the signature of a
handler that re-arms after doing its own work. Two processes run concurrently
read T = 176.016 and 176.080 ms, i.e. **the same period**, but phases of
118.172 and 31.929 ms in the shared mach epoch, i.e. **independent phase**. So
it is not one global driver heartbeat; each client has its own, built from the
same interval.

**WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE FRAME RATE.** A client can cross at most ~5.7 release
boundaries per second no matter how much it queues, so no client can present
more than ~5.7 times a second. 144 Hz needs 6.9 ms; the release quantum is
175 ms, **25x too slow**. Nothing needs to get faster — the GPU executes in
microseconds and a batch of 40 drains in one tick. **The quantum has to go
away.**

**WHAT WAS READ STATICALLY, AND WHAT IT ELIMINATES.**
- `AMDRadeonX6000_AMDHWChannel::waitForHwStamp` (`0xbe85536`) and
  `AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelChannel::waitForTimestamp` (`0xbe46f9a`) both poll at
  a **100 us** interval (`0x64`, scale 1000) with a 5 s + 20 s budget
  (`0x4C4B40` us then `0x17D7840 - 0x4C4B40`), through
  `IAMDHWInterface::pollWait` (`0xbeab6e0`) = `clock_get_uptime` ->
  `absolutetime_to_nanoseconds` -> `assert_wait_timeout(100 us)` ->
  `thread_block` on one shared global event. **A 100 us poll cannot produce
  176 ms**, and the split now shows the completion side was never the problem,
  so these are off the list.
- `IOAccelEventMachine2::enableStampInterrupt` / `disableStampInterrupt`
  (`0x14e2653c` / `0x14e26542`) are **empty stubs** — `push rbp; mov; pop; ret`
  — i.e. vendor override points, and AMDRadeonX6000 only *calls* them. The AMD
  side does implement the machinery:
  `AMDHWChannel::registerTimestampInterrupt` (`0xbe85a02`),
  `enableTimestampInterrupt` (`0xbe85904`, which returns 0 immediately unless
  `channel->0xa8 != 0`, the per-ring IRQ id from
  `AMDGFX10PM4Engine::getTimestampIRQSourcex` = `*(u32*)(this + 0x244 +
  ring*0x20)`), `timeStampInterruptCallback` (`0xbe85838`), all gated by
  `AMDHardware::useTimestampInterrupts` (`0xbea961c`) = `this->0x319 == 1 &&
  (obj->0x98 - obj->0x90) < 1e9 ns`. **This whole line is now a side issue**,
  not the frontier: it is about completion, and completion takes 45 us.
- `AMDSWScheduler::advance()` (`0xbe950e0`) walks every HwChannelCtx (0x98
  stride, count at `+0x60`) and pushes any marked `+0x71` through
  `advance(HwChannelCtx&)` (`0xbe9442a`). It has exactly **two** reachers, both
  tail jumps: `deferredCallback(IOInterruptEventSource*)` (`0xbe93e18`) and
  `timerCallback(IOTimerEventSource*)` (`0xbe9513c`) — and **`timerCallback` is
  referenced nowhere else in the kext**, so that timer is never installed.
  `advance(HwChannelCtx&)` is also called directly from `submitCommandBuffer`
  (`0xbe943e9`), so the submit path does reach the hardware push synchronously.
  Neither kext imports any `setTimeout*`/`wakeAtTime` at all — only
  `timerEventSource`, `interruptEventSource`, `clock_get_uptime`,
  `clock_interval_to_deadline`, `nextIdleTimeout`, `setIdleTimerPeriod` — so
  **whatever the 176 ms clock is, it is probably not an armed
  IOTimerEventSource**, and that is a constraint on the answer rather than an
  answer.

**NOT ESTABLISHED — do not write any of these as fact.** What produces the
176 ms is **unknown**. Its shape constrains it: free-running, per-client, the
same interval in every client, load-independent, not a round number, releasing
an unbounded batch at once. Candidates not yet separated: a doorbell write that
never reaches the command processor with something periodic re-programming the
ring pointers instead (`AMDGFX10GraphicsRing::programReadAndWritePointers`
`0xbe99da4`, and note the family of `dummyWPTRUpdateDiag` helpers that exist at
all); a user-queue attach/swap quantum (`advance(HwChannelCtx&)` calls
`AMDUserQueue::isAttached` at `0xbe94730` then `userQueueSwitch` at
`0xbe94762`); and a power/clock gating cycle. **Nothing measured here touches
the ring kick**, and rule 35 applies — instrument our own end before building
on a chain.

**Rules.** Rule 33 again, in a new form: *name which side of the work a latency
is on before attributing it.* 2wr measured two downstream clocks against each
other and called the result the defect; the number was right and the object it
belonged to was wrong. And rule 16 earned its keep positively for once — the
heavy-kernel control is the only reason the split is believable.

**Instrument.** `tools/metal_probe.m` gains `--phase [N]` (break the phase
lock, read the period off the sawtooth), `--lattice [N]` (fit the period and
the absolute phase, comparable across processes), `--busy [S]` (keep work in
flight from another process), `--heavy [N]` (the scaling control) and the
per-iteration split columns. Captures in `logs/metalphase.txt`,
`logs/metallattice.txt`, `logs/metalsplit.txt`, `logs/metalpipe.txt`.

## 2wt — THE WEDGE IS REPRODUCIBLE FROM USERSPACE IN SIX SECONDS, AND IT IS A COMPUTE USER QUEUE COUNT

No boot, boot 198 throughout. `metal_probe --queues K` creates K
`MTLCommandQueue`s in one process, warms each, then commits one buffer to each
and reads every buffer's `GPUStartTime`.

**THE TICK IS PER-PROCESS, NOT PER-QUEUE.**

    K=2    172.811  173.072                     spread 0.262 ms
    K=3    171.472  171.731  171.861            spread 0.389 ms

Every queue in a process is released by the **same** tick. Combined with 2ws's
two-process result (same period, independent phase), the object that owns the
~173 ms release quantum is the **client/process**, not the command queue and
not the device. So adding queues buys no release events, and that route to
144 Hz is closed.

**AND AT FOUR QUEUES THERE IS A CLIFF.**

    K=4    10004.996  10208.530  10208.660  10208.806
    K=4     6105.441   6105.919   6106.070   6106.217   (repeat)
    K=6    10107.057 10107.463 10107.627 10107.766 | 10281.486 10281.616

**6.1 to 10.2 SECONDS**, not 173 ms, and the value varies between runs — the
shape of a detect-and-recover timeout rather than a quantum. Three queues are
fine; four are not.

**IT IS 2we's WEDGE, CAUGHT ON DEMAND.** A sender-matched capture over the
K=4 run (478 IOAcceleratorFamily2 + AMDRadeonX6000 lines as the control):

    event timeout              5        no channel associated      5
    checkGPUProgress          16        pending stamps             5
    Signaling hardware error  16        GPURestart               412
    not hung                   5

Exactly 2we's signature — submitted, never retiring, hang check says not hung,
restart cannot find the channel. **Since 2we the wedge has only ever been
visible inside a full armed boot; it is now a userspace command that takes six
seconds.** That is the cheapest instrument this project has gained in a long
while, and it needs no kext, no arming and no reboot.

**THE CHANNELS NAME THEMSELVES, AND THAT IS THE LEAD:**

    channel  5 ComputeUQ2 event timeout; pending stamps [5..5]
    channel  6 ComputeUQ3 event timeout; pending stamps [2080..2080]
    channel  9 ComputeUQ6 event timeout; pending stamps [132..132]
    channel 33 SDMA0      event timeout; pending stamps [3155..3155]

So a Metal command queue becomes a **compute user queue**, the low ones work
and the later ones never retire a single pending stamp. That is the same shape
as the one chip fact already established about queue counts here — **one SDMA
instance where Apple's Navi 21 path builds four** (2gc/2gi) — now appearing on
the compute side.

**THE CORRESPONDENCE WORTH NAMING, AND NOT YET A CLAIM.** 2wi measured the live
accelerated desktop at *"a new frame only about every 10 seconds"*. The cliff
here costs **6.1-10.2 s**. This is the first time the desktop's own number has
been reproduced headlessly, and WindowServer plus a few apps will certainly
hold four or more command queues. **NOT ESTABLISHED**: that they are the same
defect. The desktop figure was read off a screen by eye, this one off
`GPUStartTime`, and 2wi's 10 s was also matched quantitatively by the
transaction rate (0.093 sets/s, one per 10.8 s), which is a different
mechanism. Two numbers agreeing to one significant figure is a lead, not an
identification — and rule 18 says do not build a table from it.

**WHAT THIS DOES NOT EXPLAIN.** The ~173 ms tick is untouched: K=1..3 wedge
nothing, log nothing, and still wait 173 ms with the GPU idle. There are **two
independent defects**, and the tick is the one that caps the frame rate at
5.7 Hz. The wedge adds multi-second spikes on top.

**NEXT, no boot**: `AMDHardware::mapDoorbellMemory` (`0xbea9118`),
`AMDUserQueue::updateDoorbell` (`0xbe6d14e`) and
`AMDHardware::getChannelDoorbellOffset` (`0xbeab9be`, overridden by
`AMDGFX10Hardware` at `0xbead0d2`). A doorbell write that does not reach the
command processor would leave queued work invisible to the chip until something
else poked it, which is the tick's shape; and `advance(HwChannelCtx&)` already
reads `AMDUserQueue::isAttached` before calling `userQueueSwitch`. Rule 35:
instrument before building on it.

## 2wu — EVERY ENGINE, ONE TICK. THE DRIVER HOLDS THE WORK.

No boot, boot 198. Two measurements close the characterisation.

**THE BUFFER IS "SCHEDULED" IN 92 MICROSECONDS.** `addScheduledHandler` fires
when the driver has handed the buffer on, before it completes, so it separates
a deferred submission from a chip-side delay:

    commit -> scheduled      0.092 ms
    scheduled -> GPUstart  ~174.8 ms
    GPUstart -> GPUend       0.014 ms
    GPUend -> return         0.042 ms

So **userspace is exonerated** — the dispatch source the `sample` caught
(`com.Metal.CommandQueueDispatch` -> `_submitAvailableCommandBuffers` ->
`IOAccelCommandQueueSubmitCommandBuffers` -> `IOConnectCallMethod`) runs at
once, and `kernelStartTime`'s 0.025 ms is corroborated by a clock whose meaning
is measured here rather than taken from Apple's documentation (rule 13).

**AND IT IS NOT COMPUTE-SPECIFIC.** 2wt showed a Metal command queue becomes a
compute user queue, which raised the real possibility that the tick never
touches the desktop, since WindowServer renders rather than dispatching. One
buffer per engine through the same queue, median of 8 after the random-phase
first:

    compute        wall 174.385 ms   commit->GPUstart 174.333 ms    5.7/s
    blit (SDMA)    wall 173.103 ms   commit->GPUstart 173.043 ms    5.8/s
    render (gfx)   wall 173.766 ms   commit->GPUstart 173.706 ms    5.8/s

**Identical on all three.** The graphics ring is ticked exactly like the
compute one, so the quantum *does* cap the desktop. 144 Hz needs 6.944 ms;
this is **25x** too slow.

**THE SHAPE, COMPLETE.** Collecting 2ws/2wt/2wu, the release quantum is:
every engine, every queue in a process released together, one shared cadence
per process, **independent phase between processes**, free-running, period
173-180 ms, load-independent, releasing an unbounded batch at once, with the
GPU demonstrably idle meanwhile and the work already submitted and marked
scheduled.

**THAT RULES OUT A CHIP-LEVEL MECHANISM.** Two processes submitting
concurrently throughout were released on two cadences of the same period at
**different phase**. A doorbell the command processor cannot see, an MES
timeslice, or a clock/power gating cycle are all properties of the chip and
would give every client the *same* phase. They do not. **So the decision to
release is made per client, in software, above the hardware** — which is the
first finding that points at a specific function rather than at a layer:
`AMDSWScheduler::advance()` (`0xbe950e0`), whose only two reachers are
`deferredCallback(IOInterruptEventSource*)` (`0xbe93e18`) and the never-
installed `timerCallback` (`0xbe9513c`), and which pushes exactly those
HwChannelCtx marked at `+0x71`.

**NOT ESTABLISHED.** That `advance()` is the gate, and that `deferredCallback`
is the thing running late. Everything above is measured from userspace and
*nothing* in it observes a single call inside the driver. This is precisely the
situation rule 35 names: a static chain ending at a function we have not
instrumented. The next step instruments it.

**NEXT, one boot, plugin-only.** Hook `AMDSWScheduler::submitCommandBuffer`
(`0xbe942d0`), `advance()` (`0xbe950e0`) and `deferredCallback` (`0xbe93e18`)
and publish, per second: call counts for each, and the delta from a
`submitCommandBuffer` to the next `advance()`. Said before the boot:
**advance() at ~5.7/s with submitCommandBuffer far higher** means the release
is `advance()` and the fix is to drive it from the submit path; **advance()
tracking submitCommandBuffer one-for-one** means the hold is below it and
`advance(HwChannelCtx&)`'s own gates (`AMDUserQueue::isAttached` at `0xbe94730`,
then `userQueueSwitch`) are next. Either way the counters are cheap, read-only,
and the question is settled in one boot. No framebuffer, no display, no AGDC:
`rbgpu-fb` stays **0** (rule 38 — the fb takes the panel and would freeze it
with nothing to show).

## 2ww — BOOT 199: THE MACHINE DID 632 BUFFERS/s. THE 175 ms IS A STATE, NOT A PROPERTY.

Rule 8/15/33/34 first: `rbgpu-boot` **199**, `rbgpu-arm` consumed, plugin
**`0EE32DFA`** = `build/out` exactly, `kern.boottime` **18:13:09**. `rbgpu-fb`
reads **`0`**, so the framebuffer declined and the display half is not in this
at all - though note `-rbgpuownfb` and the whole `-rbgpufb*` family ARE in
boot-args and `com.rembrandtgpu.fb` (`7A6A56A9`) is loaded from the AuxKC;
loading is not arming.

**THE USER'S OWN RUN, EARLY IN BOOT 199:**

    SERIAL median: wall 1.582 ms  gpu 0.013 ms  -> 632.0 buffers/s
    SPLIT median: commit -> GPUstart 1.522 ms, GPUend -> return 0.037 ms
    SCHEDULED median: 0.082 ms
    PIPELINED: 120 buffers in 0.050 s -> 2377.6 buffers/s
    first->last GPUstart spread = 31.776 ms over 120 buffers

**MINE, SAME BOOT, A FEW MINUTES LATER:**

    SERIAL median: wall 175.728 ms  gpu 0.014 ms  -> 5.7 buffers/s
    SPLIT median: commit -> GPUstart 175.671 ms, GPUend -> return 0.043 ms

Same boot, same binary, same `gpu` time to one microsecond - so the shader
clock is identical and this is not a faster chip. **632 buffers/s is 4.4x what
144 Hz needs.** The hardware, the driver and the completion path can all do it.
**So every reading in 2ws/2wt/2wu was taken inside one state of the machine,
and "the quantum has to go" was describing a state rather than a property.**
The characterisation (tick, per-client phase, T = 175.77 ms, R = 0.966) stands
as a description of the slow state; nothing in it was ever a property of the
hardware, and 2ws should not have written it as one from a single boot.

**WHAT `rbgpu-sched` SAYS, AND IT KILLS THE FIRST PREDICTION.** The flush runs
at the phase marks (+12/+100/+160 s), so this note covers the **fast** window:

    b=199 hk=1 sub=12191 adv=46457 smax=589 gmin=0 gmean=3412 gmax=6007470
    h=876,38808,6177,13,14,16,38,81,111,68,65,52,54,83

`advance()` ran **46 457 times against 12 191 submits** - four times more often
than work was submitted - with mean gap **3.4 ms** and **38 808 of the gaps
under 128 us**. 2wv predicted "advance() at ~5.7/s with submitCommandBuffer far
higher means advance() IS the release". It is the other branch: `advance()` runs
constantly and is **not** a 5.7 Hz gate. What is not yet known is its rate in
the SLOW state, because the note is only written at three fixed phases - the
same mistake 2wl had to fix for the crumb, in a different file. **A counter that
flushes at fixed marks cannot compare two regimes.**

**THREE CANDIDATES KILLED, ALL FREE, ALL IN THE SLOW STATE.**
1. *The wedge.* Boot 199 wedged on its own at **+19 s** (`channel 10
   ComputeUQ7`, `channel 53 SDMA0_PAGE`, `channel 52 GFX`; 31 `event timeout`,
   167 `GPURestart` within boot 199, separated from boot 198's by the
   timestamp - rule 28, the first `--last 70m` window spanned both boots).
   Churn ran 18:13:28-18:15:41 and the fast reading sits inside it, the slow
   ones after. Inducing it deliberately with `--queues 4` and benching through
   it: **180.0 / 178.7 / 179.6 ms.** Wedge churn does not restore the fast
   state and does not cause the slow one.
2. *Load.* A keep-alive of 64 light-ish buffers deep gave the keep-alive
   process **354.9 buffers/s** and a concurrent client **182.7 ms**; at depth
   128, **366.4/s** and **179.3 ms**. 354.9/64 = **5.55 batches/s** - the tick
   is untouched, it simply released 64 buffers at once.
3. *Saturation.* 64 x 5.9 ms = 378 ms of continuous GPU work per batch ran at
   **149.2 buffers/s = 2.33 batches/s (429 ms)**, and a concurrent client read
   **430.932 ms - exactly that batch period**. So releases **serialise across
   clients**. An intermediate reading that the release "follows the work with
   ~50 ms overhead" was over-fitted to `429 - 378` and is **withdrawn**: 429 is
   not a multiple of 175 either, and one number is not a model.

**AND 2ws's `--busy` TEST WAS INVALID AS RUN.** It concluded load-independence
from a generator producing 46 light buffers/s = **0.6 ms of GPU work per
second**, i.e. an idle GPU. The conclusion survives - load really does not
matter, now shown three ways - but it survives by luck. **A load generator
throttled by the thing it is testing measures nothing**, and `--busy` now takes
`--heavy` and `--depth` so it can actually saturate.

**NOT EVIDENCE (rule 14).** `PerformanceStatistics` on the accelerator carries
`Core Clock(MHz)=0`, `Memory Clock(MHz)=0`, `Total Power(W)=0`,
`Temperature(C)=0` - those fields are **not populated for this chip**, so they
say nothing about clocks either way, and `Device Utilization % = 1` beside four
dead siblings is not worth a reading. Also: the plugin's own `rbgpu_log` is
**not visible in the unified log** live (predicate matched 2 lines, both my own
command), so rule 31's lesson covers the plugin too and a live readout needs
NVRAM or the registry, not a log line.

**THE ONE NUMBER THAT MAKES THE NEXT EXPERIMENT DESIGNABLE** is when the flip
happens. The fast reading is somewhere inside the first ~2 minutes and every
slow reading is from +200 s on; the plugin's probe phases are +12/+100/+160 s,
which fits suspiciously well and makes **our own probes a suspect** (rule 16) -
`-rbgpuringprobe`, `-rbgpuringdump`, `-rbgpumcprobe` and `-rbgpuaccelprobe` are
all in boot-args. Equally consistent: anything else with a ~3 minute
constant. **Not established, and not to be written either way.**

**`tools/ratesweep.sh`** samples `--bench 6` on a clock and prints each median
against **seconds since boot**, labelling FAST (<20 ms) or slow - 20 ms is far
from both observed states, so the label cannot straddle them. Reads only; no
kext, no arming, no NVRAM writes; run it as the first thing in a boot. Its own
smoke test caught a bug in it immediately: `sed 's/.*sec = \([0-9]*\).*/\1/p'`
on `kern.boottime` is **greedy through to "usec = "** and captured the
microseconds field, printing boot+1792667083 s. Rule 16 again, and rule 26 -
the instrument was wrong in a way that still produced plausible-looking rows.

## 2wx — BOOT 200: A THIRD REGIME, AND THE WEDGE EXPLAINS TWO OF THE THREE

Rule 8/15/33/34: `rbgpu-boot` **200**, `kern.boottime` **22:21:25**,
`rbgpu-arm` consumed, `rbgpu-fb` **0** (the framebuffer declined again, so the
display half is still not involved).

**THE SWEEP, AND IT IS WORSE THAN ANYTHING MEASURED BEFORE.**
`tools/ratesweep.sh` from +117 s:

    boot+s    median(ms)   buffers/s
       117      3690.382         0.3
       151       645.148         1.6
       199      4853.574         0.2
       262     10590.280         0.1
       340     11106.244         0.1
       427      7129.548         0.1

**Seconds per command buffer**, and 10.6 s is the number 2wi read off the
screen as *"a new frame only about every 10 seconds"* - the first time that
figure has appeared in a headless measurement. (The sweep's own interval
stretched from 10 s to 34-87 s because each `--bench 6` costs six buffers; at
0.1/s that is a minute. The interval is not the instrument's error, but the
sampler should use fewer buffers.)

**AND THE SAME BOOT RECOVERED.** At +~570 s the same binary read **186-190 ms**
(`--perqueue`) and **184.396 ms** (`--bench`). So boot 200 went
seconds -> ~180 ms **within one boot**, and boot 199 went 1.582 ms -> 175.7 ms
within one boot. Three regimes now stand on one binary:

    1.582 ms   632 buffers/s     boot 199, before its first channel timeout
    ~180 ms    5.4-5.7/s         boots 198, 199 late, 200 late
    3.7-11 s   0.1-0.3/s         boot 200 while wedged

**THE WEDGE EXPLAINS TWO OF THEM, MEASURED BOTH WAYS INSIDE BOOT 200.** While
slow, the wedge ran **continuously from +20 s to +460 s** (82 `event timeout`,
139 `checkGPUProgress`, 82 `no channel associated`, 503 `GPURestart`, boot-200
lines separated from 199's by timestamp against a 1040-line control). In the
~180 ms state just now, a 3-minute window carries **0** of all three against a
6-line control. Boot 199 is the same shape from the other side: its churn ran
18:13:28-18:15:41 and **stopped**, and the rate settled at 175.7 ms. So:
**churn active -> seconds; churn quiet -> ~180 ms.**
