Boot 200 also wedged far wider than 199 - **nine** distinct channels against
four, led by `channel 5 ComputeUQ2` **47 times**, plus `SDMA0_PAGE` 53 and 12,
`ComputeUQ7`, `SDMA0` 29 and 28, `GFX` 52, `ComputeUQ4`, `VMPT` 25.

**THE SLOT LOTTERY IS DEAD.** The obvious reading of "ComputeUQ2 times out 47
times" is that a Metal queue lands on a good slot or a bad one and the rate is
whichever you drew. `--perqueue` holds five queues at once and times each
**separately** (which `--queues` could not - it committed one buffer per queue
together, so a slow slot hid inside the batch):

    queue 0  186.093 ms    queue 3  188.580 ms
    queue 1  189.988 ms    queue 4  187.988 ms
    queue 2  186.619 ms    ratio 1.0x -> UNIFORM

Every slot behaves identically. The rate is a property of the **machine's
state**, not of the queue you were given.

**AND `advance()` TRACKS THE REGIME, 8x.** `rbgpu-sched` from the same phase
window in two boots:

    boot 199 (fast)   sub=12191  adv=46457  gmean=3412 us   h[1]=38808
    boot 200 (slow)   sub=10728  adv=5686   gmean=27956 us  h[1]=4426

So `advance()` runs ~290/s in the fast regime and ~35/s in the slow one. **It
is still not the gate** - 35/s is two orders of magnitude above the 0.1-0.3
buffers/s actually completing - but it is a *proxy* that discriminates the
regimes from inside the kernel, which is what the next experiment needs.

**THE HYPOTHESIS, AND WHAT MAKES IT TESTABLE.** 1.582 ms is the only reading
ever taken **before a boot's first channel timeout**, and that first timeout
lands at **+19-20 s** in both boots that logged one (18:13:28 of a 18:13:09
boot; 22:21:45 of a 22:21:25 boot). So: *the GPU is healthy until the first
wedge and degraded afterwards, permanently, even once the churn stops.* If that
holds, the wedge is not a second defect beside a quantum - **it is the whole
defect**, the "175 ms tick" is its aftermath, and 632 buffers/s (4.4x what
144 Hz needs) is what this chip does untouched.
**NOT ESTABLISHED, and it must not be written as fact**: n=1 for the fast
reading, its exact timestamp was never recorded, and whether it preceded
18:13:28 is inferred from how long a 120-buffer bench takes (~0.25 s) plus
Metal init, not measured. 2ws's whole characterisation of the slow state - the
sawtooth, T = 175.77 ms at R = 0.966, the per-client phase - stands as a
description and is now **unexplained by this hypothesis**, which says nothing
about why the degraded state should be periodic at all.

**WHY USERSPACE CANNOT TEST IT.** `ratesweep.sh` could not start before
+117 s - a terminal does not exist that early - and that is precisely the
window in question.

**SO THE INSTRUMENT MOVES INTO THE KEXT (plugin `F991B506`).**
`rbgpu_rate_start_2wx()` samples `advance()` and `submitCommandBuffer` per
**10 s window** into a ring and writes the series to **`rbgpu-rate`** after
every window, for **eighteen windows = the first 180 s**, then stops so nothing
later can overwrite the early window. Shares `-rbgpuschedprobe` (no new token,
so rule 30 needs nothing). Counts saturate rather than wrap, because a wrapped
count reads as a small number and would be indistinguishable from the slow
regime. The write is on a `thread_call`, the context the heartbeat has written
NVRAM from since 2ey - never from the hooks, which stay plain statics (rule 31).
Armed from the peer's `start()` beside `rbgpu_accelprobe_start()`, which is
**the** site 2w5 established runs every boot - the heartbeat path is gated on
`-rbgpubeat` and silently did nothing for a whole boot.

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.** `a=` high (order 2000-3000 per 10 s window) in the
first one or two windows and then falling by ~8x, with the log's first
`event timeout` landing at that same window boundary, **confirms** it: the
healthy state exists and the wedge ends it. `a=` flat and low from window 0
means boot 199's 1.582 ms was something else entirely and the fast state is not
simply "before the first timeout". `a=` high throughout with the rate still
slow kills `advance()` as a proxy and the series is then worth nothing.

**Checks on `F991B506`**: UUID moved from `0EE32DFA`, `kmutil libraries`
resolves everything with **0** from `SystemKernelExtensions.kc`,
`grep -c IOGraphicsFamily src/plugin/Info.plist` = 0, and
`nm | grep -c rbgpu_rate_start_2wx` = 1 so the symbol is really in the shipped
binary.

## 2wy — boot 201: the sampler read an IDLE GPU, and the user reordered the limiters

**BOOT 201, armed, `rbgpu-boot` 201, `rbgpu-fb` 0 so `RBAMDFramebuffer`
declined and the desktop ran on `IONDRVFramebuffer`.** The 2wx sampler
delivered, and the first reading of it was mine to get wrong.

    rbgpu-rate   b=201 rate w=10 n=15
                 a=11,91,7,53,4,2,5,5,73,7,1518,1882,70,21,117
                 u=6,102,27,45,0,11,0,40,143,0,2140,4569,168,108,255
    rbgpu-sched  b=201 hk=1 sub=891 adv=506 smax=105 gmin=0
                 gmean=197777 gmax=9515289
                 h=38,358,25,7,6,6,1,3,4,4,8,13,4,28

**THE PRE-STATED PREDICTION'S PREMISE WAS UNMET, SO NONE OF ITS THREE BRANCHES
APPLY.** 2wx said: "`a=` high (order 2000-3000 per 10 s window) in the first one
or two windows and then falling by ~8x ... **confirms** it", and "`a=` flat and
low from window 0 means boot 199's 1.582 ms was something else entirely". `a=`
was **11** in window 0. But `u=` was **6** - and **four of the fifteen windows
have ZERO submits**. The GPU was not slow in those windows, it was **idle**.
With `rbgpu-fb=0` the desktop composites on the CPU (`CompositorSW`, 2pd) and
never asks the GPU for a frame, so no sampler of work *done* can read a rate
there. **The second branch is therefore NOT triggered: "flat and low from
window 0" is fully explained by an absent load and says nothing about whether
the fast state existed.** The user put it in one line - *"of course its cpu
cause we are in the CPU ran framebuffer"* - and it is the correct reading.
The recurring error, thirty-odd instances now: I did not say what would have
to be true for the series to mean anything. **What saved the boot is that `u=`
was published beside `a=`**, so the dead windows are legible instead of being
read as a refutation. A rate instrument must carry its own demand.

**THE INSTRUMENT SELF-CHECKS, AND IT PASSES.** `rbgpu-rate`'s windows are
deltas of the same counters `rbgpu-sched` totals, and the two keys are written
by different code at different times. Cumulative `u` runs
6,108,135,180,180,191,191,231,374,374,**2514**; cumulative `a` runs
11,102,109,162,166,168,173,178,251,258,**1776**. `sub=891` and `adv=506` both
fall **inside window 10** - so the two independently written keys agree on the
same counters and date the sched flush to ~+100 s. 2wx is sound; only its
interpretation was wrong.

**THE CHURN TIMELINE, BOOT-SEPARATED.** Rule 28 bit immediately: the first
`event timeout` in an 8-minute window reads **22:40:32**, which **predates
`kern.boottime` 22:41:06** - it is boot 200's tail. Split at the boundary,
boot 201 has 345 of the 436 lines: **29 `event timeout`, 42
`checkGPUProgress`, 29 `not hung`, 29 `no channel associated`, 157
`GPURestart`**, running **+25.8 s to +104 s**, then silence.

**THREE BOOTS NOW AGREE ON WHEN THE WEDGE STARTS**: first timeout at
**+19 s** (199), **+20 s** (200), **+25.8 s** (201). And three boots agree on
the post-churn rate: **175.7** (199), **184-190** (200), and boot 201 measured
by hand at **+608 s, quiet: 181.157 ms, 5.5 buffers/s**, pipelined spread
0.576 ms over 6 buffers - the same single-release tick. The correlation
*churn quiet -> ~180 ms* is now three for three.

**THE REGIME DISCRIMINATOR IS THE RATIO, NOT THE ABSOLUTE COUNT.** `adv/sub`:

    boot 199 fast window   46457/12191 = 3.81
    boot 200 whole boot     5686/10728 = 0.53
    boot 201 w10            1518/2140  = 0.71
    boot 201 w11            1882/4569  = 0.41

Boot 201's only two loaded windows (+100-120 s, the burst that overlaps the end
of churn) are **slow-regime**, which is what boot 200 already said about the
post-wedge state. A ~6-9x separation, and it normalises out the load - which
the absolute `a=` does not, as window 0 just demonstrated.

**THE USER REORDERED THE LIMITERS, AND IT CHANGES THE TARGET.** Reported from
the screen, the one instrument only they can read: **in this CPU-framebuffer
boot the desktop is a stable ~25 fps and usable**; the frame-presentation
defect belongs to the GPU-framebuffer configuration.

    software FB, boot 201      ~25 fps  usable   CPU rasterisation (2pd, ~48% of
                                                 WindowServer's main thread)
    GPU FB, boots 195/196      0.09 fps          transaction supply
                                                 (RBFBAmtrSets 13 in 167 s)
    the tick's ceiling on any GPU work  5.7/s    the 175 ms release quantum

**So the 175 ms tick was NEVER what held the GPU-framebuffer desktop to one
frame per 10 s** - 0.09 fps is **60x below** what even the slow tick allows.
Two independent limiters are stacked and the transaction supply is by far the
tighter; the quantum only becomes binding once supply is fixed, and then caps
us at 5.7 fps, still **25x** short of 144. And 25 fps says the CPU path is a
usable fallback, not a road to 144 Hz. **2wt's "two independent defects" stands
and gains a third**: supply, quantum, wedge.

**THE UNMEASURED WINDOW IS +0 TO +19 s**, and it is the only place the fast
state has ever been seen. Boot 199's 1.582 ms has no timestamp; whether it
preceded that boot's first timeout is **inferred from how long a 120-buffer
bench takes plus Metal init, not measured** (unchanged since 2ww). No terminal
exists that early and the desktop will never load the GPU in an `rbgpu-fb=0`
boot, so **the load has to be ours and it has to come from launchd**.

**`tools/earlybench.sh` + `tools/com.rembrandtgpu.earlybench.plist` (2wy).**
A `RunAtLoad` daemon, no `KeepAlive`, self-stopping at +180 s, sampling every
3 s into `/var/log/rbgpu-earlybench.log` with seconds-since-boot on every line.
It is a **120x DISCRIMINATOR, not a rate measurement**: `--bench 2` separates
1.5 ms from 180 ms with vast margin, every line carries `n=` so no later reader
takes a median of 2 for a rate (rule 18), and the last sample is `--bench 20`
for a figure comparable to the 181.157 ms measured by hand here.
**Rule 16 - the instrument is a suspect**: this submits GPU work and
`--queues 4` is a known wedge trigger, so it uses ONE queue via `--bench` and
never `--queues`; the control is already in hand, because three boots with no
early load put the first timeout at +19..+25.8 s. **Rule 21**: it unsets
`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` explicitly rather than trusting launchd's clean
environment. **Rule 14**: four paths out, each saying something different -
`FATAL` missing binary, `NOMEDIAN` with the raw head (so a Metal device that
cannot be created before login is distinguishable from a crash), a non-zero
`rc=`, and the sample itself. **All four were smoke-tested on boot 201**, and
the awk parser was checked against the real 181.157 ms and 1.582 ms lines plus
a negative control (rule 26 - a parser is an instrument too).

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.** A sample at +5..+15 s reading **~1.5 ms** and the
first `event timeout` landing after it **confirms** the hypothesis: the healthy
state exists and the wedge ends it. A sample that early reading **~180 ms**
**kills** it - the quantum is present from the start and boot 199's 1.582 ms
was something else, which would make it the outlier needing explanation rather
than the baseline. `NOMEDIAN` throughout means Metal needs a user session and
the daemon cannot reach that window at all, which is a result about the
instrument, not the chip. And if this boot's first timeout lands markedly
earlier than +19 s, **the load itself provokes the wedge** - also a result.
**No kext change, no boot-arg change, no plugin rebuild**; `rbgpu-fb` stays 0
(rule 38), so this boot risks nothing on the display side.

## 2wz — boot 203: THE RATE TRACKS THE WEDGE, BOTH EDGES, IN ONE BOOT

**The cleanest result in this line of work, and it refutes the hypothesis the
experiment was built to test.** 2wy's daemon put a single-queue load in the
window no terminal can reach, and boot 203 straddled both edges of the churn.

**BOOT IDENTITY FIRST (rules 8/33).** The log header printed `nonce=202` while
`rbgpu-rate` read `b=203`. They are the **same boot**: `kern.boottime`
`1793243240` equals the header's `boot_epoch` exactly and `rbgpu-boot` reads
**203**. **The daemon reads `rbgpu-boot` before the peer increments it, so the
header lags by one** - boot 202's header said 201, boot 203's said 202. Same
trap as 2wg's `RBFBCrumbBoot`. Fixed by labelling the field
`rbgpu-boot-at-start ... (LAGS by one)`; `boot_epoch` against `kern.boottime`
is the authoritative identity. **Had I correlated the b=203 series with a log I
believed was boot 202, the whole milestone would have been wrong.**

**THE TIMELINE.** Boot 203's churn, boot-split: 23 `event timeout`, 32
`checkGPUProgress`, 23 `not hung`, 23 `no channel associated`, 121
`GPURestart`, running **+21 s to +84 s**.

    t_s   wall_ms   buf/s   phase
      5   (no Metal device yet)
      9    22.352    44.7   PRE-churn
     13    35.535    28.1   PRE-churn
     16    47.074    21.2   PRE-churn
    ---- first event timeout +21 ----
     30  5916.920     0.2   DURING
     54  6104.151     0.2   DURING
     68  6005.649     0.2   DURING
     77  3869.707     0.3   DURING
    ---- last event timeout +84 ----
     85    26.985    37.1   POST-churn
     88    59.685    16.8   POST
     91   275.713     3.6   POST
     95    62.467    16.0   POST
     98   231.055     4.3   POST
    102   303.386     3.3   POST
    106   289.754     3.5   POST
    109   507.802     2.0   POST
    113   264.242     3.8   POST
    116     7.645   130.8   POST
    120   914.437     1.1   POST
    123    54.178    18.5   POST

    PRE    n= 3  min   22.352  median   35.535  max   47.074 ms
    DURING n= 4  min 3869.707  median 5961.284  max 6104.151 ms
    POST   n=12  min    7.645  median  247.649  max  914.437 ms

**COLLAPSE 265x AT THE FIRST TIMEOUT, RECOVERY 143x AT THE LAST.** The first
sample after the churn ends (+85 s) reads **26.985 ms**, materially the same as
the pre-churn 22.352 ms.

**SO "HEALTHY UNTIL THE FIRST WEDGE, THEN PERMANENTLY DEGRADED" IS REFUTED.**
That was the central hypothesis of 2ww and 2wx, written with its caveat that it
was not established. It is now **measured false**: the degradation is fully
reversible and recovery is immediate. Boot 203's +116 s sample reads
**7.645 ms, 130.8 buffers/s** - the fastest reading of the boot, taken 32 s
*after* the churn. The ordering "fast before, slow after" is simply wrong.

**AND THE 175 ms QUANTUM IS NOT A QUANTUM.** Boot 203's readings span
**7.645 ms to 6104 ms, an 800x continuum**, with no stable value anywhere near
175 ms. 2ws's lattice fit (**T = 175.77 ms, R = 0.966 over 191 periods**) was a
real measurement and is not withdrawn - but it measured a **state the machine
was in for that window**, not a property of the chip. **Do NOT write "the
quantum is just the average of a fluctuating rate"**: R = 0.966 is far too
tight for a rate that varies 800x, and nothing measured reconciles a strict
lattice with boot 203's continuum. How a stable tick and this continuum can
both be real is a **new open question**, and it is not the frontier.
Correspondingly, 2wy's "three regimes" table is withdrawn as a taxonomy - it
was three samples of a continuum, not three states.

**THE CONTENTION LEAD IS DEAD, AND BACKWARDS.** The obvious reading of boot
201's `u=2140,4569` was that something floods submissions and starves our
client. Boot 203 measures the opposite: during the slow phase submits are
**LOW** (w3-w5: `u=82, 29, 44`) and during the fast phase **HIGH** (w8/w9:
`u=2523, 4597`). A submit flood causing the slowness would need the reverse.
It makes sense in hindsight - while the wedge holds, nothing retires, so
nothing new is submitted.

**AND `adv/sub` IS NOT THE DISCRIMINATOR EITHER - 2wy's proposal is
WITHDRAWN.** The pre-churn windows at 22-47 ms read **0.73 and 0.66**, boot
199's fast window read **3.81**, and the post-churn window at 27-60 ms reads
**15.22**. Three "fast" readings, three ratios spanning 20x. One milestone old
and already refuted by the next boot; it was proposed from four points
(rule 18).

**WHAT THE PRE-STATED PREDICTION GOT.** 2wy said ~1.5 ms early confirms, ~180 ms
early kills. **Neither fired**: the earliest reading is **22.352 ms**, a value
neither branch named. Stating only two outcomes for a quantity that turned out
to be continuous was the error; the timeline is interpretable anyway because
the log carries seconds-since-boot on every line.

**BOOT 199's 632 buffers/s IS NOW A BIGGER OUTLIER, NOT A SMALLER ONE.** Boot
203's pre-wedge state is 44.7/s - **14x slower** than 632/s. So 1.582 ms is
still unreproduced, still untimestamped, and is **not** explained by "before
the first wedge". It stays open and must not be used as the baseline.

**THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS FOR THE GOAL.** 144 Hz needs **6.944 ms / 144
buffers/s**. Boot 203 measured **7.645 ms = 130.8 buffers/s = 91 % of 144 Hz**,
and boot 199 measured 632/s = **4.4x** the requirement. **The hardware does the
target rate.** Nothing needs to get faster.

**THE FRONTIER IS THE WEDGE, AND IT NEEDS NO BOOT.** Every slow reading this
project has recorded now sits inside a churn window, and the wedge is already
reducible to a **six-second userspace command** - `metal_probe --queues 4`,
K>=4 Metal command queues in one process, no kext, no arming, no reboot (2wt).
So the limiter is reproducible on demand and debuggable without spending boots.
**NAMED LEAD, NOT ESTABLISHED**: the channels that wedge are `ComputeUQ2/3/6/7`,
`SDMA0_PAGE` and `GFX`, the failure shape is *submitted, never retires, hang
check says not hung, restart reports `no channel associated with stamp_idx N`*,
and this chip has **ONE** SDMA instance where Apple's Navi 21 path builds four,
`hw->0xc2 * 2 + 2` (2gc/2gi). An index/count mismatch would produce exactly a
stamp whose channel cannot be found. That is a static read, not a boot.

**INSTRUMENT RELIABILITY, BOTH BOOTS (rule 16).** Boot 202 ran the daemon for
its full 181 s and reported `MTLCopyAllDevices: 0 device(s)` on **every one of
its 58 samples**; boot 203 had a device by +9 s. So Metal availability to a
root LaunchDaemon is **1 of 2 boots** and the daemon is not a dependable early
instrument - but the `NOMEDIAN` branch made that a legible fact instead of an
empty file, which is the whole point of rule 14. **And the daemon did not cause
the wedge**: boot 203's first timeout at **+21 s** sits inside the +19..+25.8 s
band measured in three boots that ran no early load at all.

## 2x0 — CORRECTION to 2wz: the wedge is NOT the GPU-framebuffer blocker

**2wz's closing claim "the frontier is the wedge" is WITHDRAWN**, on the user's
correction, made in one line: *"we are in CPU framebuffer instead of our own
GPU one which the problem is in... this one never had a issue."*

**THE FLAW IN 2wz'S REASONING.** Boot 203 is an `rbgpu-fb=0` boot:
`IONDRVFramebuffer` owns the panel and `CompositorSW` rasterises on the CPU.
**That boot had the wedge (+21 s to +84 s) and its desktop was fine** - a
stable ~25 fps and usable (2wy, reported from the screen). So 2wz measured the
wedge's effect on **a benchmark**, in a configuration whose desktop never had
the defect, and then promoted it to the frontier. A GPU wedge is *structurally
invisible* to a CPU-composited desktop, because that desktop never submits GPU
work; only a GPU client like `metal_probe` can see it. **Every "slow reading"
in 2wz is metal_probe's, not the product's.**

**AND THE WEDGE IS POSITIVELY ELIMINATED AS THE GPU-FB BLOCKER, BY A
MEASUREMENT ALREADY IN HAND.** 2wl recorded that in boot 196, with the GPU
framebuffer up and the desktop at ~0.09 fps, **typing into Spotlight made the
frames smooth while typing**, and *adding* characters counted while *deleting*
did not. A wedged GPU running at 0.2 buffers/s cannot produce smooth frames on
demand - it does not care what is typed. **So during boot 196's typing the GPU
was not wedged, and the 0.09 fps idle rate was therefore not a wedge.** 2wl's
frontier stands untouched: *why does a change on screen not produce a
transaction unless it is a keystroke?* The chain runs fast when asked; it is
not being asked.

**THE ~10 SECOND COINCIDENCE IS NOW THREEFOLD, AND RULE 18 APPLIES WITH MORE
FORCE, NOT LESS.** Three independent mechanisms each predict ~10 s per frame:

    2wi  transaction rate     0.093 sets/s  = one per 10.8 s
    2wt  the K>=4 wedge cliff               = 6-10 s
    2wz  0.2 buffers/s during churn, ~2 buffers per frame
                                            = one per ~10 s

CLAUDE.md already warns that two numbers agreeing on one figure is not an
identification. **Three is more suspicious, not less.** The tempting
unification - that transaction supply is low *because* the GPU cannot retire
work, collapsing 2wi's two candidates into one with the wedge upstream - is
**refuted by the typing observation above**, so it must not be written as the
story. Do not spend a boot on it.

**THE CORRECTED PICTURE.** For a GPU-composited desktop at 144 Hz, two
conditions must hold, and they are not equally binding:

    (a) transaction SUPPLY        2wl's frontier.  THE BINDING CONSTRAINT -
                                  0.09 fps, and typing proves the chain is
                                  capable and merely unasked.
    (b) the wedge not active      Caps ANY GPU client at 0.2 buffers/s while
                                  it runs, measured 265x in 2wz. But it ran
                                  only +21..+84 s in boot 203, so once (a) is
                                  fixed it is a ~60 s stutter near boot, not a
                                  standing cap - unless it runs continuously,
                                  which boot 200 showed it can (+20..+460 s).

**So the wedge is a real, measured, 265x defect and it is the SECOND problem,
not the first.** 2wt's "two independent defects" was right and 2wz got their
order wrong.

**WHAT SURVIVES 2wz UNCHANGED**, because none of it depends on the framing:
the rate tracks the churn at both edges in one boot; permanent degradation is
refuted (recovery at +85 s to 26.985 ms); the 175 ms quantum is not a quantum
(7.645-6104 ms, an 800x continuum); the contention lead is backwards (submits
low while slow, high while fast); `adv/sub` is not a discriminator; and
**144 Hz needs 6.944 ms while the chip measured 7.645 ms (91 %) and, in boot
199, 632 buffers/s (4.4x)**. The hardware does the target rate.

**RULE, PAID FOR HERE.** *A measurement of a defect in a configuration that
does not exhibit the defect does not locate the defect.* Boot 203's desktop was
healthy throughout; nothing in it could have told us what breaks the GPU
framebuffer. State which configuration a reading comes from, and whether that
configuration has the symptom, **before** promoting the reading to a frontier.
Rule 33's shape - name the object a number belongs to - applied to a whole
experiment rather than a field.

## 2x1 — the retirement experiment, made conclusive (fbkext `A57A4C4A`)

**No boot yet.** 2x0 put the frontier back on transaction **supply**, and the
candidate fix for supply has been armed for three boots and never measured.
This milestone closes the one race in it and makes the next boot answer the
question from **one `nvram` read**, with no capture.

**WHAT `-rbgpufbretire` ALREADY DOES, read from our own source.** On every
`setAttribute('amtr')` it walks the interrupt table and **force-enables every
`'vbl '` slot we did not register** (`retireEnables++`) - so Apple's handler
should then be called by `deliverVBL()` at the panel's 143.83 Hz, because that
loop calls `proc(target, ref)` for *every* enabled slot. The mechanism is
therefore already complete, and `RBFBVBL1Fires` reading 0 across boots
192/193/194 means Apple's slot was **not enabled at the moment of any tick**.

**THE ONE REAL RACE, AND IT IS CLOSED.** Our tick is ~7 ms, and at the measured
0.09 transactions/s it fires ~1500 times between transactions - so it would
catch the window easily **unless Apple re-disables its slot inside those
7 ms**, which is exactly what every `RBFBVBL1Fires` of 0 is consistent with.
So the force-enable now also **delivers immediately**, on our own
`vblKickCall`: `retireKicks++; thread_call_enter(vblKickCall)`. The enable and
the delivery are then not separated by anything Apple can observe or undo.
Same mechanism and same hazard class as 2wk's kick on the enable transition -
`thread_call_enter` plus field writes, no allocation, no logging, no blocking
on the accelerator's thread (rule 31) - and `kickVBL()` re-checks `enabled`
itself, so a window that closed anyway costs one scheduled call and is counted
(`retireKicks - retireDelivered` is how often we were late). **Kept under
`-rbgpufbretire` rather than a third boot-arg**: that arg already means "make
Apple learn a vblank happened", and an arg per refinement multiplies boots
without separating hypotheses.

**THE REAL FIX IS TO THE EXPERIMENT, NOT THE MECHANISM.** `retireEnables` and
Apple's slot fire count were **registry-only** - and the registry is
unreadable in precisely the boot that matters, because at 0.09 fps there is no
desktop to run `ioreg` from. That is why three boots in a row produced nothing:
2wi had no capture, 2wj was not installed, 2wl's crumb covered only the first
70 s. Rule 10, for the fourth time. **So the crumb now carries them**:

    E=  retireEnables   the force-enables WE performed
    A=  foreignFires()  summed fires over every 'vbl ' slot we did NOT
                        register - i.e. how often APPLE's handler actually ran

**FOUR-WAY DECISION FROM ONE `nvram rbgpu-fbcrumb`, SAID BEFORE THE BOOT:**

    E=0                      retire never ran. Check RBFBRetireArmed and t=.
                             t>0 with E=0 would mean Apple's slots were
                             already enabled, itself a new fact.
    E>0, A=0                 we enabled it, delivered immediately, and Apple's
                             handler STILL never ran -> the defect is in OUR
                             delivery, not in Apple's enable.
    E>0, A>0, rate unmoved   APPLE'S HANDLER RAN AND SUPPLY DID NOT MOVE ->
                             the VBL retirement path is ELIMINATED, and 2wl's
                             keystroke question is the whole frontier.
    E>0, A>0, rate up        FIXED.

The rate needs no capture either (2wj): **transactions/s = `t` / (`f` /
143.83)**. At the measured 0.09/s, `t/f` is ~0.0006; at 144 fps it approaches
1. Three orders of magnitude of headroom, which is all the precision this
question needs.

**`foreignFires()` IS HOSTTESTED, AND THE TEST IS MUTATION-CHECKED.** Counting
our *own* slot in `A=` would publish our 143.83 Hz tick as though it were
Apple's retirement and **read as a spectacular success** - the most expensive
mistake available here. So the new case registers one self slot and one
foreign slot, ticks the clock with the foreign slot disabled and asserts
`A == 0` while our own fires, then force-enables and kicks and asserts `A == 1`,
then ticks five more times and asserts `A == before + 5` with our own slot
firing throughout. **Mutation run**: deleting `target != this` from
`foreignFires()` fails at `assert(f.foreignFires()==0)`, line 226. Restored and
green. `RBFBForeignFires` is published **unconditionally** in
`publishVBLState()`, so it is also this build's rule-15 identity key.

**RULE 16 ON THE BOOT ITSELF.** `tools/earlybench.sh` must be **removed before
this boot**. It is a GPU client, and this is the one boot that measures how
many frames the GPU is asked for; leaving it in adds an unrelated submitter to
the measurement. It has done its job (2wz) and goes back in later if wanted.

**SAFETY, STATED.** `rbgpu-fb` must be armed, so the framebuffer takes the
panel - and 2wp's no-transaction deadline still applies: `amtrSets == 0` at
fire 18000 (125 s) consumes `rbgpu-fb` so the **next** power cycle comes up on
`IONDRVFramebuffer` with a usable desktop. 2wj's consume-by-overwrite means one
power cycle is a full disarm either way. Rule 38: **`rbgpu-arm` must be armed
too** - fb armed with the accelerator absent froze boot 197 behind a progress
bar through three power cycles. Rule 34: all four one-shots, named.

**INSTALL (rule 15, every artifact).** Plugin **`F991B506` unchanged in the
EFI** - confirmed live, because `rbgpu-rate` exists and only that build writes
it, so **no rebuild and no `efi.sh install`**. Boot-args unchanged: a
whole-token check reads `-rbgpuownfb -rbgpufbaty -rbgpufbamtr -rbgpufbhubp
-rbgpufbretire -rbgpufbflipall` already present (rule 30). **Only the fbkext
changes**, `A57A4C4A`, to the **auxiliary collection** - and per 2wa verify the
**artifact**, not `kmutil`'s exit status, which has errored `Code=34` over a
write that landed.

## 2x2 — BOOT 204: THE RETIREMENT PATH WORKS, AND IT IS NOT THE LIMITER

**fbkext `A57A4C4A`, armed, GPU framebuffer up.** Identity by field presence
(rule 15): `E=` and `A=` exist, and only this build publishes them. Rule 8:
the crumb reads `b=203` and the nonce lag of one (2wg) makes that **boot 204**;
the live box is now 205 on `IONDRVFramebuffer`, so the crumb is all there is.

    s=11 f=1000  e=6    r=1 h=0 w=1   k=1 t=1   p=0   n=0 K=4    D=4   E=0 A=4
    s=12 f=10000 e=10   r=1 h=0 w=3   k=0 t=3   p=1   n=0 K=8    D=8   E=0 A=8
    s=13 f=20000 e=1036 r=1 h=0 w=517 k=0 t=517 p=186 n=0 K=1034 D=942 E=0 A=944

**`E=0` WITH `K=1034` REFUTES THE HYPOTHESIS THIS EXPERIMENT WAS BUILT ON.**
`retireEnables` is **zero**: in 517 transactions, our force-enable never found
a foreign `'vbl '` slot disabled. And `retireKicks` is **1034**, which with
`E=0` can only have come from `setInterruptState` - i.e. **Apple performed
1034 off->on transitions on its own slot.** So 2wi/2wl's
*"Apple registers its handler, disables it and never re-enables it"* is
**measured FALSE**. `enableTransactionInterrupt` (2s5) runs, constantly, at
**exactly 2.000 enables per transaction** (1034/517; 1.996 over the typing
phase alone).

**AND THE REASON `RBFBVBL1Fires` READ 0 FOR FOUR MILESTONES IS NOW A NUMBER.**
`A=944` splits as **942 from our immediate kick** and **2 from the 143.83 Hz
periodic path**. Two catches in 20000 ticks is a duty cycle of 1.0e-4, so the
total time Apple's slot spent enabled is ~13.9 ms across 1034 windows:
**Apple's enable window is ~13 us wide, against our 6.95 ms tick** - about
500x too narrow. The periodic delivery never had a chance, and that is the
whole explanation for four boots of zero. **2x1's race was real and the
immediate kick closes it**: 942 of 1034 caught, 8.9 % too late.

**SO THE MECHANISM NOW WORKS - AND THE RATE DID NOT MOVE.**

    idle   (+7.0 -> +69.5 s)    2 transactions  =   0.032 /s   one per 31 s
    typing (+69.5 -> +139.1 s)  514             =   7.393 /s
    peak 1000-fire window       p=186           =  26.8   /s
                                                  837x the idle rate

**THE VBL RETIREMENT PATH IS ELIMINATED AS THE SUPPLY LIMITER.** Apple's
handler fires ~1.8 times per transaction, its enable path runs twice per
transaction, and idle supply is still ~0.03/s. This is 2x1's third predicted
branch reached by a route 2x1 did not name (`E=0, A>0` rather than
`E>0, A>0`), and the conclusion is the same and **stronger**, because `E=0`
refutes the premise as well as the cure. **Spend no further boot on vblank
retirement.**

**`n=0` FOR THE WHOLE BOOT REFUTES 2wm.** Not one of 517 transactions had flag
bit `0x1` clear, so **`-rbgpufbflipall` had nothing to do**, and 2wm's account
of the add/delete asymmetry - *"deleting reuses the allocation, hands us a
transaction with the bit clear, and we refuse it"* - is **false**. Deleting
does not hand us a transaction we drop. **It produces no transaction at all.**
The asymmetry is entirely upstream of our kext.

**AND OUR HALF IS COMPLETE: `w=517 == t=517`.** Every transaction handed to us
was written to the display engine, with `h=0` (HUBP set up) all boot. There is
nothing left to fix below `setAttribute('amtr')`.
*(Instrument note: `k=` reads 1 at `w=1` and 0 afterwards, because
`hubpReadback` is captured once on write #1 while `hubpLast` keeps moving.
`k` is meaningful only at `w=1`; **`k=0` at `w>1` is not a failure** and must
not be read as one.)*

**THE USER'S REPORT, WHICH IS THE SHARPEST STATEMENT OF THE DEFECT YET.**
Spamming characters into a password box: *"the screen was responding, the
faster i typed the higher the Hz, then as soon as i stop it stops until either
another write or 10s... delete key and enter dont have same behaviour, only
typing does."* The crumb's 837x and `p=186` are that sentence in numbers.

**THE FRONTIER IS NOW ONE QUESTION WITH A CONTROL ALREADY MEASURED.** Same
WindowServer, same CoreDisplay; the CPU-framebuffer boot composites
continuously and ours only on a keystroke. The one structural difference is
**which `IOFramebuffer` serves the panel** - so: *does the compositor have a
frame clock on ours?* A compositor paces on the display's vblank, which
userspace gets through CVDisplayLink -> CoreDisplay -> IOFramebuffer's vblank
timestamps. **We implement none of that surface** - a grep for `getTimeOfVBL`,
`getVBLTime`, `setVBLTiming`, `updateVBL`, `deferredVBLDisable` and `vblCount`
across `src/fbkext` returns **nothing**, while `nm` finds all six defined in
`IOGraphicsFamily` (`0x14fba970`, `0x14fc0736`, `0x14fc317c`, `0x14fc0412`,
`0x14fc0456`, plus `handleVBL` `0x14fc0484` and the throttle globals
`gIOFBVBLThrottle` / `gIOFBVBLDrift` / `gIOFBMaxVBLDelta` /
`gIOFBVblDeltaMult`). **NOT a claim that this is the cause** - `f=20000`
continuous over 139 s proves at least one slot was enabled at every tick, and
since Apple's windows are 13 us that slot must be `handleVBL`'s, so Apple's
own bookkeeping *was* being driven. Which is exactly why this needs measuring
rather than assuming.

**`tools/vblclock.m` (build `build/out/vblclock`), and its CONTROL IS ALREADY
RUN.** It creates a CVDisplayLink on the main display, counts callbacks, and
prints the nominal period beside the measured rate - because the advertised
period and the delivered one differ exactly when timestamps are published but
the interrupt never arrives. Rule 16: **on the live boot 205,
`IONDRVFramebuffer` reads `133.89 Hz` measured, nominal 140.92 Hz, mode
1920x1080 @ 144.00 Hz.** So the instrument is sound and a low reading in the
armed boot means something. Reads only; no kext, no arming, no reboot of its
own; and the armed boot can run it because **typing is the one thing that
works**, which is what a terminal is.

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.** `~134 Hz` in the armed boot **eliminates the frame
clock** and the defect is in what marks the display dirty, not in cadence -
and then the next question is why a keystroke marks it and a delete does not.
**`0` or a handful of Hz** means WindowServer has no cadence from our
framebuffer, which explains the idle rate, the keystroke dependence and the
~10 s floor together, and names a concrete API surface to implement.
Anything in between is its own reading. **No new build and no install** -
`A57A4C4A` is already in the auxiliary collection, proven by `E=`/`A=` being
published at all.

## 2x3 — BOOT 206: THE PANEL IS PARKED ON A STALE BUFFER (fbkext `4C28785D`)

**The live armed boot answered three questions and the user's own observation
answered the fourth, which is the one that mattered.**

**THE FRAME CLOCK IS ELIMINATED, POSITIVELY.** `tools/vblclock.m` creates a
CVDisplayLink and counts callbacks. On **our** framebuffer in boot 206:
**693 callbacks in 5.003 s = 138.51 Hz**, nominal period 7.214 ms. The control
on `IONDRVFramebuffer` in boot 205 read **133.89 Hz**. And
`RBFBVBL0Fires = RBFBVBLFires = 42397` - IOFramebuffer's own `handleVBL` is
driven on every single tick. **WindowServer has a perfect cadence from us**, so
2x2's named candidate (`getTimeOfVBL` / `getVBLTime` / `setVBLTiming`, none of
which we implement) is **not the defect**. Closed.

**NOTHING IN THE CHAIN IS FAILING.** Display log captured in the armed boot
(rule 36 - INFO does not survive a reboot): **0** `Fallback`, **0**
`DisplayPipeState`, **0** `Failed to submit transaction`, **0**
`IOPRESENTMENT`, against **929 WindowServer lines** plus CoreDisplay and
SkyLight subsystems as the control. Every transaction that exists succeeds.
`RBFBAmtrNoFlip = 0` and `RBFBHubpWrites == RBFBAmtrSets` (585/585) across the
whole boot: **we drop nothing and write everything.**

**THE SWAP CHAIN IS MEASURED.** Sampling `RBFBHubpLast` live shows exactly
**three** addresses cycling - `0xf4_1002_a000`, `0xf4_110e_2000`,
`0xf4_1192_a000` - about one 1920x1080x4 frame (8.29 MB) apart. **Triple
buffered.** Idle transaction supply, two independent ways: **0.071/s**
(14 s direct read) and **0.080/s** (36 transactions over 451 s).

**AN EXPERIMENT THAT MEASURED NOTHING, AND WHY.** A 75 s 4 Hz trace was
started and the phase instructions were sent *afterwards*, so the user read
them after the window had closed and ran the phases at **00:04** against a
trace that ended at **00:00:44**. The per-phase table built from it is
**WITHDRAWN IN FULL** - it described an idle machine. **Rule 28's shape applied
to an experiment rather than a log: the window and the event must be tied
together at the source.** `tools/fbphase.py` is the fix - it owns the clock AND
prompts the user itself, printing one line per phase (not a countdown, because
printing is screen damage and that is the quantity under test).
**What the dead trace does validly say**: idle behaviour is 7 transactions in
75 s at a ~6 s cadence.
**And the event was recovered anyway**, because the counter is cumulative:
00:00:44 -> 00:08:15 is 36 transactions in 451 s = **0.080/s**, a window that
*provably contains* the typing, with `RBFBAmtrPeak` still **139** and unmoved
since 23:54. So the typing produced no measurable excess of transactions.

**THE USER'S OBSERVATION IS THE DECISIVE MEASUREMENT.** *"The time like 00:07
stays like that until 00:09 when i type."* The menu-bar clock froze at 00:07,
and on the next keystroke the panel showed **00:09 - not 00:07**. **So the
compositor had been drawing every one of those minutes and we were not showing
them.** The panel was parked on a stale buffer and the keystroke re-pointed it.

**THAT RESOLVES THE CONTRADICTION.** With three buffers rotating and HUBP
pinned to one, roughly **one frame in three** is visible while anything is
being drawn, and the screen is **frozen** once drawing stops - which is exactly
"typing is smooth, stopping freezes", with no need for typing to generate
transactions at all. The transaction rate and the *frame* rate were never the
same quantity, and every milestone since 2wi that treated "transaction supply"
as the frontier was measuring the wrong thing. **2wi's "1 frame per 10 s is the
TRANSACTION rate" stands as a measurement and is withdrawn as an explanation.**

**THE FIX: FOLLOW THE SWAP CHAIN AT VBLANK RATE (`-rbgpufbpoll`).** We learn
the current surface only when a transaction arrives (0.08/s). Apple keeps the
live address in the `_AMD_PIPE_FLIP` (2wg measured the field, 2wf the struct)
and **we already hold a range-checked pointer to it** from the first
transaction. So read it on every vblank and reprogram HUBP when it moves.
`hubpPoll()` runs on our own thread_call, never Apple's thread, and allocates
nothing, logs nothing and blocks on nothing (rule 31). A torn read cannot reach
the hardware: `hubpProgram()` re-validates every address against the measured
carve-out, the 256-byte alignment and the frame size, and counts refusals
(`RBFBHubpRejects`). Gated on the boot-arg **and** on `amtrSets > 0`, so a boot
whose pipe never came up cannot poll a pointer that was never set. Rule 30
checked against all ten existing `-rbgpufb*` tokens: `-rbgpufbpoll` neither
prefixes nor is prefixed by any.
**Hosttested and mutation-checked**: the contract is *one poll per vblank*,
because one missed tick is one stale frame - the exact defect it fixes. The
case asserts `pollCalls == vblFires == 7` over seven ticks; mutating the call
site to poll on alternate fires **fails at line 257**. `RBFBPollArmed` is
published unconditionally as the rule-15 identity key, and the crumb gains
`R=` (`pollReads`) and `G=` (`pollChanges`).

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.** `R=` should run at ~143.83 per second of uptime; if
it is 0 with `-rbgpufbpoll` in boot-args, the arg or the pointer gate is wrong
and nothing else means anything. **`G=` is the whole experiment**: it counts
vblanks on which the live address differed from what we had written. `G=` in
the thousands with a smooth, self-updating desktop **confirms it** - the panel
was simply pointed at the wrong buffer. `G=` near 0 means Apple does *not*
update that field outside a transaction, the poll reads a constant, and the
address must be found elsewhere. `G=` high with the screen **still** stale, or
`RBFBHubpRejects` climbing, means we are following something that is not the
scanout surface. The user's proposal - a synthetic typing source at 144 Hz -
is deliberately **not** taken: it would force damage and still show only one
frame in three, because it treats the symptom rather than the stale pointer.

## 2x4 — the poll is DEAD by its own kill condition, and nullarc does not flip at all

**BOOT 208, live, fbkext `4C28785D` confirmed running** (`RBFBPollArmed`
present; rule 15), `-rbgpufbpoll` a whole token in boot-args (rule 30),
uptime 256 s.

    RBFBPollArmed     Yes
    RBFBPollReads     32772      of RBFBVBLFires 32985  = 99.4 %
    RBFBPollChanges   1          <-- the kill condition
    RBFBHubpRejects   0          RejectAddr 0, RejectWhy 0
    RBFBPollFirstSeen 0xf4_1002_a000
    RBFBHubpLast      0xf4_110e_2000
    RBFBHubpWrites    213  ==  RBFBAmtrSets 213   (0.83/s)

**2x3 said before the boot: "`G=` near 0 means Apple does NOT update that
field outside a transaction, the poll reads a constant, and the address must
be found elsewhere." `G=1` in 32772 reads. So `-rbgpufbpoll` is ELIMINATED**,
and cleanly - it ran on 99.4 % of vblanks, refused nothing, and simply had
nothing to follow. `_AMD_PIPE_FLIP +0x08` is a **snapshot written at
transaction time**, not a live mirror of the scanout surface. The screen is
unchanged, as the user reports.

**WHAT NULLARC ACTUALLY DOES - and it is not what 2sj recorded.** Read from
the source (MIT/GPL-2.0 + PolyForm-NC for `src/phxaccel`, **no AI
restriction**; NootedRed and NootRX remain unread under their licence).

- `Dcn314Scanout::program_scanout` writes `DCSURF_PRIMARY_SURFACE_ADDR_LO/HI`
  **once**, with the timing. **There is no flip anywhere in nullarc** - no
  `SURFACE_UPDATE_LOCK`, no `FLIP_CONTROL`, no per-frame address change. The
  grep is empty against a file that names both address registers.
- `phxfb.cpp` contains **zero** `write32`/`mmio` calls: their framebuffer
  touches no registers at all.
- `getVRAMRange()` **returns `getApertureRange(kIOFBSystemAperture)`** - the
  same single scanout buffer. (**Ours already does this**, so that is not the
  difference.)
- **The difference is who presents.** Their accelerator is *NullMoth's*,
  written against an **NVIDIA RM**: "nothing on the GPU reads those surfaces -
  **the display pipe copies finished frames by CPU**". Their "VRAM" is
  physically contiguous system memory and their GPU addresses are numbers from
  a private range **that never enter a page table**.
- They measured the copy path: through the BAR a 2560x1600 frame took
  **~110 ms (~7 fps, the whole desktop lagged)**, so they copy through the
  **system-RAM alias** of the carve-out instead, with **non-temporal stores**
  (the alias comes back write-back though it asks for write-combine, and plain
  stores stayed in the CPU cache - "stripes").

**SO NULLARC NEVER SOLVED THE FLIP PROBLEM - IT AVOIDS IT.** One fixed
scanout buffer, and every finished frame is CPU-copied into it. That is why
they need no flip registers and no transaction cadence. **Their 120 Hz is not
evidence that Apple's accelerator can be made to flip**, because their
compositor is their own and the GPU never presents.

**WHAT THAT MEANS FOR US.** We are in a strictly different configuration:
Apple's real `AMDRadeonX6000` composites into real VRAM surfaces and presents
through the display-pipe transaction, which we receive at **0.08-0.83/s**. The
fork is now explicit:

    A  COPY, nullarc's way.   Map the carve-out through its system-physical
       alias - already measured here, MC 0xF4_0000_0000 = 0x7_8000_0000 - and
       non-temporal-copy the composited surface into the scanout buffer on
       each vblank. Independent of flips entirely. Costs 8.29 MB/frame;
       1.19 GB/s at 144 Hz. Proven to work on comparable hardware.
    B  FIX THE CADENCE.  Find why Apple submits 0.08/s. Zero-copy and correct
       if it can be answered, and it is where this project has been since 2wi.

**B IS NOT YET ELIMINATED AND MUST NOT BE ABANDONED ON THE EVIDENCE SO FAR**,
because the one measurement that would settle it has never been taken
cleanly: **transactions during typing, in a window provably containing the
typing**. 2x3's trace missed its own event, and the cumulative recovery
(36 in 451 s) spans seven idle minutes around a short burst, so it bounds the
burst only weakly. `tools/fbphase.py` exists precisely for this and has not
been run.

## 2x5 — BOOT 208: THE DRIVER IS DONE. THE DEFECT IS THAT MACOS DOES NOT DRAW.

**The user found it, and the way they found it is the measurement: they opened
AnyDesk, connected it to their phone, and the desktop came alive.**
*"Without even typing... EVERYTHING is 144Hz, everything, all animations are
back, all widgets work."*

**MEASURED, with AnyDesk connected and no typing:**

    RBFBAmtrSets     0.08 /s  ->  83.43 /s      a 1000x step
    RBFBHubpWrites   0.08 /s  ->  83.43 /s      IDENTICAL, every frame written
    RBFBAmtrPeak     139      ->  671           (~96/s in a ~7 s window)
    RBFBHubpRejects  2        in the WHOLE boot
    RBFBVBLFires                 134.83 /s

**SO THE KERNEL CHAIN IS CORRECT AND COMPLETE, AND HAS BEEN ALL ALONG.**
`RBFBHubpWrites` tracks `RBFBAmtrSets` *exactly* at 58-83/s. Every frame macOS
produces, we present. The HUBP write (2wh), the `'amtr'` gate (2wc), the ATY
properties (2w9), the AGDC bridge, the gamma chain (2u6-2v7) and the VBL
delivery are all right. **144 Hz with animations and widgets has now been seen
on this panel.** Everything this project built below `setAttribute('amtr')` is
finished, and **2x4's branch A (CPU-copying frames, nullarc's way) is
unnecessary** - we are zero-copy and structurally faster than that design.

**THE DEFECT IS ENTIRELY UPSTREAM: macOS does not PRODUCE frames.** It is not
supply through a broken pipe, not a throttle, not retirement, not cadence.
WindowServer simply does not composite, and something about a live AnyDesk
session makes it.

**AND THE USER NARROWED IT FURTHER, WHICH KILLED THE FIRST GUESS:** *"no moving
in anydesk is fine, just has to be connected."* So it is not input, not cursor
motion, not damage from a remote pointer. **The session's existence is the
lever.**

**ELIMINATED TODAY, each by measurement:**

1. **Power assertions.** A connected AnyDesk holds **two**: `UserIsActive`
   ("Awake display for incoming Anydesk connection") and
   `NoDisplaySleepAssertion`. Both are reproducible with `caffeinate -d -u`
   and neither needs any permission. Held both, disconnected AnyDesk:
   **`RBFBAmtrSets` = 0.00/s**, flat frozen, with `UserIsActive 1` and
   `PreventUserIdleDisplaySleep 1` confirmed in `pmset -g assertions`. **DEAD.**
2. **`-rbgpufbpoll`** (2x4), by its own stated kill condition.
3. **The frame clock** (2x3): `vblclock` reads 138.51 Hz on our framebuffer.
4. **Failures anywhere in the chain** (2x3): 0 `Fallback`, 0 `DisplayPipeState`,
   0 submit failures against 929 WindowServer lines as control.

**AN INSTRUMENT THAT COST THREE EXCHANGES, AND THE RULE IT PAYS FOR.**
`tools/framepump.m` holds a ScreenCaptureKit stream open to act as a frame
consumer. Across three runs it reported, in order: **TCC denied** (never ran -
indistinguishable from "ran and did not help" if the output is not read);
**ran, 0 frames** at 64x36 - which is *dedup*, since SCK only delivers a
visibly changed frame and a static desktop downscales to identical pixels, so
it could neither observe the desktop nor be trusted to drive it; and **TCC
denied again, because the rebuild revoked the grant** - permission is keyed to
the binary. **Rule 14's sharpest form yet: "it didn't work" has meant three
different things in one session, and only reading the tool's own output
separated them.** A tool whose first run needs a permission grant must say so
before it is handed over, and **rebuilding it revokes that grant**.

**STILL LIVE, AND THE NEXT TEST NEEDS NO SETUP AT ALL**: that an active screen
**capture** is the lever. A connected session captures; a disconnected app does
not. It can be tested with the system's own recorder - **Cmd-Shift-5 -> Record
Entire Screen** - which is already permitted and needs no new binary, no TCC
grant and no rebuild. If the desktop runs while that recording is active, the
lever is capture and a minimal always-on stream is the bridge; if it stays
frozen, capture is dead too and what remains is whatever else a live AnyDesk
session holds open, which `lsof` on its pid will name.

## 2x6 — THE DISPLAY TRANSACTION WAITS ON A GPU STAMP, AND THE STAMP NEVER RETIRES

No boot. Everything here is read off captures already on disk plus a static
read of `IOAcceleratorFamily2` and `AMDRadeonX6000`.

### The frozen desktop's own log names the blocker 219 times

`logs/20261028-160856-plugin/display-log.txt`, a GPU-framebuffer boot with
`RBFBAmtrSets 41` against `RBFBVBLFires 46800` (= **0.126 transactions/s**, the
frozen state):

    (IOAcceleratorFamily2) AMDRadeonAccelerator: IOAccelDisplayPipe
        (fbindex=0) transaction stamp index 59 time out              x219

16:03:01.030 to 16:08:59.410 — six minutes, always **stamp index 59**,
interleaved line for line with the wedge:

    channel 12 SDMA0_PAGE event timeout; pending stamps [10..24]
    channel 12 is not hung, keep running
    restart_channel(): GPURestartSkipped stampIdx=12 type=2
    restart_channel(): no channel associated with stamp_idx 12 (type 2)

So the display-pipe transaction is **paired with a GPU stamp**, that stamp does
not retire, and the recovery machinery declines to act: the hang check reads the
hardware and says *not hung*, and the restart cannot map the stamp to a channel.

### THE DIFFERENTIAL, which is what makes this a result and not a reading

Ten consecutive captures, `display_change_handler` as the control in each:

| boot | config | stamp time outs | `event timeout` | `RBFBAmtrSets` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20261028-181533 | CPU-fb | **0** | 30 | — |
| 20261028-005656 | CPU-fb | **0** | 34 | 0 |
| 20261028-104455 | CPU-fb | 0 | 0 | — |
| 20261028-002545 | CPU-fb | 0 | 0 | — |
| 20261027-232901 | CPU-fb | 0 | 0 | — |
| 20261028-141825 | **GPU-fb** | **43** | 14 | 4 |
| 20261028-101029 | **GPU-fb** | **103** | 36 | 14 |
| 20261028-160856 | **GPU-fb** | **219** | 135 | 41 |
| 20261028-001439 | GPU-fb | 0 | 45 | no transactions |
| 20261027-233944 | GPU-fb | 0 | 41 | no transactions |

Two rows carry it. **20261028-181533 and 20261028-005656 are CPU-framebuffer
boots that HAVE the wedge — 30 and 34 `event timeout` — and ZERO stamp time
outs.** And the two GPU-framebuffer boots in which no transaction ever flowed
have the wedge and zero stamp time outs as well. The line appears **iff
transactions flow through our framebuffer**, and it scales with them: 4 -> 43,
14 -> 103, 41 -> 219.

**So this reading is taken in the configuration that exhibits the defect, and
the configuration that lacks the symptom gives zero — rule 39 satisfied in both
directions**, which is exactly what 2wz failed and 2x0 corrected.

### WHAT THIS DOES TO THE WEDGE'S STATUS

**2wl's elimination of the wedge is WITHDRAWN. It was reasoning, not
measurement.** The argument was *"a GPU wedged at 0.2 buffers/s cannot make the
screen smooth on demand"* — which treats the wedge as a throughput ceiling. It
is not one. 2we read it correctly at the time and the words were already right:
*"work is submitted and never retires; the hang check says not hung; the restart
cannot find the channel"* — a **stamp-retirement** failure. A retirement failure
is kicked by new submissions; a throughput ceiling is not. Typing submits work.
A connected AnyDesk session submits work continuously. An idle desktop submits
none.

2x0 and rule 39 stand exactly as written: boot 203's **numbers** could not
locate the defect, because an `rbgpu-fb=0` desktop cannot see a GPU wedge. The
error that followed was to drop the wedge from the candidate list on the
strength of 2wl's argument rather than re-measuring it in the configuration that
does exhibit the symptom. **The captures that settle it were already on disk
when 2wl was written.** Same shape as 2kx/2la/2lc and 2s5: read the evidence in
hand before designing the next experiment.

Nothing about the **driver** changes. 2x5 stands: `RBFBHubpWrites` tracks
`RBFBAmtrSets` exactly, 2 rejects in a whole boot, 83.43/s with AnyDesk
connected. Every frame macOS hands us still reaches the panel. What is corrected
is the **frontier**: it is not "macOS does not draw", it is "the transaction
macOS is drawing for cannot retire, so it does not draw the next one".

### THE KERNEL RETIREMENT CHAIN IS READ END TO END, AND IT IS ARMED

Static, `IOAcceleratorFamily2`. Rule 7 applied throughout.

    IOAccelDisplayPipe::transaction_queue_gated(txn)          0x14e60466
        if (pipe->0x2a4 == 0) { pipe->0x2a4 = 1;
                                pipe->vt[call 0x888 -> dump 0x898]() }
                                   /* = AMD's enableTransactionInterrupt */
        txn->0x58 = pipe->vt[call 0x8b8 -> dump 0x8c8](txn)   /* submitTransaction */
        ring: slot = pipe + 0x118 + 0x48 * (pipe->0x23c % 4); slot->0x40 = txn
        accel->0x380->vt[0x1b0](&txn->0x60)                   /* arm the stamp */
        sfence; pipe->0x23c++
        pipe->0xc0->vt[0x1d8](0,0,0)                          /* signal */

    IOAccelDisplayPipe::enableTransactionInterrupt             0x14e609ba
        pipe->vt[call 0x878 -> dump 0x888]()  /* = enableVBLInterrupt */
        pipe->0x281 = 1

    IOAccelDisplayPipe::enableVBLInterrupt                     0x14e60946
        refcount pipe->0x2a8; on 0 -> 1:
            fb->vt[0xae0](pipe->0xd8, 1)      /* IOFramebuffer::setInterruptState */

    IOAccelDisplayPipe::signalVBLInterrupt(pipe)               0x14e5dcb8
        clock_get_uptime(&pipe->0x268)
        if (pipe->0x281)      signalTransactionInterrupt(pipe)
        if (pipe->0x2a0)      pipe->0xc8->vt[0x1d8](0,0,0)

    IOAccelDisplayPipe::signalTransactionInterrupt(pipe)       0x14e5e0ec
        if (pipe->0x2a4 == 0) return;
        pipe->0x2d0 = mach_absolute_time();
        pipe->0xd0->vt[0x1d8](0,0,0)

`signalTransactionInterrupt` has **exactly one caller**, `signalVBLInterrupt`,
and `signalVBLInterrupt` is registered **once**, at `0x14e5db41` inside
`displayModeDidChange`, for `'vbl '`. There is **no second interrupt type** the
retirement wants and no page-flip-complete interrupt we are failing to deliver:
the retire path is the `'vbl '` path, and both of its gates (`0x281`, `0x2a4`)
are set by `transaction_queue_gated` on the first transaction — which is on our
path, because `submitTransaction` is called **from** it.

**So 2x1's conclusion is reconfirmed from the other side**: our VBL delivery and
Apple's handler are both correct and armed, and the retirement this chain
performs really does happen. It is the **GPU stamp** that does not retire, which
is a different object from the `'vbl '` retirement 2x1 forced, and that is why
forcing the latter moved nothing. **Rule 33 again — name the object a number
belongs to.** "Retirement" was eliminated; two different retirements wear the
name.

### AND COMPLETION IS DECIDED BY AN ATTRIBUTE WE ANSWER UNCONDITIONALLY

`AMDRadeonX6000_AMDAccelDisplayPipe::isTransactionComplete` (`0xbe4a794`):

    fbIdx = getFramebufferIndex()
    if (!pipe->0x328->vt[0x2a0]())        return true
    if (!pipe->0x330->vt[0x190](fbIdx))   return false      /* 2wc's 'amtr' gate */
    if (txn && pipe->0x248 == txn) {
        fb = getFramebuffer()
        return fb->vt[0xa30]('amtr', NULL) == 0             /* getAttribute */
    }
    return IOAccelDisplayPipe::isTransactionComplete(txn)   /* dump 0x8c0, base */

So for the **current** transaction, "complete" is literally
`getAttribute('amtr')` returning 0, and AMDFramebuffer's own answer is
`kIOReturnNotReady` while `getOutstandingDisplayPipeTransactions()` is non-zero
(2wc). `RBAMDFramebuffer` returns 0 unconditionally, i.e. **always complete** —
the optimistic answer, so it cannot be what stalls anything, and it is not a
candidate. Recorded so the next reader does not spend a boot on it.

Also found and **not** the answer, recorded to close them:
`IOAccelDisplayPipe::beginTransaction` and `signalTransactionComplete` are
`push/mov/pop/ret` **empty base stubs** (`0x14e609fa`, `0x14e60a00`), and
`ktraceStateChanged` likewise. And the 300 ms constant in
`%s: IOAccelDisplayPipeTransaction time out after 300ms. framebufferIndex=%d`
appears **0 times** in the capture — so the per-frame waiter is not that one and
the ~10 s figure does not come from it.

### THE TEST, AND IT NEEDS NO BUILD, NO BOOT, NO KEXT AND NO TCC GRANT

A connected AnyDesk session does two things at once: it **captures the screen**
and it **keeps the GPU continuously busy** encoding. 2x5 named capture as the
remaining hypothesis and never separated the two. `build/out/metal_probe
--busy` separates them: continuous GPU work on **one** command queue (never
`--queues`, which is 2wt's known wedge trigger), and **no capture at all**.

In the frozen GPU-framebuffer boot, AnyDesk disconnected:

    env -u DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES build/out/metal_probe --busy 45 --heavy 20000 --depth 16

**Said before the test.** Desktop smooth for those 45 s and frozen again after
= the lever is **GPU activity**, capture is dead, and the defect is stamp
retirement. Still frozen while it runs = GPU activity is not the lever and
capture comes back, to be tested with Cmd-Shift-5. Either way one 45-second
command settles what 2x5 left open, and the instrument reports its own buffer
rate so a dead run cannot read as a negative result (rule 39's corollary).

### WHERE THE FIX WOULD GO IF THE TEST CONFIRMS

2ws already named the software side and already named the gap, one milestone
before it was needed: the release decision is **per client, in software**,
pointing at `AMDSWScheduler::advance()` (`0xbe950e0`), which is reachable only
from `deferredCallback(IOInterruptEventSource *)` (`0xbe93e18`) and from
`timerCallback` (`0xbe9513c`) — **which is never installed**. So the only
installed trigger for advancing the scheduler is an interrupt event source. If
the stamp interrupt does not arrive (`enableStampInterrupt` /
`disableStampInterrupt` at `0x14e2653c` / `0x14e26542` are **empty base stubs**,
never overridden), nothing advances until some unrelated interrupt happens to
fire — which is what typing and a busy encoder supply.

**And we already own a 143.83 Hz timer in the right process context**: the
framebuffer's VBL `thread_call`. Driving the scheduler's advance from it would
tick retirement at **6.95 ms** where 2ws measured a free-running
**175.77 ms**, which is 25x and is exactly the 144 Hz target. **NOT
ESTABLISHED** — nothing here observes a single call to `advance()`, which is
rule 35 precisely, and 2ws said the same about it. Instrument our end first.

**NOT established either**: that the stamp timeout and the wedge are one defect.
They interleave in the log and share a shape, but the wedge lives on
GFX/SDMA/Compute user queues and the display stamp is index 59 on `fbindex=0`.
Two numbers agreeing is not an identification (rule 18).

## 2x7 — GPU ACTIVITY IS NOT THE LEVER. 2x6'S HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED BY ITS OWN TEST

`tools/setsrate.sh` on the live armed GPU-framebuffer boot, AnyDesk
disconnected. Five load profiles, one command queue in every arm (never
`--queues`, 2wt's wedge trigger), with `RBFBAmtrSets` read against the panel's
vblank counter:

| arm | what the GPU managed | `RBFBAmtrSets`/s |
|---|---|---|
| idle (control) | — | **6.83** |
| `--busy 20 --heavy 20000 --depth 16` | 32 buffers / 20.25 s = 1.6/s | 0.24 |
| `--busy 20 --depth 256` | 256 buffers / 32.07 s = 8.0/s | 0.16 |
| `--busy 20 --depth 64` | 64 buffers / 100.43 s = 0.6/s | **0.09** |
| `--bench 400` | pipelined submit 17265/s | 0.25 |

**Every loaded arm reads BELOW the control.** 2x6 said in advance that a row
near 83/s would mean GPU work is the lever and capture is dead, and that every
row near 0.1/s would mean the reverse. The rows came in at 0.09-0.25.

**So 2x6's hypothesis is REFUTED, and by the test 2x6 itself specified.** GPU
work does not kick the display transaction's stamp; it **starves** it, which is
what a transaction waiting behind the same wedged queue would do. **Capture is
back as the remaining candidate** and 2x5's open question is open again.

**2x6's stamp-timeout finding is NOT withdrawn** — the 219
`transaction stamp index 59 time out` lines and the ten-capture differential
(CPU-framebuffer boots with the wedge logging zero) are measurements and stand.
What is refuted is the *mechanism* stacked on them: that new submissions are
what retire the stamp. **Eighth instance of a correct reading with a wrong
inference attached** (rule 35), and the first one this project refuted inside a
single milestone because the prediction was written down before the test.

### THE FIRST ATTEMPT TESTED THE WRONG KNOB, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT

2x6's own first run was `--busy 45 --heavy 20000 --depth 16` and bought
**18.9 buffers/s**. That is GPU **occupancy**, not submission **rate**, and
AnyDesk's profile is many small buffers — so the knob and the hypothesis did
not match. `--depth 256` with the light kernel was added for exactly that
reason and is the arm that matters here. It also read 0.16/s.

### TWO INSTRUMENT DEFECTS THE RUN EXPOSED, BOTH IN CODE WRITTEN THIS SESSION

1. **`writes != sets` fired twice and both were FALSE ALARMS.** `setsrate.sh`'s
   `key()` ran a **separate `ioreg` per counter**, seconds apart, against a
   counter pair that advances at up to 83/s — so the 117-vs-118 and 418-vs-415
   skews are the **sampling**, not the driver. **2x5 holds.** The check was
   written to satisfy rule 38 and became rule 16's example instead: *a check is
   an instrument and can be wrong in the direction that stops the work.* A
   cross-check between two counters must read them in **one** snapshot.
2. **The idle control was contaminated by the keystroke that launched it.**
   6.83 sets/s is not the frozen 0.08/s; it is the decaying tail of pressing
   Return, because typing is the one thing that makes this machine composite
   (2wl) and the control began immediately after it. **A control for a defect
   that input suppresses must start after the input's effect has decayed** —
   the ~10 s figure has been in this journal since 2wi. Same family as 2x3's
   lost trace: the script must own the clock *and* the settle.

### AND A NEW FACT, IN THE EXHIBITING CONFIGURATION

**64 light buffers took 100.43 seconds — 1.57 s per buffer** — where the same
binary standalone, minutes earlier in the same boot, managed 18.9/s. And
`--depth 256` produced exactly 256 buffers in 32 s, i.e. **the loop body ran
once**: one batch never completed inside a 20 s window. 2wz's worst single-queue
reading was 6104 ms; this is worse and it is measured **with the display path
live**, which is the configuration 2wz could not reach (rule 39). Not yet
explained, and not attributed: the wedge may deepen because the display
transaction is itself queued behind it.

## 2x8 — THE CAPTURE TEST, WITH THE INSTRUMENT VERIFIED FIRST

`tools/levertest.sh`. No build, no boot, no kext, no sudo. Three arms, each a
discarded **15 s settle** followed by a measured **25 s window**:
**A** idle, **B** an active screen capture, **C** idle again — two controls,
not a trend (rule 18).

Every defect 2x7 exposed is fixed in it: **one `ioreg` per sample** so the
counters cannot skew against each other, a **settle before every window** so no
arm measures the keystroke that started it, and the script **owns the capture
as well as the clock** so no phase can be entered at the wrong time.

**The capture is `screencapture -v -x -D 1 -C`**, started and stopped by the
script, and **it is verified before arm B is believed**: the process must still
be alive after 4 s and the output file must be **growing** between two stats.
2x5 lost three exchanges to "didn't work" meaning three different things — TCC
denied, ran with zero frames, TCC denied again — and a capture that produced no
bytes is not a capture (rule 14). If `screencapture` exits at once it is almost
certainly TCC, and the script says so and names the GUI fallback instead of
reporting a quiet zero.

**Said before the test.** B near 83/s with A and C near 0.1/s = **capture is
the lever**; a minimal always-on stream is the bridge and the real fix is
whatever makes WindowServer treat the panel itself as a consumer. A, B and C
alike = **capture is dead too**, and what remains is whatever else a live
AnyDesk session holds open, which `lsof` on its pid will name.

## 2x9 — WINDOWSERVER NAMES THE MECHANISM: A DISPLAY STREAM FORCES A RECOMPOSITE

Live boot **208** (`kern.boottime` 00:21:13 EDT, `rbgpu-boot` 208, `rbgpu-fb`
consumed to `0`, `RBAMDFramebuffer` publishing) — rule 33 established before
anything was read.

### GEEKBENCH 7 RAN TO COMPLETION IN THIS BOOT, AND SCORED

`browser.geekbench.com/v7/gpu/340163`, uploaded 05:38 **UTC** = **01:38 EDT**,
i.e. inside boot 208, the armed GPU-framebuffer boot. Metal, device
`AMD Radeon HD GFX10 Family Unknown Prototype`, macOS 15.8.1 (24H32).
**Metal score 9336**, all eleven subtests complete, nothing zero or blank:

    Background Blur    6509    16.8 images/sec      Horizon Detection 12275  473.2 Mpixels/sec
    Face Tracking     22373    27.7 images/sec      Photo Filter      14656
    Super Resolution   5090    9.39 Kimages/sec     Video Filter       9761  2.65 Gpixels/sec
    RAW                1738    70.3 Mpixels/sec     Feature Matching  21404   40.4 Mpixels/sec
    Path Tracer       12086    21.6 Mpixels/sec     Particle Physics  18579  3330.8 FPS
    Fluid Simulation   4322    63.7 FPS

**This is a real result for the project, not just a datum**: Apple's
accelerator on an unsupported APU completes a full industry benchmark suite
without a hang, in the same boot whose desktop freezes.

**It is CONSISTENT with 2ws, not a refutation, and the distinction matters.**
2ws measured a 175.77 ms **command-buffer round-trip** tick and validated it
against a 420x control that moved GPU time while `commit->GPUstart` stayed
pinned — i.e. **work inside a buffer is unthrottled; round trips are not**.
Geekbench's figures are work throughput (3330.8 FPS, 2.65 Gpixels/s) and say
nothing about how many command buffers it used. Do **not** read them as
refuting the tick, and do not read them as confirming it either: its
submission granularity is unmeasured.
**What it does establish, with 2x7 beside it**: the same boot that runs
2.65 Gpixels/s in Geekbench took **100.43 s for 64 light command buffers**.
Few-big-buffers is at full speed; many-small-buffers is catastrophic. That is
the signature of a **per-command-buffer** cost, not a throughput limit — and
the display path is many small transactions, so it sits on the bad side. Held
as a lead; nothing here measures Geekbench's buffer count.

### THE LIVE FAST STATE, MEASURED

With AnyDesk connected (an `AnyDesk --backend` process present, pid respawning
3826 -> 3891), a 15 s settle then a 15 s window:

    RBFBAmtrSets  80830 -> 81834   = 1004
    RBFBVBLFires 623768 -> 625793  = 2025  = 14.08 s
                                   -> 71.3 sets/s

Boot average over 72 minutes is **18.66 sets/s** with `RBFBAmtrPeak 671` per
~7 s window (**95.9/s**). So the fast state is real, reproducible and live, and
it is not a few lucky frames.

### ANYDESK CAPTURES THE SCREEN — FROM ITS OWN LINK TABLE

`otool -L` / `nm -u` on `/Applications/AnyDesk.app/Contents/MacOS/AnyDesk`:

    ScreenCaptureKit.framework (weak)
    _OBJC_CLASS_$_SCStream / SCStreamConfiguration / SCShareableContent
    _CGDisplayStreamCreateWithDispatchQueue / Start / Stop / UpdateGetRects
    _kCGDisplayStreamMinimumFrameTime / _kCGDisplayStreamColorSpace
    _CVDisplayLinkCreateWithCGDisplay / GetNominalOutputVideoRefreshPeriod
    _IOSurfaceLock / GetBaseAddress / GetBytesPerRow
    _CGWindowListCreateImage

Note **`CGDisplayStream` resolves on 15.8.1**. 2x5 rewrote `framepump` *away*
from that API because it is obsoleted in 15.0; AnyDesk still links it, so the
rewrite was unnecessary and it cost the TCC grant (permission is keyed to
binary identity).

### AND WINDOWSERVER NAMES THE MECHANISM IN ITS OWN LOG

`/usr/bin/log show --last 3m --info --predicate 'sender == "WindowServer"'`,
468 lines, in the fast state:

    CreateDisplayStreamState: Display stream 0x85307 created
    0[outside of RPC]: system screen capture status 1
    WSDisplayStreamNeedsRecomposite: Display stream 0x85307 ...
    0[outside of RPC]: system screen capture status 0

**`WSDisplayStreamNeedsRecomposite`** — WindowServer has a function whose name
is *a display stream needs a recomposite*. Streams are created at 01:40:34,
01:41:00 and 01:41:44 and `system screen capture status` toggles 1/0 around
each, matching the backend pid respawning and overlapping the 71.3 sets/s
window.

**So the capture hypothesis now has a named mechanism and a system state
variable to test against**, instead of an impression. It is still a
**correlation** (rule 18): nothing here varies the stream while holding
everything else fixed, which is what `levertest.sh` does.

### AND CAPTURE WAS NEVER ACTUALLY TESTED BEFORE

Worth stating plainly, because it is why 2x5 left this open on two instrument
failures rather than a measurement: `framepump` delivered **zero** frames at
64x36 (SCK de-duplicates identical downscaled frames), then was rebuilt at
native resolution and **TCC denied it**. `vblclock` used CVDisplayLink only
and never captured. So no working capture stream has ever existed in this
project, and "capture is dead" was never a result — rule 14 twice over.

### THE INSTRUMENT, FIXED AGAIN

`tools/levertest.sh` now asks **WindowServer** whether each arm had a capture,
via `capstatus()` over the arm's own wall-clock bounds, and prints it beside
the rate. That is strictly better than checking our `screencapture` child is
alive and its file is growing (which it also does): it is the producer's own
word, and it catches AnyDesk still being connected — which would make arm A
and arm C capture arms too and destroy the contrast without saying so. Rule 16
applied to the test's premise rather than to its reading.

## 2xa — AN ACTIVE SCREEN CAPTURE IS THE LEVER. MEASURED, WITH TWO CONTROLS

Live boot **210** (`kern.boottime` 10:33:11, `rbgpu-boot` 210, `rbgpu-fb`
consumed to `0`, `RBAMDFramebuffer` publishing, **no `AnyDesk --backend`
process**) - rule 33 and the control condition both established first. Boot
average before the test: `RBFBAmtrSets 601` over `RBFBVBLFires 80656` =
**1.07 sets/s** over 9.3 minutes, so the defect is present.

`tools/levertest.sh`, three arms, each a **discarded 15 s settle** then a
**25 s measured window**:

| arm | sets | writes | vbl | window | rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** idle, no capture | 1 | 1 | 3006 | 20.90 s | **0.05 sets/s** |
| **B** capture ACTIVE | 1626 | 1626 | 3280 | 22.80 s | **71.30 sets/s** |
| **C** idle again | 2 | 2 | 3600 | 25.03 s | **0.08 sets/s** |

**A 1426x step, bracketed by two independent controls** that read 0.05 and
0.08 - which is 2x5's frozen 0.08 sets/s reproduced twice. The capture was
real: **21 858 347 bytes** of video written.

**AND THE RATE IS THE SAME NUMBER ANYDESK GIVES, TO THREE SIGNIFICANT
FIGURES.** 2x9 measured a connected AnyDesk session at **71.3 sets/s**; arm B
reads **71.30 sets/s** with no AnyDesk, no network, no input and no GPU load.
So capture accounts for the whole of AnyDesk's effect, and nothing else about
that session needs explaining. 2x5's open question is **closed**.

**`RBFBHubpWrites` tracked `RBFBAmtrSets` EXACTLY in all three arms** (1/1,
1626/1626, 2/2), from one `ioreg` snapshot per sample. **2x5 holds**, and
rule 38's cross-check is satisfied properly this time rather than firing on
sampling skew.

### WHAT IS AND IS NOT ESTABLISHED

**Established**: an active display stream takes the transaction rate from
0.05-0.08 to 71.30 sets/s, reversibly, in one boot, with the panel's own
vblank counter as the clock.
**NOT established**: *why*. `WSDisplayStreamNeedsRecomposite` (2x9) names the
mechanism on WindowServer's side - a stream needs a frame, so WindowServer
recomposites - but nothing here shows what makes WindowServer believe **the
panel itself** needs no frame. That is the remaining question and it is now
upstream of everything this project has built.
**NOT independently confirmed**: arm B's `capstatus` line read `none` with
only 1 SkyLight line in the window, so WindowServer did not corroborate the
capture *inside B's window*. The stream was created during the 9 s pre-check
before B began, and the recomposite lines are evidently not logged per frame.
What does corroborate it: the 21.8 MB file, and **arm C catching
`system screen capture status 0`** - the capture ending, exactly where it
should land.

### FIVE INSTRUMENT DEFECTS, ALL IN CODE WRITTEN THIS SESSION

The first run of this test was **void**, and said so in three places. Each
fault and its fix is in the script's header; the ones worth the rule:

1. **PARSE THE VALUE, NEVER A BYTE OFFSET.** `substr($0, RSTART+18, ...)`
   dropped the **leading digit** of every counter - 465 read as 65, 66000 as
   6000 - and once a truncated value rolled (499->500 becomes 99->00) the
   delta went **negative**. The run printed `sets -98` and `vbl -6421`, which
   is the only reason it was caught. `$NF` is the value. **An impossible
   reading is the cheapest bug report there is: print the delta, not just the
   rate.**
2. **`screencapture -v` NEEDS `-V <seconds>`.** Backgrounded without it, it
   stayed alive, wrote **0 bytes** and created no stream - indistinguishable
   from a TCC refusal, which is what 2x5 wrongly concluded about `framepump`.
   With `-V` it records and exits by itself (375 327 bytes, exit 0). **TCC was
   never the problem; the invocation was.** And `-V` buffers to disk at the
   end, so the "is the file growing" guard is ALSO wrong for this mode - it
   fired on a capture that was working perfectly.
3. **THE LOG PREDICATE'S SENDER IS `SkyLight`, NOT `WindowServer`.** The lines
   read `WindowServer: (SkyLight) [com.apple.SkyLight:default]`, so
   `sender == "WindowServer"` returned **1** line where the OR form returns
   **45**. 2x9's finding survived only because its exploratory query happened
   to carry the OR clause. **Rule 36's third instance in this project**, and
   the fix is now verified against a known-present case in the same boot: a
   6 s capture yields `CreateDisplayStreamState` 1, `status 1`, `status 0`,
   `WSDisplayStreamNeedsRecomposite` 1.
4. **The counters reset between the two runs** and the negative deltas were
   the first sign: boot 208's 80173/618000 became 465/66000, i.e. a **new
   boot** (210). Rule 33 is not a one-time check at the start of a session -
   it is a check before **every** reading.

### THE BRIDGE, AND THE REAL FIX

**The bridge is available now**: anything holding a display stream open makes
this machine usable at ~71 Hz. `screencapture -v -V` proves it but writes
~450 KB/s to disk, so the usable form is a minimal `CGDisplayStream` or
`SCStream` consumer that discards every frame - and **`CGDisplayStream`
resolves on 15.8.1** (2x9, from AnyDesk's own link table), so the obsoletion
notice that made 2x5 rewrite `framepump` was not a reason to avoid it. One
TCC grant, once, against a binary whose identity does not change.
**The real fix is the open question above**: what makes WindowServer treat the
panel as a consumer that needs frames. A workaround that needs a screen
recorder running forever is not a driver.

## 2xb — THE BRIDGE IS BUILT, AND IT IS NOT A FIX

`tools/dstream.m` + `make dstream` -> `build/out/RBDisplayStream.app`, plus
`tools/com.rembrandtgpu.displaystream.plist` (a LaunchAgent, which the **user**
installs). It holds a display stream open on the main display and **discards
every frame**, which 2xa measured as worth 0.05 -> 71.30 sets/s.

**CGDisplayStream IS ALIVE AT RUNTIME ON 15.8.1.** The SDK marks every entry
point `unavailable: obsoleted in macOS 15.0`, so the calls **will not compile**
and `-Wno-deprecated-declarations` does not help. But `dlopen` +
`dlsym` resolves `CGDisplayStreamCreateWithDispatchQueue`,
`...Start`, `...Stop` and `...UpdateGetRects`, with **`CGMainDisplayID` as a
positive control and a made-up name as a negative one** - and AnyDesk requires
the same symbols and runs here (2x9). So `dstream.m` binds them by hand.
**The first version of that check was itself wrong** and is worth recording:
it used `RTLD_DEFAULT` from a binary that linked no CoreGraphics, so it searched
nothing and reported all four `missing`. Rule 26 on a four-line probe.

**It reports its own effect.** frames/s *and* `RBFBAmtrSets`/s side by side,
with the panel's vblank as the clock, and it names the failure when a stream
creates but delivers nothing - which is the precise shape of `framepump`'s
three-exchange failure in 2x5, where "didn't work" meant TCC-denied, then
ran-with-zero-frames, then TCC-denied again.

**NOT TESTED END TO END. `CGDisplayStreamCreateWithDispatchQueue` returned
NULL under this session's shell** - Screen Recording is keyed to a code
identity and a bare CLI binary inherits whichever terminal launched it, which
here is the Claude app. The tool said so in one line instead of reporting a
quiet zero, which is the whole point of the design, but **no measurement here
shows the bridge working**; rule 14 applies to it exactly as to anything else.
The `.app` bundle exists only to give it a stable TCC identity:
**ad-hoc signed with a fixed `CFBundleIdentifier`, re-signed by the make target
rather than by hand**, because 2x5 lost `framepump`'s grant to a rebuild.

**AND IT IS A WORKAROUND.** A driver that needs a screen recorder running
forever is not a driver. The open question is unchanged and is the real fix:
**what makes WindowServer believe the panel itself needs no frame?**

### WHERE THE REAL FIX IS BEING LOOKED FOR, AND WHY IT STOPPED HERE

SkyLight has exactly one throttle symbol, **`WS::Updater::UpdateState::
add_non_throttled_display`** (`0x7ff807e2db64`), and `WS::Updater::` is the
compositing scheduler (`UpdateDisplays` `0x7ff807e2e609`, `note_will_update`,
`process_per_display_prep_data`, `prepare_coreanimation`,
`composite_windows_to_destination_and_region`). `add_non_throttled_display` is
**a plain `vector<shared_ptr<Display>>::push_back`** onto `UpdateState+0x140`,
so the decision is in its callers - of which there are **two**, both inside
