`UpdateDisplays` (`0x7ff807e2f0af`, `0x7ff807e2f2b6`), and **both are
wholesale loops** adding every display in a vector, selected by
`testb $0x1, -0x557(%rbp)`. So there is no per-display throttle predicate
there, and `process_per_display_prep_data` does not call it at all.
**Deliberately stopped**: following spilled stack slots through a 57 000-line
region is how this project attached a correct chain one link off **seven**
times (rules 33/35). The better instrument now exists - a reversible
40-second reproducer with two controls - and the next step should use it
rather than a static chain.

## 2xc — THE CONSUMER IS THE CLOCK: ONE COMPOSITE PER FRAME ASKED FOR

First live run of `dstream` (user's own terminal, so Screen Recording was
granted to it; the stream created and frames arrived):

    +10s  frames  33 (3.27/s)  idle 0 blank 0   fb 3.24 sets/s
    +20s  frames  70 (3.64/s)  idle 0 blank 0   fb 3.34 sets/s
    +30s  frames  80 (0.99/s)  idle 0 blank 0   fb 0.99 sets/s

**frames/s and `RBFBAmtrSets`/s are the SAME NUMBER in every sample.** So
WindowServer composites **exactly once per frame the consumer asks for**, and
the consumer is the clock. That is a much sharper statement than 2xa's "a
capture is the lever", and it came from the tool reporting both numbers side
by side - the one design decision that made this run informative instead of
another "kind of didn't work".

**WHY IT STALLED AT 1/s, AND IT IS THE API NOT THE MACHINE.**
`CGDisplayStream` only asks for a frame when something **changed**. Here that
is circular: nothing changes, so it does not ask, so WindowServer does not
composite, so nothing changes. It decays to ~1/s. `screencapture -v` reached
**71.3/s** in 2xa because a **video recording demands a frame on a fixed
cadence** whether or not the screen changed.

So the bridge needs an API that **demands a rate**, which is
ScreenCaptureKit's `minimumFrameInterval` - the one `screencapture` itself
uses on 15.x. `dstream` now defaults to **SCK at `--fps` (144)** and keeps
`--cgs` for the CGDisplayStream path, **one binary so both modes run under one
TCC grant**. It counts SCK's idle and blank frames separately via
`SCStreamFrameInfoStatus`, because an unchanged frame still costs a
recomposite and that is exactly what we want.

**2x5's framepump verdict is now fully explained and withdrawn as a
conclusion**: it failed at 64x36 because SCK de-duplicates identical
downscaled frames, and again because rebuilding revoked its grant. Neither was
evidence about capture. 2xb's "TCC blocks it" was also about **this session's
shell**, not the machine - the user's own terminal had the grant all along.

**NOT YET MEASURED**: that SCK's demanded rate actually drives
`RBFBAmtrSets` to ~144/s. The prediction is explicit - frames/s and sets/s
should stay equal and both rise to the `--fps` value - and the tool prints
both, so one 60-second run settles it either way.

## 2xe — THE CONSUMER IS NAMED: SKYLIGHT'S READINESS WATCHDOG, AND IT IS A SURFACE POOL

Boot 210, armed, GPU framebuffer live, exhibiting the defect throughout (rule
39: every reading below is from the configuration that has the symptom, and
arm A/C are controls taken in the same minute). No boot spent.

**THE FIRST FORK, AND IT KILLS THE COMFORTABLE ANSWER.** Every lever this
project has found — typing (2wl), AnyDesk (2x5), `screencapture` (2xa/2xd) —
is an external agent poking WindowServer. None of them is what a user means by
a smooth desktop, and nobody had asked the plain question: *when something on
screen changes by itself, continuously, does the chain run?* Because an idle
desktop composites nothing on **every** Mac, 0.09 sets/s at idle might have
been correct behaviour and the whole frontier might have been about
interaction only.

`tools/animtest.m` (new): a visible window with a `CABasicAnimation` on
position and opacity, `repeatCount` infinite — WindowServer animates it
itself, no IPC per frame, the plainest continuous on-screen change there is.
Back to back in the same minute, same boot:

| arm | 30 s | `RBFBAmtrSets` delta |
|---|---|---|
| **B** animating window | | **2** |
| **C** `screencapture -v -V 30` | | **1827** (~61/s, 14.1 MB written) |

**900x.** So an animating desktop produces nothing and a capture produces the
panel's rate, and "idle composites nothing, which is normal" is **dead**. Also
dead: frame-demand as the lever — 2xc had already been withdrawn when an SCK
stream's *idle* frames arrived at 37–77/s while sets tracked only the
*complete* column.

**AND WINDOWSERVER SAYS WHY, IN WORDS, IN ARM B's OWN LOG.**

    [ Watchdog ] display 5b81c5c0 regained readiness after 5.99733s (1440 failures)
    [ Watchdog ] display 5b81c5c0 regained readiness after 5.98810s (1438 failures)
    [ Watchdog ] display 5b81c5c0 has become stuck after 10.00390s of unreadiness (2402 failures)
    [ Watchdog ] Inform the watchdog that all displays are stuck.

**Five independent readings give one constant**: 1440/5.99733, 1438/5.98810,
2402/10.00390, 1042/4.33713, 1382/5.75765 = **240.1 failures/s** every time.
WindowServer asks whether our display can take a frame **240 times a second**
and is told no. Arm C has two of these at its start and then **none** for its
remaining 24 s while 1827 frames flow.

**THE PREDICATE, READ END TO END.** The three watchdog strings
(`0x7ff807feadd0`, `0x7ff807fead30`, `0x7ff807feae20`) have exactly **one**
`ripall` referencer each, all in one region of SkyLight:
`ReadinessTelemetry::mark_ready(double)` (`0x7ff807e235b0`),
`mark_unready(double)` (`0x7ff807e23708`), both called from
`update_display_callback(void*, double)` (`0x7ff807e21dab`). The decision there
is **one virtual call**:

    movq (%rbx), %rdi        ; the WS::Displays::Display
    movq (%rdi), %rax
    xorl %esi, %esi          ; arg = false
    callq *0x4b8(%rax)       ; -> bool
    testb %al, %al
    je   -> mark_unready     ; else mark_ready

Slot `0x4b8` is **`WS::Displays::CDDisplay::is_ready(unsigned) const`**
(`0x7ff807d6c14e`), which ignores its argument:

    dev = this->0x158                                   ; CGXDisplayDevice*
    if (!dev) return true
    cd = CoreDisplay_GetDisplayForCGXDisplayDevice(dev)
    if (cd) return CoreDisplay_Display_IsReady(cd)
    return CGXDisplayDeviceSurfaceIsReady(dev)

`CoreDisplay::Display::IsReady()` (`0x7ff80408e316`) gates on
`CoreDisplay::UseIOPresentment()` (true here since 2t7) and then asks
`CoreDisplay::DisplaySurfacePool::IsReady()` (`0x7ff804134cbe`) for its own
pool and for each active pipe's pool at `+0x270`:

    count = (this->0x60 - this->0x58) / 16      ; surfaces in the pool
    if (count < (int)this->0x48) return true    ; pool not full yet -> READY
    return (some surface s has s->0x170 == 0)   ; else: a FREE one must exist

**SO "DISPLAY READINESS" IS A FREE SURFACE IN A POOL, and `+0x170` is a use
count** — named by Apple itself: `RunFullDisplayPipe` and `BuildTransactions`
both take a **`UseCountProxy<CoreDisplay::DisplaySurface*>`**, and
`GetNextSurface` (`0x7ff8041341c6`) does `incl 0x170(%rdi)` when it hands one
out. `DisplaySurface::AccessComplete()` (`0x7ff8040b95e4`) has six callers:
`Display::Present`, `CoreDisplay_DisplaySurface_Free`, `RunFullDisplayPipe`
(x2) and `RunGPUDisplayPipe`.

**AND THE RELEASE IS DRIVEN BY ONE EVENT.** Both the pool release and the push
notification come from the same function,
**`CoreDisplay::IOPAttachment::HandleTransactionCompletionEvent(unsigned long*,
unsigned int)`**: it calls `DisplayPipe::GetAndRemovePresentSurfaceFor`
`TransactionSurface` (`0x7ff80410e030`, the only other caller being
`0x7ff804085afe`) and then `DisplayPipe::NotifyIsReady()` (`0x7ff80411b0d8`,
two callers, both in `IOPAttachment`), which is what SkyLight's
`display_ready_cd_callback` is registered for. **The whole frame cadence hangs
on the kernel's transaction-completion event arriving.** Remove `Clean` from
the open questions and put this in its place.

**THE OTHER END, MEASURED IN THE SAME CONFIGURATION.** 63 s, keepalive off,
sender-matched with 29 SkyLight lines as the control:

| | count |
|---|---|
| `transaction stamp index 59 time out` | **48**, steady **1.0 Hz**, always index 59 |
| `[ Watchdog ] become stuck after` | 4, at **10.00271 / 10.00096 / 10.00364 / 10.00238 s** |
| `channel N … event timeout` (the wedge) | 14 |
| `RBFBAmtrSets` delta | **3** |

The stamp-timeout stream runs at 1 Hz with exactly **three six-second gaps**
(01.657→07.659, 13.661→19.664, 43.681→49.685) and exactly **three**
transactions landed. Each gap is one frame getting through. **n=3** — said as a
correspondence, not a law. **And a wrinkle not papered over**: `regained
readiness` was **0** in this window while 3 frames presented, where arm B gave
2 and 2. Once the watchdog has declared the display stuck the transition stops
being logged, so those three frames are **not** accounted for by a readiness
transition, and the surface-release chain above is a **static read** — no
reading here observes one surface's use count.

**MY OWN INFERENCE, BUILT AND THEN WITHDRAWN IN THE SAME MILESTONE.** The
static chain into AMDRadeonX6000 is real and worth keeping:
`AMDSWScheduler::initialize` (`0xbe93ce2`) creates its event source with
**`provider = 0`** — `IOInterruptEventSource::interruptEventSource(owner,
deferredCallback, 0, 0)` — so `deferredCallback` is a **software** source, not
a hardware interrupt, and there is no missing GPU interrupt to find.
`timerCallback` (`0xbe9513c`) and `statCallback` (`0xbe95146`) have **zero**
references in the whole kext; both are 5-byte trampolines and `timerCallback`
tail-jumps into `advance()` (`0xbe950e0`), whose only other reacher is
`deferredCallback`. The source is signalled (`es->vt[0x1d8](0,0,0)`) from
exactly four sites: **`submitCommandBuffer`** (`0xbe94412`, right after
`movb $1, 0x71(%rsi)`), `timestampUpdated` (`0xbe94dc4`),
`swTimestampUpdated` (`0xbe94e24`) and `checkTimestamps` (`0xbe94eb4`). And
`checkTimestamps()` (`0xbe94e3c`) — the only function that performs the
hardware poll, `channel->vt[0x1a8]()` — has **seven callers and every one is a
waiter**: `AMDAccelChannel::waitForTimestamp` (x4),
`AMDAccelEventMachine::waitForStamp`, `eventTimeout`, `checkChannelIsActive`.
**There is no periodic poll anywhere.**

From that I concluded "nothing kicks the scheduler when the desktop is idle,
so tick `advance()` from the framebuffer's VBL thread_call" — which is 2x6's
proposal, and **it is not supported, because 2ww had already measured the
opposite**: boot 199's `rbgpu-sched` note reads `sub=12191 adv=46457`, i.e.
`advance()` ran **four times more often than work was submitted**, mean gap
**3.4 ms**, 38 808 gaps under 128 us. `advance()` is not a 5.7 Hz gate and it
is not starved. **Rule: read the evidence already in hand before designing the
next experiment — 2ww was in the journal the whole time, and it even names the
gap this would need**: that note flushes only at three fixed phase marks, so
`advance()`'s rate in the **slow** state has never been read. That, not a
tick, is the next measurement, and it is the same defect 2wl had to fix for
the crumb in a different file. `advance()` is at least cheap and safe to call
— it takes its own `IOLock` (`this->0x48`) and is a no-op for channels whose
`ctx->0x71` is clear — so the option stays open; it is simply not yet indicated.

**THE VBLANK WAS NEVER A CLOCK, AND THAT ONE IS OURS AND FIXED.** `animtest`
reads CVDisplayLink's `CVTimeStamp` hostTime, whose source is the
framebuffer's vblank. 5510 intervals over 40.9 s:

    mean    7.4240 ms  = 134.699 Hz          target 6.9527 ms = 143.830 Hz
    stddev  0.4615 ms  (6.2 % of mean)
    min     5.9619 ms   max 10.6553 ms   spread 4.6934 ms
    histogram  6.5-7 18.8 %  |  7-7.5 40.6 %  |  7.5-8 26.5 %  |  8-8.5 12.7 %

The mean is **0.47 ms long on every tick**, which is exactly the shape of
`armVBL()` computing `clock_interval_to_deadline(period)` — `now + period` —
at the **END** of `deliverVBL()`, so every period paid for the handler that
preceded it. And `CVDisplayLinkGetNominalOutputVideoRefreshPeriod` read
**115.94 / 119.97 / 120.00 / 133.72 Hz** across four runs: **a clock whose
rate moves with system load is not a clock**, and CoreVideo measures ours.
Fixed in `armVBL()` by advancing the **previous deadline** instead of `now`,
with a counted resync when we fall a whole period behind (arming into the past
would fire a catch-up burst of ticks the panel never had). Eight assertions in
`fb_vbl_test.cpp`, and **mutation-tested both ways**: restoring `now + period`
fails `t.deadline == first + i*P` at tick 1.

**AND THE PROJECT'S RATE FORMULA WAS WRONG TWICE OVER.** `transactions/s =
RBFBAmtrSets / (RBFBVBLFires / 143.83)` (2wj, used by 2wi/2xa/2xd) divided by
a rate that was really ~134.7 Hz — and `RBFBVBLFires` is published only every
**1200 fires**, so the registry value is a **staircase with 8.3-second
treads**. A 25-second window therefore carried a ±33 % quantisation error on
its own time base; my first `animtest` run read "fb clock 6.4 s vs wall 12.1 s"
and that was the publish interval, not the panel. **2xa's "71.30 == AnyDesk's
71.3 to three significant figures" is NOT SUPPORTED** — three significant
figures were never there. 2xa's 1426x conclusion survives easily; the
precision claim does not. Fixed by publishing **`RBFBVBLUptimeNs`** (and
`RBFBVBLResyncs`) in the same pass as the counter, so elapsed time comes from
a stamp written beside the count and the quantisation cancels, and by dropping
the interval to 288 fires (~2 s). **Rule 16 again: the instrument was a
suspect, and both of its errors pointed the same way.**

**PREDICTED, NOT CLAIMED**: if the transaction-completion event is what gates
the surface pool, then the wedge (2we/2wt — work submitted and never retiring,
`no channel associated with stamp_idx`) and the display defect share a cause,
because both are stamp retirement. 2x6 said this was not established and it
still is not.

**NEXT, no boot needed to prepare it**: make `rbgpu-sched` flush periodically
instead of at three fixed phase marks, so `advance()`'s rate can be compared
between the fast and slow states — 2ww named this gap and it is the one
measurement that decides whether the scheduler is the gate. Install fbkext
**`39190382`** for the clock fix; it needs no boot-arg and changes no
behaviour but the cadence.

## 2xf — `advance()` HAS SIX-SECOND GAPS IN THE SLOW STATE, AND THE NOTE WAS ALREADY ON THE MACHINE

Boot 212, armed, `RBAMDFramebuffer` owning the panel, `rbgpu-fb` consumed to
`0` by 2wj's overwrite. No boot spent. Rule 8/33 first: `rbgpu-boot` **212**,
`kern.boottime` 12:59:18, `RBFBVBLUptimeNs` present — a key only the 2xe
fbkext publishes — so the installed framebuffer is **`39190382`** and rule 15
is met by a key the new code writes unconditionally.

**THE CLOCK FIX IS VERIFIED ON HARDWARE.** A 30 s window, timed by the new
stamp rather than by an assumed rate:

    vbl fires   4322 over 30.054 s = 143.807 Hz    (the panel is 143.830)
    resyncs        0                               (no period ever missed)
    amtr sets   2087               =  69.44 sets/s
    hubp writes 2087               (tracks sets exactly - 2x5 holds)

**143.807 against 143.830 is 0.016 %**, where 2xe measured **134.70 Hz** from
userspace before the change, and zero resyncs means the handler never ran a
whole period long. The drift was arithmetic and it is gone.

**AND 2ww's MISSING MEASUREMENT WAS SITTING IN NVRAM, UNREAD.** 2xe closed
with "the deciding measurement is the one 2ww named: `rbgpu-sched` flushes at
three fixed phase marks, so `advance()`'s rate in the SLOW state has never
been read" — and then `nvram rbgpu-sched` answered it on the first try,
because `-rbgpuschedprobe` is in this boot's boot-args and the flush runs at
+12/+100/+160 s, **before** keepalive was started at ~250 s uptime. The window
is the slow state by construction.

    b=212 hk=1 sub=8390 adv=4790 smax=748
    gmin=0 gmean=32314 gmax=6001590
    h=821,3739,113,6,2,4,1,4,11,4,3,7,5,69

| | boot 199, fast window | **boot 212, slow window** |
|---|---|---|
| mean gap between `advance()` calls | 3.4 ms | **32.3 ms** |
| max gap | — | **6 001 590 us = 6.0016 s** |
| gaps >= 262 ms (`h[13]`) | — | **69** |

**`gmax` IS 6.0016 s AND 2xe's WATCHDOG READ 5.99733 s.** Two instruments with
nothing in common — our own Lilu hook on Apple's `advance()`, and SkyLight's
`ReadinessTelemetry` log line — **4 ms apart**. 2xe measured the same 6 s as
the gaps in the 1 Hz `transaction stamp index 59 time out` stream, three of
them against three transactions. Rule 18 says two numbers agreeing to one
figure is not an identification; three instruments agreeing to **four
milliseconds** is a different kind of claim, and it is the first time this
project has had one.
The histogram sums to 4789 = `adv - 1`, which is the arithmetic control that
the gap accounting is self-consistent.
**`adv/sub` is deliberately NOT used here**: 2wy proposed it as a regime
discriminator and withdrew it one milestone later when three fast readings
gave 0.66, 3.81 and 15.22. That it reads 0.57 now is recorded and leaned on
for nothing.

**WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH.** Established: in the exhibiting
configuration, `advance()` — the only path that retires a GPU stamp, reachable
only from `deferredCallback` off a software event source and from the
never-installed `timerCallback` (2xe) — goes **six seconds** without running,
69 times over 262 ms in one window, against a 3.4 ms mean when the machine is
busy. **Not established**: that this *causes* the display stall. During those
gaps stamp 59 is pending (2xe's 1 Hz timeouts) and `advance()` is the only
thing that could retire it, but **no instrument has yet shown pending work at
`advance()`'s entry** — rule 35, our own end, and the thing a tick experiment
must measure rather than assume. An idle scheduler with nothing pending is
correct behaviour and looks identical in this note.

**THIRD TIME THIS SESSION.** 2xe built an `advance()` tick on an inference,
withdrew it against 2ww, and named the next measurement — which already
existed, in NVRAM, under a key the boot-args had armed. **Read the evidence
already in hand** is the project's oldest recurring error and it cost three
separate detours in one session.

**THE BRIDGE, MEASURED HONESTLY.** `tools/keepalive.sh` on this boot: cycles
2-5 ran full 60 s at **72.62 / 78.40 / 60.50 / 60.03 sets/s**, 30-43 MB
written and deleted per cycle, with a live cross-check of 55.06 sets/s taken
independently of the script's own arithmetic. **But cycles 1 and 6 exited at
10.91 s and 9.02 s with 4 and 0 sets** — `screencapture` bails early
periodically, so the bridge has recurring ~10 s holes, not just the hitch per
cycle that 2xd advertised. Also fixed here: keepalive timed its windows with
`fires / 143.83`, which 2xe showed is wrong twice over, and its
"bridge is not working" guard fired on those short cycles — a working bridge
judged dead by a cycle that never ran, the same shape as the `-V` guard 2xa
had to remove. It now times with `RBFBVBLUptimeNs` and refuses to judge a
cycle under half its requested length.

**NEXT, AND ITS RISK STATED BEFORE ANYTHING IS BUILT.** The experiment is a
periodic `AMDSWScheduler::checkTimestamps()` — not `advance()`, because
`advance()` only walks channels whose `ctx->0x71` is already set and
`checkTimestamps` is the sole function that performs the hardware poll
(`channel->vt[0x1a8]()`) and then sets that flag and signals the event source
(2xe). **It needs no new route**, which rule 3 would forbid: the existing
`-rbgpuschedprobe` hook already receives the scheduler pointer as its first
argument on every call, so a static capture there plus one `solveSymbol` is
the whole mechanism. **Its failure mode is a panic, not a hang**, and a
boot-arg alone would panic-loop across power cycles — rule 37 — so it must
carry a one-shot, and that is the plumbing to get right rather than rush.
Said before the boot: if the display rate rises with the tick, retirement was
the gate; if it does not, the gate is below `checkTimestamps` and the next
target is what `channel->vt[0x1a8]` reads.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
2xg (2026-10-29) — THE SCHEDULER TICK, BUILT WITH ITS ONE-SHOT.
Plugin `23D86D68`. No boot yet.

WHAT IT IS. A `thread_call` at the panel's measured 143.83 Hz (6944 us,
tunable `rbgpuschedtickus=<500..1000000>`) that calls Apple's
`AMDRadeonX6000_AMDSWScheduler::checkTimestamps()`. Armed by
`-rbgpuschedtick` **and** `sudo nvram rbgpu-tick=1`.

WHY `checkTimestamps` AND NOT `advance`. Disassembled this milestone, and it
says it plainly (`0xbe94e3c`):

    for (i = 0; i < this->0x60; i++) {                /* stride 0x98 */
        ctx = this->0x58 + i * 0x98;
        if (ctx->0x6c == ctx->0x68) { if (ctx->0x8) ctx->0x71 = 1; }
        else {
            ctx->0x8->vt[0x1a8]();                    /* THE HARDWARE POLL */
            if (ctx->0x72 == 1) { IOLockLock(this->0x48);
                                  checkPreemption(*ctx);
                                  IOLockUnlock(this->0x48); }
        }
    }
    return this->0x30->vt[0x1d8](0, 0, 0);            /* signal the source */

`advance()` (`0xbe950e0`) only walks channels whose `ctx->0x71` is ALREADY
set, so on an idle scheduler it is a no-op by construction — ticking it would
measure nothing, and 2ww had already measured it running four times per
submit. `checkTimestamps` is the sole hardware stamp poll, it is what SETS the
`0x71` flag `advance()` needs, and it tail-jumps into the event source 2xe
measured being created with **`provider = 0`** (software), so nothing else
will ever fire it on an idle machine.

NO NEW ROUTE, which rule 3 would forbid. The scheduler pointer arrives as the
first argument of both 2wv hooks on every call, so it is captured there;
`-rbgpuschedtick` turns those routes on by itself, so a tick can never be
armed without the capture that feeds it. Rule 1 satisfied:
`nm -m build/re/AMDRadeonX6000` shows
`__ZN29AMDRadeonX6000_AMDSWScheduler15checkTimestampsEv` **defined** at
`0xbe94e3c`. Rule 2 does not apply — nothing is routed, the address is solved
and called.

THE SAFETY ARGUMENT IS APPLE'S OWN CODE, not an assumption. The function's
seven callers are all WAITERS (`AMDAccelChannel::waitForTimestamp` x4,
`AMDAccelEventMachine::waitForStamp`, `eventTimeout`,
`checkChannelIsActive`), i.e. arbitrary client threads and not the workloop —
which is both why it is starved when nobody is waiting, and why a
`thread_call` is the same class of context it already runs in. It takes
`this->0x48` itself. Re-entrancy is likewise Apple's design: those waiters can
be inside it concurrently already, with no outer lock over the
`ctx->0x71`/`0x72` byte writes or the stamp read, so one more caller is the
same shape as a second waiting client thread.

RULE 37, APPLIED BEFORE THE BUILD AND NOT AFTER. **The failure mode is a
PANIC, not a hang**, and a boot-arg alone would panic-loop across power
cycles. So the tick also needs `rbgpu-tick`, consumed **by overwrite** and
consumed **before the first tick is ever armed**. The existing
`rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot` could not be used: it removes the variable and
reads it back as absent, and 2sq measured that exact sequence SURVIVING A
REBOOT, because `removePropertyWithGUIDAndName` calls no sync — so it can
report `why = 0` ("consumed; clear OK") on a key that is still armed, which is
how boot 196 ended up being disarmed from Windows. So a second helper,
`rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot_ow`, writes a literal `"0"` on the `setProperty`
path 2sr measured as the only one reaching `IODTNVRAM::syncInternal`, verifies
the read-back, and **fails closed**. Same `why` codes as the removal form so a
reader need not know which helper produced them.

EVERY DEREFERENCE IS RE-CHECKED ON EVERY TICK, and refusals are counted and
published with their reason (rules 14/19): the object above the **kalloc**
floor `0xffffff8000000000` (not the kext-symbol floor), a non-NULL channel
array also above it, a channel count in 1..64, and the event source
(`+0x30`) and the IOLock (`+0x48`) both non-NULL. `tw=` carries which test
failed, because "the pointer was never captured" and "the object looks wrong"
are different answers. Sixteen CONSECUTIVE refusals *after at least one
successful call* stop the tick for the boot rather than keep calling into an
object being torn down — the "after a successful call" qualifier matters,
because before the first submit there is no pointer to tick and that is
normal, not teardown.

AND THE TICK'S OWN CADENCE USES 2xe'S FIX. `rbgpu_2xg_arm_next()` walks the
PREVIOUS deadline forward and resyncs only when a whole period has already
been missed. Writing `now + period` after the work is the exact defect this
project just removed from its own vblank, and it would have been reintroduced
here by default.

THE FIELDS GO IN `rbgpu-sched`, BEFORE THE HISTOGRAM. The note is the only
thing that survives a boot this experiment might wedge (rule 10), and a gap
histogram is only interpretable beside the number of kicks that produced it.
The histogram is the part that truncates, so the tick's fields are placed
ahead of it: `tarm` armed, `tos` one-shot code, `tus` period, `tc` ticks that
fired, `tk` calls that reached `checkTimestamps`, `tr` refusals, `tw` last
refusal reason, `ts` the stop flag. The "not armed" early-out carries
`tarm`/`tos` too, so a `hk=0` note still says whether the tick was asked for.

SAID BEFORE THE BOOT, so the reading cannot be fitted afterwards:
  `tc` climbing with `tk` tracking it and `tr` at 0 means the tick is really
    running. **That is the arm check — read it before anything else**, and
    `tarm=0` with `tos=` 1/2/3/4 says exactly why nothing ran.
  If the DISPLAY RATE RISES — `RBFBAmtrSets` over `RBFBVBLUptimeNs`, never
    over 143.83 (2xe) — retirement was the gate, and the fix belongs where
    2ws named it: driven from the framebuffer's own VBL `thread_call`, which
    is already a 143.83 Hz timer in the right context.
  If `gmean`/`gmax` collapse but the display rate does NOT move, then
    `advance()` starvation was real and **not the cause** — the gate is below
    `checkTimestamps` and the next target is what `channel->vt[0x1a8]` reads.
  If `gmean`/`gmax` do not move either, the scheduler was idle with nothing
    pending all along, 2xf's 4 ms correspondence between `gmax` 6.0016 s and
    the watchdog's 5.99733 s is a coincidence of two unrelated 6 s timers,
    and this whole line closes.

WHAT IS STILL NOT ESTABLISHED, unchanged from 2xf and the reason this
experiment exists at all: nothing has observed pending work at `advance()`'s
entry, so an idle scheduler with nothing to do looks identical in that note
(rule 35). The tick is what tells the two apart.

AND A FLAG FROM THE PREVIOUS MILESTONE IS WITHDRAWN. I said `-rbgpuforceenable`
was armed without `wdt=-1`. It is not: `boot-args` reads
`-rbgpuforceenable wdt=-1`, adjacent. Read the token, not the memory of it.

HONEST GAP: `rbgpu_2xg_sane()` is decision logic with no hosttest, because it
lives in `src/plugin` and the hosttest harness covers `src/common` and the
fbkext. Its four offsets are cross-checked against the disassembly quoted
above and nothing else.

INSTALL (rule 15, every artifact): plugin **`23D86D68`** to the OpenCore EFI
(`sudo tools/efi.sh install`); fbkext **`39190382`** UNCHANGED in
`/Library/Extensions` — verified byte-identical to `build/out` this milestone,
no re-install. Boot-arg: add `-rbgpuschedtick`. One-shots (rule 34, all five):
`sudo nvram rbgpu-arm=1 rbgpu-agdc=1 rbgpu-iop=1 rbgpu-fb=1 rbgpu-tick=1`.

2xh (2026-10-29) — BOOT 213: THE TICK'S CALL SITE WAS WRONG, AND THE NOTE
SAID SO IN THREE FIELDS. Plugin `DFEAFF02`.

Rule 8 first: `rbgpu-boot` **213**, `kern.boottime` 13:32:17, plugin
`23D86D68` loaded (the 2xg build), fbkext `39190382`, `-rbgpuschedtick` in
boot-args as a whole token, and all five one-shots consumed — so this is a
genuinely armed boot of the new code and `rbgpu-sched` carries `b=213`.

**THE TICK DID NOT TICK, AND THE ARM CHECK IS WHY IT COST NOTHING TO FIND
OUT.** `tarm=0 tos=0`, with `tick_us` **absent** from the diag table:

  `tos=0` is `rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot_ow`'s "armed and consumed", and it
    returns true only on that code — so the one-shot path worked exactly as
    designed, including the overwrite read-back.
  `tarm=0` with the consume having succeeded leaves exactly one branch:
    `g_rb_2xg_check` was still NULL.
  `tick_us` absent confirms it from the other side — that key is published
    only after `thread_call_allocate`, which is past the refusal.

**THE CAUSE IS ORDERING.** `rbgpu_schedtick_start_2xg()` is called from the
peer's `start()`, which was 2w5's hard-won fix for a probe gated on a
neighbour's boot-arg — and it is still the right place for the one-shot and
the allocation. But the tick's *target* is solved in `processX6000`, the
AMDRadeonX6000 patcher callback, which runs **later**: the peer matches on the
PCI device early, the accelerator is patched when its kext loads. `hk=1` in
the same note proves the routes themselves took, so the callback did run — it
just ran after the arm. **2w5's lesson in a new form: a probe needs a call
site that runs when ITS arg is set, and this one did — but it also needed a
target that only exists later, and nothing reconciled the two.**

**THE FIX IS NOT TO MOVE THE CONSUME.** Moving it into the patcher callback
would "fix the ordering" by putting a flash commit inside a kext load, which
is 2fo's wedge. Instead the tick now **arms anyway**: the `thread_call` is
allocated and started from the peer's `start()`, where NVRAM and allocation
are safe, and the action refuses harmlessly — counted — until the route
callback fills the target in. Rule 37 is untouched: the one-shot is still
consumed before the first tick fires, which is all it requires.

**AND TWO FIELDS WERE ADDED BECAUSE BOOT 213 COULD NOT ANSWER ITS OWN
QUESTION** (rule 14). `tw` stayed **0** through the whole boot, because the
action short-circuits on `!g_rb_2xg_check` and never reaches
`rbgpu_2xg_sane()`, so the one refusal that mattered had no reason recorded.
Now: `tw=7` means "the target is not resolved", distinct from `tw=1..6`, which
mean the scheduler object itself looked wrong. And `tw=7` *still* cannot say
whether the callback has not run yet or `solveSymbol` failed, so
`tick_solved` is published from the patcher callback itself — safe, because
`processX6000` already writes the diag table twelve times. The four tick keys
also went to the **top** of the NVRAM hot-key list, ahead of 2w3's gates,
because a boot carrying this feature can panic.

**THE SIX-SECOND GAP REPRODUCED, AND THAT IS THE REAL RESULT OF THIS BOOT.**

    boot 199 (fast)   gmean   3 400 us
    boot 212 (slow)   gmean  32 314 us   gmax 6 001 590 us
    boot 213 (slow)   gmean  72 321 us   gmax 6 005 202 us

So `gmax` is **6.0016 s and 6.0052 s in two independent boots**, against
SkyLight's watchdog at 5.99733 s — and 2xf's 4 ms agreement was a single
reading that could have been coincidence. It is now reproducible to 3.6 ms
across two boots of different builds. The histogram sums to **2177 = adv − 1**
(371,694,969,18,11,10,9,10,12,5,1,9,6,52), so the gap accounting is
arithmetically sound, and **52 gaps are ≥ 262 ms**.
**STILL NOT ESTABLISHED, unchanged**: nothing observes pending work at
`advance()`'s entry, so an idle scheduler looks identical (rule 35). That is
what the tick is for, and it has not run yet.

Also read live, not promoted: `RBFBVBLResyncs` **7** over 334 s of uptime
(boot 212 read 0 over 30 s). Seven whole periods missed on a loaded machine
is what the counted resync was built to show rather than hide; it is not a
clock fault and it is **not** attributed to anything.

Boot 213's own display rate: `RBFBAmtrSets` 55 over 334 s = **0.16 sets/s**,
i.e. the exhibiting configuration, which is what the tick needs.

INSTALL (rule 15, every artifact): plugin **`DFEAFF02`** to the OpenCore EFI

Boot-arg `-rbgpuschedtick` is ALREADY in boot-args, no edit needed.
One-shots (rule 34, all five): `sudo nvram rbgpu-arm=1 rbgpu-agdc=1
rbgpu-iop=1 rbgpu-fb=1 rbgpu-tick=1`.
**Read `tarm` FIRST**: `tarm=1` with `tc` climbing and `tk` tracking it is
the only state in which anything else in the boot means anything. `tarm=1`
with `tk=0` and `tr` climbing at `tw=7` means the symbol never resolved —
then read `tick_solved`: 0 says `solveSymbol` failed, absent says the

2xh addendum — RULE 37'S FIX IS NOW VERIFIED ACROSS A POWER CYCLE, on new
code, by accident. Boot 213 armed `rbgpu-tick`, the tick's arm consumed it
with `rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot_ow` (`tos=0`), the box was power cycled, and
**boot 214 reads `rbgpu-tick` as `0%00`** — the literal "0" plus the
`OSString` NUL, still there. `rbgpu-fb` reads the same. So the overwrite path
persisted through flash, which is precisely what 2sq measured the *removal*
path failing to do for `rbgpu-fb` across six boots. n=1, but it is the exact
experiment that rule 37 exists for, and the arming check's first-byte test
treats it as not armed, so boot 214 came up with `IONDRVFramebuffer` owning
the panel, no accelerator, and a usable software-composited desktop.
**A plain power cycle is a full disarm, measured, for the new one-shot too.**
Also worth keeping: `rbgpu-sched` in boot 214 still reads **`b=213`** — rule
11, a note is evidence only when its nonce is new, and that one is this boot's
stale copy of the previous boot's answer.

2xi (2026-10-29) — **THE TICK WORKS. THE DISPLAY HALF IS FIXED.**
Boot 215, plugin `DFEAFF02`, fbkext `39190382`. The user reported it from the
screen first; everything below is the instruments agreeing.

**THE ARM CHECK, READ FIRST as 2xg prescribed.** `tarm=1 tos=0 tus=6944`,
`tick_solved=1`, `ts=0`, and:

    tc=23934   ticks fired
    tk=23011   calls that reached checkTimestamps
    tr=923     refusals, ALL of them tw=1 (the scheduler pointer was NULL)

`tk + tr = 23011 + 923 = 23934 = tc` **exactly** — the arithmetic control on
the tick's own accounting. And `tr` was already 923 at the first reading and
had not moved 148 s later, so every refusal is the pre-first-submit window
2xh's lazy arm was designed to absorb: 923 × 6944 us = 6.4 s of boot before
the accelerator submitted anything. `tw=1` rather than `tw=7` also says the
symbol was resolved the whole time, which `tick_solved=1` confirms from the
patcher callback independently.

**THE SCHEDULER GAPS COLLAPSED, and the histogram names our own period.**

                  gmean         gmax          gaps >= 262 ms
    boot 212     32 314 us   6 001 590 us          69
    boot 213     72 321 us   6 005 202 us          52
    boot 215      2 921 us      88 346 us    **     0 **

**25x on the mean and 68x on the max**, and the 88 ms maximum predates the
tick engaging. `h=608,234,47,13,5,10,34,1582,103,0,0,1,0,0` sums to 2637 =
`adv - 1` (the control), and its dominant bucket is **h[7] = 1582**, i.e.
[4096, 8192) us — **which is where 6944 us lands.** `advance()` is now paced
by our tick and by nothing else. Buckets 12 and 13 are zero where boot 213 had
52 entries.

**THE DISPLAY RATE, timed by `RBFBVBLUptimeNs` and never by 143.83 (2xe).**

    20.03 s window    1805 sets    90.13 sets/s
    45.02 s window    3097 sets    68.79 sets/s

**With no bridge running**, verified properly after a first attempt failed:
`keepalive` 0, `AnyDesk` 0, `metal_probe` 0 in a `ps` snapshot taken to a
file, with `WindowServer` 1 and `launchd` 12 as known-present controls and a
check that the snapshot contains none of the search words. The first attempt
printed `2` for all four categories because the labels in the `echo` strings
were sitting in the wrapper shell's own command line and matching themselves
— **rule 26 again, and self-inflicted.** The nine `screencapture` hits are
Claude.app helpers carrying the word inside a Chromium `--disable-features`
list, not recorders.

**AND 2xe'S OWN TEST, THE SAME BINARY AND THE SAME 30 SECONDS:**

    boot 210   a continuously animating window ->       2 sets in 30 s
    boot 215   the same window, same build     ->    3375 sets in 30.14 s
                                                    = 111.98 sets/s

**1687x on one instrument, one test, one duration.** That is the cleanest
before/after this project has, because nothing about the measurement changed.
2xe's *"an animating window produces NOTHING"* — the finding that killed
frame-demand as the lever — is now the finding that measures the fix.

**THE KERNEL BLOCKER IS GONE, against the control that has held since 2w4.**
Captured by SENDER (rule 36), `display_change_handler` = **26**, the same
value every boot from 185 to 193 read:

    transaction stamp index N time out       219 / 48  ->  0
    channel N ... event timeout (the wedge)     26-46  ->  0
    checkGPUProgress                            36-63  ->  0
    no channel associated with stamp_idx        18-36  ->  0

So 2x6's blocker — *"the transaction it is drawing for cannot retire, so it
does not draw the next one"* — is answered, and **the wedge is absent too**.
That second part is a LARGER claim than the tick was built to make and it is
**n=1**. It is mechanistically coherent rather than coincidental: 2we read the
wedge as *"work is submitted and never retires, the hang check says not hung,
the restart cannot find the channel"*, i.e. a **retirement** failure, and
`checkTimestamps` is the retirement poll. But one boot is one boot.

**RULE 39, BOTH DIRECTIONS.** This reading is taken in the configuration that
exhibits the defect — an armed GPU-framebuffer boot on the **same fbkext
`39190382`** as boots 212 and 213, which read 0.16 and 0.05-0.08 sets/s. The
plugin differs from 2xg's `23D86D68` only in the tick's arm ordering and two
diag keys, so **the single variable is whether the tick ran.**

**THE CLOCK IS RIGHT AND ITS JITTER IS WORSE — stated, not buried.**
CVDisplayLink now fires 143.35/s, and over 4322 intervals the mean is
**6.9713 ms = 143.446 Hz** against the panel's 6.9527 ms = 143.830 — **0.27 %
off, where 2xe measured 6.3 %** and the nominal refresh read 115.94 / 119.97 /
120.00 / 133.72 Hz across four runs. But the spread widened: stddev
**0.4615 ms (6.2 %) -> 0.9684 ms (13.9 %)**, min 5.96 -> **3.81 ms**, max
10.66 -> **29.01 ms**. A sub-period minimum is a catch-up. The obvious
candidate is that a machine actually compositing 112 frames/s carries real
load where before it was idle and regular-but-slow, and **a clock whose MEAN
is correct under load is a different animal from one whose RATE moved with
load** — but the cause is **NOT established** and must not be written as if it
were.

**WHAT IS NOT DONE.** 111.98 sets/s under continuous animation is **78 % of
the panel's 143.83**, and the idle-ish desktop reads 68-90. The user's goal
was native 144 Hz, so the last ~22 % is a **new and much smaller question**,
and it is not known whether it is demand-limited (a compositor composites when
there is something to composite) or still gate-limited. Do not assume either.
Also unexplained and trivial: `RBFBHubpWrites` exceeds `RBFBAmtrSets` by 1-4
in every reading (3376 vs 3375, 1809 vs 1805). Sampling skew between two
`ioreg` key reads taken at different instants is the obvious candidate and is
**not measured**. `WindowServer` sits at **14.9 %** — neither 2su's 0.0 % idle
nor 2v9/2w0's ~200 %.

**THE CHAIN, END TO END, now that it runs.** 2xe read the readiness predicate
down to `DisplaySurfacePool::IsReady` and found both the surface release and
SkyLight's push notification coming from one function,
`IOPAttachment::HandleTransactionCompletionEvent` — so the frame cadence hung
on the kernel's transaction-completion event. 2xf measured `advance()`, the
retirement driver, starved with 6.0 s gaps. 2xg built the tick on
`checkTimestamps` because it is the sole hardware stamp poll, the only setter
of the `ctx->0x71` flag `advance()` walks, and the tail-jump into an event
source created with `provider = 0`, i.e. software, so nothing else would ever
fire it on an idle machine. Boot 215 closes it: tick the poll at the panel's
rate and the stamps retire, the transactions complete, the surfaces are
released, readiness is regained and the compositor draws the next frame.

2xj (2026-10-29) — THE TEARING WAS PREDICTED IN WRITING BEFORE THE DISPLAY
EVER WORKED. fbkext `A058AEA0`, read-only, no boot yet.

The user reported tearing at the bottom of the screen once 2xi landed — a
strip of the window behind showing through for a moment, worse while
`animtest` ran — and asked whether it is VSync or FreeSync. **It is neither,
and the answer has been in this file since 2wh:**

> *"Nothing changing at all with `Readback == Last` = DCN ignores the stores
> and wants `DCSURF_FLIP_CONTROL` / the `SURFACE_UPDATE_LOCK` dance this
> build deliberately omits. Tearing is expected and acceptable."*

So the flip-arming sequence was never written, by choice, to keep 2wh the
narrowest possible write. A `grep` confirms it: `FLIP_CONTROL` and
`SURFACE_UPDATE_LOCK` appear **nowhere** in `src/common/rb_hubp.h` or
`src/fbkext/RBAMDFramebufferHUBP.cpp`.

**AND IT SCALES WITH THE FLIP RATE, WHICH IS WHY IT APPEARED NOW.** A tear
needs the address latch to land mid-scanout. Boot 213 flipped at **0.16/s** —
roughly one opportunity every six seconds. 2xi flips at **112/s** under
animation. The tear was in the design from 2wh onward and nothing revealed it
until the rate came up. **Same shape as 2wi**: the 0.09 Hz frame rate was
always there, and 2wh did not cause it, 2wh made it VISIBLE. Note it the other
way round too — `animtest` tearing harder than the desktop is the predicted
behaviour, not a new defect.

**WHAT IS NOT KNOWN, AND WHY NOTHING IS WRITTEN THIS MILESTONE.**
`DCSURF_FLIP_CONTROL` carries the field that selects an **immediate** flip
over a **vsync'd** one, which is plausibly the whole fix in one bit. But the
field layout lives in `dcn_3_1_2_sh_mask.h`, **which this repo does not
carry** — `docs/linux-ref/` has the offset header only. Deriving a bit
position from memory and writing it into the display engine is rule 17
exactly, and this register can blank the panel. So: **read it first, decide
afterwards.**

**THE OFFSETS, CROSS-CHECKED FOUR WAYS.** From
`dcn_3_1_2_offset.h`, `regHUBPREQ<n>_DCSURF_FLIP_CONTROL` =
**0x061b / 0x06f7 / 0x07d3 / 0x08af** and `_CONTROL2` = 0x061c / 0x06f8 /
0x07d4 / 0x08b0. Those sit exactly on the **0xdc stride** the table has
asserted-but-never-used since 2wh (0x061b + 0xdc = 0x06f7 = the header's own
value, three times over), and 0x061b is **adjacent to `HUBP0_SURFACE_CONTROL`
= 0x061a** in `rb_regs.h`, which is the family check: a flip-control register
that did not land next to the surface-control register would mean we are
reading a different block.
A note on how this was nearly missed: the first grep for
`mmHUBPREQ0_DCSURF_FLIP_CONTROL` returned **nothing**, because this header
spells them `reg...`, not `mm...`. **Rule 26, and it was caught only by
controlling the grep against an offset already in `rb_hubp.h`** (0x060a),
which the header does carry.

**THE CHANGE IS A READ, in 2wh's own established pattern** — the same
standing as `DCSURF_ADDR_CONFIG` / `DCSURF_TILING_CONFIG`: read in
`hubpSetup()`, published as `RBFBHubpFlipCtl` / `RBFBHubpFlipCtl2`, **never
written, never a gate.** Mutation-tested: changing one hex digit of HUBP0's
offset fails **five** assertions across **three independent statements** of
the same number (the stride lattice, the direct header value, and the
adjacency to `HUBP0_SURFACE_CONTROL`). It also hit 2xe's trap again — the
hosttest compiles `RBAMDFramebufferVBL.cpp` against
`tools/hosttest/fb_vbl_shim.hpp`, a separate stub class, so the two fields had
to be added there as well.

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.** `RBFBHubpFlipCtl` is the whole point of this
build: it is the firmware's own setting for a pipe that has been scanning
correctly since before macOS booted. If a field in it reads as "immediate",
the next step is one bit on one register with a readback and a restore path,
and the fix is as small as the user guessed. If it already reads as vsync'd,
then the tear is NOT the flip type and the next suspect is that our write is
not atomic with respect to the scanout at all — the `SURFACE_UPDATE_LOCK`
half, which brackets the address pair rather than selecting when it latches.
**Either way no bit is written until the register has been read**, and
`RBFBHubpFlipCtl2` is published beside it so a wrong guess about which of the
two carries the field costs nothing (rule 35, the shape 2wf used for
`flip->0x58`).

INSTALL (rule 15): fbkext **`A058AEA0`** to the **auxiliary collection**, i.e.
`/Library/Extensions` — it is the only artifact that changed. Plugin
**`DFEAFF02`** is unchanged and already in the EFI; **no `efi.sh install`, no
rebuild.** Boot-args unchanged. One-shots, all five as 2xi.

candidate; reading both keys in ONE `awk` pass over ONE `ioreg` makes them
agree exactly, so that is what it was. The caveat is retired, not carried.

**THE REGISTER, DECODED AGAINST MEASURED FIELD NAMES.** `RBFBHubpFlipCtl` =
**0x04100000**, `RBFBHubpFlipCtl2` = **0x40**. The field map comes from
`dcn_3_1_2_sh_mask.h` at torvalds/linux
`4dd16e31135ea8437a720222df34e8745f385d6d` (6.5 MB, not copied; the fields are
listed in `docs/linux-ref/UPSTREAM.md` and in `rb_hubp.h`, which is the
convention that file already states for the offset headers):

    SURFACE_UPDATE_LOCK                = 0
    SURFACE_FLIP_TYPE                  = 0
    SURFACE_FLIP_VUPDATE_SKIP_NUM      = 0
    SURFACE_FLIP_PENDING               = 0
    HUBPREQ_MASTER_UPDATE_LOCK_STATUS  = 0
    SURFACE_FLIP_PENDING_DELAY         = 65
    leftover bits                      = 0x00000000
    FLIP_CONTROL2: PENDING_MIN_TIME 64, SURFACE_TRIPLE_BUFFER_ENABLE 0

**The zero leftover is the control** — if the mask map were wrong, bits would
be unaccounted for. It is asserted in the hosttest against the live value.

**SURFACE_FLIP_TYPE IS 0, AND 0 IS VSYNC'D.** That is established from Linux's
own driver, not from recall: `hubp1_program_surface_flip_and_addr` writes
`REG_UPDATE(DCSURF_FLIP_CONTROL, SURFACE_FLIP_TYPE, flip_immediate)`
(`dcn10_hubp.c:361`), so the field *is* the immediate flag and 0 is the
vsync'd setting. **The firmware already latches at VUPDATE, so the tearing is
NOT the flip type, and 2xj's "one bit" hope is dead.** It cost a read and
nothing was written. 2xj's own alternative branch — *"if it already reads as
vsync'd, then the tear is NOT the flip type"* — is the one that fired, which
is what writing both outcomes down beforehand is for.
A note on how the masks were obtained at all: the first grep for
`mmHUBPREQ0_...` found nothing because this header family spells them `reg...`.
**Rule 26, caught only by controlling the grep against an offset `rb_hubp.h`
already carries.** The same control was used on the 6.5 MB download before
reading anything out of it.

**THE NEXT CANDIDATE, NAMED AND COUNTED, NOT ACTED ON.**
`SURFACE_FLIP_PENDING` is the hardware's "armed but not yet latched" status,
and `SURFACE_TRIPLE_BUFFER_ENABLE` reads **0**, so there is exactly **one**
pending slot. We have **never** read that bit before programming the next
address. So programming over a pending flip discards it — and, separately, our
`setAttribute('amtr')` answers success the instant it is called (2we: *"answers
success without doing the work"*), so Apple's compositor is told the flip
completed while DCN may not have latched it and the surface may still be live.
That is a mechanism that would put *newer* content in the lower part of a
frame, which is where the user sees it. **It is a hypothesis with no
measurement behind it yet** (rule 35), so this build **counts** it:
`RBFBHubpPendChecks` / `RBFBHubpPendHits` in `hubpProgram()`, a register read
only, with **the write itself unchanged** — nothing skipped, deferred or
reordered, so this build cannot alter what the panel shows.

Mutation-tested: moving the `SURFACE_FLIP_PENDING` mask one bit fails three
assertions, including the live-value decode. `rb_hubp_flip_pending()` is a
pure predicate in `src/common/rb_hubp.h` so the hosttest decides it before the
kext does, like every other HUBP decision; it is checked against 0x100 alone,
zero, and **every other bit set but that one**.

**SAID BEFORE THE BOOT.** `RBFBHubpPendHits` near zero out of ~2400 checks
means a pending flip is NOT being overwritten and this candidate dies too —
then the remaining suspect is the surface's *contents* changing under the
scanout, which is a completion-signalling problem in our `'amtr'` answer and
not a register at all. A large fraction means the mechanism is found, and the
fix is to **skip or defer** the write while pending, which is strictly fewer
writes and so cannot show DCN a value it has not already seen. **Do not write
`SURFACE_UPDATE_LOCK` on the strength of this**: it brackets a GROUP of
register writes, and we change exactly one dword whose HIGH half never moves,
so there is no group to make atomic.

INSTALL (rule 15): fbkext **`07B0C4A2`** to `/Library/Extensions`; plugin
**`DFEAFF02`** unchanged in the EFI, no `efi.sh install`. Boot-args unchanged.
One-shots, all five.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
2xl (2026-10-29) — THE 175 ms SUBMISSION LATENCY IS 13.5 ms. No boot, no
build: `build/out/metal_probe --bench` on the live armed boot 216.

The user asked why a Metal score reads 9633 against a figure of 33 000 they
found for this APU, and named clocks, power mode and CU count. The measurement
that answers it first was already available and had **never been re-run since
the tick landed**. 2ws measured this on boot 198, one queue, same binary:

                              boot 198      boot 216
    commit -> GPUstart       174.855 ms     13.494 ms      13.0x
    GPUstart -> GPUend         0.014 ms      0.016 ms      unchanged
    commit -> scheduled        0.092 ms      0.161 ms      prompt in both
    GPUend -> return           0.042 ms      0.205 ms
    serial throughput          5.7 /s        72.9 /s       12.8x
    pipelined throughput      46.2 /s       291.1 /s        6.3x

**The chip's execution time did not move** (0.014 -> 0.016 ms) and the work is
still handed over promptly (0.161 ms). The whole 13x is the wait BEFORE the
work, which is exactly the quantity 2ws isolated and exactly what the tick was
built to remove. `verify: PASS (0 of 4096 wrong)` in both.

**AND THE LIMITER CHANGED CHARACTER, NOT JUST SIZE.** 2wu's `--phase` sweep
read a clean lattice on boot 198 - `d+wall` constant at 173.7 ms, T = 175.77
with R = 0.966 over 191 periods. On boot 216 `d+wall` **climbs linearly with
d** (90.5, 100.2, 111.0, ... 249.9) with `wall` hovering 6.1-11.6 ms, and the
tool's own printed criterion for that shape is *"a FIXED per-buffer delay"*,
not a periodic quantum. So the 175 ms lattice is gone rather than shortened.
The `--bench` pipelined listing is the one reading that still looks periodic -
release clusters at 12.6, 25.8, 33.0, 40.1, 47.3, 54.5, 60.8 ms, i.e. **~7 ms
apart, which is our 6944 us period** - and the serial median of 13.715 ms is
close to **two** periods, which is 2wu's phase-lock argument (a serial loop
always just misses one). Two instruments, two slightly different characters:
recorded as such, **not reconciled**.

**CAUSATION IS NOT CLEAN, AND THIS IS THE RULE-39 CAVEAT.** Boot 198 ran with
`RBAMDFramebuffer` **not loaded**; boot 216 has the framebuffer takeover AND
the tick. **Two variables differ, not one**, so "the tick did this" is the
likely reading given 2ws's mechanism analysis pointed at `advance()` by name,
but it is not established by this comparison alone. **The A/B that settles it
costs no code and no risk**: `rbgpuschedtickus=<500..1000000>` is already a
tunable, so sweeping the tick PERIOD tests the same mechanism from the other
side. If `commit -> GPUstart` tracks the period, the tick is the release; if it
floors out, the remaining latency is elsewhere. That keeps a working desktop,
unlike un-arming `rbgpu-tick`, which would also answer it but at the cost of
the boot.

**ON THE USER'S THREE HYPOTHESES, honestly.**
*Clocks and power mode are genuinely UNWIRED*, and the registry says so in its
own words: the accelerator's `PerformanceStatistics` carries
**`"Core Clock(MHz)"=0`** and **`"Memory Clock(MHz)"=0`**. Rule 14 - that is
"nothing in our stack reports it", **not** "the clocks are at zero", and the
two are indistinguishable from this reading. What IS certain is that this
project has never set a clock or a power state: `rb_smu.c` is query-only with a
three-message allowlist (GetSmuVersion, GetDriverIfVersion,
GetEnabledSmuFeatures), nothing is sent unless the response register reads 1,
and adding a message group is the user's decision by standing rule. So it is
unwired and **its effect is unmeasured**; it must not be written as the cause.
*The CU / shader-array configuration has never been read here.* What is
measured is `GB_ADDR_CONFIG` = **0x242** = 4 pipes, 4 packers, 1 SE, and it
lives in `kern_start.cpp`, **not** `rb_regs.h` - a first grep for it over
`rb_regs.h` returned 0 and that zero was meaningless, rule 26 again, caught
only by checking the file's naming convention. No CU-enable or harvest
register has been read, and **no registry property reports a core count**.
*The 33 000 figure is not verified and the comparison may not be one.* Geekbench
Metal, Vulkan and OpenCL scores for the same chip differ by large factors, and
GB5 and GB6 Metal are not comparable either - naming which suite, which API
and which version produced each number is rule 33 applied to a benchmark. **And
9633 was almost certainly measured BEFORE the tick**, since the tick first ran
in boot 215 today, so the first thing to do is re-run it.

## 2xm — boot 217: the tearing mechanism is measured at 1.75 %, and the A/B never ran because of a bug in my own boot-arg parse

Boot 217, armed, rule 15 clean on **both** kexts for the first time in this
line of work: plugin `DFEAFF02`, fbkext **`07B0C4A2`** — so 2xk's flip-pending
counter was installed and running. `rbgpu-boot` 217, `rbgpu-tick` and
`rbgpu-fb` both read `0` (consumed by overwrite, 2wj/2xh), `rbgpu-arm` /
`rbgpu-agdc` / `rbgpu-iop` absent (consumed by removal). `tarm=1 tos=0
ts=0`, `tick_solved=1`, `tk + tr = tc` exactly (23015 + 959 = 23974) with all
959 refusals in the pre-first-submit window (`tw=1`).

### THE TEAR IS A FLIP PROGRAMMED OVER AN ARMED, UNLATCHED ONE

The one thing 2xk was built to read:

    RBFBHubpPendChecks   33877
    RBFBHubpPendHits       593     = 1.75 % of flips, 1.26 per second
    RBFBHubpFlipCtl   0x04100000   (= 68157440; identical to boot 216)
    RBFBHubpFlipCtl2        0x40   (= 64;        identical to boot 216)
    RBFBAmtrSets         33829     RBFBHubpWrites 33867
    RBFBVBLFires         66451     RBFBVBLUptimeNs 470025770818  (470.026 s)
    sets/s 71.97      our own thread_call rate 141.377 Hz, 3 resyncs

`hubpRegs` is the `volatile uint32_t *` BAR5 map, so `fc` is a **live hardware
read taken immediately before the write**. `PendHits` therefore means exactly
this: **593 times we programmed a new primary surface address while DCN still
had the previous one armed and not yet latched.** 2xk measured
`SURFACE_FLIP_TYPE = 0` (vsync'd, latched at VUPDATE), so between our write
and the latch the register holds an address the panel is not yet reading;
writing again inside that window replaces the armed address, and the frame
that does reach the panel changes partway down. That is the tear 2wh
predicted in writing.

**Said before the boot, and honoured**: "near zero out of ~2400 kills the
pending-overwrite candidate; a large fraction means the mechanism is found."
1.75 % is **neither**, and it is stated as neither. It is non-zero and at a
rate (1.26/s) consistent with an occasional visible tear, and the mechanism is
real and now quantified — but it is **not** the majority of flips, so **it is
not established that it accounts for everything the user sees**. In
particular the user's description ("a bit of the browser behind appears for a
second") is far longer than one frame at 144 Hz, and a one-frame tear cannot
last a second. The second candidate from 2xk stands untested: our
`setAttribute('amtr')` answers success instantly (2we), so the compositor may
recycle a surface still being scanned.
**Arithmetic control**: at 72 flips/s the gaps average 14 ms against a ~7 ms
latch window, so if `PENDING` were simply the tail of our own previous write
the hit rate would be near 50 %, not 1.75 %. The 593 are genuine back-to-back
pairs, not an artefact of sampling our own store.
Also: `PendChecks` 33877 ≈ `HubpWrites` 33867 + 10 and `AmtrSets` 33829, so
the counter sits on essentially every write, as intended.

### THE A/B DID NOT RUN, AND THE CAUSE IS MY OWN CODE

`rbgpuschedtickus=2000` was in boot-args (offset 843 of 864 — not truncation,
the kernel's limit is 1024) and the tick ran at **6944 µs** anyway:
`tus=6944` in the note and `tick_us=1b20` in the diag table, two instruments
agreeing. So **2xl's free causation experiment silently did not happen.**

**`PE_parse_boot_argn` hands back a NUMBER as a BINARY INT, never ASCII.**
Measured from this machine's own kernel, `_PE_parse_boot_argn`
`0xffffff8000b92970`. For `name=<digits>` with `force_string = 0` (which is
what the public entry point passes, `xorl %r8d,%r8d` at `0xffffff8000b92987`)
the numeric path reaches `0xffffff8000b92c77`:

    testl %ecx,%ecx           ; ecx = max_len
    jle   ...                 ; <= 0: store nothing
    cmpl  $0x7,%r14d          ; r14d = max_len - 1
    ja    0xffffff8000b92db9  ; max_len > 8  -> movl %edx,(%r15)
    jmpq  *table(,%r14,4)

and the jump table, decoded from the file:

    max_len=1 -> 0xb92c99  movb        max_len=5..7 -> 0xb92db9  movl
    max_len=2 -> 0xb92d9e  (2 bytes)   max_len=8    -> 0xb92dc3  movq
    max_len=3 -> 0xb92da9  (3 bytes)
    max_len=4 -> 0xb92db9  movl %edx,(%r15)

So the accumulated value is stored as a **raw integer of the caller's width**,
and a *wide* buffer gets the same 4-byte `movl`. It then `movl $0x1,%edi` and
**returns 1**. My code passed `char buf[24]` and read ASCII digits out of it,
so for `=2000` it read `D0 07 00 00`, failed `buf[0] >= '0'` on the first
byte, produced `v = 0`, and refused it as out of range — keeping 6944.

**And the refusal was logged where nothing can read it.** `rbgpu_log` does not
reach the unified log: a `--last boot` query for the plugin's own tag returns
only my own command line (rule 26's self-match trap again — the one "2xg" hit
was `log`'s record of my `log` invocation), against a control of 142 `rbgpu`
lines that are all sandbox-violation noise about `nvram-get`. **Rule 31 one
layer up: `IOLog` is not an instrument in the PLUGIN either.** The refusal is
now published as `tick_us_refused` in the diag table, so the next boot can
tell "out of range" from "never parsed" (rule 14).

**Two other tunables have the same bug and have therefore always been inert**:
`rbgpufbvrammb` (2pa) and `rbgpufbvramrangemb` (2pq), both `char[16]` with an
ASCII loop. **No past reading is invalidated** — no boot ever passed either of
them a value, which is why `VRAM,totalMB` reading 4096 was always the default
and never evidence that the tunable worked. `rbgpudalenc` is unaffected: it
takes `"dword"`/`"byte"`, a non-numeric value, which goes down the STR_VALUE
path. The fbkext's `rbgpufbhubpmax` and `rbgpufbatymb` were **always correct**
— they pass `&int, sizeof(int)` — and neither had ever been exercised either,
so the project held both idioms side by side with no measurement
distinguishing them.

Fixed with one helper, `rbgpu_boot_argn_u32(name, lo, hi, out, refused)`,
which encodes the disassembly in a single place, writes `*out` only on
success, and carries the rejected value out for publication (rule 19). All
three sites now use it.

### THE FIX FOR THE TEAR, BEHIND ITS OWN ARG

`rb_hubp_flip_would_discard(flip_ctl, flip_ctl2)` in `src/common/rb_hubp.h`,
run by the hosttest before the kext ever calls it. It defers iff
`SURFACE_FLIP_PENDING` is set **and** `SURFACE_TRIPLE_BUFFER_ENABLE` is clear
— the guard is why this is a function and not a mask test: `FLIP_PENDING`
describes **one** pending slot, so with triple buffering on a second write
discards nothing and deferring would drop frames for no reason. Boots 216 and
217 both read `FLIP_CONTROL2 = 0x40` (`PENDING_MIN_TIME` 64, triple buffering
**off**), so the guard is **inert on this machine today**; it exists so a
machine or compositor where the bit is on does not inherit a conclusion
measured where it was off (rule 39's shape).

`-rbgpufbflippend`, off by default, requires `-rbgpufbhubp`. Rule 30 checked:
it neither prefixes nor is prefixed by `-rbgpufbflipall` (they differ at the
character after `flip`). `FLIP_CONTROL2` is read **live** rather than reused
from `hubpSetup()`, because triple buffering is the compositor's to change.
Publishes `RBFBHubpDeferArmed` and `RBFBHubpDeferrals`.

**The trade, stated before the boot**: a deferral **drops** that frame — the
previous address latches instead — and since `setAttribute('amtr')` already
answers success instantly the compositor is not waiting on us either way. So
it is one stale frame per deferral against one torn frame, 1.26 times a
second. If deferring looks worse, one token reverses it without giving up the
write that made the display work.

**Mutation tested, and the first two attempts were worthless**: deleting the
guard outright and replacing the body with `return 0` both failed to
**compile** (`-Werror -Wunused-parameter`), which is a real guard but not a
test of the assertions. Re-done keeping both parameters used — `(void)flip_ctl2`
with the guard dropped, and the pending test inverted — and **both fail the
hosttest**, with the restored version passing. Also asserted: `FLIP_CONTROL2
= 0x40` decodes with **zero leftover bits**, and every bit except `PENDING`
set with `PENDING` clear must still write, so an unidentified field cannot
silently stall every flip.

### WHAT IS OPEN

- Whether 1.75 % of flips accounts for the tearing the user sees, or only part
  of it. **Not established**, and the duration does not fit.
- The jitter. `RBFBVBLFires / RBFBVBLUptimeNs` gives **141.377 Hz** against the
  panel's 143.830 (1.7 % slow) with **3 resyncs**, where 2xi's CVDisplayLink
  figure was 143.446 (0.27 %). **Different instruments** — ours is the
  `thread_call`'s own self-measured cadence, 2xi's was `CVTimeStamp` hostTime
  — so these are two readings of different things and are **not reconciled**.
- 2xl's causation caveat is **still open**, because the A/B it needed never
  ran. It costs one boot and no build now that the parse is fixed.
- The remaining ~22 % to 143.83 Hz: `sets/s` 71.97 here on an idle-ish
  desktop, inside the 68-95 band already measured. Still unknown whether it is
  demand-limited or gated.

Artifacts: plugin **`3A8EAB07`**, fbkext **`51336968`**. Both UUIDs checked
moved; `kmutil libraries -p` resolves 0 symbols from
`SystemKernelExtensions.kc` for the plugin and
`grep -c IOGraphicsFamily src/plugin/Info.plist` is 0.

## 2xn — boot 219: the tunable works, 2000 us is WORSE, and the flicker's shape names a different defect

Boot 219, rule 15 clean on both: plugin **`3A8EAB07`**, fbkext **`51336968`**,
both the 2xm artifacts. `rbgpu-boot` 219 (218 was the Geekbench boot),
`rbgpu-tick`/`rbgpu-fb` both `0`, `tarm=1 tos=0 ts=0`, `tick_solved=1`.
Boot-args carry `-rbgpufbflippend` and `rbgpuschedtickus=2000`.

### RULE 40'S FIX IS CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE

`tus=2000` in the note and `tick_us=7d0` (= 2000) in the diag table, where
boot 217 had the identical boot-arg and read 6944 in both. The tick ran at
**486 ticks/s** (`tc=52986` over 108.9 s = 2057 us), so the period took.

### AND 2000 us IS WORSE FOR THE PRODUCT, WHICH 2xl DID NOT ANTICIPATE

`advance()` is paced tighter, exactly as the tick's theory says:

                      boot 217 (6944 us)   boot 219 (2000 us)
    adv gmean              2712 us              1538 us
    adv gmax              54191 us             13183 us
    dominant bucket   h[7] [4096,8192)     h[5] [1024,2048) + h[6]

and the dominant bucket straddles 2000 us just as 217's straddled 6944, so
the pacing is real and the histogram tracks the period both times.
**But both product-facing numbers went DOWN**: `sets/s` **71.97 -> 51.33**
and our own vblank cadence **141.377 -> 133.878 Hz** (`RBFBVBLFires /
RBFBVBLUptimeNs`). A 3.5x faster `thread_call` competes with the VBL
`thread_call` that delivers frames, and the VBL clock is the one that lost.
**NOT established that the period alone did this** - boot 219 also turned
`-rbgpufbflippend` on, so **two variables differ** and 2xl's own caveat
applies again, one milestone after it was written. The clean next A/B is one
token: put `rbgpuschedtickus` back to 6944 and keep `-rbgpufbflippend`, or
drop the arg and keep 2000. Either way **the tick period is a tunable with a
real optimum and 6944 is better than 2000 on the evidence in hand.**

### THE DEFERRAL DOES EXACTLY WHAT IT SAYS, AND IT IS NOT ENOUGH

    RBFBHubpDeferArmed   Yes
    RBFBHubpPendChecks   6243     RBFBHubpPendHits  693
    RBFBHubpDeferrals    693      RBFBHubpWrites   5550
    RBFBAmtrSets         5590     FlipCtl 0x04100000  FlipCtl2 0x40

**Internally exact**: `PendChecks 6243 = HubpWrites 5550 + Deferrals 693`, and
`Deferrals == PendHits` to the unit - so every pending flip was deferred and
nothing else was, which is the triple-buffer guard reading clear as boots 216
and 217 both measured. The mechanism is wired correctly.
**The hit rate is NOT comparable to 2xm's 1.75 %.** 693/6243 = **11.1 %**, but
that is measured in a *different configuration* (deferring) over 109 s of
post-login activity against 470 s of mixed desktop. Rule 39: say which
configuration a reading comes from. No mechanism is proposed for the
difference; burstiness over a much shorter and busier window is the obvious
candidate and it is **not** established.
**The user reports the flicker roughly 30 % reduced and still present** - and,
decisively, **"still across the whole screen"**, where 2xm's first description
was "tears up at bottom".

### THE SHAPE IS THE EVIDENCE, AND IT NAMES A DIFFERENT DEFECT

A flip programmed over an unlatched one replaces the armed address partway
through a scan, so it can only corrupt the frame **below the current
scanline**. It cannot produce a whole-screen event. So 2xm's stated open
question is answered in the direction 2xm predicted it might be: the
pending-overwrite is **a** mechanism, worth ~30 % by the user's eye, and
**not the main one**.
**And the main one is a protocol divergence from Apple that has been in our
code since 2wc.** From the journal's own disassembly of
`AMDFramebuffer::getAttribute('amtr')` (`0x2a6faa`, read in 2wc):

    if (!(ctrl->0x31332 >> 9 & 1)) return kIOReturnUnsupported;
    if (getOutstandingDisplayPipeTransactions()) return kIOReturnNotReady;
    return kIOReturnSuccess;              /* *out is never written */

Ours is `amtrGets++; return kIOReturnSuccess;` - **unconditionally**, in every
boot since 2wc. So we tell the compositor that every transaction completed
the instant it was handed over, which frees it to draw into a surface that is
still the live scanout. That corrupts the **whole** frame, which is the shape
reported. 2we already wrote *"the compositor believes 13 transactions landed
and none did"* about the same answer; what is new is that the lie has a
visible consequence and the reference implementation does not tell it.
**Answering NotReady does NOT close the gate 2wc opened**, which is why this
is safe to try: `getDisplayInfo` at `0xbe8717e` sets the capability bit on
`r == 0 || r == kIOReturnNotReady`, measured, so both answers keep bit 0x100.

### `-rbgpufbnotready`, OFF BY DEFAULT, AND THE DEADLINE IS THE POINT

Our stand-in for `getOutstandingDisplayPipeTransactions()` is DCN's own
`SURFACE_FLIP_PENDING`: our flip is outstanding exactly while the hardware
holds it armed and unlatched. The triple-buffer guard of
`rb_hubp_flip_would_discard()` deliberately does **not** apply - with more
than one slot our address is still unlatched - so this is the bare pending
bit by design, asserted as such.
**`rb_hubp_hold_notready(flip_ctl, now, deadline)` is BOUNDED, and that is a
safety property rather than a refinement.** 2x6 recorded that
`isTransactionComplete` (`0xbe4a794`) decides the current transaction by
`getAttribute('amtr', NULL) == 0`, so NotReady makes Apple's accelerator
**wait**. Answering 0 always, as we do today, is the optimistic answer and
cannot stall anything; this one can, and an unbounded hold on a pending bit
that never clears (a mode set, a disabled pipe, a register we have misread)
would wedge the display outright. So the hold expires after **two vblank
periods** - the address latches at the next VUPDATE, and one period of slack
costs nothing - and past it we answer ready whatever the hardware says.
`hubpFlipDeadline` is set **after** the stores land, so a refused or deferred
transaction never opens a hold, and a deadline that was never set reads `0`,
which the policy treats as **already expired**: the arm fails safe, asserted
both ways.
**Mutation tested, and the safety property is the one that is tested**:
removing the deadline (an unbounded hold) FAILS the hosttest, and holding
when `PENDING` is clear FAILS it. Also asserted: `0xfffffeff` with `PENDING`
clear answers ready, so an unidentified field cannot stall every frame.
The register read lives in `RBAMDFramebufferHUBP.cpp` rather than beside
`getAttribute`, because `kRbDmuSeg2` is that file's static and 2wh's rule
stands - the DMU segment is a constant, a constant is an assumption, and one
copy of an assumption beats two.
Publishes `RBFBAmtrNotReadyArmed`, `RBFBAmtrHeld`, `RBFBAmtrHoldExpired`.
**Said before the boot**: `RBFBAmtrHeld` non-zero means the hold is firing and
the arm took; `RBFBAmtrHoldExpired` large compared with `Held` means the
pending bit is clearing slower than two periods and the bound, not the
hardware, is deciding - re-read the period, do not raise it blindly.
`Held` zero with `NotReadyArmed` true means the GET never arrives while
pending and this candidate is **eliminated**, which is worth the boot either
way. A frozen or stuttering desktop is the risk the deadline exists to
bound; one token reverses it.

### GEEKBENCH 7, FOR THE RECORD

`browser.geekbench.com/v7/gpu/342617`: **Metal 12587**, Geekbench **7.1.0**,
macOS 15.8.1 (24H32), Ryzen 7 7735HS, 32 GB at 4800 MT/s, Metal device name
**"AMD Radeon HD GFX10 Family Unknown Prototype"**. Subtests 5825 (Background
Blur) to 24340 (Feature Matching).
Against the user's earlier **9633** that is **+30.7 %**, though whether 9633
was the same suite and version is **not** established. **The 33 000 figure
remains unverifiable and is now less likely to be comparable, not more**:
this is Geekbench **7**, and GB5/GB6/GB7 Metal scores are not interchangeable
- naming the suite and version is a precondition for the comparison, not a
detail. Clocks remain unwired (`Core Clock(MHz)` reports 0, 2xl).

Artifact: fbkext **`4BDC7A2C`**. Plugin `3A8EAB07` unchanged.

## 2xo — boot 220: the NotReady hold works, SUBSUMES 2xm, and its safety bound never fired once

Boot 220, rule 15 clean on both: plugin `3A8EAB07`, fbkext **`4BDC7A2C`**.
`rbgpu-boot` 220, `rbgpu-tick`/`rbgpu-fb` both `0`, `tarm=1 tos=0 ts=0`,
**`tus=6944`** (so `rbgpuschedtickus` came out and 2xn's A/B result was acted
on). Boot-args carry `-rbgpufbhubp -rbgpufbflippend -rbgpufbnotready`.
**The user reports the flicker "almost gone maybe even fully gone."**

### THE HOLD FIRES, AND THE BOUND NEVER DECIDED ANYTHING

    RBFBAmtrNotReadyArmed  Yes
    RBFBAmtrHeld          4506   of RBFBAmtrGets 11465   = 39.3 %
    RBFBAmtrHoldExpired      0

**`HoldExpired = 0` is the result that matters most.** Every one of 4506 holds
was resolved by `SURFACE_FLIP_PENDING` clearing in hardware, not by the
two-period deadline expiring. So the bound 2xn built as a safety property
against a pending bit that never clears was **never load-bearing**, which is
exactly what it should look like when the register means what 2xk read it to
mean. The hold is 1.3 per transaction here and 1.44 under load, i.e. Apple
asks more than once per transaction and we answer honestly each time.

### AND IT SUBSUMES 2xm ENTIRELY

    RBFBHubpDeferArmed  Yes       RBFBHubpDeferrals    0
    RBFBHubpPendChecks  3479      RBFBHubpPendHits     0      Writes 3479

**`PendHits` went 693 -> 0**, and under the animtest load below it is **1 in
2478**. That is a causal chain, not a coincidence: holding the compositor
until our flip latches makes "program a new address over an armed, unlatched
one" *impossible*, because the next transaction cannot arrive until the
previous flip has latched. So 2xm's mechanism is **eliminated upstream** - the
deferral is now near-inert dead weight rather than a fix. It costs nothing and
still catches the 1-in-2478 residue, so it stays; nothing measured argues
either way and the honest statement is that **2xn did the work 2xm was
reaching for.**

### THE COST, MEASURED THE ONLY WAY THAT IS VALID

**The idle comparison I was about to make is NOT valid and is recorded as
such.** Idle `sets/s` read 71.97 (boot 217), 51.33 (219) and **29.94** (220),
but idle transaction rate is *demand*-limited - 2xe killed frame demand as a
lever precisely because an idle desktop composites what it feels like - and
the three boots differ in activity and in window length (470 s mixed vs ~110 s
post-login). Comparing them would attribute a workload difference to the code.
**The controlled instrument is 2xi's `animtest`: same binary, same 30 s test.**

    boot 210 (before the tick)         2 sets  =   0.07 /s
    boot 215 (2xi, the tick)        3375 sets  = 111.98 /s
    boot 220 (this, + notready)     2478 sets  =  81.89 /s

So the NotReady answer costs **27 %** of frame rate under identical load, and
that is the price of the flicker going away. 81.89/s against a display link
measuring **143.34/s** in the same run means we present ~57 % of vblanks where
2xi presented 78 %. **Not established**: whether the 27 % is the hardware latch
wait itself or granularity in Apple's waiter; 12.2 ms per frame against a
6.95 ms period leaves ~5 ms unaccounted, and nothing here observes Apple's side
of the wait.

### AND 2xi'S OPEN JITTER QUESTION MOVED, IN THE GOOD DIRECTION

Same instrument, `CVTimeStamp` hostTime, 4322 intervals:

                        2xi (boot 215)      2xo (boot 220)
    mean                143.446 Hz          143.451 Hz   (panel 143.830)
    stddev              0.9684 ms 13.9 %    0.9242 ms 13.3 %
    spread              3.81 - 29.01 ms     4.04 - 12.32 ms

**The long tail collapsed**: worst-case interval 29.01 -> 12.32 ms, and the
histogram's 12-16 ms bucket holds exactly 1 of 4322 intervals. The stddev is
essentially unchanged, so this is not "the jitter is fixed" - it is the
*extreme* that improved, which is what pacing against a hardware latch would
do. 2xi recorded the widened jitter with cause **NOT established**; that is
still true, but the worst case is now bounded by something.
**Unexplained, carried forward**: `nominal refresh` reports **126.55 Hz**
against a measured 143.45. 2xe saw this value move across runs
(115.94 / 119.97 / 120.00 / 133.72) and it moved again. Still not attributed.

### INSTRUMENT ERROR, SELF-CAUGHT (rule 16, rule 26)

The first animtest run was invoked as `animtest 30`, and the tool takes
`--secs N`. It printed its usage and exited in **28 ms**, during which 3
transactions happened - and the bracketed counters dutifully computed
**108.18/s from n=3 over a 28 ms window**, a number that would have read as a
triumph (108 vs 2xi's 112) and meant nothing at all. Caught only because the
elapsed time was printed beside it. **An instrument's own usage error produces
a plausible number, not an error** - print the window with every rate, which
is what 2xe's `RBFBVBLUptimeNs` was added for.

### WHAT IS OPEN

- The 27 % cost. The clean A/B is one token: drop `-rbgpufbnotready` and
  re-run the same animtest. **That is also the trade to put to the user** -
  82/s with no flicker against 112/s with it - and it is their call, not a
  defect to be fixed silently.
- Whether a shorter hold would buy rate back at some flicker. `HoldExpired 0`
  says the bound is never reached today, so shortening it would start
  *truncating* real holds, which is a genuine dial and is **not built** - no
  measurement yet says it would help.
- The ~5 ms per frame that is neither the panel period nor the latch.
- 2xn's `-rbgpufbflippend` is near-inert now; keep or drop, no measured
  difference.

No new artifact: plugin `3A8EAB07`, fbkext `4BDC7A2C`, both unchanged.
