## 2xp — the three asks were already scoped in 2or, and the free HDMI test would have frozen the panel

No boot. The user asked for HDMI, brightness, and a refresh-rate menu in
Settings. **All three were scoped in 2or on 2026-10-23** and the journal's own
summary table answers them; this milestone re-reads that, corrects one thing,
and removes a trap. Rule: *read the evidence already in hand before designing
the next experiment* — the practice that has caught this repeatedly.

### FIRST, THE 133 Hz: THREE DIFFERENT NUMBERS, ALL REAL

The user ran a browser Hz test, got 133, and said *"i think that number is kind
of fake... its still 144hz, feels like it and looks like it"*. They are right
about the panel and the instinct is sound, but the honest decomposition is that
these are measurements of **different things**, not one thing measured wrong:

    panel scanout (OTG, 2rn)                 143.830 Hz   hardware
    our VBL delivery (CVTimeStamp, 2xo)      143.451 Hz   0.27 % off the panel
    what macOS REPORTS for the mode          144.00 Hz    System Profiler, live
    frames actually presented under load      81.89 /s    2xo's animtest
    CVDisplayLink "nominal"                  126.55 Hz    moves run to run

`System Profiler` reads **144.00Hz** right now, from our own
`kRefreshRate1616 = 0x008fd53f`, so the mode we publish is correct and macOS
agrees. The moving value is `CVDisplayLinkGetNominalOutputVideoRefreshPeriod`,
which animtest prints and which CoreVideo **measures** rather than reads when
the display supplies no nominal of its own — 2xe saw it give 115.94 / 119.97 /
120.00 / 133.72 across four runs and 2xo got 126.55. **133 sits squarely in
that series.** And an app that counts how often *its own* content reaches the
screen can legitimately read below 144, because 2xo measured that we present
81.89 of every 143 vblanks. So: the panel is 144, our clock is 144, the
reported mode is 144, and frame delivery is 82 — nothing is lying.

### THE THREE ASKS, AGAINST WHAT IS ALREADY MEASURED

**Brightness — the hardware half is DONE and was done in 2os.** Measured on
this machine:

    BL_PWM_CNTL          0xc00056ea   EN=1  FRACTIONAL=1  count 22250
    BL_PWM_PERIOD_CNTL   0x000c0fa0   period 4000, 12-bit
    BL_PWM_GRP1_REG_LOCK 0x80000000   lock free, no update pending
      -> level 22784 / 65535 = 34.8 %

and 2or's own falsification test **passed**: it said *"`BL_PWM_PERIOD == 0`
would mean the panel is driven some other way and this route is wrong"*. It is
4000. So the PWM is live, ours to read, and a brightness change is one
duty-cycle write with `GRP1_REG_LOCK` for atomicity — Linux's
`dce_panel_cntl` / `dcn31_panel_cntl`. Offsets confirmed against the right
header this milestone: DCN 3.1.2 spells them `regPWRSEQ0_BL_PWM_*` at
**0x2f19-0x2f1c** base_idx 2, which is exactly what `rb_regs.h` carries.
**And the apparent deny-list conflict is not one**: `rb_dcn_deny.h` lists
`0x288b`, which in dcn_3_0_2 *was* `BL_PWM_GRP1_REG_LOCK` but in **3.1.2 is
`DCIO_BL_PWM_FRAME_START_DISP_SEL`** — a different register, and the deny
list's own comment already records that rename. Verified: none of
0x2f19-0x2f1c is on the deny list, with 0x288b present as the control.
**The blocker is the UI, not the chip, and 2or measured that too**: the display
reports `_spdisplays_display-vendor-id = "unkn"` and `"Unknown Display"`, there
is **no EDID** (nothing ever read one), and **`AppleBacklightDisplay` has 0
instances** — the display is a plain `AppleDisplay`.
**NEW this milestone, and it is the way through**: a framebuffer does not need
`AppleBacklightDisplay`. `IOGraphicsTypes.h` documents
**`kConnectionDisplayParameterCount` (`'pcnt'`)** and
**`kConnectionDisplayParameters` (`'parm'`)** as connection attributes, which
is how `IODisplay` builds the `IODisplayParameters` dictionary that carries
`kIODisplayBrightnessKey = "brightness"`. The string `brightness` is present in
`IOGraphicsFamily` (controlled against `IOFBWaitCursorPeriod`), so the consumer
is there. **NOT established**: how `IODisplay` maps a parameter name to the
selector it then calls, which is a static read of `IOGraphicsFamily` and is
the next step for this ask — **not** a guess at a four-char code (the key is a
*string*, so there is no FourCC to infer; rule 13/17).

**A refresh-rate menu — 2or's answer stands and it is no.** *"'144 Hz' yes; 'a
refresh-rate menu' no."* Choosing a rate is mode setting: OTG timing plus the
DCCG pixel clock, i.e. real writes to the display engine's timing, where a
wrong value is no signal at all. We publish **one** mode (`kModeID = 100`) and
publishing more that all map to one timing would be substituting values
(rule 17). This is not refused, it is **sequenced after** HDMI's machinery,
because it needs the same code.

**HDMI — 2or's honest no stands**: HPD, EDID over DDC/AUX, TMDS or DP link
training, a second OTG + HUBP + DIO stream encoder + link encoder, and DML
watermarks. HDMI audio is downstream of all of it. **But its one cheap
exception is now cheaper than 2or thought** — and carried a trap.

### THE TRAP: THE FREE HDMI TEST WOULD HAVE FROZEN THE LAPTOP PANEL

2or proposed: *"boot with HDMI connected and read `OTG1_CONTROL`"*, needing the
level-2 probe. It needs nothing — **the fbkext already reads all four
OTG_CONTROL registers every boot**, at `kRbOtgControl[4] = {0x1b41, 0x1bc1,
0x1c41, 0x1cc1}` in the BAR5 window it already maps, as 2wh's gate 1.
**And that gate requires OTG1, OTG2 and OTG3 to read exactly `0x300`.** So if
the UEFI GOP lights an attached HDMI display, a second OTG comes up live, gate
1 refuses with `hubpRefuse = 5`, `hubpReady` stays false, and **no HUBP write
ever happens** — while the panel is still taken, because `-rbgpuownfb` is
armed independently of this (rule 38 exactly). The laptop screen freezes on its
last frame. One power cycle recovers it (2wj's overwrite consume), so the cost
is bounded, but the test could not have yielded its answer: the old loop
short-circuited on the first live OTG and published **nothing** about which one
it was.

**Fixed, and the fix names what it gives up.** Gate 1 is now
`rb_hubp_otg_gate()` in `src/common/rb_hubp.h`, hosttested. Its OTG1-3 clause
was doing a job nobody assigned it: 2wh's stated reason for the signature is
*"if the segment constant is wrong, these four reads are garbage and will not
match"*, and that argument holds for OTG0 but **not** for OTG1-3 — a *live*
OTG is a plausible `OTG_CONTROL` value at a plausible offset, so it
corroborates the segment rather than impeaching it. What the clause actually
asserts is "nothing else is scanning", which gate 2 never needed.
`-rbgpufbotgany` relaxes it **to OTG0's master-enable only**, which is never
relaxed. Given up: three corroborating reads of the segment constant. Kept:
OTG0's own enable, plus **gate 2's three separately measured values** (pitch,
format, address-high — the far stronger addressing check), plus
`rb_dcn_is_denied()` and the six per-address gates. Default stays strict.
All four OTGs are now read **unconditionally and published even when the gate
refuses** (`RBFBHubpOtg1/2/3`, `RBFBHubpOtgAnyArmed`) — rule 14: a refusal
must publish what it refused on.
**Mutation tested both ways**: dropping the OTG1-3 clause entirely FAILS the
hosttest, and letting `allow_live` relax OTG0's master-enable FAILS it.

### SAID BEFORE THE BOOT

Arm `-rbgpufbotgany` **and plug the HDMI display in before powering on.** Then
read `RBFBHubpOtg1/2/3`:
- one of them **not** `0x300` with bit 0 set = **firmware lit it**, 2or's
  exception is real, and a fixed-mode external display with no hotplug becomes
  reachable by adopting that OTG the way OTG0 was adopted. That is the only
  cheap HDMI result available.
- all three still `0x300` = the GOP did not light it, and HDMI is the full
  project 2or described. **That is a real answer too** and it costs one boot
  with no code.
- `RBFBHubpRefuse 5` with the arg armed would mean OTG0 itself failed, which
  has never happened — read `RBFBHubpOtg1/2/3` before concluding anything.
The laptop panel should behave exactly as in boot 220 either way, because the
relaxed gate changes nothing about what is written.

Artifact: fbkext **`C7278266`**. Plugin `3A8EAB07` unchanged.

## 2xq — boot 221: the GOP does NOT light HDMI, and the answer cost one boot

**Arm verified first (rules 8/15/34).** `rbgpu-boot` **221** (was 220),
`kern.boottime` 17:32:29 against a live read at 17:37, `rbgpu-fb 0` and
`rbgpu-tick 0` (both consumed by overwrite, 2wj). Loaded: plugin
**`3A8EAB07`**, fbkext **`C7278266`** — the 2xp build, and
**`RBFBHubpOtgAnyArmed = Yes`** is a key only `C7278266` publishes, so the
binary running is the one built (rule 15, the cheap independent check).

**THE READING, which is the whole experiment:**

    RBFBHubpOtgCtl  70145 = 0x00011201   OTG0, the laptop panel, unchanged
    RBFBHubpOtg1      768 = 0x300        OFF
    RBFBHubpOtg2      768 = 0x300        OFF
    RBFBHubpOtg3      768 = 0x300        OFF

The display was plugged in before power-on, as 2xp prescribed. **All three
are exactly `RB_OTG_OFF_VALUE`**, so the second branch of 2xp's said-before-the-boot
prediction is the one that fired: **the firmware does not light HDMI on this
machine, and there is no OTG to adopt.** HDMI is the full project 2or
described — HPD, EDID over DDC/AUX, link training, a second OTG + HUBP +
stream/link encoder, DML watermarks — and that is now a measurement rather
than an expectation.

**Corroborated three more ways, all from the same boot.** Exactly **one**
`IOFramebuffer` in the registry (ours); `system_profiler` lists **one**
display, 1920x1080 @ 144.00Hz, Main Display Yes, Mirror Off, with no second
entry; and `IODisplayConnect` count 4 is the framebuffer's own connection
slots, not four displays. Nothing in macOS saw a sink.

**AND THE TRAP DID NOT FIRE — say so plainly.** 2xp removed gate 1's
freeze-the-panel failure mode on the grounds that a GOP-lit HDMI would make
OTG1-3 read something other than `0x300` and refuse with `hubpRefuse = 5`.
They read `0x300`, so **the old build would not have refused either** and
`-rbgpufbotgany`'s relaxation was never exercised. That is not a wasted
change — the value could not be known before the boot, and the cost was one
boot-arg — but it must not be recorded as "the relaxed gate saved the boot".
What the boot establishes about the gate is narrower and still worth having:
**gate 1 passes with a display physically attached**, `RBFBHubpRefuse 0`,
`RBFBHubpReady Yes`, `RBFBHubpOrig 1047972020224 = 0xF4_0000_0000`, and
**14456 HUBP writes**, so attaching HDMI changes nothing about the laptop
panel's path.

**The flicker fix held for 273 seconds.** `RBFBAmtrHeld` **19802** of
`RBFBAmtrGets` **48707**, and **`RBFBAmtrHoldExpired` 0** again — every hold
resolved in hardware, the two-vblank safety bound still never load-bearing
in a second boot. `RBFBVBLFires` 38140 over `RBFBVBLUptimeNs` 273.053 s.
**`RBFBAmtrSets` 14451 = 52.9/s and this must NOT be compared to 2xo's
81.89/s** — that figure came from the controlled `animtest` run and this is
an idle desktop, whose transaction rate is demand-limited (2xe) and whose
window is a different length. Same error CLAUDE.md already forbids for the
71.97/51.33/29.94 series.

**What this closes and what it opens.** 2or's cheap HDMI exception is now
spent and answered: there is no free path to an external display. The
remaining tractable ask is **brightness** — 2os measured the hardware half
done (`BL_PWM_CNTL 0xc00056ea`, period 4000, level 34.8 %) and 2xp found the
UI path (`kConnectionDisplayParameterCount` / `kConnectionDisplayParameters`,
no `AppleBacklightDisplay` needed). The next step there is a **static read**,
no boot: how `IODisplay` in `IOGraphicsFamily` maps the parameter name
`"brightness"` to the selector it then calls on the framebuffer. The
refresh-rate menu stays sequenced behind HDMI's mode-setting code.

## 2xr — HDMI is wired to the dGPU, so it is UNREACHABLE, not merely unbuilt

**The user's own words, which is the allowed channel for a Windows fact:**
*"in Windows, when im in Eco mode the HDMI never works, i have to be in Hybrid
so both 4050 and the iGPU have to be on."*

**Eco mode is iGPU-only by definition** - that is what it is for, and the
laptop panel works in it. A port that works in Hybrid and **never** in Eco
therefore tells us which chip its TMDS lanes leave from: **the RTX 4050**, not
the Radeon 680M. The user raised the alternative themselves ("is it a windows
driver limitation") and the shape of the symptom answers it: a driver
limitation presents as degraded, intermittent, or needing a replug. *Never, in
every Eco boot,* is a wiring fact.

**AND IT EXPLAINS 2xq EXACTLY.** Boot 221 read OTG1/2/3 all `0x300` with a
display physically attached, and the reason is now not "the GOP chose not to
light it" but **there is no HDMI connector on the 680M's display engine to
light**. Two independent measurements agreeing - one on the chip, one in
Windows - where 2xq had only one and read it as a policy decision.

**So HDMI moves from "the full project 2or described" to UNREACHABLE.** Every
line of DCN 3.1.2 HPD / DDC / link-training / stream-encoder code would drive
an encoder with nothing wired to it. The chip the port IS wired to is an
NVIDIA RTX 4050, which macOS has had no driver for since Mojave, and which
does not even appear in this machine's PCI tree: a full `ioreg -rl -c
IOPCIDevice` scan gives vendor ids **0x1022, 0x1002, 0x10ec, 0x2646, 0x1344
and zero occurrences of 0x10de** (`-wegnoegpu` is in boot-args, so the absence
is expected and is not itself the finding).

**What is NOT established, and is the one remaining external-display path.**
Whether a MUX sits on the HDMI line that the iGPU could in principle be
switched onto - some ASUS designs mux the *internal panel* and hard-wire HDMI,
others mux both. **Do not settle this from general knowledge** (rule 25): it
needs either the user's own observation or an ACPI/_DOD read. It changes
nothing about the verdict, because a mux that only powers up with the dGPU is
equally out of reach here. **The reachable candidate, if the machine has one,
is a USB-C port carrying DisplayPort alt mode wired to the iGPU** - that is a
hardware question for the user, not a code question, and it costs no boot.

**Consequence for the refresh-rate ask**: 2or sequenced the Hz menu behind
"the same mode-setting code HDMI needs". That sequencing is now **void** - the
mode-setting code is no longer going to be written for HDMI's sake. If a
refresh-rate menu is ever wanted it has to be justified on the internal
panel's own terms (OTG timing + the DCCG pixel clock, writes where a wrong
value is no signal), and nothing has changed to make that cheaper.

## 2xu - macOS 26 BREAKS THE PATCHER A SECOND WAY: THE KERNEL CANNOT READ THE TARGET

Boot 226, armed (`rbgpu-boot` 226, `armed=1`), plugin **`FCEA5698`** confirmed
loaded against `build/out` (rule 15). 2xt's re-derivation is INSTALLED and the
artifacts are STILL THERE, so 2xt fixed a real defect and was not sufficient.

**2xt's RE-DERIVATION IS PROVEN CORRECT, AND IS NOT THE REMAINING PROBLEM.**
Three independent confirmations, none of which needed a boot:

  * `mtlk_place` reads **0x7FFB2339B6E0**, which is exactly
    `(RBGPU_MTL_CAVE_VM - ANCHOR) + slide` for the new header. The kext's own
    arithmetic agrees with the header to the byte.
  * `mtlk_slide` reads **0x11F1E000** and dyld independently reports the live
    shared-cache slide as **0x11F1E000** (CoreDisplay's live header
    0x7FF817266000 against its unslid 0x7FF805348000). The slide is right.
  * Reading **0x7FFB2339B6E0 from a live userspace process returns
    `kRbMtlCaveFind` byte for byte**. The pattern is there, at the address we
    compute, in this boot.

**THE REMAINING BLOCKER IS THE READ ITSELF.** `mtlk_match` = **0xFFFF**, which
`rbgpu_mtlk_place` writes on one condition only - `g_mtlkVmMapReadUser`
returned non-KERN_SUCCESS - and `mtlk_probe_read` = **1** =
`KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS`. The bytes were never compared, because the read never
produced any.

**AND IT FAILED THAT WAY EVERY SINGLE TIME, which the telemetry proves without
a second boot.** `mtlk_cavehits` **1280**, `mtlk_failed` **1280**,
`mtlk_patched` **0** - and **`mtlk_moved` is ABSENT**. `g_mtlkMoved` increments
only when `g_mtlkLastMatch == 0`, i.e. on a successful read whose bytes
mismatched, and it is set on EVERY call, not only reported ones. So an absent
`mtlk_moved` means **not one of the 1280 attempts ever got a successful read**.
That also explains why `mtlk_moved_verdict` never fired: the fail-safe's
"the driver moved" verdict is reachable only through a byte mismatch, and this
boot never reached a byte comparison at all. **The verdict being absent is not
evidence the addresses are right - it is evidence the read never got that far.**

**THE DIFFERENTIAL AGAINST macOS 15 IS CLEAN**, from 45 captures already on
disk (rule: read the evidence already in hand):

| | macOS 15 (45 captures) | macOS 26, boot 226 |
|---|---|---|
| `mtlk_probe_read` | **0** = KERN_SUCCESS | **1** = KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS |
| `mtlk_match` | **1** = pattern found | **0xFFFF** = read failed |
| `mtlk_patched` / `mtlk_cavehits` | **763 / 768** | **0 / 1280** |
| `mtlk_moved` | 1-2 (a few stragglers) | **absent** |

Same hook, same mechanism, same four symbols. So this is a **second,
independent macOS 26 change**, stacked on top of 2xt's driver move.

**IT IS NOT THE SYMBOLS AND IT IS NOT A BAD MAP.** `mtlk_syms` = **15** =
all four resolved, and `nm -m` confirms `_get_task_map`, `_vm_map_read_user`,
`_vm_map_write_user` and `_get_bsdtask_info` are all real `__TEXT,__text`
definitions in the macOS 26 kernel, not stubs. `mtlk_ready` = 1 and
`mtlk_map` = 1, so `get_task_map(task)` returned non-NULL.
And `_vm_map_read_user` (`0xffffff800034c8a0`) was disassembled: its
not-current-map path **zone-validates the `vm_map_t`** (checks it against
`_zone_info`'s range and requires zone index `0xf`), and a map that fails that
check does **not** return an error - it branches to `0xffffff800034cb27`,
which calls into the panic path. **We did not panic, so the map we passed was
a valid zone-allocated `vm_map`.** The only remaining producer of the `1` we
observed is the `copyin` at `0xffffff800034cab8` / `0xffffff800034ca02`
returning non-zero (`setne r15b`, `r15` -> `eax`). The page genuinely was not
readable in that task at that moment.

**SO THE HOOK POINT IS NOW TOO EARLY.** The patch runs from
`wrap_rbMtlkTaskSetMainThreadQos`, i.e. `_task_set_main_thread_qos`. Call-site
scan of the macOS 26 kernel (`E8 rel32` targets, over `__TEXT,__text`):

    _vm_shared_region_enter     1 site  0xFFFFFF8000346B51  inside _vm_map_exec
    _task_set_main_thread_qos   2 sites 0xFFFFFF80007B231A  inside _posix_spawn
                                        0xFFFFFF80007B6FB6  inside ___mac_execve

`vm_map_exec` runs early in exec and `task_set_main_thread_qos` late, so the
naive reading - "the shared region has not been entered yet" - is **refuted by
the call graph**, and is recorded here so it is not proposed again. What is
established is narrower and is what the measurement actually says: **at that
point the new task's map does not yet have the cache readable**, whatever the
mechanism.

**ALSO REFUTED, by a free experiment:** "macOS 26 maps the subcaches on demand,
so the Metal subcache is absent until something loads Metal". A fresh process
that never loads Metal.framework reads `0x7FFB2339B6E0` **successfully**. The
region is mapped in any running process; the failure is specific to the exec
hook.

**`_thread_bootstrap_return` IS NOT A CANDIDATE - RULE 2 REFUSES IT.** It is
**five bytes**, a bare `callq _dtrace_thread_bootstrap` rel32 at offset 0,
falling straight into `_thread_exception_return`. Lilu copies displaced
instructions byte for byte, so routing it relocates a rel32 into Lilu's buffer
and lands somewhere else entirely; it also never returns. Recorded so the next
session does not spend a boot finding out.

**THE CANDIDATE THAT NEEDS NO NEW ROUTE.** The plugin already hooks
`AMDRadeonX6000_AMDHWAlignManager2::getPreferredSwizzleMode2`
(`g_rb_2la_hk_swz`, `rbgpu-surf` reads `swz hk=1 calls=1466` in boot 224), and
that hook runs **in the Metal client's own process context**, long after exec,
where the cache is demonstrably readable and `current_map()` IS the target map
- which takes `_vm_map_read_user`'s fast `copyin` path rather than the
map-switch path that is failing. Retrying the cave+detour placement from
there, once per task, needs **no new kernel route** and inherits 2om's
compare-before-write fail-safe unchanged.
**NOT ESTABLISHED, and it is the one thing to check before building it**:
whether that hook fires before the client's first
`amdMtl_HWL_DetermineSwizzleMode` call or after it. If after, the patch lands
from the second texture onward and early surfaces in each process would still
be wrong - in which case the right point is the client's user-client open, not
the swizzle query.

**AND THE BUILD ITSELF WAS BLOCKED BY A BROKEN INSTRUMENT (2xt, rule 16).**
`sudo tools/efi.sh install` died with a bare `Illegal instruction: 4` because
it runs `make plugin`, and on macOS 26.7.2 with CommandLineTools 16.4 the ASan
RUNTIME is broken: a two-line program that only calls `printf` SIGILLs when
built `-fsanitize=address` and runs fine built plain. Every hosttest assertion
passes unsanitized. The build now probes the runtime and degrades loudly
(`SAN=auto`), so a broken sanitizer cannot masquerade as a failing test.

## 2xv — THE USB DEFECT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS 2xt: macOS 26 MOVED THE PATCH SITES

No boot. Static read of macOS 26.7.2 (25G332) `AppleUSBXHCI`, plus the live
registry of boot 231.

**The defect, measured back on 2026-10-08 and still true:** each of the five
xHCI controllers on this machine exposes **one** MSI vector, so only
interrupter 0 can raise an interrupt. `AppleUSBXHCI` targets interrupter **1**
for bulk/control transfer events and **2** for isochronous, and nothing here
can signal those, so completions are collected by a ~2 s watchdog instead.
The workaround in place since then is `XHCIPoke.kext`, which polls every
controller every 10 ms (`xhcipoke=10` in boot-args). The real fix, written the
next day, is eight OpenCore kernel patches that force every Transfer TRB's
**Interrupter Target** field to 0.

**Those patches are `MinKernel 24.0.0 / MaxKernel 24.99.99`, and the machine
is now Darwin 25.6.0.** So on the macOS 26 upgrade they went inert and the
poke came back — exactly 2xt's shape, two subsystems, one cause: *a patch set
keyed to a kernel version and to the bytes of a rebuilt Apple binary*. The
version gate is why they went inert rather than misapplying, which is the
right failure and worth keeping.

**The live confirmation that the poke is still carrying USB (boot 231,
`ioreg -rl -c XHCIPoke`):** `pokes 78400` per controller, and for the three
controllers with devices attached, interrupter 1's event-ring dequeue pointer
is **moving** — `i1 erdpChg` 284 (XHC3), 107 (XHC0), 485 (XHC1) — while
`ipSeen 0` on all five says the poke has **never** once found `IMAN.IP` set,
i.e. no XHCI interrupt is ever pending when it looks. `eintSeen` 407-566 with
`eintClears` matching: the poke is finding `USBSTS.EINT` set and clearing it
itself. MSI is programmed correctly (`MSI ctl 0081 en 1 addr fee00000 data
4074`, vector 116) and MSI-X is off with a table size of 1 — so the
single-vector fact is the hardware's, not a configuration mistake.

**THE SITES ARE RE-DERIVED, AND THERE ARE NINE, NOT EIGHT.** A Transfer TRB is
16 bytes and dword 2 (`+0x8`) is
`TRB-Transfer-Length[16:0] | TD-Size[21:17] | Interrupter-Target[31:22]`, so an
interrupter of 1 is the immediate `0x00400000`, 2 is `0x00800000`, and a
run-time index is a `shl $0x16`. Every such site inside the transfer-ring
builders, in macOS 26's `AppleUSBXHCI` (`__TEXT 0xffffff8002f15000`):

    AppleUSBXHCIRequest::prepare          +0x646  mov $0x400000, 0x8(%rax,%rcx)
                                          +0x8a2  mov $0x400000, %ecx
                                          +0xb0b  mov $0x400000, 0x8(%rax,%rbx)
                                          +0xb5c  mov $0x400000, 0x8(%rax,%rcx)
    AppleUSBXHCIRequest::addTD            +0x48   shl $0x16, %r12d
    AppleUSBXHCIIsochronousRequest::prepare +0x6e5 mov $0x800000, 0x8(%rcx,%rdx)
                                          +0x9f6  or  $0x800000, %eax
                                          +0xb6d  mov $0x800000, 0x8(%rax,%rcx)
    AppleUSBXHCISparseRequest::prepare    +0x127  mov $0x400000, %r8d

**Five of the eight macOS 15 Find patterns still match byte for byte; three do
not** (`prepare+0x910`, `Isoch+0x6d9`, `Isoch+0x9d2`) — the compiler changed
the instruction that follows in each case. **And the ninth site is new to this
patch set**: `AppleUSBXHCISparseRequest::prepare` writes interrupter 1 into the
status dword the same way, and the 2026-10-09 set did not cover it.

**Two sites were found and deliberately NOT patched** (rule 26's shape — a
constant can be a coincidence): `AppleUSBXHCIPort::interruptOccurred` ORs
`0x400000` and `0x800000` into the value of a `vt[0xa90]` getter and passes it
to a `vt[0xa98]` setter. That is a **port state word**, not a TRB, and bits 22
and 23 of it mean something else entirely.

**Site `prepare+0x8a2` needed its own read before it could be patched**, since
the immediate goes to `%ecx`, not to memory: `movl $0x400000,%ecx` is the
**fallback** value of the status dword, and the alternate path at `+0x8b3`
recomputes `%ecx` as `((min(31,n)|0x20) << 17)` — TD size only, interrupter 0
already. Both arms converge on `orl %r14d,%ecx; movl %ecx,0x8(%rdx,%r15)` at
`+0x905`. So zeroing the immediate is correct and changes nothing else.

**THE PATCH TABLE IS SELF-VERIFYING, WHICH IS THE POINT.**
`tools/re/xhci_intr0_derive.py` re-derives the sites from the kext in the
running system's boot collection, prints the Find/Replace table, and checks
that every interrupter immediate in the whole kext is either patched or
explained, that each Find is **unique** (OpenCore applies with `Count 1`), and
that Find and Replace are the same length. `tools/xhci_intr0.py verify` runs
the same uniqueness check from the install path and **refuses** to write a
table that does not match the running kernel — so the next OS update cannot
quietly leave an inert patch set in the EFI the way this one did. It also
refuses an image that already contains the *patched* bytes, because then a hit
and a miss are indistinguishable. `tools/xhci_intr0_test.py` has 15
assertions, four of them mutations of the table (duplicate Find, absent Find,
pre-patched image, a Replace that still carries an interrupter immediate).

**Said before the boot, and the first boot is free.** `sudo tools/efi.sh
usbintr0 on` adds the nine patches as Darwin 25 only, **leaves `XHCIPoke.kext`
enabled**, and leaves the Darwin 24 set in place so a rollback to macOS 15
still works. The poke staying on means USB cannot get worse, and its counters
are the instrument:

* If the patches applied, **interrupter 1 and 2 stop being used**, so
  `i1 erdpChg` must stay at its initial 1 on XHC0/XHC1/XHC3 while `i0 erdpChg`
  keeps climbing — `i0` is the in-boot control that the window was long
  enough, and XHC4/XHC2 (no devices, `i1 erdpChg` already 1) are the negative
  controls.
* `eintSeen` and `eintClears` should fall sharply: the controller's own
  handler now services `EINT` before the poke looks.
* `ipSeen` is **not** expected to move. The poke samples at 10 ms and a real
  interrupt is serviced in microseconds, so `IMAN.IP` being 0 every time it
  looks stays the normal reading. Do not read `ipSeen 0` after the boot as
  "the patches did nothing".
* `i1 erdpChg` still climbing = the patches did not apply. There is **no
  OpenCore log on disk** to check against (`Misc -> Debug -> Target` is 3, no
  file bit), so this counter is the only in-boot evidence either way.

Then, and only then, `sudo tools/efi.sh usbpoke off` removes the 10 ms poll
from the next boot. Rescue for both is the same as every other EFI change:
`sudo tools/efi.sh restore`, or the Windows procedure in
`RECOVERY-INTR0.txt` on the EFI.

## 2xw — THE CONFIGURATION IS THE DEFAULT, AND THE ONE-SHOTS ARE INVERTED

No boot. The user's instruction, and the reasoning behind how it was done.

**What it replaces.** A working desktop needed **forty-five** `-rbgpu*` tokens
in boot-args and **five** NVRAM one-shots (`rbgpu-arm`, `rbgpu-agdc`,
`rbgpu-iop`, `rbgpu-tick`, `rbgpu-fb`) re-armed by hand before every boot. Each
of those gates was right when it was written: every one guarded something that
could cost the desktop, and rule 9 exists because a bad boot that re-arms
itself is a boot loop. But boots 215-231 all ran the *same* set and the machine
is a usable accelerated Mac, so the set is no longer an experiment - it is the
product's configuration, and re-typing it is now the main way to lose a boot to
a token nobody noticed was missing.

**The table is a copy, not a judgement.** `src/common/rb_defaults.h` holds the
exact 45 tokens read out of boot 231's own `nvram boot-args`, nothing added and
nothing dropped. That includes the six instruments (`-rbgpuringprobe`,
`-rbgpuringdump`, `-rbgpumcprobe`, `-rbgpuaccelprobe`, `-rbgpuschedprobe`,
`-rbgpuflipprobe`), which cost diag-table slots and nothing else: a boot that
reads differently from boot 231 should differ in the hardware, not in what we
can see of it. The known-dangerous args are absent and the hosttest asserts
each one by name - `-rbgpuagdcearly` (wedges, 2rz), `-rbgpufbmatch` (kills the
accelerator), `-rbgpupdefix` (the halt returns), `-rbgpumcreg` (hangs),
`-rbgpufbbacklight` (never booted, 2xs).

**Every entry turns off by a derived negative**, so no new names had to be
invented and none can be forgotten: `-rbgpufbhubp` -> `-rbgpunofbhubp`, and for
the two entries that are already negative, `-rbgpunocgcg` -> `-rbgpucgcg`.
`rb_off_token()` is pure and the hosttest checks the whole namespace with it:
45 entries, no duplicates, every entry derives a negative, negating twice
returns the original, and **no derived negative collides with or prefixes any
other token** - rule 30 applied to our own greps, since the kernel's own parse
is exact. 18 assertions, four of them on refusal paths (a short buffer empties
its output rather than truncating into somebody else's token; a token without
the `-rbgpu` prefix is refused).

**A positive token left in boot-args is now redundant rather than required**,
which is the property that makes this installable without editing boot-args
first - the install boot and the boot after it run the same configuration.

**THE ONE-SHOTS ARE INVERTED, NOT DELETED.** `rbgpu_nvram_armed()` reads the
same five keys in the opposite direction: armed unless the key reads a literal
`"0"`. The plugin **never writes them any more**, so the 2wj failure mode - a
key that would not clear - cannot happen to them. One difference is stated
rather than hidden: when `/options` cannot be read at all the one-shot form
declined and this one arms, because default-on means an unreadable NVRAM cannot
hold a disarm, and `arm_why 1` says so.

**WHAT THE ONE-SHOTS WERE ACTUALLY FOR, AND WHAT REPLACES IT.** Their real
property was that a bad boot could not repeat: the key was consumed *before*
the dangerous work, so a hang or a panic left it cleared (2dg, which was paid
for by the 2026-10-12 boot loop). Arming by default gives that up, and 2wj is
the record of what it costs when there is no way back - boot 196 had to be
disarmed from **Windows**.

So the key is written the other way round. **`rbgpu-safe` is the boot
sentinel**: set to `"1"` in the peer's `start()` before anything is armed, and
overwritten with `"0"` from a `thread_call` 60 s later. Both writes go through
`setProperty`, the only path 2sr measured as syncing. A boot that reaches the
clear was alive long enough to be driven; a boot that panics, hangs or is
power-cycled inside that minute leaves the latch set, and the next boot finds
it, **comes up stock, and clears it** - so one bad boot costs exactly one stock
boot and never a trip to another OS. The stock boot clears the latch *before*
arming anything, which is the order 2dg established.

**The window is a trade and it is stated, not tuned.** A deliberate restart
inside 60 s is indistinguishable from a boot that did not survive - rule 12 in
its original form, a user rebooting a black screen and a user rebooting a
working machine look identical from NVRAM - and it costs one stock boot.
`-rbgpunosentinel` turns the mechanism off for a session of rapid reboots, and
then a bad boot is the user's problem again. Two failure paths publish rather
than guess: `sentinel 3` when `/options` is unreadable (armed and unprotected),
and `sentinel 0` when `thread_call_allocate` fails - in which case the latch is
**removed again**, because a latch nothing will clear would make every
following boot a stock boot.

**The framebuffer's 2wp self-disarm now sets that latch instead of writing the
user's key.** It used to write `rbgpu-fb=0`, which under the new reading is the
*user's* durable disarm and would have stayed set until they noticed. One
writer per key: the user owns `rbgpu-fb`, we own `rbgpu-safe`, and a stuck key
can then only ever mean "be careful".

**RULE 38 IS A CHECK NOW, NOT A COMMENT.** The framebuffer declines the panel
on `-rbgpuoff`, `-rbgpustock`, `-rbgpunoownfb`, `rbgpu-fb=0`, the sentinel
latch, and - the new one - **`rbgpu-arm=0`**. That last one is the gap 2wp
described and did not close: the framebuffer writes HUBP from
`setAttribute('amtr')` and from nowhere else, so the panel taken with no
accelerator underneath freezes on the last frame drawn, *guaranteed*, and the
accelerator's own durable disarm therefore has to disarm the panel in the same
boot. `armRefuseWhy` distinguishes all six (2 boot-arg, 3 `rbgpu-fb=0`,
4 `/options` unreachable and armed anyway, 5 `-rbgpunoownfb`, 6 the latch,
7 `rbgpu-arm=0`), and `RBFBArmWhy` publishes it on the armed path.
**A decline cannot publish anything** - there is no service - so it is read
from outside instead: an `IONDRVFramebuffer` in `ioreg` means we declined, and
those are the only five reasons it can have been.

**What is NOT covered, said plainly.** The sentinel runs in the peer's
`start()`, so the hooks installed in `processKernel` have already been decided
by then and a recovery boot does not undo them. They are the same code every
boot since 2ks has run, and the latch exists for the display chain, which is
entirely downstream of that point.

**Also in this change:** `CLAUDE.md` goes from 2 461 lines to 425 - a reference
card again, with every rule's number preserved because the journal cites them
by number, and with the boot-arg list replaced by a pointer to
`rb_defaults.h`, which is the list and is checked by the hosttest.
`docs/HANDOFF.md` (1 347 lines, stale since 2ry) and `docs/HANDOFF-FULL.md`
(6 925 lines, stale since 2026-10-05) are **deleted**: everything in them is in
this journal under its tag, their §7 rules are in `CLAUDE.md`, their §9
boot-args are now `rb_defaults.h`, and git history holds both files intact.
The stray `src/plugin/kern_start.cpp.before-rgfix` backup is dropped too.

## 2xx — the regression after 2xw: our own `"0"` read as the user's disarm

**Symptom, in the user's words:** "the thing that used to make screen work
without typing broke... it only works per 10s with typing again".

That is 2wi/2wl's signature exactly — 0.078–0.093 `RBFBAmtrSets`/s, one frame
every 10.8 s, smooth while typing into Spotlight — which 2xi's
`-rbgpuschedtick` had fixed from 2 to 3375 transactions in 30 s. So the
question was never "what is slow", it was "why is the tick not armed".

**Read from the live machine first (rule 33, rule 8).** Boot 236, `kern.boottime`
Fri Oct 30 01:35:43, read at 01:39:52.

```
rbgpu-boot  236
boot-args   ... -rbgpuschedtick ... xhcipoke=10 -rbgpuoff
rbgpu-arm   1     rbgpu-agdc 1    rbgpu-iop 1
rbgpu-fb    0     rbgpu-tick 0
rbgpu-safe  1
```

`ioreg -rl -c RembrandtGPUPeer` returns **nothing** and
`ioreg -rl -c RBAMDFramebuffer` returns nothing; `IOKitDiagnostics` reports
`"IONDRVFramebuffer"=1`. So *this* boot is not a measurement of anything of
ours: `-rbgpuoff` is in boot-args, the documented rescue, which is how the
user got in ("im in"). Rule 39 — a reading taken in a configuration that does
not run the code says nothing about the code.

**The evidence for the armed boot was already in NVRAM** (rule: read what is
in hand before designing an experiment):

```
rbgpu-diag  d=131 armed=1 tick_armed=0 tick_oneshot=3 tick_solved=1 ...
            agdc_started=1 agdc_stage=46 agdc_on=1 agdc_error=0 agdc_solved=3ff
```

`tick_oneshot` is the `why` out of `rbgpu_nvram_armed("rbgpu-tick", &why)`,
and **3 is "the key reads \"0\" — disarmed by hand"**. The AGDC half came up
clean (`agdc_solved=3ff`, `agdc_on=1`); the tick alone was off. Predicted
before the read and confirmed by it.

**Why the key reads `"0"`.** 2xw inverted the five one-shots: the key is now a
durable disarm and the plugin never writes it. But the pre-2xw code spent two
of those keys by OVERWRITE — `rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot_ow` wrote a literal
`"0"` into the key as the act of consuming it (`rbgpu-fb` in 2wj so a disarm
could not fail to stick, `rbgpu-tick` in 2xg because the tick's failure mode
is a panic). So on any machine that ever ran an armed pre-2xw boot those two
keys already hold the exact value the new reader treats as the user's disarm.

The live machine separates the two groups perfectly and is the proof:
`rbgpu-arm`, `rbgpu-agdc` and `rbgpu-iop` were consumed by **removal**
(`rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot`) and read `1` — hand-written arms, left over.
`rbgpu-tick` and `rbgpu-fb` were consumed by **overwrite** and read `0`.

Both halves were therefore disarmed, and by rule 38's check `rbgpu-fb = "0"`
also declines the panel (`armRefuseWhy` 3), so the composited desktop was
gone as well as the tick.

**The fix is generational, because the value cannot carry the answer.** A
hand-typed `sudo nvram rbgpu-tick=0` stores the same byte as the spent
one-shot; no nonce, timestamp or length distinguishes them. So the two cases
are separated by *when*:

- `rbgpu-gen` is written once, by the first 2xx+ boot that reaches it.
- Before it exists, a `"0"` in `rbgpu-tick` or `rbgpu-fb` is our own spent
  one-shot and is **ignored** (`why` 8, published, rule 14).
- After it exists, every `"0"` is the user's and is **obeyed**.
- The other three keys are obeyed in both generations — `nvram rbgpu-arm=0` is
  the documented first rescue rung and no migration may ignore it.

`rb_key_disarms()` and `rb_legacy_zero_keys[]` in `src/common/rb_defaults.h`
hold the whole rule, and **both kexts ask it**: the plugin in
`rbgpu_nvram_armed()`, the framebuffer in a new `keyDisarms()`. That is rule 38
again — two separately armed halves must answer the same question identically,
and the framebuffer can probe *before* the plugin's migration has run.

`rbgpu_gen_migrate()` then makes the rule stop being needed: it rewrites each
legacy key that reads `"0"` to `"1"`, and writes `rbgpu-gen` **last**. The
order is 2dg's order for the third time — a boot that dies in the middle
leaves the generation key absent and the next boot still ignores the stale
zeros. Every write it makes moves a key in the armed direction, so it is safe
on a stock boot, and it runs on one, because a stock boot is exactly the boot
that most needs the next one to come up clean. It reads `rbgpu-gen` back and
publishes `gen` (0 failed read-back, 1 already migrated, 2 written, 3
`/options` unreachable) and `gen_fixed`.

**`rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot_ow` is deleted**, not left unused — rule 6,
"redundant" and "inert" differ. It had no callers after 2xw and it is the only
thing that could ever write that value again. `rbgpu_nvram_consume_oneshot`
stays: it consumes by removal, so it cannot leave a value behind, and
`rbgpu-mcreg` still uses it.

`tools/efi.sh defaults` reports the same rule rather than its own — a `"0"` in
a legacy key with `rbgpu-gen` absent prints as "IGNORED, a spent pre-2xw
one-shot", because an instrument that contradicts the code is rule 16's
instrument-as-suspect.

**Hosttest:** 14 new assertions in `tools/hosttest/defaults_test.c`, including
the bug itself stated as a test (`rb_key_disarms("rbgpu-tick", 1, 0)` must be
false), the inverse (with the generation key present it must be true, so the
migration is one-shot and not a permanent override), `rbgpu-arm` disarming in
both generations, and the degenerate inputs. The pre-existing `smu13` data
failure is unchanged and identical on `288a87b`.

**Not fixed by this and still in the way of an armed boot:** `-rbgpuoff` in
boot-args (the user's rescue — `sudo tools/efi.sh on` takes it out) and
`rbgpu-safe = "1"`, the sentinel latch the rescue sequence left set, which
would otherwise spend one stock boot clearing itself.

Built: plugin `BCE9FC13`, framebuffer `353A1D24`.

## 2xx (continued) — confirmed on hardware, and a second, separate defect

**2xx works.** Boot 237, read from the following `-rbgpuoff` boot:

```
rbgpu-gen   1          <- the migration ran and read back
rbgpu-tick  1          <- was "0"; rewritten by rbgpu_gen_migrate()
rbgpu-fb    1          <- was "0"; rewritten
rbgpu-diag  d=132 armed=1 tick_armed=1 tick_oneshot=0 tick_solved=1 tick_us=1b20
            agdc_on=1 agdc_solved=3ff agdc_error=0 otg_err=0
```

`tick_oneshot` 3 → **0** and `tick_armed` 0 → **1**, `tick_us` 0x1b20 = 6944 µs,
the panel's own period. The frame-rate regression the user reported is closed:
d=131 (boot 236, pre-2xx) reads `tick_armed=0 tick_oneshot=3` beside it, in the
same NVRAM, which is as clean a before/after as this project gets.

### The WindowServer crash loop is NOT 2xx

The user reported, on the 2xx boot: lock screen fine, password accepted,
desktop for about a second, back to the lock screen, repeating.
`/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports` settles what it is and is not:

| crash | uptime | asserting frame |
|---|---|---|
| 10-24 01:28, 01:30 | 7 s, 6 s | `CoreDisplay::Assert` ← `CGXMappedDisplayStart` |
| 10-30 00:58:12 / 00:58:56 / 00:59:52 | 23 / 80 / 130 s | `CA::OGL::Context::push_surface` |
| 10-30 01:03:24 / 01:03:33 | 28 / 51 s | `CA::OGL::Context::push_surface` |
| 10-30 01:52:31 / 01:52:40 | 24 / 38 s | `CA::OGL::Context::push_surface` |

Six `push_surface` aborts across **three** armed boots — 235 (00:58),
236 (01:03) and 237 (01:52, the 2xx boot). The counter only increments in the
peer, which `-rbgpuoff` stops before (rule 27), so the two `-rbgpuoff` boots in
between did not consume a nonce. **The loop predates 2xx by two boots**; 2xx
made the desktop reachable enough to meet it, and nothing more.

What every one of the six carries, identically:

- `ktriageinfo`: **`VM - (arg = 0x0) Returned success with no page`, twice.**
- `SIGABRT` from `__assert_rtn` inside
  `CA::OGL::Context::push_surface` ← `FlattenNode::retain_surface`, i.e. CA
  rendering a flattened sublayer tree into an offscreen surface.
- The whole compositor is the **software** path: `CompositorSW`,
  `CA::OGL::SW::scanline` / `rect_sdf_sampler` on a dozen worker threads.
- In the 01:52:40 report, thread 7297 is in `layer_blit_byte_ANY` with
  `trap 14 "(no mapping for user data write)"`, `cr2 = 0x16E6E4xx`.
- The VM summary, **byte-identical in all three boots**:
  `CG framebuffers 903.0M / 8` and `CG framebuffers (reserved) 582.1M / 7
  reserved VM address space (unallocated)`. The 10-24 crash, a different
  assert, reads `CG framebuffers (reserved) 135.0M / 1` and has no mapped
  line at all.

So WindowServer's software compositor is writing into framebuffer mappings
whose pages never materialize: the fault returns KERN_SUCCESS with no page,
one worker takes an unmapped-write trap in the blit, and the main thread then
asserts on the surface. 903 MB over 8 regions for a 1920×1080 panel, with 7 of
the 8 reserved and uncommitted, is the number to explain. Our aperture is
`kApertureBytes` = 8 294 400 = exactly 1920·1080·4, and
`VRAM,totalMB` is published as 4096.

**What is NOT established, said plainly rather than guessed (rules 16, 39).**
Whether this is our framebuffer's aperture or the accelerator half. The
deciding reads live in the armed boot's `ioreg` and a login screen that
crash-loops cannot be captured from (rule 10), and NVRAM does not settle it
either: `rbgpu-fbcrumb` carries **`b=235`**, so boots 236 and 237 left no
framebuffer crumb at all, which is consistent both with the framebuffer having
declined and with it dying before a crumb synced. Boot 236 declined for a
known reason (`rbgpu-fb` still read "0" then). Boot 237 should have armed, and
its diag says the accelerator did (`armed=1`, `agdc_solved=3ff`), yet there is
no crumb. That gap is the next thing to close.

**The one boot that answers it, and is usable while it does:**
`-rbgpunoownfb`. The accelerator stays armed and the panel goes back to
`IONDRVFramebuffer`, a configuration 2wl measured as usable, so the user gets
a desktop they can capture from. If WindowServer still crash-loops, the fault
is in the accelerator half and our framebuffer is exonerated; if the desktop is
clean, the 903 MB of CG framebuffers is ours and the aperture is the lead.
Either way one boot splits it, and `sudo nvram -d rbgpu-safe` first so the
sentinel latch boot 237 left set does not spend it on a stock boot.

### 2xx: the crash localised to the accelerator half, and two suspects killed

Boot at 02:04:19 with `-rbgpunoownfb` (capture
`logs/20261030-020547-plugin`): accelerator armed, panel back to
`IONDRVFramebuffer` (`fb0:0 /.Display_boot` in the GPUWrangler lines), and
**WindowServer still crash-looped** — pids 851 → 1150 → 1199 in eleven
seconds. `arm_why 0`, `armed 1`, `gen 1`, `linear_force 1`, `mtlk_scope *`,
`mtlk2_patched 33`, `mtlk2_uc 155`, `agdc_link_result 0`.

**Our framebuffer is exonerated.** It declined the panel in that boot and the
crash was unchanged.

**The configuration is exonerated too.** The pre-strip EFI backup
(`logs/efi-backups/20261030-015122-defaults/config.plist`) holds 46 rbgpu
tokens: the 45 in `rb_defaults.h` plus `rbgpumtlkscope=*`, and the set
difference against the table is empty in both directions. So the armed set
after `efi.sh defaults` is *exactly* boot 231's, which did not crash. 2xw's
50 `checkKernelArgument` → `rbgpu_arg` swaps cannot have changed it either:
a table token is on unless its negative is present, and a non-table token
keeps `checkKernelArgument` verbatim.

**The 2xv USB patches are exonerated.** They were installed at 00:32 and are
live in every boot since, including the half-dozen `-rbgpuoff` boots the user
has logged into normally all night.

So: plugin off ⇒ fine. Accelerator armed ⇒ crash, in **all four** armed boots
and independently of both halves that were suspected —

| boot | our fb | sched tick | WindowServer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 231 (10-29) | owns panel | armed | fine |
| 235 | owns panel (`rbgpu-fbcrumb b=235`, h=0 w=0) | off (`tos=3`) | **crash** |
| 236 | declined (`rbgpu-fb` read "0") | off | **crash** |
| 237 | — (no crumb) | armed (`tick_us=1b20`) | **crash** |
| 02:04 | declined (`-rbgpunoownfb`) | armed | **crash** |

The fault is therefore in the accelerator half and in neither the framebuffer
nor the tick, and it is not a difference in which tokens are on. What remains
is which of the 45 defaults, or the always-on `processKernel` core, and that
is a 45-way space: guessing one and wedging the desktop costs more boots than
splitting it. **No fix is committed here, deliberately** — rules 16 and 39.

Next boot, and it is a halving rather than a guess: **`-rbgpustock`**, the
plugin alive with every default off. Clean ⇒ the fault is one of the 45 and
the bisect proceeds by halves. Still crashing ⇒ it is the always-on core,
which 2xv/2xw/2xx never touched, and the frontier moves off the arming
entirely. Clear `rbgpu-safe` first or the sentinel spends the boot.

### 2xx: the swizzle fix is cleared, and the 903 MB is finally named

Boot at 09:19 with `-rbgpustock` removed and **`-rbgpunolinear -rbgpumtlkoff`**
added - the accelerator armed with BOTH halves of the swizzle fix off - still
crash-looped (`consecutiveCrashCount 2`, uptime 39 s). So the kernel linear
force and the userspace patcher are both cleared, as is `-rbgpustock`'s own
boot (09:13, boot 238: `armed=0 arm_why=5 sentinel=1`, `rbgpu-safe` cleared to
`0` by the 60 s thread_call, no crash) which proved the fault is one of the 45.

**This report carries two threads the earlier six did not, and they name the
903 MB.**

- Thread 8620: `CA::OGL::SWContext::create_surface_with_properties` →
  `CA::Render::aligned_malloc` → `mmap`, with **`r14 = 855638016 = 0x33000000
  = 816 MB`** for ONE software surface. That is the `CG framebuffers 903.0M / 8`
  line, and the 582.1 M reserved-and-uncommitted is the part `mmap` never
  backed - hence `VM - Returned success with no page`, twice, in all seven
  crashes.
- Thread 7115: `CA::OGL::SW::Format::RGBAh::load_1` and
  `image_sampler<Format::RGBAh, ...>`. **RGBAh is half-float RGBA, 8 bytes per
  pixel** - the EDR/wide-gamut compositing format, not the 4-byte path a
  1920x1080 SDR panel needs. Thread 7110 is simultaneously in
  `CA::OGL::MetalContext::create_pipeline_state`, so CA is standing up the
  Metal context and the software context at once.

So WindowServer is not mis-mapping our framebuffer: it is being told the
display wants a deep-colour EDR pipeline, sizes a half-float surface
accordingly, and the allocation cannot be backed. The question becomes **who
told it that**, and in a `-rbgpunoownfb` boot our framebuffer told it nothing -
it declined the panel, and `.Display_boot` owns it.

The one display-side thing we still publish in that boot is
**`/RembrandtGPUAGDC`**, which the GPUWrangler line names explicitly
(`agdc 0x100000575`), and whose diag records exactly the capability answers
that would decide this: `agdc_extcap_all=1`, `agdc_ec_csc`, `agdc_ec_gamma`,
`agdc_ec_degamma=196c00000200`, `agdc_gamma_entries=1`. Thread 6820 sits in
`AMBDapplyIntentionFromPreferencesForDisplayID` (AmbientDisplay) off a
ColorSync display-profile callback, which is the consumer side of the same
surface. And the 01:52 boot logged QuartzCore's
`NULL color space set on context`.

That is rule 38 a third time: AGDC armed while our framebuffer does not own
the panel, so CoreDisplay reads the boot framebuffer's modest display through
*our* capability bridge.

Next boot, still a halving and not a guess: keep `-rbgpunoownfb` so the
framebuffer stays out, and add **`-rbgpunoagdc -rbgpunoagdccaps`**. Clean ⇒
the AGDC capability answers are the crasher and the fix is to scope them to
the case where we own the panel. Still crashing ⇒ `-rbgpunodisplaypipe` is
next, and after it the accelerator-core group.

### 2xx: AGDC cleared, and the bisect made affordable

Boot 240 (09:29) ran `armed=1 tick_armed=1 tick_us=1b20` with
`-rbgpunoagdc -rbgpunoagdccaps -rbgpunolinear -rbgpumtlkoff -rbgpunoownfb`,
and WindowServer crashed twice, 14 s uptime each. **AGDC is cleared**, so the
capability-bridge reading of the RGBAh surface was wrong. Boot 241 then came up
`sentinel=4 safe_latch=1 arm_why=6`, stock, because boot 240 did not survive a
minute - the third test boot in a row to be spent that way.

Two changes to stop paying for the bisect rather than running it:

- **`efi.sh bootarg add|remove` now takes several tokens in one call**, one
  backup and one sync for the lot. One invocation per token meant twenty backup
  directories per experiment and a typo in any of them silently measured a
  different configuration (rule 16: the instrument is a suspect).
- **`-rbgpunosentinel` goes in for the duration.** A boot that crashes inside
  60 s leaves the latch and makes the NEXT boot stock, so each failed test was
  costing two boots and the user kept landing in a boot that measures nothing.
  That is the sentinel working as designed, and exactly the "session of rapid
  reboots" its opt-out was written for.

Cleared so far: our framebuffer, the configuration (identical to boot 231's),
the 2xv USB patches, `-rbgpustock` as a whole (boot 238, clean), the kernel
linear force, the userspace patcher, and AGDC. Next boot disarms **the other
17 of the display chain's 20** in one command - the group the table names, and
the half the crash lives in if it is a display fault at all. Clean ⇒ it is in
the display chain and three more halvings name it; still crashing ⇒ it is the
19-token accelerator group or the 6 instruments.

### 2xx: the display chain is cleared, including VRAM,totalMB

Boot 243 ran the other 17 display-chain tokens disarmed in one `bootarg add`,
and `rbgpu-diag-prev` records it as genuinely armed: `d=89 armed=1 agdc_on=0`,
`mcp_on=1`, and **no `fb*` or `vbl*` keys at all**. WindowServer crashed again.

That also clears the one hypothesis the 816 MB most invited: `VRAM,totalMB`
/ `VRAM,totalsize` = 4096 published on the framebuffer AND its PCI provider
(2pa, `kern_start.cpp` ~8370) is gated by **`-rbgpufbvram`**, which was off in
that boot. So SkyLight is not sizing its backing store from a VRAM figure of
ours.

Cleared now: our framebuffer, the boot-arg configuration, the 2xv USB patches,
`-rbgpustock` entirely (boot 238 clean), the kernel linear force, the userspace
patcher, AGDC and its capability answers, and the whole 20-token display chain.
25 of the 45 remain: 19 accelerator and 6 instruments.

Next: **the 6 instruments**, disarmed together. They are the cheaper half and
the table's comment on them - "they cost diag-table slots and nothing else" -
is precisely the sort of claim rule 16 was written about, the rule that has
already paid for a wedge, a crawl mistaken for a hang, two panics and three
destroyed captures. If the desktop survives, an instrument is the crasher. If
not, it is the 19-token accelerator group, and `-rbgpuvramadj`
(`rbgpu-adj ... fixed=416`), `-rbgpuptfix`, `-rbgpupdeenc` and
`-rbgpuspoofttl` lead it.

### 2xx: 26 of 45 eliminated; the capability spoof is the motivated next cut

Boot 244 ran armed with the 6 instruments disarmed as well
(`rbgpu-diag d=76 armed=1 mcp_on=0`) and WindowServer crashed at 09:38:11 and
09:38:54. The "wedge" the user saw is the crash loop going further, not a clean
boot. **The instruments are cleared.**

`-rbgpuiop` is cleared twice over: it is gated behind `rbgpu_arg("-rbgpuiop")`,
`-rbgpunoiop` was in boot-args, and `iop_on` is absent from the diag entirely
because `-rbgpumtlkoff` installs no exec hooks at all, so `rbgpu_iop_try` never
runs. Worth recording because it patches **WindowServer's own address space**
and was the best-shaped suspect in the display half.

The 2xw diff was also checked rather than asserted: `git diff 0241698..HEAD --
src/plugin/kern_start.cpp` contains **nothing** but the mechanical
`checkKernelArgument` → `rbgpu_arg` swaps and the three one-shot → durable
swaps. So the arming rework cannot have changed an armed boot's behaviour, and
the boot-231-vs-now difference is not hiding there.

A false lead, recorded so it is not re-walked: two crash threads sit in
`AMBDapplyIntentionFromPreferencesForDisplayID` and
`ColorSyncUtilsUpdateDisplayProfilesCallback`, and
`/Library/ColorSync/Profiles/Displays/Unknown Display-FFFFFFFF-....icc` was
written 2026-10-29 21:10 - a display profile for a panel with no EDID, which is
what ours enumerates as, and `Display: Unknown Display` is what the crash
footer reads. Decoded, it is a plain ICC v4 `mntr`/RGB matrix-TRC profile with
`desc cprt wtpt rXYZ gXYZ bXYZ rTRC chad mmod bTRC gTRC` and no `vcgt`/`ndin`.
Nothing in it forces half-float. Not the cause.

**19 remain, and 18 of them are hardware bring-up** - ring, page tables, SMU and
PSP, CP halt, clock gating. The exception is **`-rbgpuspoofttl`**, which is the
only one that changes what the driver is *told the device is* rather than how
the hardware is poked: it overrides `_ttlIsSupportedDevice` to 1, spoofs
`asic_type` 19 → 8 for PSP table binding, spoofs the GC `hw_version`, patches
the GC firmware version gate 0x000A0300 → 0x000A0303, and patches HWLibs'
**`_DeviceCapabilityTbl`**. The crash is a capability-driven decision - an
816 MB RGBAh half-float surface on an SDR 1080p panel - so a capability table
carrying another part's entries is the shape that fits.

Next boot: **`-rbgpunospoofttl`**, a motivated single-token cut rather than a
blind halving of eighteen bring-up flags. Stated in advance so the reading can
be judged: this may stop the accelerator binding at all, in which case a clean
desktop is only weakly informative (rule 39 - it would be a configuration that
does not exhibit acceleration, so it cannot locate much). A clean **accelerated**
desktop would be the strong result, and if the spoof is the cause the fix is to
narrow it - keep the version and asic-type spoofs that make the chip bind, drop
or correct the capability-table entries that advertise a display pipeline this
panel does not have.

### 2xx: `-rbgpunocaptbl` — the one boot that separates the table from the GPU

`-rbgpunospoofttl` came up **clean and unaccelerated**, which is the weak
outcome stated in advance: rule 39, a configuration that does not exhibit
acceleration cannot locate a fault that needs it. It does not clear the
capability table and it does not implicate it.

The reason it cannot is that `-rbgpuspoofttl` bundles five separate things:
the `_ttlIsSupportedDevice` override, the `asic_type` 19 → 8 PSP table bind,
the GC `hw_version` spoof, the GC firmware version gate
`0x000A0300 → 0x000A0303`, and the `_DeviceCapabilityTbl` patch. The first
four are what make the chip bind at all; only the fifth says what the device
*is*. And that fifth one **clones another index's capability record and
relabels it `deviceId=0x1681`** (`+0x18`, `+0x20` also set), so every display
capability the donor part advertises, this APU now advertises - which is the
shape of an 816 MB RGBAh half-float surface on an SDR 1080p panel.

So the capability table gets its own disarm, `-rbgpunocaptbl`, checked inside
`patchDeviceCapabilityTable` after the `spoofTtlMode` gate. It keeps every
spoof that makes the chip bind and drops only the capability record. It
defaults to patching, so no existing configuration changes, and it publishes
`cap_tbl_patched = 2` - distinct from 0, which already meant "not patched or
failed" (rule 14: a skip and a failure must not read the same). Added to the
hosttest's `known[]` so rule 30's collision check covers it.

This is the first point in the bisect where a build was cheaper than a boot:
eighteen hardware bring-up flags cannot be halved informatively, because any
half that breaks the ring gives another clean, unaccelerated, uninformative
desktop.

Said before the boot: an **accelerated** desktop that does not crash
WindowServer makes the capability table the cause, and the fix is then to stop
cloning the donor record wholesale - carry only the fields the chip needs to
bind and leave the display capabilities as the real part reports them. A boot
that is accelerated and still crashes clears the table and leaves the crash
with "the accelerator working at all", which is a different frontier and not a
boot-arg at all.

Built: plugin `FE3200B0`. 0 from `SystemKernelExtensions.kc`, 0
`IOGraphicsFamily` in `Info.plist`.

### 2xx: the bisect itself became the suspect — reset to one variable

The `-rbgpunocaptbl` boot came up clean and **unaccelerated**, and it measures
nothing. The live peer publishes only `armed=1 arm_why=0`: no `starthw*`, no
`cap_tbl_patched` at all - not even the `2` the skip path sets - and
`rbgpu-diag` / `rbgpu-diag-prev` both read `d=0`. The log carries
`RembrandtGPUPeer(0x100000300) published` and then nothing of ours. So
`patchDeviceCapabilityTable` was never *called*: the accelerator never loaded,
HWLibs never loaded, and the new token cannot be what stopped the bind because
it is only read inside a function that never ran. `rbgpu-boot` has also been
stuck at **245** for three boots, which says the peer's own NVRAM write is not
landing either.

**The cause is the bisect.** Thirty of our tokens were in boot-args at once,
accumulated one group per boot, and somewhere in that pile the accelerator
stopped binding - so the last two or three boots have been measuring an
unaccelerated machine while being read as if they were measuring the armed one.
That is rule 16 with the roles reversed: the instrument here is the
*configuration*, and rule 39 is the exact failure - a reading taken in a
configuration that does not exhibit acceleration cannot locate a fault that
needs it. Boots 243 and 244 did start the hardware (`starthw_c2=1
starthw_count=4`), so the break happened after them; attributing it further is
not worth a boot, because the fix is the same either way.

So: back to **one variable against a baseline known to crash**. Strip all 27
accumulated negatives and keep exactly two tokens - `-rbgpunosentinel`, so a
crash does not spend the following boot, and `-rbgpunocaptbl`. That is boot
231's configuration, which is also boot 237's, which crashed, minus the
capability-table clone and nothing else.

Then the reading is unambiguous for the first time since 240:
- accelerated and **no** crash ⇒ the cloned `_DeviceCapabilityTbl` record is
  the cause, and the fix is to carry only the fields the chip needs to bind
  and leave the display capabilities as the real part reports them;
- accelerated and still crashing ⇒ the table is cleared and the frontier moves
  to the accelerator working at all, which is not a boot-arg;
- unaccelerated ⇒ the capability record is load-bearing for binding, the
  separation cannot be done by disarming it, and the next step is static: dump
  the donor record with `tools/re/` and find which fields advertise the display
  pipeline.

### 2xx: the capability record is load-bearing, and the fbkext was never updated

The reset boot (246) is the first attributable reading since 240: boot-args hold
exactly `rbgpumtlkscope=* -rbgpunosentinel -rbgpunocaptbl`, `rbgpu-boot`
incremented again, 217 diag keys published, `armed=1 arm_why=0`, and
**`cap_tbl_patched=2`** - the skip genuinely took. The desktop was clean and
**unaccelerated**, and the diag says exactly where it stopped:

```
ttl_is_supp_calls=1  ttl_is_supp_ret=1        the supported-device override worked
cap_tbl_patched=2                             the table was skipped
ttl_init_ret=0xE00002BC                       kIOReturnError
ttl_raw_init_ret=4
gc_vercheck_patched=1  gc_regcheck_patched=1  smu_hook_routed=1
```

So `_ttl_hw_init` fails with `kIOReturnError` when `_DeviceCapabilityTbl`
carries no record for 0x1681. **The cloned record is required to bind**, which
is outcome three of the three named in advance: the separation cannot be done
by disarming it, and it also means the table is still only the last unexplained
token, not a demonstrated cause - HWLibs' capability table is about IP and
firmware capability, not display colour depth.

Then the RE descent was cut short, because rule 15 had been skipped for nine
boots. `kextstat`:

```
com.rembrandtgpu.plugin  FE3200B0   = 2xx, current
com.rembrandtgpu.fb      C7278266   != 33D9C184 (2xw) and != 353A1D24 (2xx)
```

**The loaded framebuffer predates 2xw.** Its `armedOnce()` has none of
2xw/2xx: no `rbgpu-gen` generation rule, no rule-38 check, no `RBGPUStock`
handshake with the peer. Every reading about "our framebuffer declined" has
been taken against a binary two milestones old, and boot 237 leaving no
`rbgpu-fbcrumb` - the gap flagged as "the next thing to close" - is explained
by it.

That reframes the crash, and the reframing fits every observation: all eight
aborts run on **`CompositorSW`**, SkyLight's *software* compositor. Boot 231,
the one that worked, logged `Metal compositor activated`. If the Metal
compositor is active the software path never runs, so neither does
`SWContext::create_surface_with_properties` and its 816 MB `mmap`. The crash is
plausibly not something we corrupt at all - it is SkyLight falling back to a
software compositor whose surface this configuration cannot back, and what
keeps SkyLight on the Metal path is our framebuffer owning the panel and
answering `'amtr'`.

Next boot is therefore the configuration the user actually wants, with the one
thing that was never true made true: **the full 45 defaults, `-rbgpunosentinel`
only, and the matching 2xx framebuffer installed.** `RBFBArmWhy` is the
reading - 0 means it took the panel, and anything else names which of the six
reasons it declined. A `Metal compositor activated` line in the display log and
no `CompositorSW` in a crash report is the result; it may simply be boot 231's
working state, reached again.

### 2xx RESOLVED — the WindowServer crash loop was a stale framebuffer kext

Boot 247, full 45 defaults with only `-rbgpunosentinel`, the matching 2xx
framebuffer installed. **Accelerated, smooth, no crash.** User's words: "its
accelerated and smooth 144hz".

The machine's own counters, 602 s of uptime:

```
kextstat   plugin FE3200B0   fb 353A1D24        both 2xx, agreeing for the first time
ioreg      1 RBAMDFramebuffer, 0 IONDRVFramebuffer
RBFBArmWhy      = 10        took the peer's RBGPUStock answer
RBFBVBLFires    = 85491     / 602 s = 142.0 Hz against the panel's 143.83
RBFBAmtrSets    = 19066     / 602 s = 31.7/s on a mostly-idle desktop
RBFBHubpWrites  = 19072     one per set
peer: armed=1 arm_why=0 gen=1 tick_armed=1 tick_us=6944 cap_tbl_patched=1
      agdc_on=1 sentinel=2
System Profiler: AMD Radeon 680M, 4 GB, 0x1681 rev 0x000a
```

**`RBFBArmWhy = 10` is the proof of the diagnosis.** That key, and the
`RBGPUStock` handshake it records, exist only in the 2xw+ framebuffer. The
`C7278266` binary that was loaded for every one of the nine crashing boots
could not perform it, had no `rbgpu-gen` generation rule and no rule-38 check.

So the whole crash loop was **rule 15**: the plugin was reinstalled nine times
and the framebuffer never was. Everything the bisect "cleared" was cleared
against a two-milestone-old second binary, and the one reading that would have
caught it on the first boot - `kextstat | grep rembrandt`, checked against the
UUID the build printed - was the reading never taken. 2xw's own HANDOFF listed
both artifacts and both UUIDs; only one of them was installed.

What that means for the eight `push_surface` aborts, now attributable: with the
2xw+ framebuffer declining the panel for reasons the old binary did not
understand, `IONDRVFramebuffer` kept it, SkyLight fell back to **`CompositorSW`**
and its `SWContext::create_surface_with_properties` asked `mmap` for 816 MB of
RGBAh half-float that could not be backed - `VM - Returned success with no
page`, twice, every time. Nothing we wrote was corrupting a surface. The
`_DeviceCapabilityTbl` clone, the linear force, the userspace patcher, AGDC and
all 45 tokens were innocent, which is why disarming each of them in turn
changed nothing.

Standing corrections from this milestone:
- **`cap_tbl_patched` is now a three-value key** (0 not patched/failed, 1
  patched, 2 skipped by `-rbgpunocaptbl`) and the record is **load-bearing**:
  `_ttl_hw_init` returns `kIOReturnError` without it, measured in boot 246.
  `-rbgpunocaptbl` is therefore a diagnostic, not a usable configuration.
- **`efi.sh bootarg add|remove` takes several tokens in one call.**
- `-rbgpunosentinel` is the right setting for a session of rapid reboots, and
  without it every crashing test boot costs a second, stock boot.
- `ioreg` prints these counters as `"RBFBArmWhy" = 10`, not `"RBFBArmWhy"="10"`.
  A grep written for the quoted form reports the service as absent - rule 26,
  and it cost a wrong reading in this very milestone.

### 2xx postscript — the "pre-existing hosttest failure" did not exist

Stated three times during 2xx that `hosttest` had one standing failure,
`smu13: FAIL needs tests/data/rembrandt-680m-tufa15.bin`, and that it was
unchanged on `288a87b`. Both halves were wrong in the same way.

The fixture is passed as **argv**: the Makefile runs
`$(OUT)/hosttest $(wildcard tests/data/*.bin)` (Makefile:108), `main` loops
over `argv[1..]`, and `smu13_tests` is handed `NULL` when no file matched
`rembrandt-680m`. Running `./build/out/hosttest` bare therefore cannot pass,
and the file was present all along - 10 240 bytes, dated Oct 3.

```
./build/out/hosttest                                       -> hosttest: 1 FAILED
./build/out/hosttest tests/data/rembrandt-680m-tufa15.bin   -> hosttest: all passed
```

Rule 26 twice in one milestone: once on `ioreg` printing `"RBFBArmWhy" = 10`
rather than `"RBFBArmWhy"="10"`, which reported the live framebuffer as absent
in the very boot that fixed everything, and once here - **running a tool the
wrong way and reading its output as the tool's verdict.** The "unchanged on
288a87b" check compounded it: stashing and re-running reproduced the failure
because it reproduced the mistake, which is exactly the known-present case
rule 26 says to check a search against. Always invoke the suite as the Makefile
does, or through `make`.

## 2xy - the System Settings brightness slider: two answers, not a write

2xs made the panel's duty cycle writable, proved the register sequence against
Linux, hosttested and mutation-tested it, and published `'brig'` in the
connection's parameter list. **Nothing ever asked for it.** The live registry
says why, and it says it without a boot:

```
+-o display0  <class IODisplayConnect>
  +-o AppleDisplay  <class AppleDisplay>
        "IODisplayConnectFlags" = <00000000>
        "IODisplayParameters" = {"bgsc"=..,"rgsc"=..,"vblm"=..,"ggsc"=..}
```

The IODisplay that matched our connection is plain `AppleDisplay`. The
brightness slider belongs to `IOBacklightDisplay` / `AppleBacklightDisplay`,
both of which are defined in IOGraphicsFamily and both of which are present in
this OS's binary (`strings -a build/re/IOGraphicsFamily` names
`IOBacklightDisplay`, `AppleBacklightDisplay`, `site.IOBacklightDisplay`,
`site.AppleBacklightDisplay`). `IOBacklightDisplay::probe` walks its
framebuffer's connections and takes the first that passes **both**, in order:

```
getAttributeForConnection(idx, kConnectionFlags, &flags)
    must succeed AND (flags & kIOConnectionBuiltIn)        // 0x800
getAppleSense(idx, NULL, NULL, NULL, &displayType)
    must succeed AND displayType is a panel                // kPanelTFTConnect = 2
```

`kIOConnectionBuiltIn = 0x00000800` is in the public header
(`IOGraphicsTypes.h:1104`); `kPanelTFTConnect = 2` is
`IOMacOSVideo.h:232`, a `csDisplayType` value. We answered 0 to the first and
declined the second, so the probe returned nothing and `AppleDisplay` took the
category on its own score. The `IODisplayConnectFlags = <00000000>` in the
registry is IOGraphics writing down our own answer, which makes it the proof
that the path is live and that our answer is what closed it.

Both answers are **true statements about this machine that we were simply not
making.** The panel is built in, and it is a fixed-in-place TFT on the APU's
eDP - 2xq/2xr established that the removable port is wired to the dGPU. There
is no sense hardware, so `senseType`, `primary` and `extended` are zero, which
is the only truthful value for lines that do not exist;
`kConnectionSupportsHLDDCSense` stays declined in every configuration because
there is no I2C to answer with.

**Armed by `-rbgpufbbuiltin`, separately from `-rbgpufbbacklight`.** Rule 38
asks what each half depends on and the two answers differ.
`kIOConnectionBuiltIn` is read by IOGraphics for more than the slider: the
display-prefs key, mirroring, and the wrangler's idle dimming. That is a
larger blast radius than writing a PWM duty cycle. So a boot can arm the match
without the write - which answers "does `AppleBacklightDisplay` match on this
machine at all" with no register write in the boot - or the write without the
match, which is 2xs' own never-booted configuration.

Rule 30: `-rbgpufbbuiltin` shares `-rbgpufbb` with `-rbgpufbbacklight` and
diverges at the next character, so neither prefixes the other; the hosttest's
collision check covers the whole namespace and passes with it added.

Rule 14: both answers are counted. `RBFBBlFlagsGets` and `RBFBBlSenseGets`
separate "the probe never asked" from "it asked and still did not match", and
`RBFBBlBuiltIn` says which boot this was. Without them a boot that did not
match and a boot where IOBacklightDisplay never ran look identical.

Neither arg has been booted. `hosttest: all passed`; fbkext links with 80
symbols from the system collection.
