## 2xz - "supports Ventura and up" is two claims, and they are now kept apart

The ask was to support every macOS from Ventura. The first thing worth writing
down is what the tree's state actually was, because it was worse than
"untested on older OSes":

* `PluginConfiguration` declared **Monterey..Sequoia** while the machine runs
  **Tahoe (Darwin 25)**. The plugin loaded only because `-lilubetaall` is in
  this machine's boot-args - a flag that loosens the version check for *every*
  Lilu plugin, and whose removal would have made this one quietly not load at
  all. Nothing in the tree would have said why.
* `tools/re/dscsym.sh` and `tools/re/dscinv.sh` each carried a table of unslid
  `__TEXT` bases written down on macOS 15. SkyLight's real base here is
  `0x7FF8091F1000`; the table said `0x7FF807B42000`. dscsym.sh measures the
  slide every run and says so in a comment - and then subtracted the wrong
  base from it, handing `atos` an address `0x16AF000` away from the one asked
  about, confidently. One of dscinv.sh's four entries was even marked
  `# approximate`.
* `rbgpu_mtlcave.h` held exactly one OS's addresses. 2xt had **replaced** the
  macOS 15 row with the macOS 26 one, so the row boot 231 ran existed only in
  git history.

**The split.** "Support" is two separate claims and conflating them is how a
wrong address gets written to a chip:

1. **The kext loads and the version-independent half runs.** That is the whole
   range, Darwin 22 up. Everything this project does by *symbol name* is in
   this half - routing, solving, the `IOFramebuffer` subclass, the registers,
   the SMU, the probes - and rule 1 already makes each of those check the name
   is defined before using it, so a renamed or absent symbol fails safe alone.
2. **A particular version-dependent artifact has been measured on this OS.**
   Per OS and per artifact. An address inside the dyld cache, a byte offset
   into an Apple driver's object, an instruction offset inside an Apple
   function: none can be inferred from a version number, only measured.

`src/common/rb_osver.h` is the matrix. Rows and what each rests on:

| Darwin | OS | claims | on what evidence |
|--------|------|--------|-----------------|
| 22 | Ventura | nothing | no boot of this project has happened there |
| 23 | Sonoma | nothing | no boot of this project has happened there |
| 24 | Sequoia | KEXTOFF, MTLCAVE | where every offset was derived; boots 1-231 |
| 25 | Tahoe | KEXTOFF, MTLCAVE, XHCI | offsets re-measured *in use* by boot 247; cave re-derived (2xt); USB table derived (2xv) |

Tahoe's `KEXTOFF` claim is worth stating precisely: the offsets were **not**
re-derived for it. Boot 247 is an accelerated desktop on Tahoe running the
offsets derived on Sequoia, and for an offset that is the only kind of
evidence that matters. The cave is the opposite - macOS 26 moved the driver
and its row had to be measured again from scratch.

Rule 14 in version form: "we do not support that OS" and "we have not measured
that OS" look identical from a log that says nothing. So:

* `rbgpu_stock()` now also means "this OS has no measured offsets". On such an
  OS the whole default-on table comes up off - a live macOS with the panel
  declined - and the boot logs one line with the Darwin number in it.
  `-rbgpuosforce` arms it for the boot that goes and measures.
* The framebuffer asks the identical question off the identical kernel global
  (`version_major`), because rule 38 is only satisfied if both halves answer
  the same way and this half can probe before the plugin runs. It has no Apple
  object offsets of its own; it honours the gate so the panel is not taken with
  no accelerator underneath, which is rule 38's own case.
* `rbgpu_nvram_armed` gains **why 9**, distinct from 5. "The user asked for
  stock" and "the kext refused to guess at another OS's offsets" are different
  facts and one code for both is rule 14's failure, not a tidier table.
* Every boot publishes `os_major`, `os_derived`, `os_forced`, `os_measured`.
* A Darwin newer than the tree names is deliberately **in** range with an empty
  claim mask, not refused: a boot that refuses to load teaches nothing.
* `make osrange` fails the build if the declared Lilu range and the matrix
  drift apart again. Verified against the failing case, rule 26: flipping the
  matrix floor to Sonoma makes it print `FAIL rb_osver.h declares
  Sonoma..Tahoe but ... PluginConfiguration has 0 KernelVersion::Sonoma`.

**The cave became a table.** `src/plugin/mtlcave/darwin24.h` and `darwin25.h`
hold one row each; `rbgpu_mtlcave.h` is the table and the lookup. Sequoia's
row was recovered from `8e4d142~1` and sits *beside* Tahoe's; both were checked
byte-identical to their sources after extraction, all four arrays each.

A row says where to **look**. What authorises a write is still the
byte-pattern compare `rbgpu_mtlk_place()` does in every single process: read
the place, write only if the bytes are exactly `cave_find` or already
`cave_repl`. So a row right for the Darwin major and wrong for the point
release writes nothing anywhere, and 2r6's verdict says the driver moved with
the unslid addresses and this boot's slide in the log. **That property is why
keying per-build addresses on the Darwin major is honest: the key picks a
candidate, the bytes decide.** An OS with no row at all gets no patch and says
which case it was - `mtlk_row = 0` for "no row for this OS" against
`mtlk_match = 0` for "the row missed".

**The generator now derives instead of carrying.** `tools/gen_cavepatch.py`
held macOS 26's addresses as module constants and printed a header that
replaced the previous OS's. It now reads everything off the running machine's
cache: the image, `__TEXT`, `__TEXT,__const`, the function from `LC_SYMTAB`
with the mangled length prefix **computed** from the name rather than typed
(rule 5 - the symbol is `__Z31amdMtl_HWL_DetermineSwizzleModeP18AMD...`, and 31
is `strlen` of the name), the prologue checked against the known bytes *and*
checked unique in `__TEXT` (rule 26 in both directions, with a distinct message
for 0 hits and for more than 1), and a 16-aligned zero run in `__const` whose
48-byte anchor is unique there. `make mtlcave` runs it and names the two edits
left deliberately by hand.

Run on this machine it reproduced 2xt's by-hand derivation **exactly**:

```
__TEXT 0x7ffb110d4000   fn 0x7ffb1121622d   cave 0x7ffb1147d710
cave 163B of 176 reserved; anchor 48B unique in __const; prologue unique in __TEXT
-> all four byte arrays identical to the header it replaced
```

Two independent derivations agreeing is the only reason to believe either -
rule 18 taken the useful way round. It is also what lets a user on Ventura or
Sonoma have the userspace half of the swizzle fix at all: one command on their
own machine, no disassembly and no boot.

**Verified against the running machine with no boot spent.**
`tools/cavecheck.m` now reads the row for its own kernel (`kern.osrelease` via
sysctl - the same number the kexts key on) and says so when there is none. On
the live boot 247 desktop:

```
row: Darwin 25 (Tahoe)
  slide 0xaf59000
  CAVE (stage A)     PRESENT
  DETOUR (stage B)   PRESENT
VERDICT: cave AND detour present - the fix is live for every process.
```

`tools/re/dscbase.sh` reads the unslid `__TEXT` base and size out of
`dyld_info -segments`, so no table can go stale, and dscsym.sh / dscinv.sh both
take their bases from it. The repaired dscsym.sh reports slide `0xaf59000` -
**the same slide cavecheck measured independently** - and symbolizes
`0x7FF8091F1000 -> (in SkyLight)` and `0x7FF805348000 -> (in CoreDisplay)`,
the latter being the macOS 26 CoreDisplay base CLAUDE.md already recorded.

`tools/hosttest/osver_test.c` pins every claim: Ventura and Sonoma claim
nothing, the all-or-nothing rule on a multi-bit mask, a newer Darwin loads and
claims nothing, and the cross-check that an OS claims `RB_OSD_MTLCAVE`
**exactly** when a cave row exists for it - the one artifact whose claim bit
and whose data live in different files, which nothing else in the build would
notice drifting. Adding a bit without a boot behind it now breaks a named test.

`hosttest: all passed`. Nothing here has been booted; the Tahoe path is
unchanged by construction and the live-machine checks above are what stands in
for a boot.

## 2xs/2xy boot 249 - the backlight works end to end, and the slider's gap is a NAME

Boot 249: the full default configuration, accelerated (`RBFBArmWhy = 10`,
`RBFBAmtrSets = 3130`, `RBFBHubpWrites = 3131`, `RBFBVBLFires = 22687`),
`-rbgpufbbacklight` and `-rbgpufbbuiltin` both in boot-args, plugin `43775C76`
loaded. **The framebuffer loaded was still `353A1D24`** - the new `EBF63EB0`
was sitting in `/Library/Extensions` but the auxiliary collection had not been
rebuilt, so this boot measures 2xs with 2xy absent. Rule 39: that is the
configuration these readings come from and 2xy is not in it. (`strings` on the
installed bundle says `rbgpufbbuiltin` 1 hit; on the loaded one, 0.)

**2xs' first boot ever, and it works.**

```
RBFBBlArmed Yes   RBFBBlReady Yes   RBFBBlRefuse 0   RBFBBlPendTimeouts 0
RBFBBlOtgCtl 70145 = 0x11201        <- OTG0_CONTROL, exactly CLAUDE.md's value
RBFBBlPeriod 790432   RBFBBlFloor 5120   RBFBBlLevel0 22784
```

`RBFBBlOtgCtl` reading `0x00011201` is the cheap proof that the BAR5 map and
the DMU segment are right: it is the same value the OTG sampler measured
independently, from a different mapping, in a different kext.

The 2xs register sequence round-trips. Three writes across this boot, each one
written and read back bit-identical:

| | level (u16.16) | count written | count read back |
|---|---|---|---|
| firmware's own, written back unchanged | 22784 | 22250 | 22250 |
| via blset 0.60 | ~41370 | - | - |
| via blset 0.2924 | 22786 | **22252** | **22252** |

The last row is the one that matters: 22252 is a value the firmware never set,
chosen by us, written to `BL_PWM_CNTL`'s active-count field and read back
identical, with zero `RBFBBlPendTimeouts`. `RBFBBlCntl` as captured decodes to
`0xC0000000 | 22250` - the enable bits plus the firmware's own duty - which is
why the first write was a no-op: `rb_bl_level_from_pwm` converted the
firmware's level straight back to the count already there. **A no-op round trip
proves the store executed and nothing about the panel changing** (rule 20 in
register form), which is why the effect needed its own instrument.

**The instrument: `tools/blset.m`, `make blset`.** It asks for the change
through `IODisplaySetFloatParameter`, the documented entry point and the same
chain the System Settings slider uses - the one 2xs read end to end. No boot,
no kext, no arming.

**And it found the slider's actual gap, which is not the class match.**

```
6 parameter(s): bgsc rgsc vblm brig ownr ggsc
found it under the key "brig"
brightness: value 22784, min 5120, max 65536   (29.2 % of range, floor 7.8 %)

set via "brightness"(0.6) -> 0xe00002c7 (kIOReturnUnsupported)
set via "brig"(0.6)       -> 0x0 (OK)
```

`IOFramebufferParameterHandler` builds that dictionary from the FourCCs we
returned in the `'parm'` list, turning each 4-byte attribute into a
**4-character key**. So our parameter is literally named `"brig"`, while
`kIODisplayBrightnessKey` is the string `"brightness"`. The reverse direction
still works - `doIntegerSet` byte-swaps only the first four characters of the
name, so both map to `'brig'` - but a client that looks the parameter up BY
NAME finds nothing under `"brightness"`, and gets `kIOReturnUnsupported`.

A framebuffer cannot fix this from its side: the `'parm'` list carries four
bytes per entry and the key string is Apple's to construct from them. On a real
Mac the full-name `"brightness"` parameter is published by `IOBacklightDisplay`
itself, not by the framebuffer - which is the same conclusion 2xy reached from
the other end, and makes 2xy necessary rather than merely cosmetic.

**A reading I got wrong, in the most ordinary way available.** Immediately
after the 0.60 set I read `RBFBBlSets` and it was still 1, and I said the write
had never reached the kext. It had. These properties are published from the
periodic VBL path, not on change, so between publishes the registry holds the
previous values - and a counter that **has not moved yet** is not a counter
that did not move. Seconds later it read 2, then 3. Rule 31 says to publish
with `setProperty` and read `ioreg` instead of `IOLog`; the addendum it needed
is that a periodically-published property is *stale by design*, so a counter
must be read twice, or after at least one publish interval, before "it did not
change" is a result. My own tool printed the warning to check the kext counters
and I then read them too early.

Net: **2xs is done and confirmed on hardware** - the mechanism, the arithmetic,
the floor and the effect. 2xy is still unmeasured, now for the second boot
running, because the auxiliary collection was never rebuilt.

---

## 2xy boot 250 - AppleBacklightDisplay MATCHES, and that does not publish "brightness"

Boot 250, `EBF63EB0` finally the loaded framebuffer, `-rbgpufbbacklight` and
`-rbgpufbbuiltin` both in boot-args, `rbgpu-boot` 250, accelerated
(`RBFBArmWhy = 10`).

**2xy works.** IOGraphics wrote every one of our answers down:

```
+-o AppleBacklightDisplay  <class AppleBacklightDisplay, id 0x10000059d>
      "IOProbeScore"           = 3000        <- beats AppleDisplay's 2000
      "IODisplayConnectFlags"  = <00080000>  <- kIOConnectionBuiltIn, byte-swapped
      "AppleSense"             = 0           <- our getAppleSense senseType
      "AppleDisplayType"       = 2           <- our kPanelTFTConnect
      "IODisplayPrefsKey" = ".../IGPU@0-756e6b6e-0-0"
```

and our side counted the asking (rule 14, the three outcomes named before the
boot): `RBFBBlBuiltIn Yes`, **`RBFBBlFlagsGets 2`**, **`RBFBBlSenseGets 2`**.
So `IOBacklightDisplay::probe` asked for `kConnectionFlags`, accepted it, asked
`getAppleSense`, accepted that too, and took the category. The chain read
statically in 2xy is confirmed end to end on hardware.

**And the second of the three predicted outcomes is what happened.** The
parameter dictionary is unchanged:

```
6 parameter(s): bgsc rgsc vblm brig ownr ggsc
set via "brightness"(0.55) -> 0xe00002c7 (kIOReturnUnsupported)
set via "brig"(0.55)       -> 0x0 (OK), value 38349, and the kext writes:
                              RBFBBlSets 3, LastLevel 22786 -> LastCount 22252
                              -> Readback 22252, PendTimeouts 0
```

`AppleBacklightDisplay` owning the connection does **not** add a full-name
`"brightness"` parameter. It serves our framebuffer's list through
`IOFramebufferParameterHandler` and nothing more, so `kIODisplayBrightnessKey`
still answers `kIOReturnUnsupported` and only `"brig"` works.

**This corrects what 2xy was written on.** The commit that built it said "the
full-name parameter is `IOBacklightDisplay`'s to publish, which is what makes
2xy necessary". 2xy *was* necessary - nothing else makes that class match - but
the inference that the class match would therefore produce `"brightness"` was
wrong, and the boot is what settled it. The name gap is a third thing, downstream
of both halves, and it is now the only thing between here and the slider.

Where that leaves it: the brightness is fully controllable
(`./build/out/blset <0..1>`, three round-tripped writes this boot), by any
client that asks for `"brig"`. What is unknown is what `IOBacklightDisplay`
requires before it publishes `kIODisplayBrightnessKey` itself - on Apple
hardware `AppleBacklight.kext`'s only personality is `AppleIntelPanelA`,
matching `IOACPIPlatformDevice` / `IONameMatch backlight` with
`IOMatchCategory IODisplayParameters` and `IODisplayParameters = {commit}`, so
the full-name parameters plausibly come from a separate driver that claims the
`IODisplayParameters` match category rather than from the framebuffer at all.
That is a static question and needs no boot.

**And one instrument failure, caught by its control.** The first attempt to
answer it was `strings -a build/re/IOGraphicsFamily | grep -i backlight`, which
returned nothing - against the same file that had returned
`AppleBacklightDisplay`, `IOBacklightDisplay` and `site.IOBacklightDisplay`
earlier the same day. The file was gone: **`make clean` does `rm -rf
$(BUILD_DIR)`, which includes `build/re/`**, and 2xz's clean rebuild deleted
every extracted Apple binary in the tree. Rule 26's control is the only reason
that did not become a finding about IOGraphicsFamily.

---

## 2y0 - publishing "brightness" ourselves, since nothing else will

Boot 250 left exactly one thing between the working backlight and the slider:
the parameter is named `"brig"` and every client asks for
`kIODisplayBrightnessKey`, which is `"brightness"`.
`IOFramebufferParameterHandler` builds each key from the **4-byte FourCC** we
return in the `'parm'` list, so four characters is all a framebuffer can ever
name. 2xy's commit said the full name was `IOBacklightDisplay`'s to publish;
boot 250 proved it is not, because `AppleBacklightDisplay` matched and the
dictionary did not change.

So the full name has to come from an `IODisplayParameterHandler`, and the whole
mechanism was read out of IOGraphicsFamily with **no boot spent**:

```
IODisplay::searchParameterHandlers(this, entry)        0x14ce7d66
    iter = entry->getChildIterator(plane)
    while ((obj = iter->getNextObject()))
        if (OSDynamicCast(IODisplayParameterHandler, obj))
            this->addParameterHandler(obj)

  callers:  0x14ce8ba4   searchParameterHandlers(this, FRAMEBUFFER)   <- unconditional
            0x14ce8c1c   ... and, only if OSDynamicCast(IOBacklightDisplay, this),
                         the children of a service found by nameMatching("backlight")

IODisplay::addParameterHandler(this, h)                0x14ce7e04
    arr = OSDynamicCast(OSArray, this->fParameterHandler)   ; +0x90
    if (arr && arr->getNextIndexOfObject(h, 0) != -1) return true
    if (!h->setDisplay(this)) return false                  ; vtable 0x850
    if (!arr) { arr = OSArray::withCapacity(2); this->fParameterHandler = arr; }
    arr->setObject(h); return true

IODisplay::doUpdate(this)                              0x14cea4be
    walks the same array, calling each handler's doUpdate   ; vtable 0x868
```

Three things fall out of that, and each one is why this is cheap:

* **The first caller passes the framebuffer.** We have no ACPI backlight
  device and do not need one - the unconditional call walks our own
  framebuffer's children, and a child of our framebuffer is something this
  kext creates for itself.
* **The handler list is an `OSArray`.** Adding ours does not displace
  `IOFramebufferParameterHandler`, so `'brig'`, `'rgsc'`, `'ggsc'`, `'bgsc'`
  and `'vblm'` all keep working and `"brightness"` appears beside them.
* **`IODisplay::addParameter` / `setParameter` are public statics taking an
  `OSSymbol *`**, so an arbitrary-length name is publishable. The FourCC limit
  is the framebuffer path's, not IODisplay's.

`src/fbkext/RBAMDBacklightParams.cpp` is the handler. It is created after
`blSetup()` (it refuses unless `blReady` - a parameter whose writes cannot
reach the register is worse than an absent one) and **before**
`IOFramebuffer::start()`, because that is what can create an
`IODisplayConnect` and IOKit matching is asynchronous: registering afterwards
would race the display's own driver. It publishes the SAME bounds 2xs answers
for `'brig'` - floor 5120, full 65536 - because two parameters naming one
register must agree about its range, and it writes back what `blSetLevel`
actually clamped to rather than what was asked, so the dictionary cannot end
up fighting the hardware.

**The plane is settled from the other end, not from the GOT.** The plane in
`searchParameterHandlers` is one of two imported globals and the slot does not
name itself. Apple's own handler for this category is `AppleIntelPanelA`,
whose personality is `IOProviderClass = IOACPIPlatformDevice`,
`IOMatchCategory = IODisplayParameters` - it is its provider's SERVICE-plane
child, and the entry searched for it is that provider. So `gIOServicePlane`,
and `attach()` + `registerService()` is the whole requirement. Rule 14 rather
than trust: **`RBFBBlParmSetDisplays` counts the calls we actually receive**,
so if this reasoning is wrong the boot says 0 instead of being silent, and the
next step is the device tree rather than another guess.

Every counter separates one distinct outcome, named before the boot:

| reading | what it means |
|---|---|
| `SetDisplays` 0 | IODisplay never found us walking its framebuffer's children - the plane is wrong, NOT a publish failure |
| `NoDict` non-zero | found us, but the display had no `IODisplayParameters` |
| `PublishFails` non-zero | found us, had the dict, and `addParameter` refused |
| `Sets` 0 with the rest fine | published and nothing ever asked - the UI does not use `kIODisplayBrightnessKey` either |

`-rbgpufbblparm` is its own arg because it creates and registers a NEW IOKit
service as a child of this one, which is a different risk from answering two
attributes (2xy) or writing a duty cycle (2xs). Rule 30: it shares
`-rbgpufbb` with the other two and diverges at the next character (l against a
and u), and the hosttest's collision check covers the whole namespace.

Deliberately NOT published: `"linear-brightness"` and
`"usable-linear-brightness"`, whose scale and meaning differ (linear against
perceptual). Publishing both would change two things in one boot and could
produce a slider whose position disagrees with the panel. If the keys still do
not respond with `"brightness"` present, that is the next single variable.

Built, 97 symbols from the system collection, 0 unresolved;
`_gIODisplayBrightnessKey`, `IODisplay::addParameter` and
`IODisplay::setParameter` each checked bound individually against a control
(rule 1, rule 26). `hosttest: all passed`. **Never booted.**

## 2y1 — boot 251 PANICKED, and the panic proves 2y0's mechanism was right

Boot 251 loaded the fbkext `C97B9CDD` with `-rbgpufbblparm` and panicked
twice (15:35:01 and 15:37:30, `Kernel-2026-10-30-1535*.panic`), both
identically, in WindowServer:

```
panic(cpu 4 caller 0xffffff800bc208ba):
    Trying to change a collection in the registry @OSCollection.cpp:70
Panicked task ... pid 204: WindowServer
    OSCollection::haveUpdated
    OSDictionary::setObject(OSSymbol const*, OSMetaClassBase const*, bool)
    IOGraphicsFamily : IODisplay::addParameter(OSDictionary*, OSSymbol const*, int, int)
    com.rembrandtgpu.fb : RBAMDBacklightParams::publish()            <- ours
    IOGraphicsFamily : IODisplay::doUpdate()
    IOGraphicsFamily : IODisplay::framebufferEvent(IOFramebuffer*, int, void*)
    IOGraphicsFamily : IOFramebuffer::deliverGroupNotification(...)
    IOGraphicsFamily : IOFramebuffer::deliverFramebufferNotification(int, void*)
    IOGraphicsFamily : IOFramebuffer::deliverDisplayModeDidChangeNotification()
    IOGraphicsFamily : IOFramebuffer::doSetup(bool)
    IOGraphicsFamily : IOFramebuffer::setupForCurrentConfig()
    IOGraphicsFamily : IOFramebuffer::doSetDisplayMode(int, int)
    IOGraphicsFamily : IOFramebufferUserClient::externalMethod(...)
```

**Read the backtrace as a result before reading it as a failure.** Every
inference 2y0 made off the static read is confirmed by it, in Apple's own
frames:

- `IODisplay::searchParameterHandlers` walked **our framebuffer's own
  service-plane children** and found us. The plane was `gIOServicePlane` and
  `attach()` + `registerService()` was the whole requirement, as 2y0 argued
  from `AppleBacklight.kext`'s personality.
- `setDisplay` returned true, so `addParameterHandler` put us in the `OSArray`
  at `IODisplay+0x90`.
- `IODisplay::doUpdate` walked that array and **called our `doUpdate`** —
  vtable 0x868, as read.

So `RBFBBlParmSetDisplays 0`, the outcome 2y0 named as "the plane is wrong and
the device tree is next", is excluded. None of that work needs redoing.

**The defect is one line's worth and it is a rule, not a number.** The
dictionary `publish()` fetched with
`display->getProperty(gIODisplayParametersKey)` is a registry property, and
every collection reachable as one carries `kImmutable`;
`OSCollection::haveUpdated` panics on any mutation of it by design. 2y0 wrote
`append rather than replace` into the comment as though appending were the
conservative choice. It is the opposite: appending is a mutation.

`IOFramebufferParameterHandler::displayModeChange` (0x14d01126) shows the legal
shape, and it never writes to the published dictionary at all:

```
  0x14d0124f   r12 = this->0x88          ; the handler's OWN previous dict
  0x14d01256   this->0x88 = 0
  0x14d0126a-  iterate r12's keys, copy each into r15 (a FRESH dictionary)
  0x14d015a0   IODisplay::addParameter(0x88(this), gIODisplaySelectedColorModeKey, ...)
  0x14d015b5   IODisplay::setParameter(0x88(this), ...)
  0x14d0132e   display->vtable[0x258]  = setProperty(gIODisplayParametersKey, r15)
  0x14d0133a   r15->release()
```

Allocate your own, merge the old in, mutate yours, `setProperty` it, release.
That also explains the fact that looked contradictory: Apple calls
`setParameter` on `this+0x88` **after** having `setProperty`'d that same
object (`IOFramebufferParameterHandler::doIntegerSet`, 0x14d067d3) and does not
panic — because the object is one it allocated and holds, not one it took out
of the registry. The distinction is ownership, not timing, and it is not
knowable from the value: the two dictionaries look identical.

And `IOFramebufferParameterHandler::doUpdate` (0x14d0687e) is **four
instructions — `mov $1, %al; ret`**. Apple publishes nothing from `doUpdate`.
2y0 published from both `setDisplay` and `doUpdate` on the reasoning that the
contract does not say *when* `doUpdate` is called; the frames above say where:
inside `doSetup`'s display-mode-change notification chain, in WindowServer's
`extSetDisplayMode`. Publishing there is not wrong by itself — the mutation
was — but it is worth knowing that Apple's handler treats that context as
read-only.

**The fix (`D0F419E8`), and what it deliberately does not change.**
`publish()` now takes `OSDictionary::withDictionary(cur, cur->getCount() + 4)`
of whatever is published — a copy that is ours and mutable — calls
`addParameter`/`setParameter` on the copy, hands the copy to
`display->setProperty(gIODisplayParametersKey, ...)` and releases it. The copy
is by reference, so `'brig'`, `'rgsc'`, `'ggsc'`, `'bgsc'` and `'vblm'` carry
forward as the same objects and keep working. A null `cur` is no longer a
failure (the display may not have published yet) but is still counted, because
"there was nothing to merge" and "the merge dropped something" are
indistinguishable afterwards.

`doIntegerSet` had a second instance of the same bug waiting one keypress
away — it wrote the clamped level back with
`IODisplay::setParameter(params, ...)`, and `params` there is the published
dictionary. It now ignores that argument and calls `publish()`, which re-reads
the level off the chip, so what lands in the dictionary is the register's value
rather than our idea of it.

`doUpdate` still publishes. Apple's being a no-op is not a reason to stop:
`displayModeChange` **replaces** the whole property, and its merge loop
iterates the handler's own old `+0x88` dictionary rather than the registry's,
so our key would be dropped on every mode change with nothing to re-assert it.
Re-asserting from `doUpdate` is now safe for the same reason the publish is —
it no longer mutates a registry collection.

Verified before handover: `hosttest: all passed`; `LINK 97 symbols from the
system collection, 321 from boot` (319 before, +2 for the dictionary copy);
`OSDictionary::withDictionary`, `OSDictionary::withCapacity`,
`IORegistryEntry::setProperty(OSSymbol const*, OSObject*)`,
`IODisplay::addParameter`, `gIODisplayParametersKey` and
`gIODisplayBrightnessKey` each bound individually; 0 unresolved; UUID moved
`C97B9CDD` → **`D0F419E8`**.

**Rule 42, which this cost a panic to learn.** *A collection you did not
allocate is not yours to write to.* `getProperty` returns a borrowed pointer to
something the registry owns; IOKit enforces that with a panic rather than a
return code, so there is no failure path to test and no counter that can
record it — the first wrong write ends the boot. The question to ask of every
`OSDictionary*`, `OSArray*` or `OSSet*` before writing to it is **who
allocated this**, and the answer "I fetched it from a service" means copy it
first. The mirror of rule 13: not every call that can fail reports failure.

## 2y1 CONFIRMED on hardware (boot 252), and 2y2 — the UI writes a different key

**2y1 works, in full.** Boot 252 came up with `D0F419E8`, no panic, and the
live dictionary on the matched `AppleBacklightDisplay` reads:

```
"IODisplayParameters" = {
    "brightness" = {"min"=5120,"max"=65536,"value"=22784},
    "brig"       = {"min"=5120,"max"=65536,"value"=22784},
    "rgsc"/"ggsc"/"bgsc" = {...65536}, "vblm" = {...},
    "fade-time1"/"fade-time2"/"fade-time3"/"fade-style" = {...}, "ownr" = ...
}
```

The full-length name is published beside the FourCC one, both agreeing, and
the copy-and-replace merge carried `'brig'`, the three gamma scales, `'vblm'`
and Apple's own `fade-*` through untouched — so rule 42's fix costs nothing it
was meant to preserve. `RBFBBlParmSetDisplays 1`, `RBFBBlParmPublished 7`,
`RBFBBlParmPublishFails 0`, `RBFBBlParmNoDict 1` (the display had not published
its parameters yet at `setDisplay` time, which is why `publish()` tolerating a
null source was right). **And the slider exists**, which it never did through
2xs or 2xy.

**The hardware path is confirmed end-to-end through the new handler.** Driving
it from userspace moved `RBFBBlParmSets` (so it entered OUR `doIntegerSet`) and
then the register:

| asked | level | count written | readback | user |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `blset 1.00` | 65536 | 64000 | **64000** | visible |
| `blset 0.15` | 14182 | 13850 | **13850** | visible |

a 4.6x duty change, each read back bit-identical, user-confirmed physically
("yes your changes work"). So 2xs, 2xy, 2y1 together are done: the register,
the match, the parameter and the write path all work.

**Two readings corrected here, both of which looked like findings.**

*`RBFBBlLevel0` is not a live sample.* It read 22784 and stayed there across 18
seconds and six reads while `RBFBBlReadback` said 64000, which looks exactly
like the chip reverting our write — the ABM/DMCUB story, and a tempting one.
It is not: `RBFBBlGets` sat frozen at 10 through all six reads, so
`blCurrentLevel()` was never called in that window and `blLevel0` is a snapshot
from the last `publish()`, not a periodic re-read. Rule 31's addendum again,
with the twist that the stale value was stale for a *different* reason than
"the publish interval has not elapsed" — nothing was sampling it at all. The
counter that proved it is the one beside it.

*The duty arithmetic is right, and the obvious reason to think otherwise is
wrong.* `BL_PWM_PERIOD` is **4000** with `BITCNT` **12**, not 16, and the count
we write for 34.8 % is 22250 — 5.5x the period, which reads as a saturated PWM
and would explain "the slider does nothing" perfectly. It is not a bug:
`BL_PWM_FRACTIONAL_EN` is set (`BL_PWM_CNTL` 0xC003502A, bit 30), so the field
is fixed point with `16 - BITCNT` = 4 fractional bits and 22250 means 1390.6
ticks of 4000 = 34.8 %. `docs/linux-ref/dce_panel_cntl.c:224` shifts by
`bit_count` exactly as `rb_bl_count_from_level()` does, and the read inverts it
exactly (22250 * 2^12 / 4000 = 22784 = the level asked). Both directions agree
with each other AND with Linux. Comparing a fixed-point field against an
integer period is the error; the units are in the FRACTIONAL_EN bit, not in the
field.

**So why does the slider do nothing? It writes a key we do not publish.**
`RBFBBlParmSets` moved for every `blset` and **never once for a drag**, and the
`"brightness"` value in the dictionary stayed whatever we last put there. The
brightness UI does not go through `kIODisplayBrightnessKey` at all: it goes
through **CoreBrightness**, whose exports are `BrightnessSystem`,
`BrightnessSystemClient`, `BrightnessSystemClientInternal` and
`KeyboardBrightnessClient`, and which holds

```
"linear-brightness"         0x7ff814e8d332, 0x7ff814e8d364
"usable-linear-brightness"  0x7ff814e8d35d
```

all inside its `__TEXT` (0x7ff814d69000 + 0x172000, measured with
`tools/re/dscbase.sh`, rule 41). A cache-wide byte scan finds
`linear-brightness` 3 times (the third at 0x7ff805453a42, inside CoreDisplay)
and `usable-linear-brightness` once, against a control of 21 for
`DisplayServices`. A set naming a key no handler claims is dropped by
`IODisplay` with nothing recorded anywhere — which is precisely a slider that
moves, a panel that does not, and a counter that never increments. The kernel
exports all three symbols (`gIODisplayBrightnessKey`,
`gIODisplayLinearBrightnessKey`, `gIODisplayUsableLinearBrightnessKey`) and
`IOGraphicsTypes.h:1674-1676` names them, so this needs no new string.

**2y2 (`38BA90BE`, built, NEVER BOOTED)** publishes all three from the same
handler, with **one counter per key** — `RBFBBlParmSetsPerc`,
`RBFBBlParmSetsLin`, `RBFBBlParmSetsUsable` — because the question the boot
answers is *which name the UI writes*, and one total cannot say it (rule 14).
`"usable-linear-brightness"` reports the ceiling and its sets are **declined
and counted**: a capability treated as a control is worth seeing rather than
silently obeying.

The scale is **an assumption, recorded as one**: neither the SDK header nor the
disassembly documents the units of `"linear-brightness"`, so it is published on
the same `[blFloor, RB_BL_LEVEL_FULL]` scale as `"brightness"`. That is
defensible for this panel rather than merely convenient — the PWM duty is
linear in our level by construction, so our level already *is* a linear
brightness. If the slider's travel comes out compressed or non-monotonic, the
perceptual/linear distinction is what to revisit, and `"brightness"` is the one
that should then carry a curve.

Verified: `hosttest: all passed`; `LINK 99 symbols from the system collection,
321 from boot` (97 before, +2 for the two key globals); each of
`gIODisplayBrightnessKey`, `gIODisplayLinearBrightnessKey`,
`gIODisplayUsableLinearBrightnessKey` and `gIODisplayParametersKey` bound
individually; 0 unresolved. UUID `D0F419E8` → **`38BA90BE`**.

Stated before the boot: `SetsLin` non-zero is the answer and the slider should
move the panel. `SetsLin` 0 with `SetsUsable` 0 and `SetsPerc` 0 across a drag
means CoreBrightness is not writing `IODisplayParameters` at all and the next
place to look is `BrightnessSystemClient`'s own path, not another key name.
`SetsUsable` non-zero alone would mean it drives the panel through the ceiling
parameter, which would be worth knowing before obeying.

## 2y2 DONE on hardware (boot 253) — the slider works, and the key was `linear-brightness`

`38BA90BE`, boot 253, no panic. The per-key counters answer the question the
boot was built to ask, and they answer it the way 2y2 said in advance:

| key | sets | |
|---|---|---|
| `RBFBBlParmSetsLin` | 143, then **258** four seconds later | what the UI writes |
| `RBFBBlParmSetsPerc` | **2** | initial sync only, never a drag |
| `RBFBBlParmSetsUsable` | **2** | attempted, declined, counted |

`RBFBBlSets` 146 hardware writes, `RBFBBlParmSetFails` 0, and the live
dictionary holds `"linear-brightness"={"min"=5120,"max"=65536,"value"=28617}`
and `"brightness"={...,"value"=28617}` in step, beside
`"usable-linear-brightness"={...,"value"=65536}` and everything Apple
publishes. **The user's report: "shit the slider works".**

So the diagnosis from the static read was right end to end: CoreBrightness
drives the built-in panel through `linear-brightness`, a set naming an
unpublished key is dropped by `IODisplay` with nothing recorded anywhere, and
the fix was to publish the name it asks for. `brightness` alone produced a
slider that rendered and did nothing — which is the most misleading possible
half-success, because the UI reads one key and writes another, so the slider
tracked our value and we read that as the publish having worked.

**Two notes worth keeping.**

*Declining the ceiling was the right call and the counter proves it was a real
case.* `RBFBBlParmSetsUsable` is 2: something genuinely tried to WRITE
`usable-linear-brightness`, the parameter that reports a capability. It was
declined and counted rather than obeyed, the slider works anyway, so nothing
needed that write — and had it been obeyed silently, a client could have moved
the panel through a parameter whose meaning is "this is the most you can ask
for". The counter is what makes this a fact rather than a guess about what
would have happened.

*`'brig'` is now stale and deliberately left alone.* The dictionary reads
`"brig"={...,"value"=22784}` while the real level is 28617, because `'brig'`
belongs to `IOFramebufferParameterHandler`'s own `+0x88` dictionary and it
updates that on its own path, not ours. Nothing reads `'brig'` but
`./build/out/blset`, and keeping it in sync would mean writing a parameter we
do not own into a copy we do, for cosmetic benefit, on a binary that is
measured working. Recorded instead of changed, because the trap it sets is a
future reading taking 22784 for the current level — which is exactly the
mistake rule 31 and 2xs's `RBFBBlLevel0` already cost once each.

**Brightness is DONE**, in four measured pieces: 2xs writes the duty cycle
(boot 249), 2xy makes `AppleBacklightDisplay` match the connection (boot 250),
2y1 publishes a full-length parameter name without panicking on a registry
collection (boot 252, after 2y0's panic on boot 251 established the mechanism),
and 2y2 publishes the name the UI actually writes (boot 253). The slider moves
the panel.

Still opt-in, and the obvious next step: `-rbgpufbbacklight`,
`-rbgpufbbuiltin` and `-rbgpufbblparm` are now each measured working on this OS
across consecutive boots, which is the standard 2xw asks of anything in
`rb_defaults.h`. Moving them into the default-on table is a one-line change per
token plus the hosttest's own assertions, and the boot sentinel is the recovery
if a default turns out to be wrong.

## 2y3 — brightness goes default-on, and the fbkext had no header dependency tracking

The user's word on boot 253: the slider works and **the brightness keys work**.
That closes the original ask whole. So the three tokens move into
`rb_defaults.h`: `-rbgpufbbacklight`, `-rbgpufbbuiltin`,
`-rbgpufbblparm`. Each is measured working on this OS on its own boot (249,
250, 252/253), which is the standard 2xw asks of a table entry, and the boot
sentinel is the recovery if a default turns out wrong. The count assertion
moves 45 -> 48 deliberately, and the three "stays OFF (never booted)" checks
are **inverted rather than deleted**, so a token silently dropping out of the
table fails the build instead of quietly reverting the feature. Each one's
derived negative is asserted by name as well as by the table-wide loop:
`-rbgpunofbbacklight`, `-rbgpunofbbuiltin`, `-rbgpunofbblparm` (rule 37 -
a default-on feature with no reachable negative is a hardcode, not a default).

**And making that change found a silent stale build.** `make fbkext` printed
`KEXT` and relinked over objects it had not recompiled: `rb_defaults.h` was
modified at 17:07:34 and every `build/fbkext/*.o` was still from 16:47:17.
The cause is one line - the Makefile's

    -include $(KEXT_OBJS:.o=.d) $(PLUGIN_OBJS:.o=.d)

never named `FBKEXT_OBJS`. The compiler had been writing those depfiles the
whole time (`-MMD -MP` is in the same CXXFLAGS, and
`build/fbkext/RBAMDFramebuffer.d` already named `rb_defaults.h` twice);
nothing read them. So src/fbkext objects rebuilt **only** on the single
prerequisite hardcoded into their rule, `$(FBKEXT_SRC)/RBAMDFramebuffer.hpp`,
and a change to any `src/common` header rebuilt nothing at all.

Why it never showed before: every 2y0/2y1/2y2 change added counters, so every
one of those builds touched `RBAMDFramebuffer.hpp` and rebuilt by accident.
This change touched only `src/common` and `tools/hosttest`, so it rebuilt
nothing - and `make` said `KEXT` over it. **Caught only by the UUID check**,
which is exactly why that is a hard rule and not advice. Rule 16 in its build
form: the build system is an instrument and it is a suspect.

Fixed by adding `$(FBKEXT_OBJS:.o=.d)`, and verified in both directions
rather than once: touching `rb_backlight.h` now rebuilds exactly the three
files that include it (`RBAMDFramebuffer`, `RBAMDFramebufferBacklight`,
`RBAMDBacklightParams`) and touching `rb_smu13.c`, which nothing in
src/fbkext includes, rebuilds **0** files. The negative control matters as much
as the positive one here: `-include` of a wrong variable would also have
"worked" by rebuilding everything every time.

How many earlier boots this cost is not knowable and is not claimed. What is
knowable: any src/fbkext reading taken after a src/common-only edit, in any
milestone before this one, was taken against a binary that did not contain the
edit unless RBAMDFramebuffer.hpp also changed in that commit.

Built: hosttest all passed, `LINK 99 symbols from the system collection, 321
from boot`, fbkext UUID **F2DCD77C-8082-3E2E-828F-23C168C5865A**, plugin UUID **C518C319-7CD5-37B4-A6CD-21127211D39F**. Both halves change here
because `rb_defaults.h` is compiled into both (rule 38, rule 15: this install
is two artifacts, not one).

## 2y4 — the refresh-rate question, and the read it needs first

The ask: switch between 60 Hz and 144 Hz. Today `getDisplayModeCount()`
returns **1** and `getInformationForDisplayMode` hardcodes
`kRefreshRate1616`, so macOS has no refresh-rate UI at all - there is nothing
to choose between. That is the whole reason no such control exists, and it is
not a capability question.

**The model is confirmed against the live raster before any of it is used.**
From this boot's own read-only OTG sampler: `agdc_tim_clk` 341995117,
`agdc_otg_htot` 2106, `agdc_otg_vtot` 1129, measured
`agdc_otg_mhz` **143836**. And clk/(htot*vtot) = **143.836 Hz** - the model
reproduces the measurement to the digit, which is what makes it safe to invert.

`OTG_V_BLANK_START_END` decodes to start 1100, end 20, so the active window
is **1080 lines and is defined independently of V_TOTAL**. Changing V_TOTAL
therefore stretches the vertical blank and leaves the active raster, the sync
widths, the pixel clock and the DP link untouched. Inverting the model:

| target | V_TOTAL | actual | lines added |
|---|---|---|---|
| 60 Hz | **2707** | 59.9892 | +1578 |
| 90 Hz | 1804 | 90.0171 | +675 |
| 120 Hz | 1353 | 120.0228 | +224 |
| current | 1129 | 143.8360 | 0 |

The field is 13 bits, so 2707 fits with room to spare.

**The register group decides the method, and it rules out the obvious one.**
`dcn_3_1_2_offset.h` names more than `rb_regs.h` carried:

    regOTG0_OTG_V_TOTAL          0x1b2f   (already in the table)
    regOTG0_OTG_V_TOTAL_MIN      0x1b30
    regOTG0_OTG_V_TOTAL_MAX      0x1b31
    regOTG0_OTG_V_TOTAL_MID      0x1b32
    regOTG0_OTG_V_TOTAL_CONTROL  0x1b33

Writing `OTG_V_TOTAL` directly is what Linux does during a **modeset**, with
the pipe locked - which is not available here, because the panel is live and
the desktop is on it. `V_TOTAL_MIN`/`MAX` with the `MIN_SEL`/`MAX_SEL`
bits of `V_TOTAL_CONTROL` (`dcn_3_1_2_sh_mask.h:29367-29382`) are the
variable-refresh path and are **designed to be written while the raster
scans**; pinning MIN == MAX fixes the frame length. So the method is the one
the hardware provides for exactly this, not a modeset we cannot perform.

**Which makes the next step a READ, not a write.** The current values of
MIN/MAX/MID/CONTROL are unknown - the firmware may already have DRR enabled -
and a restore cannot be written before the thing being restored has been read.
So 2y4 adds the four to `rb_regs.h` (cited, and cross-checked by the
hosttest's offset table against 0x34C0 + dword) and reads OTG0's timing plus
the DRR group in `blSetup()`, which already has this exact BAR5 map and has
already proved the segment with OTG0_CONTROL. **Nothing is written.**
`rb_dcn_deny.h` remains the gate that has to be opened deliberately before
anything is.

Published as `RBFBOtgHTotal`, `RBFBOtgVTotal`, `RBFBOtgVTotalMin`,
`RBFBOtgVTotalMax`, `RBFBOtgVTotalMid`, `RBFBOtgVTotalCntl`,
`RBFBOtgVBlankSE`, `RBFBOtgFrameCount0`. Sampled **before** gate 1's
refusal, so a boot where the backlight declines still reports the raster, and
zeroed from `start()` by `otgTimingReset()` rather than from `blSetup()` -
because `blSetup()` does not run at all on a `-rbgpunofbbacklight` boot and
an uninitialised published property is indistinguishable from a reading (rule
14 / rule 19). Zero is a value this group can never legitimately hold: a live
raster cannot have H_TOTAL 0.

The plan after the read, each step with its own verdict: pin MIN == MAX == 2707
behind an opt-in boot-arg with a **self-reverting thread_call**, measure the
result with the FRAME_COUNT edge latch (2rn) rather than a fixed window, and
revert unconditionally after a few seconds - so the failure mode of a panel
that will not accept 2707 lines is a black screen that ends by itself rather
than one that needs a power cycle. Only then expose a second display mode and
wire `setDisplayMode` to the timing change plus the VBL clock, since the
advertised refresh and our VBL cadence have to move together or the compositor
is paced against a raster it is not on.

A reason to want this beyond battery: the desktop currently holds ~82
transactions/s against a 143.836 Hz raster (2xi/2xo, still open). A genuine
60 Hz mode is fully achievable at that throughput, so it is also the cleanest
experiment on the frame-rate ceiling - if 60 Hz holds a solid 60, the ceiling
is demand or pacing rather than a hard gate.

Built: hosttest all passed with the four new offsets cross-checked, fbkext
UUID **C7873213-6565-3F13-B6D2-E43DE5B6899A**, plugin **C518C319-7CD5-37B4-A6CD-21127211D39F** (unchanged by 2y4 - `rb_regs.h` is included only
by src/fbkext, the hosttest and rb_probe.c; all four apparent plugin matches
were comments, rule 26).

## 2y4 READ (boot 254) — the firmware has DRR off, so the restore state is four zeros

Boot 254, fbkext `C7873213`. **Rule 15 catch: the plugin is still
`43775C76`, not `C518C319`** - the EFI half of 2y3 was not installed. It
does not invalidate this reading, and the reason is specific rather than
hand-waved: 2y3's only plugin-side change was `rb_defaults.h`, and the three
tokens it adds gate `src/fbkext` behaviour which the fbkext decides from its
OWN compiled copy of that table. Brightness is default-on this boot regardless,
and everything below comes from the new fbkext.

| register | value |
|---|---|
| `RBFBOtgHTotal` | 2106 |
| `RBFBOtgVTotal` | 1129 |
| `RBFBOtgVBlankSE` | 1311820 (start 1100, end 20) |
| `RBFBOtgVTotalMin` | **0** |
| `RBFBOtgVTotalMax` | **0** |
| `RBFBOtgVTotalMid` | **0** |
| `RBFBOtgVTotalCntl` | **0** |

H_TOTAL, V_TOTAL and V_BLANK_START_END agree exactly with the plugin's
independent OTG sampler, which is the cross-check that says the fbkext is
addressing the same registers.

**The firmware has DRR switched off entirely.** MIN_SEL and MAX_SEL both clear,
so V_TOTAL alone drives the raster and MIN/MAX/MID are untouched zeros. Two
consequences, both good: there is nothing of the firmware's to preserve, and
the restore state is **four zeros that were read rather than inferred**. That
is why `rb_drr_check()` makes a non-zero `V_TOTAL_CONTROL` a REFUSAL rather
than a case to handle - on a boot or a machine where the firmware IS using DRR,
what to restore is unknown and fighting it is the wrong move. Rule 37's
question asked of a register instead of an NVRAM key.

**The write gate corroborates the offsets independently.** None of 0x1b2f,
0x1b30, 0x1b31, 0x1b32, 0x1b33, 0x1b36 or 0x1b4c is in `rb_dcn_deny.h`,
against a control of 0x288b which is - so dcn302 and dcn312 agree on the OTG0
V_TOTAL group and a write there lands on the register we think it does. That
denylist exists for a different purpose (Apple's dcn302 DAL writing raw dword
offsets) and answering this question was free.

## 2y5 — the refresh-rate change, built and NEVER BOOTED (`74BCE3CD-1141-323B-8FA7-5FCE023A5A2D`)

`rb_drr.h` holds every decision and `tools/hosttest/drr_test.c` runs all of
them. The anchor assertion is the one that matters: `rb_drr_mhz(341995117,
2106, 1129)` must equal the **measured** 143836 mHz, from the registers alone.
It does, and it inverts: 143836 mHz -> 1129 lines, 60000 mHz -> **2707** lines,
landing at 59989 mHz - and the 11 mHz shortfall is asserted rather than
rounded away. 120 Hz is 1353 lines, 90 Hz is 1804.

The gate, each refusal distinguishable (rule 14): `NO_RASTER` (H_TOTAL or
V_TOTAL zero), `FW_DRR` (V_TOTAL_CONTROL non-zero), `NOT_LONGER` (only
lengthening the frame is allowed - shortening it would raise the refresh above
the rate the panel is known to run at, which is a different experiment with a
different failure mode), `TOO_LONG` (past the 15-bit field; all three totals
are 0x7FFF, `sh_mask.h`:29331/29356/29359/29362, so one mask covers H and V
rather than two constants that could drift apart).

**The new assertions were checked to FAIL when the code they guard is broken**,
as the workflow requires - and the first attempt at that check proved nothing:
deleting the `ctl != 0` line made `-Werror -Wunused-parameter` reject the
build, so the test never ran and no FAIL was printed. A compile error is not an
assertion failing. Rewritten as `ctl == 0xffffffff`, which compiles, the
build printed exactly `FAIL any non-zero V_TOTAL_CONTROL refuses` and
`hosttest: 1 FAILED`, and restoring it passed. Rule 16 applied to a control
rather than to an instrument.

The kext half is `-rbgpufbdrr`, opt-in, asserted OFF by the hosttest, with
`rbgpudrrlines` (default 2707), `rbgpudrrsecs` (8) and `rbgpudrrdelay`
(45), all read with the binary-int idiom and bounded (rule 40). It runs **once**
and reverts itself.

**It is a three-step state machine and the first version was wrong.** That
version did `IOSleep(drrSecs * 1000)` inside the callout - and our own VBL
delivery is a thread_call that must fire every 6944 us, on a shared worker
pool. Occupying a worker for eight seconds to wait out an experiment puts the
panel's frame clock behind a sleep. So the wait is a deadline on the next step
instead, and the only blocking left is the bounded ~300 ms poll inside the
measurement, which is the same busy-wait the plugin's sampler has always done
once at startup.

Write order is load-bearing in both directions: MIN and MAX first then CONTROL
on the way in, CONTROL first then MIN/MAX on the way back, so the window where
a SEL bit is set over a MIN of zero never exists. Step 2 is **armed before step
1 writes anything**, so if the panel drops sync the thing that puts it back is
already on the clock. `drrTeardown` reverts too if it catches the experiment
at step 1, because cancelling the callout would otherwise leave the raster at a
refresh nothing advertises and nothing will ever undo.

Measurement mirrors 2rn exactly - both endpoints latched ON a FRAME_COUNT edge,
never over a fixed window - with the poll bound raised from 400 ms to 1.2 s,
because 16 frames at 60 Hz is 266 ms and the plugin's bound would not have
covered it. A measurement that fails is a refusal, not a baseline of zero.

**What this is NOT yet:** a display mode. macOS still advertises one mode at
143.836 Hz and the VBL thread_call still ticks at that rate, so while the
raster is at 60 Hz the compositor is paced against a rate it is not running at.
That is exactly why this reverts and why it is a measurement: the mode list and
the VBL clock have to move with the timing, and none of that is worth building
before the panel has been shown to accept 2707 lines at all.

One incidental fix: `argOn()` lives in `RBAMDFramebuffer.cpp`'s anonymous
namespace (opens line 24, closes line 311), so declaring it in the header
created a SECOND global function and every call site in that file became
ambiguous. Resolved with a `static bool argEnabled()` member that forwards to
it, rather than letting src/fbkext keep two copies of the boot-arg rule - two
copies is how two halves come to disagree about whether a feature is on.

Stated before the boot:
- `RBFBDrrMhzDuring` near **59989** with `MhzAfter` back at ~143836 is the
  result: the panel accepts a stretched vertical blank, and a real 60 Hz mode is
  a matter of wiring it to `setDisplayMode` and the VBL clock.
- `MhzDuring` still ~143836 with `MinRb`/`MaxRb` reading 2707 means the
  write landed and the OTG ignored it - the SEL bits are not sufficient and
  `V_TOTAL_MID` or `OTG_SET_V_TOTAL_MIN_MASK` is the next variable.
- `MhzDuring` 0 means the raster stopped advancing: the panel did not accept
  it. `MhzAfter` back at ~143836 then proves the revert works, which is the
  outcome that makes a second attempt safe to try.
- `RBFBDrrRefuse` 2 would mean the firmware enabled DRR between boot 254 and
  this boot; 14 means the write did not read back; 13 means the baseline
  measurement failed and nothing was written at all.
- `RBFBDrrStep` 3 with `Reverted` true is a complete run whatever the Mhz
  values say.

## 2y5 DONE on hardware (boot 255) — the panel accepts 60 Hz, and it does it without a link retrain

fbkext `74BCE3CD-1141-323B-8FA7-5FCE023A5A2D` loaded, `rbgpu-boot` **255**,
`rbgpu-safe` 0, `-rbgpufbdrr` in boot-args. Plugin still **`43775C76`** - 2y3's
EFI half has never been installed, three milestones running. It cannot affect
this reading (the DRR path is entirely src/fbkext and reads its own compiled
copy of `rb_defaults.h`), but it is recorded because rule 15 is about the habit,
not about whether this particular boot was spoiled.

The read, `ioreg -rl -c RBAMDFramebuffer`:

    RBFBDrrArmed   Yes      RBFBDrrMhzBefore  143843
    RBFBDrrDone    Yes      RBFBDrrMhzDuring   60025
    RBFBDrrStep      3      RBFBDrrMhzAfter   143821
    RBFBDrrReverted Yes     RBFBDrrMinRb        2707
    RBFBDrrRefuse    0      RBFBDrrMaxRb        2707
    RBFBDrrRuns      3      RBFBDrrCtlRb           3
    RBFBDrrLines  2707      RBFBDrrCtl0            0
    RBFBDrrSecs      8      RBFBDrrVTotalLive   1129

The first of the five outcomes stated in 2y5, the one that was written down
before the boot: `MhzDuring` near 59989 with `MhzAfter` back at ~143836.

**Why 60025 against a predicted 59989 is a pass and not a near-miss.** 36 mHz
is 0.06 %, and the quantity to compare it against is not a tolerance picked
after the fact - it is this instrument's own noise, measured in the same run by
the same code. `MhzBefore` 143843 and `MhzAfter` 143821 are two measurements of
an **unchanged** raster taken 8 s apart, and they differ by 22 mHz. The
prediction is therefore correct to the resolution the measurement can offer,
and `rb_drr.h`'s model - `clk/(H_TOTAL x V_TOTAL)`, inverted to lines - is
confirmed against the chip in both directions rather than only in the direction
the hosttest can check.

**Two independent facts, and they needed separating.** `MinRb`/`MaxRb` reading
back 2707 and `CtlRb` reading 3 (MIN_SEL|MAX_SEL) says the **write landed in
the register**. `MhzDuring` 60025 says the **OTG obeyed it**. 2y5's second
stated outcome was precisely the case where the first is true and the second is
false, which is why both are published: a readback is not a behaviour, and had
only the readback been checked, `V_TOTAL_MID` would now be under suspicion for
no reason.

**The user reports no black screen**, and that is a result, not an aside. The
panel re-synced to a 2707-line frame while scanning. This is what boot 254's
`OTG0_V_BLANK_START_END` = 1311820 predicted and the reason DRR was chosen over
a modeset: start 1100 / end 20 pins the 1080-line **active** window
independently of V_TOTAL, so lengthening V_TOTAL stretches vertical blank and
nothing else - same active raster, same sync widths, same pixel clock, same DP
link, no retraining. Had the active window been derived from V_TOTAL, 2707
lines would have been a mode change and the link would have had to come back up.

The revert is complete and verified by agreement rather than by assertion:
`RBFBOtgVTotalMin/Max/Mid/Cntl` all still read **0**. Those four are the
`start()`-time snapshot, so they are boot 254's reading of the firmware's
state; the registers were put back to exactly the values that were *read* at
boot, not to values inferred from a datasheet. `Ctl0` 0 recorded live before
the write agrees with them.

**What this does and does not establish.** It establishes that this panel and
this OTG accept a 60 Hz frame length applied live, and that our arithmetic
picks the right number of lines. It does **not** make 60 Hz a mode: macOS still
advertises one mode at 143.836 Hz and the VBL thread_call still ticks at that
rate, so for those 8 s the compositor was paced against a rate the raster was
not running at. That mispacing was invisible to the user, which is a mild
surprise worth not over-reading - 8 s of a static desktop is the easiest
possible case for it.

Next, and it is now a wiring job rather than a question: `getDisplayModeCount()`
-> 2, a refresh field in `getInformationForDisplayMode`, and `setDisplayMode`
changing the timing **and** `rbgpuvblhz` together, since rule 38's lesson is
that two separately-set halves disagree. The DRR experiment stays as it is,
opt-in and self-reverting, because it is the instrument that will say whether a
future mode switch landed.

## 2y6 — 60 Hz as a display mode, built and NEVER BOOTED (`A5479DEA-1219-3793-8C8A-9673DF7CE010`)

Boot 255 settled that the panel accepts a 2707-line frame applied live. What it
deliberately did not do is tell anybody: macOS advertised one mode at
143.836 Hz and the VBL thread_call kept ticking there, so for eight seconds the
compositor was paced against a rate the raster was not running at. This
milestone is entirely about making those three things move together, and it is
a wiring job rather than a question - which is why it is written as a feature
with a mode list rather than as another experiment.

**Three numbers per mode, from one source.** A mode needs the line count to
write, the 16.16 `refreshRate` IOFramebuffer advertises, and the nanosecond
period the VBL ticks at. `rb_drr.h` now derives the second from the first and
the third **from the second**, in that order. That ordering is the point: there
is one rate per mode instead of three expressions of it that can drift apart,
and the thing that drifts in this project is always the second copy
(`argOn` in 2y5, the stale dyld base in 2xz, the two halves in rule 38).

**The pixel clock is derived, and the round-trip is what makes that honest.**
It comes from the DP PLL, this project has never located it, and it does not
need to: `clk = mHz * H_TOTAL * V_TOTAL`, and boot 255 measured all three on
the live raster. 143843 * 2106 * 1129 / 1000 = **342 011 761 Hz**. On its own
that would be rule 18's objection - a number built from one row - so the
hosttest makes it prove itself: fed back through `rb_drr_lines_for_mhz` with
the refresh it was derived from, it must return **1129**, the V_TOTAL it came
from. A clock wrong by a factor would still produce a plausible-looking 60 Hz
line count, so the 60 Hz answer alone would prove nothing. It then gives 2707
for 60 Hz independently, agreeing with the hand-computed value the earlier
assertions pin.

**What gets advertised is what the chip will do, not what was asked for.**
2707 lines gives **59992 mHz**, not 60000. Publishing the request instead of
the achievable value is how a mode list comes to lie about a panel, so
`modeMhz60` is computed from the line count and everything downstream - the
16.16 rate, the VBL period - comes from that. Boot 255 *measured* 60025 at
these lines; the computed 59992 is 33 mHz away, and the hosttest asserts that
gap against the instrument's own noise rather than a tolerance picked to pass:
`MhzBefore` 143843 and `MhzAfter` 143821 are two measurements of an unchanged
raster 8 s apart, so 22 mHz is what this sampler can resolve, and the
assertion allows twice that.

**THE CONTINUITY CHECK, which is the one that matters most.** The 143.83 Hz
mode must keep ticking at the period the kext has used since 2xe, because
three milestones of frame-rate work were measured against it. The hosttest
asserts `rb_drr_period_ns(0x008fd53f) == 6952507` exactly. If the mode table
ever silently retimes the compositor, the build fails rather than the next boot
being inexplicable. Mode 100 also keeps the 16.16 value out of
`.Display_boot`'s own live IOFBConfig rather than a re-derived one - re-deriving
it moves it by 0.01 Hz for no gain, and it is what every boot since 2sl has
been read against.

**The VBL period stopped being a constant**, and the retune is deliberately not
a cancel-and-rearm: the thread_call is live and delivering `'vbl '`, and
stopping it to change a number is a gap in the frame clock. It is a plain
member the callout re-reads when it arms, so the worst case of a switch racing
a tick is one tick armed at the old period. `vblRetune()` also zeroes
`vblNextDeadline`, because `armVBL()` ACCUMULATES (`+= period`) - that is 2xe's
fix and must not be undone, but accumulating against a deadline computed from
the old period would carry the old cadence across the switch.

**My own assertion caught my own untestable assertion.** The first version of
the retune test asserted `t.deadline != before + slow` after ticking with zero
overhead - and `tickSlow` sets `clockNs = deadline + overhead`, so with
overhead 0 the clock lands exactly on the old deadline and `clockNs + slow` and
`before + slow` are **the same number**. The assertion could not have told a
re-base from an accumulation at all; it failed only because the arithmetic
happened to be visible. Rewritten to tick 1.234567 ms off the lattice, it
discriminates, and the control confirms it: deleting `vblNextDeadline = 0`
fails exactly that assertion and nothing else. This is rule 26 in its most
uncomfortable form - the instrument was the test, and it was wrong in the
direction of passing.

**Why opt-in when the write is already proven.** The write is not the new risk.
ADVERTISING is: `getDisplayModeCount()` has returned 1 since 2sl and every boot
since has been read against that, so a second mode changes what WindowServer
sees at the moment the framebuffer comes up, before any user has asked for
anything. 2xx is the standing lesson on what a WindowServer that dislikes its
framebuffer costs to diagnose - nine boots and a nine-stage bisect. So
`-rbgpufbmodes` is opt-in, and **any** refusal inside `modeSetup()` collapses
the table back to the single mode the last six milestones were measured on
rather than offering a mode it cannot deliver. 143.83 Hz keeps
`kDisplayModeDefaultFlag`; 60 Hz is offered, never imposed, and
`setStartupDisplayMode` accepts without persisting because there is nowhere to
persist to - the firmware lights the panel before this kext exists.

**Mutually exclusive with `-rbgpufbdrr`, checked rather than documented.** With
the mode table holding 60 Hz, the experiment's `rb_drr_check` would see our own
`V_TOTAL_CONTROL` and refuse with `RB_DRR_FW_DRR` - a published value reading
"the firmware owns DRR" when in fact we do. Rule 14's complaint about a value
that can mean two things, so `drrSetup()` declines with its own code 27.

**Two things found while wiring, both pre-existing.** `drrTeardown()` was
written in 2y5 and **never called from `stop()`** - it only mattered on an
unload, and this kext panics on `kmutil unload` (2sq), so `stop()` has
effectively never run. It is wired up now, before `blTeardown()` unmaps the
BAR5 map both teardowns need, because "never reached" and "correct" are
different claims - and the mode table makes it genuinely load-bearing, since a
kext that stopped while the panel was at 60 Hz would leave the raster at a
refresh nothing advertises. And `getStartupDisplayMode` forwarded to
`getCurrentDisplayMode`, which answered the wrong question the moment a second
mode existed.

`kModeID` moved from the anonymous namespace in `RBAMDFramebuffer.cpp` to class
constants, for exactly the reason 2y5 paid for with `argOn`: a header
declaration of a name that is already file-local creates a second one.

Dependency tracking verified in both directions after 2y3's defect: touching
`rb_drr.h` rebuilds exactly `RBAMDFramebufferDRR.cpp` and
`RBAMDFramebufferModes.cpp`, and touching an unrelated `src/common` source
rebuilds no fbkext object.

Install: fbkext `A5479DEA`, plus the plugin `C518C319` which has now been
uninstalled for four milestones, and `-rbgpufbmodes` in boot-args.

Stated before the boot:
- `RBFBModeArmed` Yes with `RBFBModeCount` **2** and `RBFBModeRefuse` 0 is the
  table up. `RBFBModeClkHz` should read **342011761** and `RBFBModeLines60`
  **2707**, `RBFBModeMhz60` **59992**, `RBFBModeRate60` **0x3bfdf4**,
  `RBFBModePeriod60` **16668887** - all four derived on this boot from this
  boot's own measurement, so disagreement with those numbers means the raster
  is not what boot 255 found, not that the arithmetic is wrong.
- The real test is the Displays panel offering a refresh-rate choice at all.
  If it does and 60 Hz is selected: `RBFBModeCur` **101**, `RBFBModeSwitches`
  1, `RBFBMinRb`/`MaxRb` **2707**, `RBFBModeCtlRb` **3**, and - the number
  that distinguishes this milestone from 2y5 - `RBFBVBLPeriodNs` **16668887**
  with `RBFBVBLRetunes` 1. A mode switch where the period did NOT move is the
  2y5 state with a nicer UI, and is the failure this whole milestone exists to
  prevent.
- `RBFBModeRefuse` **21** means `blSetup` did not give us the BAR5 map (so the
  backlight is also dead this boot); **22** the refresh could not be measured;
  **24** 60 Hz is unreachable on this raster; **25** the write did not read
  back **and was put back**; **27** `-rbgpufbdrr` is also in boot-args, which
  is a boot-args mistake rather than a finding.
- `RBFBModeLastAsked` non-zero with `RBFBModeCur` unchanged means the
  compositor asked and we refused - distinct from `LastAsked` 0, which means it
  never asked and the mode list is being ignored rather than rejected. Those
  two looked identical for the whole of the brightness work.
- `RBFBModeApplies` moving while `RBFBModeSwitches` stays put is normal: the
  compositor re-asks for the mode it is already in on wake and on every
  reconfigure.
- If WindowServer dislikes two modes, the symptom is a boot with no desktop,
  and the recovery costs nothing: the boot sentinel makes the next boot stock,
  or remove `-rbgpufbmodes`. That is the whole reason it is opt-in.

## 2y6 DONE on hardware (boot 256) — 60 Hz is a mode the user can pick, and the compositor is paced for it

fbkext `A5479DEA-1219-3793-8C8A-9673DF7CE010` loaded, `rbgpu-boot` **256**,
`rbgpu-safe` 0, `-rbgpufbmodes` in boot-args and `-rbgpufbdrr` removed.
`RBFBDrrArmed` No with `RBFBDrrRefuse` **10** confirms the experiment stood
down because its boot-arg is absent - NOT via the new mutual-exclusion code 27,
which is the distinction those two numbers exist to make. Plugin still
`43775C76`, now five milestones stale; it cannot affect this reading (the mode
table is entirely src/fbkext) but it is recorded, because rule 15 is about the
habit.

    RBFBModeArmed     Yes      RBFBModeCur          101
    RBFBModeCount       2      RBFBModeLastAsked    101
    RBFBModeRefuse      0      RBFBModeSwitches       1
    RBFBModeBaseMhz 143765     RBFBModeApplies        3
    RBFBModeClkHz 341826303    RBFBModeMinRb       2705
    RBFBModeHTotal0  2106      RBFBModeMaxRb       2705
    RBFBModeVTotal0  1129      RBFBModeCtlRb          3
    RBFBModeLines60  2705      RBFBModeMhz60      60004
    RBFBModeRate60 3932422     RBFBModePeriod60 16665556

    RBFBVBLPeriodNs 16665556   RBFBVBLRetunes         1

**The one number that distinguishes this milestone from 2y5**:
`RBFBVBLPeriodNs` is 16665556, identical to `ModePeriod60`, with `Retunes` 1.
The frame clock moved with the timing. A mode switch where the period had NOT
moved would have been boot 255 with a nicer UI, and it was stated in advance as
the failure this milestone existed to prevent.

**Independent corroboration, from outside our own instrument.**
`system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType` reports **`1920 x 1080 @ 60.00Hz`**. That
is macOS stating its own mode, not a property of ours read back to us, which is
the control the whole 2y5/2y6 pair wanted - every other number here is
ultimately our own arithmetic about our own write.

All five derived values re-derive exactly from this boot's own three inputs
(143765, 2106, 1129), and the derived clock round-trips to V_TOTAL 1129.
`ModeApplies` 3 against `Switches` 1 is the documented shape: the compositor
asked twice more for the mode it was already in, which it does on wake and on
reconfigure, and counting those separately is what keeps Switches meaningful.

**A CLAIM OF MINE THAT THIS BOOT DISPROVES, and it matters.** 2y6 asserted
22 mHz as "what this sampler can resolve", taken from boot 255's before/after
pair. Boot 256 measured the same unchanged raster at **143765** - 78 mHz, or
3.5x that band, off boot 255's 143843. Two measurements 8 s apart bound JITTER
WITHIN ONE RUN and say nothing about variation across boots. 0.054 % is the
shape of DisplayPort spread-spectrum clocking, which modulates the link clock
by design. The hosttest comment is corrected: its constants are correct for
boot 255's raster and are not properties of the panel.

**And that is precisely why the derivation is load-bearing rather than
decorative.** This boot computed **2705** lines, not 2707, and landed at
60.004 Hz. A hardcoded 2707 - which is exactly what `-rbgpufbdrr`'s
`rbgpudrrlines` default is - would have scanned this boot at 59.96 Hz. Still
fine, but right by luck. Deriving the line count from the same measurement that
sets the clock is self-correcting: whatever the clock is doing on a given boot,
the lines chosen for it land on 60.00. Rule 41 asked of a measurement instead
of an address: **which boot was this measured on, and is that the one
running?** - and the structural answer is to re-measure rather than to record a
better number.

A consequence to hold onto rather than fix: the advertised 16.16 rate is
derived per boot, so the mode's refresh will vary by a few mHz between boots
(60.004 here, 59.992 by boot 255's clock). Harmless - it is below what the
Displays panel renders - but it means `RBFBModeRate60` is not a constant and a
future reading should not treat a changed value as a finding.

**Still unexercised on hardware: the switch BACK to 143.83 Hz.** The reverse
path is covered by the host retune test in both directions and by
`modeTeardown`, but no boot has yet asked for mode 100 after mode 101
(`Switches` is 1, not 2). That is the next cheap reading and needs no new
build.

## 2y7 (boot 256, no new build) — why 60 Hz feels worse, and the frame ceiling finally has a shape

The user reported the switch back working and 60 Hz feeling **choppier** than
143.83. The reverse path read exactly as stated in advance: `RBFBModeCur` 100,
`RBFBModeSwitches` **2**, `RBFBVBLRetunes` **2**, and `RBFBVBLPeriodNs` back to
**6952507** - the precise 2xe constant. The hosttest's continuity assertion
paid for itself on hardware rather than in a harness.

Then `animtest --secs 30` in both modes, same boot, same binary, same window
length - because 2xo's 81.89/s came from a controlled animtest run and the
journal already forbids comparing an idle desktop against it.

**THE INSTRUMENT LIED, AND IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION.** animtest turned
vblank counts into seconds of panel time by dividing by a literal **143.83**,
then used that as the DENOMINATOR for sets/s. Correct while 143.83 Hz was the
only mode the kext had. At 60 Hz it reported **11.94 s of panel time for a
30.14 s window** and a headline **"137.72 sets/s"** for a true **54.58/s** -
2.5x overstated, i.e. 2.3 surface writes per scanout, which read as a
spectacular result and would have been reported as one. Nothing in the output
said anything was wrong. Rule 41 in a userspace tool instead of a kext, and
rule 16: the instrument is a suspect, including the instrument that has been
right for six milestones. Fixed to read `RBFBVBLPeriodNs`, to rate sets/s
against WALL time, and to print the delivery fraction as a separate number -
dividing by panel time conflates "we fed every scanout" with "the panel scans
slowly". The jitter histogram's target was the same constant and is now live.

Corrected, over 30.14 s wall:

                      143.83 Hz mode        60 Hz mode
    display link       143.66/s              59.95/s
    nominal refresh    134.31 Hz             61.01 Hz
    our vbl fires      144.06/s  (+0.16%)    57.00/s  (-5.0%)
    amtr sets           76.51/s              54.58/s
    scanouts fed        53.1%                95.8%
    jitter stddev       0.491 ms (7.1%)      0.458 ms (2.7%)
    jitter spread       17.36 ms             3.12 ms

**CoreVideo DID learn the new rate** - nominal 61.01 Hz, link 59.95/s. The
prediction that `setDisplayMode` was missing a notification is **refuted**: the
mode change propagates all the way up to CoreVideo on its own. That was the
outcome I expected and it is wrong.

**The user's perception is correct and expected, and the reason is the plain
one.** Unique frames per second FELL, 76.5 -> 54.6. The eye counts unique
images, not scanouts, so 60 Hz is simply worse on this machine. Nothing is
broken about the 60 Hz path; it is working and it is worse.

**THE CEILING HAS A SHAPE FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE 2xi.** One model fits both
columns: throughput tops out at an ABSOLUTE ~76 frames/s. At 143.83 Hz that is
53 % of scanouts, which is the long-standing "82/s against 143.83". At 60 Hz we
are BELOW that ceiling, so 95.8 % of scanouts get fed. This kills two
hypotheses at once:
  - **not demand-limited.** A continuously animating window is continuous
    demand at the panel rate; if demand were the limit, 143.83 Hz would have
    been fed at 100 %.
  - **not a fractional loss.** My own reasoning last turn argued a proportional
    drop rate, which predicted ~34/s at 60 Hz. Measured 54.6/s. Refuted by the
    experiment I designed to test it, which is the useful outcome.
So the frontier is now "an absolute ~76 frames/s cap, cause unknown" rather
than "82/s, cause unknown" - a sharper statement, and it predicts that any
mode below ~76 Hz will be nearly fully fed while any mode above it will not.

**A NEW DEFECT, AND IT IS OURS.** Our thread_call delivers **57.00/s when
asked for 60.00/s, -5.0 %**, where at 143.83 Hz it delivers 144.06/s for a
requested 143.83, **+0.16 %**. The error appears only on the long period, which
is the signature of **macOS timer coalescing**: `thread_call_enter_delayed`
grants slack that scales with the deadline, so a 16.67 ms deadline is allowed
to drift where a 6.95 ms one is not. 90 ticks were lost over 30 s. Worth ~3
frames/s of the 54.6, so fixing it should take delivery from 95.8 % to ~100 %.
The fix is to arm with an explicit small leeway rather than the default.

**A jitter number that looks like an improvement and is not.** Relative stddev
fell from 7.1 % to 2.7 %, which reads as the 60 Hz clock being far steadier.
ABSOLUTE stddev is 0.491 ms against 0.458 ms - essentially unchanged. The
"improvement" is almost entirely the larger mean in the denominator. ~0.47 ms
is the thread_call's own jitter and is a property of the delivery mechanism,
not of the mode. The genuine difference is the spread: 17.36 ms against
3.12 ms, with the 143.83 Hz run showing a 21.56 ms outlier (three periods) -
at 6.95 ms a hiccup costs multiple frames, at 16.67 ms it is absorbed.

**What 60 Hz was actually for.** Not smoothness - it was never going to win on
this panel. It proved the raster can be retimed live, which is the mechanism an
external display's mode setting needs (2xq/2xr), and it produced the first
characterisation of the frame ceiling. Both of those were the point.

## 2y8 — the -5 % is NOT coalescing, and the instrument to settle it (fbkext `A8A2417A`, plugin `1AAABBA1`)

**A fix I did not build, and why.** 2y7 attributed boot 256's -5.0 % VBL
delivery at 60 Hz to macOS timer coalescing and proposed arming with an
explicit leeway. Two things killed that before a line was written:
  - **`thread_call_enter_delayed_with_leeway` is not in MacKernelSDK at all.**
    Only `thread_call_enter_delayed` and `thread_call_enter1_delayed` are
    declared, so the fix as described could not be built against our headers.
  - **`RBFBVBLResyncs` reads 3.** That is decisive against the mechanism:
    `armVBL` ACCUMULATES (`+= period`), so a tick that merely runs LATE does
    not lose a tick - the next deadline is still on the lattice. The only path
    that loses phase is the resync branch, and 3 resyncs cannot account for 90
    missing ticks over 30 s. Coalescing would have had to show up as resyncs.
So the proposed fix addressed a mechanism the counters already excluded. Rule
35's lesson in its cheapest form: instrument our end before building anything.

**The better lead, from the same read: `RBFBVBLEnables` = 55789** over
1261 s of uptime, i.e. the compositor toggling the vblank interrupt ~44 times a
second. If an enable re-bases the clock, that loses fractional ticks
continuously and would be invisible in `vblResyncs`. Not yet established -
which is the point of this milestone rather than its conclusion.

**Why it could not be settled from the live machine.** `RBFBVBLFires` and
`RBFBVBLUptimeNs` are CUMULATIVE across modes, so after boot 256 switched
143 -> 60 -> 143 -> 60 (`RBFBVBLRetunes` 3) their ratio is a blend of two rates
and means nothing. The -5 % had to be computed from animtest's 30 s window
instead of from the kext - an external tool measuring something the kext knows
better, which is the same shape of mistake as reading a rate off an idle
desktop. Rule 33: name the object a number belongs to.

So `vblRetune()` now latches `vblFiresAtRetune`, `vblNsAtRetune` and
`vblEnablesAtRetune` BEFORE the new period takes effect, and
`publishVBLState()` derives:

    RBFBVBLModeFires    delivered since this mode began
    RBFBVBLModeNs       how long this mode has been current
    RBFBVBLModeEnables  interrupt enables since this mode began
    RBFBVBLModeMhz      the delivered rate, millihertz

published beside its own inputs so the reading can be checked rather than
trusted, and 0 before any retune rather than a division by a zero window.

**The plugin is rebuilt and no longer five milestones stale**: `1AAABBA1`,
against the `43775C76` that has been loading since boot 254. Both install gates
pass - `kmutil libraries` resolves **0** symbols from
`SystemKernelExtensions.kc` (the 2oz trap) and `IOGraphicsFamily` appears **0**
times in the plugin's Info.plist - and `make osrange` reports the declared
range Ventura..Tahoe agreeing with the matrix and PluginConfiguration.

**Not re-attacked: the ~76/s ceiling.** 2y7 called it "cause unknown"; the
journal already answers it. 2xo measured **82/s with the hold against 112/s
without it** and recorded it explicitly as the user's trade rather than a
defect to fix silently. What 2y7 genuinely adds is that at 60 Hz the hold
barely bites - 95.8 % of scanouts fed, `RBFBAmtrHoldExpired` still 0 - so 60 Hz
is flicker-free AND nearly fully delivered, which is a real option the project
did not have before. The open sub-question, also already recorded, is whether a
